The old samplex annotation reads: "It is provided by jurisprudence ... (Atty. Uribe does not subscribe to this ruling)." So answer (c) in the MCQ, following Merced and Zapanta, even though he personally disagrees. In an essay, you may state the ruling and add the criticism: bigamy is consummated upon the celebration of the second marriage, and a voidable marriage is valid until annulled.
      Tenebro v. CA (423 SCRA 272, February 18, 2004)

      Tenebro, while married to Villareyes, married Ancajas. That second marriage was later declared void on the ground of psychological incapacity. He argued there was no bigamy because the second marriage was void. Doctrine: The declaration of nullity of the second marriage on the ground of psychological incapacity is not an indicator that it lacked the essential requisites for validity. All the essential and formal requisites were present. Although a judicial declaration of nullity under Art. 36, FC retroacts to the celebration insofar as the vinculum is concerned, the marriage is not without legal effects: children conceived or born before the judgment are legitimate. One of those consequences is incurring criminal liability for bigamy. To hold otherwise would render the penal laws on bigamy nugatory and let people deliberately flaw each marriage. "The nullity of a second marriage is not per se an argument for the avoidance of criminal liability for bigamy." So an Art. 36 petition on the second marriage is not a prejudicial question to bigamy.

      Pulido v. People (G.R. No. 220149, July 27, 2021)

      Pulido married Arcon, and while that marriage subsisted, married Baleda. Charged with bigamy, he argued that the first marriage was void ab initio for lack of a marriage license, and pending the case both marriages were judicially declared void. Doctrine (En Banc): (1) Art. 40, FC requires a judicial declaration of nullity of a previous void marriage only for purposes of remarriage. It was not intended to amend Art. 349, RPC. (2) A void ab initio marriage is void from the beginning. It is not "valid until declared void," which is the rule for voidable marriages. (3) A judicial declaration of nullity, even one obtained after the second marriage or after the filing of the bigamy case, retroacts to the celebration of the marriage. (4) Hence the accused may raise the void ab initio nature of the first marriage as a defense in the bigamy case, even without a prior judicial declaration, and may present evidence of its nullity there. Contrary rulings (e.g., Mercado v. Tan, Jarillo) were abandoned. (5) Bigamy also requires that the second marriage have all the essential requisites for validity, i.e., that it would have been valid were it not for the subsisting first marriage. So the accused may also show that the second marriage is void on a ground other than its being bigamous. Pulido was acquitted. The second marriage remains void under Art. 40 for civil purposes, and Art. 40 still applies to remarriage.

      Uribe (2025 class, on Pulido): "Bigamy is committed if there is no judicial declaration prior to the second marriage because a void marriage is valid until declared void. Is this correct?" No. That is the voidable rule, and "the declaration of nullity retroacts to the celebration of marriage, so no valid prior marriage." On a pending action to declare the first marriage void: "if the accused can prove that the first marriage is void then he cannot be found guilty of bigamy," so grant the motion to suspend. On a pending action to declare the second marriage void on a ground other than its being bigamous: the fourth element fails, since it would not have been valid even without the first marriage, so there is no bigamy. On Tenebro: "I will maintain Pulido. The only ground for the declaration of nullity which is not a defense to bigamy is that the second marriage is a bigamous marriage. No qualification for any other ground, including psychological incapacity. If the Court maintains such view, wala nang Tenebro. If [it gets] similar facts as Tenebro, baka sumunod sa majority decision." He also stressed that Pulido concerns void marriages. A problem about annulment (voidable) is not answered by Pulido.
      Note: what to write. (1) MCQ "may involve a prejudicial question in bigamy" → annulment of the second marriage (Merced/Zapanta), per his key. (2) "Nullity of the second marriage due to psychological incapacity" → per Tenebro, no prejudicial question, and the key treats it as wrong. If asked in an essay, cite Tenebro, then note that Pulido's fourth element (the second marriage would have been valid but for the first) casts doubt on Tenebro, which Uribe says he would "maintain." (3) Under Pulido, a previously instituted action to declare the first marriage void ab initio is now determinative of guilt, so a motion to suspend may be granted. The accused may also simply prove the nullity in the criminal case itself. (4) The bank (V-66) follows Uribe: a second marriage void for lack of license → no bigamy. Santiago v. People (2015) refused this defense to an accused who knowingly married without a license, so mention it if writing an essay.
      Beltran v. People (2000)

      A husband charged with concubinage moved to suspend the case because of his pending petition to declare his marriage void under Art. 36, FC. Doctrine: No prejudicial question. A party cannot judge for himself the nullity of his marriage, and the Art. 40 judicial declaration requirement applies. Even if the marriage is later declared void, he is presumed married while cohabiting with his paramour. He who cohabits with another before a judicial declaration assumes the risk of prosecution for concubinage. (Decided before Pulido, but it concerns concubinage, where the marriage at the time of the act is what counts.)

      Pimentel v. Pimentel (2010)

      The husband was charged with frustrated parricide. Weeks later, the wife filed a petition to declare the marriage void under Art. 36, and the husband moved to suspend. Doctrine: No prejudicial question. (1) The civil action must be previously instituted, and here it was filed after the criminal case. (2) The issue is not determinative: relationship is an element of parricide, and at the time of the attack the parties were married. A later declaration of nullity would not change that for purposes of the crime.

      Dreamwork Construction v. Janiola (2009)

      Doctrine: Under Rule 111, Sec. 7 (2000 Rules), the civil action must be previously instituted. A civil case for rescission filed after the B.P. 22 informations is not a prejudicial question. The change is consistent with Art. 36, which leaves the matter to the Rules of Court, and it prevents delaying tactics.

      People v. Carmenforte (2021, as reported in the B29 repository)

      A final civil judgment upheld the genuineness of signatures on deeds of sale. The accused was charged with falsification for allegedly forging those signatures. Doctrine: Res judicata did not apply because the People was not a party to the civil case. But the civil finding was a prejudicial question that negated the element of falsification, and the dismissal of the criminal cases was affirmed. A prejudicial question exists when the civil issue is a logical antecedent of the criminal issue and determines whether the criminal case may proceed.

      Note: The B29 case repository describes Pulido v. People as "an example of settling pre-judicial questions." That is imprecise. Pulido was decided on the merits of the bigamy defense: the accused may prove the nullity of a void marriage in the criminal case itself, and the retroactive judicial declaration negates an element. It did not hinge on a motion to suspend. Also, B29 suggests "pre-judicial" and "prejudicial" questions are different. They are the same concept: Art. 36 uses the hyphenated spelling, Rule 111 does not.

      Bigamy and actions on marriage as prejudicial questions: decision matrix

      Elements of bigamy (Art. 349, RPC, as summarized in Pulido): (1) the offender is legally married; (2) the first marriage has not been legally dissolved, or, if the spouse is absent, has not been declared presumptively dead; (3) he contracts a second or subsequent marriage; and (4) the second marriage has all the essential requisites for validity, i.e., it would have been valid were it not for the first. Bigamy is consummated upon the celebration of the second marriage.

      Pending civil action (filed before the criminal case)Prejudicial question?Reason
      Legal separation (either marriage)NoLegal separation does not sever the bond (FC 63). It has nothing to do with guilt.
      Annulment of the FIRST marriage (voidable, any ground)NoA voidable marriage is valid until annulled. When the second marriage was celebrated, a valid first marriage subsisted, and bigamy was consummated. A later annulment does not retroact (Uribe 2025 class; bank P-61).
      Annulment of the SECOND marriage, filed by the accused, alleging his consent was obtained by force, threat or intimidationYesIf proved, he did not voluntarily contract the second marriage (Merced v. Diez; Zapanta v. Montesa; Landicho/Donato dicta). This is the answer in Uribe's MCQ key, though he does not subscribe to it personally.
      Annulment of the SECOND marriage, filed by the second spouse alleging the accused's deceitNoDonato v. Luna. The ground (his own concealment of the first marriage) does not negate his guilt, and the accused cannot profit from his own fraud.
      Declaration of nullity of the SECOND marriage for being bigamousNoThe second marriage is void precisely because it is bigamous. Its nullity confirms the crime (Tenebro; Capili; Pulido).
      Declaration of nullity of the SECOND marriage under Art. 36 FC (psychological incapacity)No per Tenebro (and the MCQ key). Arguably yes per Uribe's reading of PulidoTenebro: a void marriage still produces legal effects, including criminal liability for bigamy. Uribe: Pulido's fourth element would make it a defense, and "wala nang Tenebro" if Pulido is maintained.
      Declaration of nullity of the SECOND marriage on another ground (no license, no ceremony, etc.)Yes (post-Pulido)The fourth element fails because the marriage would not have been valid anyway (Pulido; Uribe; bank V-66). Compare Santiago v. People (2015).
      Declaration of nullity of the FIRST marriage (void ab initio)Pre-2021: No (Landicho; Mercado; Jarillo). Post-Pulido: Yes / determinativeThe judicial declaration retroacts, so there was no valid prior marriage. The accused may also prove the nullity directly in the bigamy case.
      First "marriage" with no ceremony at all (only signed a contract)No suspension needed: acquittal on the meritsMorigo v. People (2004). It "bears no semblance to a valid marriage," so there is no first marriage to speak of.

      A married B. While that marriage subsisted, A married C. A few months later, A was charged with bigamy. A moved to suspend, citing a case he had earlier filed to annul his marriage to B on the ground of fraud. Rule on the motion.

      Answer: Deny. The action concerns the first marriage, which is merely voidable and therefore valid until annulled. When A married C, the first marriage subsisted, so bigamy was consummated. Even if the first marriage is later annulled, the annulment does not retroact to erase the crime. The civil case is not determinative of guilt, so there is no prejudicial question. (Uribe's model answer: it depends on which marriage is the subject. If the first, no PQ. If the second, look at who filed and on what ground.)

      Same facts, but the pending action (filed by A before the bigamy case) is for annulment of his marriage to C, alleging that C's brothers forced him at gunpoint to marry her.

      Answer: Grant the motion and suspend the criminal proceedings. If the civil court finds A's consent was obtained by force or intimidation, he did not freely and voluntarily contract the second marriage, an element of the crime (Merced v. Diez; Zapanta v. Montesa). The civil action was previously instituted, involves an intimately related issue, and its resolution determines whether the criminal action may proceed (Rule 111, Sec. 7). Suspension does not mean acquittal. A must still prove the duress in the civil case.

      Same facts, but it was C who filed (before the criminal case) to annul her marriage to A because A deceived her by concealing his existing marriage to B.

      Answer: Deny (Donato v. Luna). The ground, A's own deceit, is not determinative of A's guilt. Annulment of the second marriage is prejudicial only when it is the accused's consent that was vitiated by force or intimidation. The claim of prejudicial question is a mere ploy to delay the prosecution.

      A married B in 2010 without a marriage license (no exemption applies). In 2015, without any judicial declaration, A married C. In 2020, B filed a bigamy complaint. A had already filed a petition to declare his marriage to B void, and he now moves to suspend the criminal case. Rule.

      Answer: Grant (post-Pulido). The civil action was previously instituted, and its issue, the nullity of the first marriage for lack of a license, is determinative. A judicial declaration of nullity of a void ab initio marriage retroacts to its celebration, so there would be no valid prior marriage, an essential element of bigamy. Under Pulido, A may even prove the nullity directly in the criminal case. The Art. 40 judicial declaration is required only for purposes of remarriage, so A's marriage to C is still void under Arts. 40 and 35(6), FC as a civil matter. Before Pulido (Landicho; Mercado v. Tan), the motion would have been denied because A "assumed the risk."

      While validly married to B, A married C. That second marriage was later declared void under Art. 36. Does that nullity bar a bigamy conviction?

      Answer: No, under Tenebro v. CA. The second marriage had all the essential and formal requisites, and a marriage void under Art. 36 still produces legal effects, among them criminal liability for bigamy. "The nullity of a second marriage is not per se an argument for the avoidance of criminal liability." (Add for Uribe: Pulido's fourth element arguably undermines Tenebro, and Uribe says he would maintain Pulido, under which only a bigamous-ground nullity is no defense.)

      Breach of promise to marry (syllabus VII.A.3)

      Related provisions: NCC 19, 20, 21 (above), NCC 2176, and NCC 1403(2)(c).

      Art. 2176, NCC. Whoever by act or omission causes damage to another, there being fault or negligence, is obliged to pay for the damage done. Such fault or negligence, if there is no pre-existing contractual relation between the parties, is called a quasi-delict and is governed by the provisions of this Chapter.
      Art. 1403(2)(c), NCC. The following contracts are unenforceable, unless they are ratified: x x x (2) Those that do not comply with the Statute of Frauds as set forth in this number. In the following cases an agreement hereafter made shall be unenforceable by action, unless the same, or some note or memorandum thereof, be in writing, and subscribed by the party charged, or by his agent; evidence, therefore, of the agreement cannot be received without the writing, or a secondary evidence of its contents: x x x (c) An agreement made in consideration of marriage, other than a mutual promise to marry; x x x
      Quiz trap: The Statute of Frauds covers an agreement made in consideration of marriage, other than a mutual promise to marry. A mutual promise to marry may be proved orally (it is outside the Statute). A promise by a parent to give a dowry or to build a house in consideration of the marriage must be in writing. Unenforceable contracts can be ratified, including by failure to object to oral evidence (Art. 1405).

      The rule and its basis

      • General rule: a mere breach of promise to marry is not an actionable wrong. No action for damages lies purely for the breach, and marriage cannot be compelled by specific performance, since consent to the actual marriage must be freely given (FC 2[2]).
      • History: the Code Commission's draft contained a chapter (ten articles) on "Promise of Marriage," which provided for material and moral damages for breach and determined who may sue and who may be liable. Congress deliberately eliminated the whole chapter. The Senate Special Committee cited the US experience that breach of promise suits are prone to abuse by "designing women and unscrupulous men" (the "heart balm" statutes being abolished in many states). It reaffirmed De Jesus v. Syquia (58 Phil. 866, 1933): "the action for breach of promise to marry has no standing in the civil law, apart from the right to recover money or property advanced by the plaintiff upon the faith of such promise." The Family Code did not change this.
      • Exceptions (where damages are recoverable): not because of the breach itself, but because of an independent wrong:
        1. Art. 21 / Art. 19: the breach is accompanied by acts palpably and unjustifiably contrary to good customs, e.g., walking out on a formally set and publicized wedding (Wassmer), or abusive, capricious withdrawal;
        2. Moral seduction / fraud: the promise was a deceptive device to obtain the woman's consent to sexual intercourse (Baksh; cf. Tanjanco for the limits);
        3. Recovery of money or property advanced on the faith of the promise (De Jesus v. Syquia; Domalagan, unjust enrichment under Art. 22); return of conditional gifts;
        4. Actual damages caused by fault, e.g., inducing the woman to resign her job (Garcia v. Del Rosario, 33 Phil. 189, quasi-delict); the expenses of pregnancy and childbirth and support of the child (Hermosisima).
      Tolentino (contract to marry): When parties agree to marry in the future there is a contract to marry (the engagement), a purely executory contract. It differs from ordinary contracts because neither party's promise can be enforced by court action: consent to the marriage itself must be purely voluntary. No form or ceremony is needed. A promise to marry needs only to be made so that the injured party may reasonably believe it, judging from the antecedents, the persistence and repetition of the offer, and the like. A request to postpone the marriage for reasonable cause is not a repudiation. A party who develops a disease making it unsafe to marry may have the ceremony postponed. There is repudiation when one declares he will not go through with it, refuses to communicate, or puts himself in a position where he cannot perform (as by marrying another).
      Damages: an action based purely on breach of the contract to marry will not lie. A young woman whose suitor changes his mind, absent seduction or abuse of right, has no cause of action, even if she suffers wounded feelings and mental anguish (elements of moral damages under Art. 2217), because there must first be a right of action. But if the action is based on tort or quasi-delict, or on Arts. 19, 21 or 22, there is a legal basis.
      Seduction: Tolentino criticizes old cases (e.g., Batarra v. Marcos) for treating carnal intercourse and the contract to marry as identical. The sexual relation is apart from the contract and is rarely its consideration. If the promise was the means of accomplishing the seduction, the woman may recover not on the promise but on the tortious seduction, a breach of trust "as plain as any advantage gained by a trustee." The essence of the action is the wrong accomplished through the deceitful promise.
      Abuse of right: even without seduction, under Art. 19 a party who repudiates capriciously may be liable, especially just before the wedding and after a long engagement. "Where a woman has been wantonly deserted after a long engagement ... the result to her feelings ... are all matters to be considered."
      Unjust enrichment: Art. 22 is another basis, essentially the basis of Domalagan v. Bolifer. Gifts to a fiancée are generally conditional on the marriage and recoverable on breach by the donee, particularly the engagement ring and jewelry. Absolute gifts (e.g., Christmas presents) are not recoverable.
      Oral agreements: Tolentino thinks writing is not necessary in an action for damages for breach, because the Statute of Frauds should apply only when the action is to enforce the contract, and it is unjust to let the party who received the consideration hide behind it.
      Cabague v. Auxilio (92 Phil. 294, November 26, 1952)

      Felipe Cabague and his son Geronimo sued Matias Auxilio and his daughter Socorro. The defendants had promised that Socorro would marry Geronimo if the Cabagues improved the Auxilios' house and spent for the wedding, which they did. Socorro then refused to marry Geronimo. The trial court dismissed under the Statute of Frauds. Doctrine: There were two kinds of agreement: (1) the agreement between Felipe Cabague and the defendants in consideration of the marriage, and (2) the agreement between the two lovers, a mutual promise to marry. For breach of the mutual promise, Geronimo may sue Socorro for damages, and evidence of that oral promise is admissible since it is excepted from the Statute of Frauds. But Felipe's action may not prosper, because it seeks to enforce an agreement in consideration of marriage, which must be in writing. As between Felipe and Matias, the action cannot be maintained on the theory of "mutual promise to marry," nor may it be regarded as an action by Felipe against Socorro on a mutual promise to marry.

      Domalagan v. Bolifer (33 Phil. 471, February 8, 1916)

      The plaintiff paid the defendant ₱516 in consideration of the defendant's promise that his daughter would marry the plaintiff's son. The daughter married another man. The plaintiff sued to recover the money, and the defendant invoked the Statute of Frauds. Doctrine: Verbal agreements made upon the consideration of marriage, other than a mutual promise to marry, are not invalid for not being in writing. The law only says such agreements cannot be proved in court if not in writing. Since the defendant did not object to the oral evidence, he waived the Statute (cf. Art. 1405, ratification by failure to object). The defendant was ordered to return the ₱516. Tolentino reads the case as essentially resting on unjust enrichment (now Art. 22).

      Hermosisima v. CA (109 Phil. 629, 1960)

      Soledad Cagigas, a school teacher, had intimate relations with Francisco Hermosisima, an apprentice pilot about ten years her junior, who promised to marry her. She became pregnant and gave birth, but he married another woman. The CA awarded moral damages for breach of promise. Doctrine: The SC deleted the moral damages. A mere breach of promise to marry is not an actionable wrong: Congress deliberately eliminated from the draft Code the provisions that would have made it so, and an action for breach of promise has no standing apart from the right to recover money or property advanced on the faith of the promise (De Jesus v. Syquia). Damages could be claimed if seduction were involved, but here, given that she was older than he by about ten years and a mature woman, it could not be said that he seduced her. The award of actual damages (pregnancy and delivery expenses) and support for the child was maintained.

      Wassmer v. Velez (12 SCRA 648, December 26, 1964)

      Beatriz Wassmer and Francisco Velez applied for a marriage license and set their wedding. Invitations were printed and distributed, the gown, trousseau and reception were prepared, and bridal showers were given. Two days before the wedding, Velez left a note: "Will have to postpone wedding — My mother opposes it." The next day he wired that nothing had changed and he would return. He never appeared. Doctrine: Mere breach of promise to marry is not an actionable wrong. But "to formally set a wedding and go through all the above-described preparation and publicity, only to walk out of it when the matrimony is about to be solemnized, is quite different. This is palpably and unjustifiably contrary to good customs for which defendant must be held answerable in damages in accordance with Article 21." Actual damages (wedding expenses), moral damages (Art. 2219[10]) and exemplary damages were awarded, though the Court reduced the moral and exemplary damages as excessive. The defense that the judgment was by default and that he was not given a chance to settle was rejected.

      Estremos v. Ephan (CA, 83 O.G. 4022, No. 35)

      Doctrine (per Uribe's doctrines outline): A mere breach of promise to marry is not an actionable wrong. Congress deliberately eliminated from the draft of the new Civil Code the provisions that would have made it so. The SC has, however, laid down exceptions, as in Wassmer v. Velez: under Art. 21, formally setting a wedding and going through the preparation and publicity, only to walk out when the marriage is about to be solemnized, is different from a mere breach. It is palpably and unjustifiably contrary to good customs, making the defendant answerable in damages under Art. 21.

      Tanjanco v. CA (18 SCRA 994, December 17, 1966)

      Tanjanco courted Araceli Santos, a woman of legal age, and promised to marry her. She consented to sexual relations and they had repeated intercourse for about a year. She became pregnant, had to resign from her job, and suffered mental anguish, and he refused to marry her. Doctrine: No cause of action under Art. 21. Seduction connotes essentially the idea of deceit, enticement, superior power or abuse of confidence on the part of the seducer, to which the woman yields against her will. "In an action by the woman, the enticement, persuasion or deception is the essence of the injury; and a mere proof of intercourse is insufficient to warrant a recovery." A woman of adult age who maintained intimate relations for a year, with repeated acts, shows a mutual passion incompatible with seduction. The Code Commission's example in Art. 21 refers to seduction, not mere sexual intercourse or breach of promise.

      Baksh v. CA (G.R. No. 97326, February 19, 1993)

      Gashem Shookat Baksh, a foreign medical student, courted Marilou Gonzales, a 22-year-old restaurant waitress, and promised to marry her. Relying on the promise, she lived with him and surrendered her virginity, and her parents agreed to the live-in because of the promised marriage. He later maltreated her and repudiated the promise. Doctrine: Where a man's promise to marry is in fact the proximate cause of the woman's acceptance of his love, and his representation that he will fulfill it is the proximate cause of her giving herself to him in sexual congress, proof that he had no intention of marrying her and that the promise was only a subtle scheme or deceptive device to entice her could justify damages under Art. 21, "not because of such promise to marry but because of the fraud and deceit behind it and the willful injury to her honor and reputation which followed thereafter." The injury must have been committed in a manner contrary to morals, good customs or public policy. She surrendered her virginity "not because of lust but because of moral seduction," the kind illustrated by the Code Commission's example. He could not be held liable for criminal seduction under RPC 337 or 338 because she was above 18. In pari delicto does not apply because her fault, if any, was not equal to his. She was the victim of his deceit and was not in equal fault. Moral damages were awarded.

      Uribe (doctrines outline summary): "Prior decisions of this Court clearly suggest that Article 21 may be applied in a breach of promise to marry where the woman is a victim of moral seduction." The progression to memorize is: Hermosisima (no action for mere breach; no seduction where the woman is older) → Wassmer (walking out on a publicized wedding is contra bonos mores, so Art. 21 applies) → Tanjanco (mutual passion is not seduction, so no recovery) → Baksh (fraudulent promise as a device for moral seduction, so Art. 21 applies).
      Garcia v. Del Rosario (33 Phil. 189)

      The plaintiff, a school teacher, resigned her position at the defendant's instance, relying on his promise of marriage, which he then broke. Doctrine: The defendant was held liable for the damage caused by her loss of employment. Liability rests not on the breach of the contract to marry as such but on his fault in inducing her to resign (cf. Art. 2176). (Cited by Tolentino and in B29: the breach directly led to the injured party's loss of employment.)

      Bunag, Jr. v. CA (1992)

      After an abduction, the man and the woman applied for a marriage license, but he later withdrew his application and refused to marry her. The criminal case for abduction had been dismissed. Doctrine: While a mere breach of promise is not actionable, the circumstances, including the abduction and deflowering followed by the deceitful promise and its repudiation, made the man liable for moral and exemplary damages under Art. 21. Dismissal of the criminal case did not bar the civil liability.

      Abanag v. Mabute (2011)

      Doctrine: Voluntary intimacy between two unmarried, consenting adults, neither under any impediment to marry and with no deceit, is neither criminal nor so grossly immoral as to warrant administrative sanction. (Related: no "seduction" without deceit.)

      Related Family Code rules on donations and gifts

      • FC 81: stipulations in the marriage settlement in consideration of a future marriage, including donations between the prospective spouses made therein, are rendered void if the marriage does not take place.
      • FC 86(1): a donation by reason of marriage may be revoked by the donor if the marriage is not celebrated or is judicially declared void ab initio, except donations made in the marriage settlements, which are governed by Art. 81.
      • Muslim Code (P.D. 1083), Art. 22: listed in Uribe's doctrines outline under this heading (not in the syllabus). Unlike the Civil Code, the Muslim Code has its own provision on liability for breach of a promise to marry (betrothal). Read the exact text before the exam; it is not reproduced here.
      Claim after a broken engagementRecoverable?Basis
      Moral damages for the mere breach (hurt feelings)NoHermosisima; Estremos; Congress deleted the chapter
      Specific performance (compel marriage)NeverConsent must be freely given (FC 2)
      Wedding expenses, moral and exemplary damages when the groom walks out on a publicized, prepared weddingYesArt. 21 (Wassmer)
      Damages when the promise was a fraudulent device to obtain sexual consent (moral seduction)YesArt. 21 (Baksh); Tolentino
      Damages for voluntary intercourse between adults over a long period, without deceitNoTanjanco; Hermosisima
      Money or property advanced on the faith of the promiseYesDe Jesus v. Syquia; Domalagan; Art. 22
      Engagement ring and conditional giftsYes (conditional on the marriage). Absolute gifts: noTolentino; FC 86 (donations propter nuptias)
      Lost salary after being induced to resignYesGarcia v. Del Rosario (fault or quasi-delict)
      Pregnancy expenses; support of the childYesHermosisima (actual damages and support maintained); law on support
      Claim by a plaintiff who acted in bad faith (e.g., concealed his own existing marriage)NoGuevarra v. Banach
      Third person's oral agreement in consideration of the marriage (e.g., parent's promise)Unenforceable unless in writing or ratified (waived by failure to object)Art. 1403(2)(c); Cabague; Domalagan

      B and F set their wedding date. Invitations were distributed, the gown and reception arranged, and bridal showers given. Two days before, F left a note saying his mother opposed the wedding, then wired that "nothing changed," but never showed up. B sues for damages. Which is correct? (a) B cannot recover since breach of promise is not actionable; (b) B may recover only expenses as damages for breach of contract; (c) B may recover actual, moral and exemplary damages under Art. 21; (d) B may compel F to marry her.

      Answer: (c). Wassmer v. Velez. The award is based on Art. 21 (walking out of a formally set and publicized wedding is palpably contrary to good customs), not on the breach of contract as such. Marriage can never be compelled.

      Statements: (1) "A promise to marry has obligatory force; hence its breach is per se an actionable wrong." (2) "A prospective bride or groom who capriciously breaks an engagement without reason, causing moral and material injury, may be held liable for damages, especially where the break occurs just before the wedding."

      Answer: No. 1 is FALSE and No. 2 is TRUE (Tolentino; Arts. 19 and 21; Wassmer).

      Felipe and his son Geronimo orally agreed with Matias and his daughter Socorro that Socorro would marry Geronimo if Felipe repaired Matias's house. Felipe spent ₱700. Socorro backed out. Felipe and Geronimo sue. Matias objects to oral evidence under the Statute of Frauds. Rule.

      Answer: Cabague v. Auxilio. (1) Geronimo's claim against Socorro rests on a mutual promise to marry, which is excepted from Art. 1403(2)(c), so oral evidence is admissible and he may sue. (2) Felipe's claim rests on an agreement in consideration of marriage, which is unenforceable unless in writing, so with a timely objection his oral evidence is inadmissible. Had Matias failed to object, the defect would have been waived (Domalagan). Felipe may also explore recovery of what he spent under Art. 22 (unjust enrichment), per Tolentino.

      X, 25, and Y, 28, both single, had a sexual relationship for two years. Y repeatedly promised to marry X but never set a date. Y then married another woman. X sues Y under Art. 21. Will it prosper?

      Answer: As a rule, no (Tanjanco; Hermosisima). A mere breach of promise is not actionable. Voluntary intercourse between adults over a long period indicates mutual passion, not seduction, because there is no deceit, enticement, superior power or abuse of confidence. It would be different if X proves that Y never intended to marry her and used the promise only as a device to obtain her consent (Baksh), or that Y's withdrawal was attended by acts contrary to good customs (Wassmer). Support for any common child and actual expenses are separate matters.

      More application drills (Uribe style)

      True or False: "Every person who, contrary to law, wilfully or negligently causes damage to another, shall indemnify the latter for the same." / "Any person who wilfully or negligently causes loss or injury to another in a manner that is contrary to morals, good customs or public policy shall compensate the latter for the damage."

      Answer: The first is TRUE (Art. 20 verbatim). The second is FALSE because Art. 21 requires a wilful act. "Or negligently" is not in Art. 21.

      True or False: "The classical rule that he who uses a right injures no one is maintained in the Civil Code." / "Under Art. 19, the absence of good faith is essential to abuse of right."

      Answer: The first is FALSE. The Code abandoned qui jure suo utitur neminem laedit, and only the legitimate exercise of a right (with prudence and good faith) is protected. The second is TRUE (Tolentino).

      During a severe typhoon emergency, a wealthy family throws a lavish week-long fireworks party broadcast online. A neighbor, a private individual, asks the court to stop it. Will it prosper?

      Answer: Not at the neighbor's instance. Art. 25 allows thoughtless extravagance for pleasure or display during acute public want or emergency to be stopped by court order only "at the instance of any government or private charitable institution." The neighbor may sue only if he has his own cause of action, e.g., under Art. 26 or as a nuisance.

      A mayor, without just cause, refuses for six months to act on X's complete application for a business permit, which by ordinance must be issued upon compliance. X loses a supply contract. Remedy?

      Answer: An action for damages and other relief against the mayor under Art. 27 for refusal or neglect, without just cause, to perform an official duty owed to X, causing material (and moral) loss. It is "without prejudice to any disciplinary administrative action." Good faith or a superior's order is no defense, though it may mitigate damages.

      A was charged with serious physical injuries for mauling B. Without making any reservation, B filed a separate civil action for damages based on Art. 33. A moves to suspend the civil case until the criminal case is decided. Rule.

      Answer: Deny. Under Art. 33 and Rule 111, Sec. 3, the civil action for physical injuries is entirely separate and distinct, proceeds independently of the criminal prosecution, and needs only a preponderance of evidence. Under the 2000 Rules no reservation is required. B may not, however, recover twice for the same act.

      A, charged with homicide, was acquitted. The decision stated that the prosecution's evidence "creates doubt" as to A's participation, without an express statement that it was on reasonable doubt. Can the heirs still sue A civilly for the same act?

      Answer: Yes. Under Art. 29, par. 2, absent an express declaration it "may be inferred from the text of the decision" whether the acquittal was on reasonable doubt, and here it was. The civil action requires only a preponderance of evidence, and upon A's motion the court may require the heirs to post a bond against a malicious suit. Had the court declared that A was not the author of the act or that the act did not exist, the civil action ex delicto would be barred (Rule 111, Sec. 2).

      B complained to the prosecutor that A committed an offense for which the law grants no independent civil action. The prosecutor refused to file the case. B sued A for damages. A year later the prosecutor, on new evidence, filed an information. What happens to B's civil case?

      Answer: Under Art. 35, par. 2, the civil action shall be suspended until the termination of the criminal proceedings. (Contrast: if the offense had an independent civil action, such as defamation, the civil case would continue.)

      Last-minute checklist

      • Art. 19: "in the exercise of his rights AND in the performance of his duties": (1) act with justice, (2) give everyone his due, (3) observe honesty and good faith. Elements: legal right or duty, bad faith, sole intent to prejudice. Sanction via Art. 20 or 21. Absolute rights include a parent's refusal of consent to a minor's marriage.
      • Art. 20: "contrary to law, wilfully or negligently," "indemnify." General sanction for laws without their own sanction. Prudence, not charity: no liability for failing to save a drowning man.
      • Art. 21: "wilfully" only, "contrary to morals, good customs or public policy" (three, and NOT "law"), "compensate." Covers legal acts. Moral damages under 2219(10).
      • Art. 22: "without just or legal ground," "shall return." Accion in rem verso has four requisites: enrichment, loss, no just ground, no other action (subsidiary). Recovery is capped at the enrichment.
      • Art. 23: "Even when not due to fault or negligence ... shall be liable ... if benefited." Damage to property. Example: flood drives cattle onto a neighbor's highland. Liability up to the extent of the benefit.
      • Art. 24: moral dependence, ignorance, indigence, mental weakness, tender age, other handicap. "Courts must be vigilant." Covers contractual, property or other relations.
      • Art. 25: thoughtless extravagance in expenses for pleasure or display, during acute public want or emergency, stopped by court order "at the instance of any government or private charitable institution."
      • Art. 26: dignity, personality, privacy, peace of mind. (1) prying into privacy of residence; (2) meddling with private life or family relations; (3) intriguing to alienate from friends; (4) vexing or humiliating on account of religious beliefs, lowly station, place of birth, physical defect, other personal condition. "Following and similar acts," "though they may not constitute a criminal offense," "damages, prevention and other relief."
      • Art. 27: public servant "refuses or neglects, without just cause," "material or moral loss," "without prejudice to" administrative action. Nonfeasance only.
      • Art. 28: unfair competition in agricultural, commercial, industrial enterprises or labor through force, intimidation, deceit, machination, or other unjust, oppressive or highhanded method. Need not be a crime.
      • Art. 29: acquittal on reasonable doubt allows a civil action for the same act, by preponderance. Bond "upon motion of the defendant," "may." The court "shall so declare," or it may be inferred from the text. Acquittal because the act did not exist or the accused was not the author bars the civil action ex delicto (Rule 111, Sec. 2).
      • Art. 30: separate civil action ex delicto with no criminal proceedings during its pendency: preponderance.
      • Art. 31: obligation not arising from the felony: proceeds independently and regardless of the result (contract, quasi-delict).
      • Art. 32: public officer or private individual, "directly or indirectly," 19 rights, whether or not a crime, independent, preponderance. Moral damages "shall" be included; exemplary "may." Judges are liable only if the act violates the Penal Code or another penal statute. Malice and good faith are irrelevant (Lim v. Ponce de Leon; Vinzons-Chato). Aberca: superiors are liable, and suspension of the writ is no bar.
      • Art. 33: defamation, fraud, physical injuries: entirely separate and distinct, "only a preponderance." Physical injuries include death (Madeja v. Caro). Fraud includes estafa.
      • Art. 34: police refuses or fails to aid. Officer primarily liable, city or municipality subsidiarily (NOT solidarily). Independent, preponderance. No diligence-in-selection defense.
      • Art. 35: no independent civil action plus no reasonable ground found or prosecutor refuses: civil action by preponderance, bond on the defendant's motion. If an information is later filed, the CIVIL action is suspended.
      • Moral damages, Art. 2219(10): Arts. 21, 26, 27, 28, 29, 30, 32, 34, 35 (not 19, 20, 22–25, 31, 33).
      • Rule 111 (2000): only civil liability ex delicto is deemed instituted. Reservation must be made before the prosecution presents evidence. Independent actions (32, 33, 34, 2176) need no reservation. No double recovery. B.P. 22: no reservation allowed. Death of the accused pending the case extinguishes ex delicto liability only.
      • Art. 36: "Pre-judicial questions ... before any criminal prosecution may be instituted or may proceed ... governed by rules of court ... not in conflict with this Code."
      • PQ elements (Rule 111, Sec. 7): (a) previously instituted civil action with an issue similar or intimately related to the issue in the subsequent criminal action; (b) its resolution determines whether or not the criminal action may proceed. Traditional third requisite: jurisdiction is in another tribunal.
      • PQ procedure (Sec. 6): file with the prosecutor or the court conducting preliminary investigation, or, if already in court, in the same criminal action before the prosecution rests. Effect: suspension only, not acquittal (Uribe).
      • Bigamy MCQ: PQ answer = annulment of the SECOND marriage (accused's consent vitiated by force or intimidation: Merced v. Diez, Zapanta v. Montesa). Uribe personally disagrees but keys (c).
      • Not a PQ: legal separation; annulment of the first marriage (voidable = valid until annulled); annulment of the second filed by the second spouse for the accused's deceit (Donato v. Luna); nullity of the second marriage for being bigamous; Art. 36 nullity of the second marriage (Tenebro); civil case filed after the criminal case (Pimentel; Dreamwork).
      • Landicho v. Relova: parties cannot judge the nullity of their marriage themselves, and one who remarries before a judicial declaration "assumes the risk" of a bigamy prosecution. This was abandoned by Pulido as to void ab initio marriages.
      • Pulido v. People (2021): Art. 40 applies only for remarriage, not for bigamy. A void marriage is not valid until declared void. A judicial declaration retroacts. The accused may prove nullity of the first (void) marriage, or of the second on grounds other than bigamy, even without a prior declaration. Uribe: "wala nang Tenebro" if Pulido is maintained.
      • Morigo: no ceremony means no first marriage at all, so no bigamy and no judicial declaration needed.
      • Ritter: acquittal on reasonable doubt does not extinguish civil liability. Art. 21 applies even if no penal law punishes the act. Ardiente: water cut off without notice is an abuse of right, with three elements.
      • Breach of promise: mere breach is NOT actionable (Hermosisima; Estremos; De Jesus v. Syquia; Congress deleted the chapter). Exceptions: Art. 21 walkout on a publicized wedding (Wassmer); fraudulent promise as a means of moral seduction (Baksh, with no in pari delicto since fault is unequal); recovery of money or property advanced (Domalagan; Art. 22); lost job (Garcia v. Del Rosario). No seduction where there is mutual passion between adults (Tanjanco). The plaintiff must be in good faith (Guevarra v. Banach).
      • Art. 1403(2)(c): agreement in consideration of marriage, OTHER THAN a mutual promise to marry, must be in writing. Cabague: the son may sue the fiancée on the mutual promise, but the father may not sue on the oral agreement in consideration of marriage. Domalagan: failure to object to oral evidence = waiver, and the ₱516 had to be returned.
      • Marriage can never be compelled by specific performance. Donations propter nuptias are revocable if the marriage is not celebrated (FC 86[1]). Those in marriage settlements are void if the marriage does not take place (FC 81).

      Civil Personality, Restrictions on Capacity to Act, Domicile, and Effectivity of the Family Code

      Covers syllabus III to VI. That is: persons and personality (NCC 37–39); commencement of personality (NCC 40–41, Const. Art. II Sec. 12, PD 603 Art. 5, FC 164, RPC 256–259); death (NCC 42); survivorship (NCC 43 vs. Rule 131 Sec. 3[jj]–[kk]); juridical persons (NCC 44–47); the presumption of capacity and each restriction or modification of capacity to act (minority, insanity, deaf-mutism, prodigality, civil interdiction, family relations, alienage, absence under NCC 381–396, insolvency and trusteeship); citizenship in brief (NCC 48–49); domicile (NCC 50–51, FC 68–69); and the Family Code's effectivity, repeal and retroactivity (EO 209, EO 227, RA 6809, RA 7160, FC 253–257). Includes every syllabus case, Tolentino (Vol. I, pp. 153–217), and Uribe's quiz keys and recitation remarks.

      Uribe (why this part matters): Arts. 1–51 of the Civil Code "were not modified or repealed" by the Family Code. The Family Code begins with marriage, and the repeal starts at NCC Art. 52. He warns that the bar asks questions on these provisions, "esp. under juridical personality." Expect T/F items that copy the codal word for word except for one dropped qualifier ("favorable," "by contract," "habitual," "called to succeed each other," "of less than seven months"). Expect also an essay problem on posthumous children and simultaneous deaths.

      Persons, personality and status: basic concepts

      Person

      • Etymology. From the Latin persona, the mask worn by Roman actors. The word later came to mean the character, or the actor who played it (Tolentino).
      • Juridical sense. A person is any being, physical or moral, real or juridical and legal, that is susceptible of rights and obligations, or of being the subject of legal relations (Tolentino).
      • "Person" is wider than "man." It includes entities with no physical existence, such as corporations and partnerships, that the law endows with legal existence. Since slavery was abolished, every human being is a person, whatever his intelligence or will. Infants and the insane are persons. Even twins who are physically joined are two distinct persons (Tolentino).

      Classes of persons

      Natural personsJuridical (artificial, fictitious, moral) persons
      NatureHuman beings, individual and physical, perceptible to the sensesEntities formed by association of men; no physical existence; exist only in contemplation of law
      OriginProducts of procreationProducts of legal fiction
      Personality beginsBirth (Art. 40), retroacting to conception for favorable purposesAs provided by law (Art. 44), e.g., public-interest entities "as soon as they have been constituted according to law"; private corporations upon issuance of the certificate of incorporation
      Personality endsDeath only (Arts. 37, 42)Termination of existence under the governing law (dissolution)
      CapacityFull range, including family rightsPatrimonial relations only. No family rights, cannot make a will, no rights that presuppose physical existence

      Personality

      • Concept. Personality is the quality derived from being a person. A person is a being. Personality is that being's aptitude to be the subject, active or passive, of juridical relations. It is born with man and stays until his death, and the law extends it to juridical persons (Tolentino).
      • Characteristics (Tolentino): (1) it is a quality of certain beings, not a being itself; (2) it is a juridical concept, not a physical element; (3) it cannot be the object of a contract or of possession, and cannot be impaired by agreement; (4) it is a matter of public interest.
      • Relation to capacity. Sanchez Roman treats personality as the product of capacity. In the general sense it cannot be limited, because it flows from juridical capacity, which flows from human nature. In a specific sense it may be limited, because it results from capacity to act. Most civil-law writers, however, treat personality as identical to juridical capacity, and Tolentino says the terms are used interchangeably in the law.

      Status

      • Definition. Status is the legal condition or class to which one belongs in society, or one's legal position with regard to the rest of the community. It determines the nature and number of a person's rights and obligations.
      • Kinds: political (e.g., citizenship and suffrage) or civil (from private law). Civil status is grouped three ways: (1) as a member of society (resident or non-resident, citizen or alien); (2) as a member of a family (single, married, widowed or divorced; parent, child, sibling; legitimate, illegitimate or adopted); (3) as to the person himself (age, mental condition, sex). Profession is not a status. It depends on an accidental element, the occupation, and is not inherent in the person (Tolentino).
      • Characteristics of status: it is outside the commerce of man. Hence it is (1) inalienable, (2) imprescriptible, (3) not the object of compromise (NCC 2035(1): "the civil status of persons"), and (4) the action to claim it cannot be renounced, and (5) the rights arising from it cannot be exercised by creditors (Tolentino).
      Uribe (precision of language): He corrected a student who said a child "received juridical personality." "A person does not receive juridical personality." Say instead that personality begins or is acquired at birth, that the conceived child is considered born, and that personality is extinguished by death.

      Art. 37: juridical capacity vs. capacity to act

      Art. 37, NCC. Juridical capacity, which is the fitness to be the subject of legal relations, is inherent in every natural person and is lost only through death. Capacity to act, which is the power to do acts with legal effect, is acquired and may be lost. (n)

      Source: Sanchez Roman and Art. 11 of the Swiss Civil Code. The union of the two capacities is full civil capacity; these are the elements of civil capacity (Tolentino).

      Point of comparisonJuridical capacityCapacity to act
      Definition (codal)"the fitness to be the subject of legal relations""the power to do acts with legal effect"
      Refers toAptitude for the holding and enjoyment of rights (passive)Aptitude for the exercise of rights (active)
      How obtained"inherent in every natural person"; attaches by the mere fact of being a man"acquired"; requires intelligence and will
      How lost"lost only through death""may be lost" (e.g., insanity, civil interdiction) or restricted
      NatureOne, indivisible, irreducible, the same for all menConditional and variable; differs from person to person
      LimitationCannot be limited (except by death)Restricted, modified or limited by the circumstances in Arts. 38–39
      IndependenceCan exist without capacity to act (an infant, an insane person)Cannot exist without juridical capacity; the existence of capacity to act implies juridical capacity
      SynonymsLegal capacity; personality"Capacity" in the ordinary sense
      • Capacity is a matter of public interest. It is fixed by law and cannot be modified, extended or restricted by agreement. Both capacities are qualities of persons, not rights, so they cannot be alienated or renounced (Tolentino).
      • An infant has full juridical capacity (it can own, inherit and be a donee) but no capacity to act. A person with capacity to act necessarily has juridical capacity.
      Uribe ("who has no juridical capacity?"): A corpse (dead person), because death extinguishes it. He also gave a corporation not registered with the SEC, since it never acquired personality. He added that under the present law corporations have perpetual existence (Revised Corporation Code), so they do not really "die."
      Quiz traps (Uribe keys):
      • "Juridical capacity, which is the fitness to be the subject of legal relations, is inherent in every natural person and is lost only through death": TRUE.
      • "Juridical capacity, which is the power to do acts with legal effect, is acquired and may be lost": FALSE. That is the definition of capacity to act.
      • "Capacity to act: (a) is the fitness to be the subject of legal relations; (b) is inherent in every natural person; (c) is acquired and may be lost; (d) all; (e) none": answer (c). Choices (a) and (b) describe juridical capacity.
      • 2012 Bar: which is NOT an attribute of juridical capacity? "Juridical capacity cannot exist without capacity to act." It is the other way around.

      Arts. 38–39: restrictions vs. modifications or limitations on capacity to act

      Art. 38, NCC. Minority, insanity or imbecility, the state of being a deaf-mute, prodigality and civil interdiction are mere restrictions on capacity to act, and do not exempt the incapacitated person from certain obligations, as when the latter arise from his acts or from property relations, such as easements. (32a)
      Art. 39, NCC. The following circumstances, among others, modify or limit capacity to act: age, insanity, imbecility, the state of being a deaf-mute, penalty, prodigality, family relations, alienage, absence, insolvency and trusteeship. The consequences of these circumstances are governed in this Code, other codes, the Rules of Court, and in special laws. Capacity to act is not limited on account of religious belief or political opinion.
      A married woman, twenty-one years of age or over, is qualified for all acts of civil life, except in cases specified by law. (n)

      The two lists compared

      Art. 38: "mere restrictions on capacity to act" (6)Art. 39: "modify or limit capacity to act" (11, "among others")
      MinorityAge
      Insanity or imbecilityInsanity; imbecility
      State of being a deaf-muteState of being a deaf-mute
      ProdigalityProdigality
      Civil interdictionPenalty
      —Family relations
      —Alienage
      —Absence
      —Insolvency
      —Trusteeship

      Memory aid for Art. 39 (11): A-I-I-D-P-P-F-A-A-I-T (Age, Insanity, Imbecility, Deaf-mute, Penalty, Prodigality, Family relations, Alienage, Absence, Insolvency, Trusteeship). Art. 38's six all reappear in Art. 39, with minority as "age" and civil interdiction as "penalty." The five only in Art. 39 are family relations, alienage, absence, insolvency and trusteeship.

      Rules

      1. Art. 38 circumstances do not touch juridical capacity. They only restrict the exercise of rights. The incapacitated person keeps his rights to support, to inherit, and to damages for injuries (Tolentino).
      2. Incapacity does not exempt from "certain obligations." The codal examples are obligations arising (a) from his acts, and (b) from property relations, such as easements. Tolentino says the incapacitated person may have obligations from all sources except contracts:
        • Law: family obligations, legal easements (he cannot contract a voluntary easement), taxes.
        • Crimes: he is civilly liable even when exempt from criminal liability (RPC 101).
        • Quasi-delicts: NCC 2180–2182. Under Art. 2182, if the minor or insane person has no parents or guardian, he answers with his own property, through a guardian ad litem.
        • Quasi-contracts: no one may unjustly enrich himself at another's expense. A minor who receives money as a loan acquires ownership but no contractual duty to pay. He must still return what he received or the amount of his enrichment (Art. 22; also Arts. 1241, 1399, 1971).
        • Necessaries: Art. 1489 par. 2. He must pay a reasonable price.
      3. The Art. 39 enumeration is not exclusive ("among others"). Arts. 38 and 39 are general statements of principle. The controlling rules are the specific articles in the Code, other codes, the Rules of Court and special laws (Tolentino). Physical condition is one unlisted circumstance: impotence is a ground for annulment (FC 45(5)), and a person who is blind, deaf or dumb cannot witness a will (Art. 820).
      4. Circumstances that do NOT limit capacity: religious belief and political opinion (express). Tolentino adds race and nobility, which no longer affect capacity though they once did.
      5. Sex no longer limits capacity. The last paragraph of Art. 39 should now read "eighteen years" because of RA 6809 (Tolentino). The Family Code abolished the old differences, such as the wife's lower marrying age, the 300-day bar on her remarriage, and the unequal adultery and concubinage grounds for legal separation. See also Const. Art. II Sec. 14 (fundamental equality of women and men).

      Restriction vs. modification or limitation

      The Code uses "restrictions" for the Art. 38 list and "modify or limit" for the Art. 39 list, but it attaches no different legal effect to the labels. Tolentino treats all of them together as "causes of incapacity." In both cases, what a person may or may not do is found in the specific provisions.

      Reintegration of capacity (Tolentino): some incapacities end automatically: minority on reaching majority, and civil interdiction on service of the principal penalty. Others need a judicial declaration of restored competency. A person declared incompetent (e.g., insane or prodigal under guardianship) must petition the court that he is now competent (Rules of Court on guardianship).

      Tolentino (omission criticized): Old Civil Code Art. 32 expressly said incapacitated persons "are susceptible of rights." The present Art. 38 kept the reference to their obligations but dropped the reference to their rights. Tolentino calls this "unfortunate and conducive to confusion," since it might suggest the Code meant to suppress their rights. Other provisions show it did not.
      Quiz traps (Uribe keys):
      • "The following circumstances modify or limit capacity to act, except: (a) alienage (b) insanity (c) civil interdiction (d) all (e) none": answer (e) none of the above. All three limit capacity. Alienage is in Art. 39, insanity in both, and civil interdiction in Art. 38 (as "penalty" in Art. 39). (The quiz bank notes that one samplex key marked (c). That key is wrong on the codal, because Art. 39 lists "penalty" and is not exclusive. Uribe's reasoning for (c) was that civil interdiction appears by name only in Art. 38. If this exact item appears, answer (e) and, if space allows, add one line: "civil interdiction is a 'penalty' under Art. 39 and a restriction under Art. 38.")
      • "...modify or limit capacity to act, except: (a) age (b) insanity (c) penalty": none of the above. All three are in Art. 39.
      • "The following modify or limit capacity to act: (a) imbecility (b) prodigality (c) alienage (d) all": (d).
      • "Minority, insanity... are mere restrictions on capacity to act, and exempt the incapacitated person from all obligations": FALSE. They "do not exempt... from certain obligations."
      • "Capacity to act is not limited on account of religious belief or political opinion": TRUE.

      Arts. 40–41: commencement of personality and the conceived child

      Art. 40, NCC. Birth determines personality; but the conceived child shall be considered born for all purposes that are favorable to it, provided it be born later with the conditions specified in the following article. (29a)
      Art. 41, NCC. For civil purposes, the foetus is considered born if it is alive at the time it is completely delivered from the mother's womb. However, if the foetus had an intra-uterine life of less than seven months, it is not deemed born if it dies within twenty-four hours after its complete delivery from the maternal womb. (30a)

      Related provisions (syllabus)

      1987 Constitution, Art. II, Sec. 12. The State recognizes the sanctity of family life and shall protect and strengthen the family as a basic autonomous social institution. It shall equally protect the life of the mother and the life of the unborn from conception. The natural and primary right and duty of parents in the rearing of the youth for civic efficiency and the development of moral character shall receive the support of the Government.
      PD 603 (Child and Youth Welfare Code), Art. 5. Commencement of Civil Personality. - The civil personality of the child shall commence from the time of his conception, for all purposes favorable to him, subject to the requirements of Article 41 of the Civil Code.
      Art. 164, FC (par. 1). Children conceived or born during the marriage of the parents are legitimate.
      RPC Arts. 256–259 (abortion), in substance. Art. 256, intentional abortion: reclusión temporal if violence is used on the pregnant woman; prisión mayor if, without violence, the offender acts without her consent; prisión correccional (medium and maximum) if she consented. Art. 257, unintentional abortion: prisión correccional (minimum and medium) on one who causes an abortion by violence, but unintentionally. Art. 258: abortion practiced by the woman herself or by her parents, with a lower penalty if done to conceal her dishonor. Art. 259: abortion by a physician or midwife (penalty of Art. 256 in its maximum period), and a pharmacist who dispenses an abortive without prescription (arresto mayor and fine).

      The syllabus pairs these with Arts. 40–41 to show that the law protects the unborn although it has no personality yet. Criminal law punishes its destruction as a separate crime (abortion, not homicide or infanticide), and the Constitution protects its life from conception. Civil personality, however, still depends on birth.

      Rule, exception and condition

      1. General rule: birth determines personality. "Birth" means the removal of the foetus from the mother's womb, naturally or by surgical means (e.g., caesarean). Before birth the foetus is not a person but part of the mother's internal organs (Tolentino).
      2. Exception (presumptive or provisional personality): the conceived child is considered born "for all purposes that are favorable to it." This makes its legal existence, if it is born alive, retroact to the moment of conception.
      3. Condition: "provided it be born later with the conditions specified in" Art. 41. If it is not so born, its provisional personality disappears as if it had never existed.

      Tolentino lists two characteristics of the conceived child's personality: (1) it is essentially limited, because it covers only favorable purposes; and (2) it is provisional or conditional, because it depends on the child being born alive later.

      When is the foetus "considered born" (Art. 41)?

      Intra-uterine lifeRequirement to be considered bornResult if not met
      7 months or moreAlive at the time it is completely delivered from the mother's womb. The length of extra-uterine life is immaterial; even an instant suffices.Stillborn: never a person
      Less than 7 monthsAlive at complete delivery and does not die within 24 hours after complete delivery (i.e., must survive 24 hours)Dies within 24 hours: "not deemed born" and never acquired personality
      • Complete delivery. Total separation is produced by cutting the umbilical cord, whether the removal was natural or surgical (Tolentino).
      • Alive. The child must have an independent extra-uterine life of its own, not a mere continuation of intra-uterine life. The general opinion is that independent life is shown by complete respiration. The cry of the child is evidence of it but not a necessary sign. Another indication is the floating of the lungs in water. Pulsations, convulsive movements and incomplete respiration may be mere continuations of intra-uterine life (Tolentino).
      • Viability is not required. French law requires viability; ours, like the German, requires only that the child be alive, even for an instant. In effect, the law conclusively presumes viability if the foetus is alive at complete separation (Tolentino).
      • Premature birth (less than 7 months). The child must live 24 hours. This holds even if it was killed before the 24 hours lapsed and could have survived but for the wilful act, and likewise if death came by accident. Conversely, personality is acquired even if the 24-hour survival was due only to medical or scientific means (Tolentino).
      • Source and change. Old Civil Code Art. 30 required a "human form" and 24 hours' life for every foetus. The Code Commission dropped the human-form requirement (science shows every foetus born alive has human form; monsters are not born alive) and dropped the 24-hour rule for full-term children, because "the fact of being alive is the significant fact."
      • Period of conception. Science cannot fix the exact moment. Legally, in a normal child, it is the first 120 days of the 300 days preceding birth (Tolentino). Art. 41 is hard to apply because conception cannot be dated exactly.
      • Burden of proof. Some writers say the child is presumed alive and the burden is on whoever alleges otherwise; others put it on whoever claims a right through the child's personality. Tolentino reasons that Art. 41 makes being alive at birth a condition, so it cannot be presumed, and whoever claims the condition was fulfilled must prove it. Once live birth is shown, continuity of life is presumed, and for a premature child the burden of proving it did not live 24 hours shifts to whoever alleges it. Art. 43 does not govern this question, because it presumes two living persons who both died.
      Uribe (count the intra-uterine life, not the father's death): The 7-month figure refers to the intra-uterine life of the foetus, not to the interval between the father's death and the birth. A child born five months after the father died may have had nine months of intra-uterine life. On "within" 24 hours: "Kapag sinabing less than 24, edi kapag 24 hrs na, okay na." A premature child that lives a full 24 hours is considered born. He also stresses that the second sentence of Art. 41 is only a qualification of the first.
      Quiz traps (Uribe keys):
      • "Birth determines personality; but the conceived child shall be considered born for all purposes, provided..." is FALSE. It must be "for all purposes that are favorable to it."
      • "For civil purposes, the foetus is considered born if it is alive at the time it is completely delivered from the mother's womb" (standing alone) is FALSE, because it is not absolutely true. The 24-hour qualifier for an intra-uterine life of less than 7 months is missing.
      • "...it is not deemed born if it dies within 24 hours after complete delivery, if: (a) the child is born less than 7 months from the death of the father; (b) ...6 months...; (c) ...5 months...; (d) all; (e) none": (e) none of the above. The test is intra-uterine life. Variants use 9, 8 and 7 months "from the death of the father," and the answer is still none.
      • Watch "seven" changed to six or eight, "twenty-four hours" changed to 48 or 72, and "completely delivered" changed to "conceived" or "partially delivered."

      Rights of the conceived child (favorable purposes)

      • Donations. It may receive donations, accepted by those who would legally represent it if already born (NCC 742).
      • Succession. It may inherit by will or by intestacy. Under NCC 1025, the heir must be living, or at least conceived, at the moment the succession opens.
      • Support. It is entitled to support from its progenitors even while in the womb (Quimiguing v. Icao).
      • Compensation. Its interests "embrace both personal and property rights, including the right to compensation for personal injuries wrongfully inflicted" (Tolentino, citing US cases).
      • Acknowledgment. It may be acknowledged as a child before birth (De Jesus v. Syquia).
      • Insurance. It may be named an insurance beneficiary (Marian bar problem below).
      • Nothing unfavorable. Provisional personality cannot be used to impose obligations or burdens on the unborn.
      Geluz v. Court of Appeals (2 SCRA 801, July 20, 1961)

      Nita Villanueva had her pregnancy aborted by Dr. Antonio Geluz without the knowledge of her husband, Oscar Lazo. It was her third abortion by the same doctor. The CA awarded the husband ₱3,000 as the minimum indemnity "for the death of a person." Doctrine: Reversed. (1) The minimum award for the death of a person does not cover an unborn foetus, which is not endowed with personality and is incapable of having rights and obligations. (2) Since an action for pecuniary damages for personal injury or death pertains primarily to the one injured, no such right could accrue derivatively to the parents or heirs of an unborn child. The provisional personality of Art. 40 operates only for purposes favorable to the child and only if it is born alive. An aborted foetus never acquired personality, so no right of action ever vested in it to be transmitted. (3) The parents may recover only damages for injury to themselves: moral damages for the illegal arrest of the normal development of the foetus (the distress and anguish of its loss and the disappointment of their parental expectations) and exemplary damages if warranted (Art. 2230). On the facts, the husband showed indifference to the repeated abortions and more concern with damages than with the loss, so moral damages were not justified.

      Quimiguing v. Icao (34 SCRA 132, July 31, 1970)

      Carmen Quimiguing alleged that Felix Icao, a married man, had carnal intercourse with her through force and intimidation, and that she became pregnant. She sued for support of the unborn child and damages. The trial court dismissed the complaint because it did not allege that the child had been born, reasoning that the support obligation between parents and illegitimate children (old Art. 291) does not cover unborn children. Doctrine: Reversed. "A conceived child, although as yet unborn, is given by law a provisional personality of its own for all purposes favorable to it, as explicitly provided in Article 40." It has a right to support from its progenitors, even while in the womb, enforceable through an action on its behalf. It may also receive donations (Art. 742). The lower court's theory violated Art. 40. The mother may separately recover damages for the injury to herself (the Court cited Arts. 21 and 2219).

      De Jesus v. Syquia (58 Phil. 866, November 28, 1933)

      Cesar Syquia had a relationship with Antonia Loanco, who became pregnant. Before the birth he wrote a note to the priest asking him to baptize the expected child, referring to it as his, and letters showing paternal interest. After the birth he lived with mother and child for about a year, and left when she became pregnant again. The child was christened Ismael Loanco rather than "Cesar Syquia, Jr." Doctrine: "It is a universal rule of jurisprudence that a child, upon being conceived, becomes a bearer of legal rights and capable of being dealt with as a living person. The fact that it is yet unborn is no impediment to the acquisition of rights." Recognizing an unborn child is no different from recognizing a child already born and named; only the means of identification differ. The note to the priest could not be read two ways. It referred to a child then conceived and expected in June, and the child's identity was clear despite the different name. The writing was sufficient for compulsory acknowledgment.

      Tolentino: De Jesus v. Syquia shows that letters written before birth can ground an action for compulsory acknowledgment after birth. Note, however, that actions for compulsory recognition were abolished by the Family Code, which now speaks of establishing filiation (FC 172–175).
      Roe v. Wade (410 U.S. 113, US Supreme Court, January 22, 1973)

      A challenge to Texas laws criminalizing abortion. Doctrine (as Uribe's outline uses it): Pregnancy litigation is "capable of repetition, yet evading review." The normal 266-day gestation will end before the usual appellate process is complete, so the case is an exception to the rule that an actual controversy must exist at every stage of review. On the merits, the Court recognized a constitutional right to abortion grounded in privacy, with State interests growing through the trimesters, and held that the unborn is not a "person" under the Fourteenth Amendment.

      Note: Roe v. Wade was overruled by the US Supreme Court in Dobbs v. Jackson Women's Health Organization (2022). In any case, Roe is foreign law and contrasts with our own framework: the 1987 Constitution "shall equally protect the life of the mother and the life of the unborn from conception" (Art. II Sec. 12), and the RPC criminalizes abortion. Civil personality, however, remains tied to birth (Arts. 40–41), which is why Geluz denies indemnity "for death" of an unborn foetus.
      Continental Steel Manufacturing Corp. v. Montaño (October 13, 2009) — related case, not in syllabus

      An employee claimed CBA bereavement leave and death benefits after his wife's premature delivery ended in the death of their unborn child. The employer argued that the child never acquired personality and so could not have "died." Doctrine: Benefits granted. The Civil Code does not say that only those who have acquired juridical personality can die. Death is the cessation of life, and life is not synonymous with civil personality. The unborn child was a "dependent" of the parents. Contrast Geluz: Continental Steel concerns a labor contract (CBA) construed in the worker's favor, not indemnity for the death of a "person" under the Civil Code.

      (2012 Bar) Ricky donated ₱1 million to the unborn child of his pregnant girlfriend, and she accepted. After six months of pregnancy the foetus was born and baptized Angela, but she died 20 hours after birth. May Ricky recover the money?

      Answer: Yes. The donation is favorable, so the conceived child had provisional personality and could be a donee, with acceptance by its would-be representative (Arts. 40, 742). But Angela had an intra-uterine life of less than seven months and died within 24 hours of complete delivery, so she is not deemed born (Art. 41). Her provisional personality never became definite, and she never had juridical capacity to be a donee. The donation never took effect, and retaining the money would be unjust enrichment (Art. 22). Baptism is irrelevant.

      (2022 Bar) Gavin's will devised his rest house to his daughter Remy's unborn child. Gavin and Remy, then seven months pregnant, were in a car accident on December 1, 2021. Gavin died instantly, and Remy prematurely delivered the same day. The baby died at 8:30 A.M. on December 3, 2021. Is the devise valid?

      Answer: Yes. The devise is favorable, and the child was conceived when Gavin died (Art. 1025). With an intra-uterine life of seven months, the baby was considered born if alive at complete delivery, and it was. The 24-hour rule applies only to a foetus of less than seven months, and in any case the baby lived about two days. It acquired personality and therefore the devise, which passes to its own heirs.

      (2011 Bar, MCQ) X's negligence caused a vehicular accident in which Y, who was pregnant, suffered an abortion. Y sued X for ₱1,000,000, among other damages, for the death of a family member. Is Y entitled to indemnity for the death of the foetus?

      Answer: No. "Since birth determines personality, the accident did not result in the death of a person" (Geluz). Y may still recover damages for her own injuries, moral damages for her own anguish, and exemplary damages if the negligence was gross.

      (Uribe class problem, "Mr. Luna") Mr. Luna died leaving ₱10 million. Four months after his death his widow gave birth to a child, who died five hours after birth. Two days later the widow died of complications. Luna's parents and the widow's parents both claim the estate. Who is entitled?

      Answer: It depends on the child's intra-uterine life, which "four months after Luna's death" does not tell you.
      (a) Less than seven months, and died within 24 hours (5 hours): the child is not deemed born and never inherited. Luna's heirs are his legitimate parents and his widow, who share the estate (one-half to the parents, one-half to the widow, NCC 997). On the widow's death, her share passes to her own heirs, her parents.
      (b) Seven months or more, and alive at complete delivery: the child was born, became Luna's heir, and excluded Luna's parents. It concurs with the widow. When the child died, its estate passed to its mother. When she died, everything she held passed to her parents.
      Uribe's critique of the student's answer: it ignored that the persons now fighting are the two sets of parents, because "patay na ang mga tao na yan" and the dead have no personality. Trace the succession from death to death, and remember that "somebody else might have acquired their rights by succession."

      (Uribe situationer) X had five children. A became a New York citizen before X died. B is serving a sentence with civil interdiction. C died before the filing of the estate proceedings. D was born six months after X's death and died six hours after birth. Who may inherit from X by intestacy?

      Answer (Uribe): A may inherit. Persons not incapacitated by law may succeed (NCC 1024), and alienage is no bar to succession. B may inherit but cannot accept personally; it is done through the guardian (civil interdiction restricts capacity to act, not juridical capacity). For C, it depends on whether C died before or after X. If after, C inherited and transmits to his own heirs. If before, his descendants may represent him. D "MAY inherit, if his intra-uterine life was 7 months."
