      • Abandonment requires "a deliberate and provable choice of a new domicile, coupled with actual residence in the place chosen, with a declared or provable intent that it should be one's fixed and permanent place of abode, one's home" (Tolentino).
      • Whoever alleges that a person abandoned his domicile of origin must prove it by preponderance of evidence (Abella).
      Abella v. COMELEC (201 SCRA 253, September 3, 1991)

      Adelina Larrazabal ran for Governor of Leyte, claiming residence and registration as a voter in Kananga, Leyte. The COMELEC found that she actually resided in Ormoc City, an independent component city whose voters cannot vote for provincial officials, where she lived with her husband. It disqualified her, relying in part on the Family Code provisions that spouses must live together (FC 68) and jointly fix the family domicile (FC 69). She argued that under election law residence is a matter of intention, the animus revertendi, and that she had never abandoned Kananga. Doctrine: Disqualification upheld. (1) "Mere absence from one's residence or origin-domicile to pursue studies, engage in business, or practice his avocation, is not sufficient to constitute abandonment or loss of such residence." (2) "The determination of a person's legal residence or domicile largely depends upon intention which may be inferred from his acts, activities and utterances. The party who claims that a person has abandoned or left his residence of origin must show and prove preponderantly such abandonment or loss." (3) On the facts, there was no evidence that she left Kananga temporarily in 1975 to pursue a calling or business. What was clear was that she established her residence in Ormoc City with her husband and considered herself a resident there, so animus revertendi to Kananga was absent. Occasional visits do not show intent to keep a residence, because "it is common among us Filipinos to often visit places where we formerly resided." (The second-placer, Abella, could not be proclaimed in her place.)

      Romualdez-Marcos v. COMELEC (248 SCRA 300, 1995)

      Imelda Romualdez-Marcos filed her certificate of candidacy for Representative of the First District of Leyte. She first wrote that she had resided there "seven months," then amended it to "since childhood." She was challenged for failing the one-year residency requirement. Doctrine: (1) For election purposes, "residence" is synonymous with domicile. (2) Her domicile of origin was Tacloban/Tolosa, Leyte, where she was brought as a child and schooled. Her later stays in Manila, San Juan and Batac, Ilocos Norte, as a student, wife of a congressman and President, and later, did not show an intent to abandon it. (3) To change domicile there must concur (a) an actual removal or change of domicile, (b) a bona fide intention of abandoning the former residence and establishing a new one, and (c) definite acts corresponding to the purpose. Absent these, the domicile of origin continues. Domicile, once acquired, is retained until a new one is gained. (4) A wife does not automatically lose her domicile of origin by marriage. Old Art. 110 let the husband fix the family "residence," which means actual residence, not domicile. At most she gained a new residence, and after her husband's death she could freely return to her domicile of origin. (5) The one-year requirement is a separate constitutional qualification. It is not an element of a change of domicile.

      Poe-Llamanzares v. COMELEC (2016) — related (B29)

      A former US citizen who returned for good in 2005 and reacquired Philippine citizenship in 2006 claimed ten years' residence for the 2016 presidential election. Doctrine: Residence may be reckoned from her return in 2005, as shown by acts evidencing intent to stay (enrolling the children, selling the US home, relocating assets), even before reacquiring citizenship. A new domicile requires (1) residence or bodily presence in the new locality, (2) an intention to remain there, and (3) an intention to abandon the old domicile.

      Family domicile (FC 69)

      • General rule: joint. "The husband and wife shall fix the family domicile." In case of disagreement, the court decides (through a summary proceeding, FC 253 in relation to FC 69). Under the old Code (Art. 110) the husband alone fixed the residence. The Family Code reflects the spouses' equality.
      • Exemption (par. 2): the court may exempt one spouse from living with the other (a) if the latter lives abroad, or (b) for other valid and compelling reasons. The exemption is discretionary, not automatic.
      • Exception to the exemption: it "shall not apply if the same is not compatible with the solidarity of the family."
      • Note the change from NCC 110. The old Code exempted only the wife, and only if the husband lived abroad "unless in the service of the Republic." Under FC 69, either spouse may be exempted, there is no "service of the Republic" proviso, and there is the family-solidarity limit.
      • The duty to live together (FC 68) cannot be enforced by compulsion or contempt. Its sanction lies in other remedies, e.g., support, legal separation for abandonment, and separation of property (see Arroyo v. Vasquez de Arroyo in the spouses section).
      Quiz traps (Uribe keys):
      • "For the exercise of civil rights and the fulfillment of civil obligations, the domicile of natural persons is the place of their actual residence": FALSE. The codal says "habitual residence."
      • "When the law creating or recognizing them... does not fix the domicile of juridical persons, the same shall be understood to be the place where their legal representation is established or where they exercise their principal functions": TRUE (Art. 51). Watch for "and" swapped in for "or," or "principal office" swapped in for "principal functions."
      • "The family domicile shall be fixed by: (a) the husband; (b) the wife; (c) H and W, and in case of disagreement the husband's decision prevails; (d) ...the family court shall decide; (e) ...the court shall decide": (e), the exact codal wording. Choice (c) states the old Civil Code rule (NCC 110).
      • "In case of disagreement as to the family domicile, the decision of the husband shall prevail, subject to the wife's recourse to the court": FALSE. Contrast FC 96/124 (administration of the community or conjugal property), where the husband's decision prevails, subject to the wife's recourse to the court, and FC 211 (parental authority), where the father's decision prevails unless there is a judicial order to the contrary.
      • "To effect a change of domicile, the following must concur, except: ... continuous physical presence in the new place for at least one year": that is the exception. No minimum period is an element of a change of domicile.

      H, a career diplomat, is posted abroad. W refuses to join him because she runs a business in Manila and the children study here. H petitions the court to require W to live with him abroad. Rule.

      Answer: The court may exempt W from living with H, since H lives abroad and there are valid and compelling reasons (her business, the children's schooling), unless the exemption is not compatible with the solidarity of the family (FC 69 par. 2). The husband's choice does not prevail, and W cannot be compelled by contempt to cohabit. H's posting abroad does not change H's own domicile (Tolentino: a diplomat's assignment is no abandonment of his Philippine domicile).

      B, born and raised in Lucena, studied and worked in Quezon City for eight years, renting a condominium there while keeping his voter registration, his family home and his business permit in Lucena, where he goes home most weekends. He runs for councilor in Lucena. Is he a resident?

      Answer: Yes. Lucena is his domicile of origin. Absence to pursue studies or a calling does not constitute abandonment (Abella), and his acts (registration, home, permit, regular returns) show animus revertendi. Whoever claims abandonment must prove an actual removal, a bona fide intent to abandon, and corresponding definite acts (Romualdez-Marcos). Quezon City is merely a residence.

      The Family Code: effectivity, retroactivity, repeal and amendments

      Enactment and effectivity

      • EO 209 was issued by President Corazon C. Aquino on July 6, 1987, under her legislative powers before the Congress convened. It was drafted by the Civil Code Revision Committee (UP Law Center).
      • EO 227 (July 17, 1987) amended EO 209 before it took effect. Among its changes were the second paragraph of Art. 26 (a foreign divorce obtained by the alien spouse capacitates the Filipino spouse to remarry) and the texts of Arts. 36 and 39.
      • Effectivity: FC Art. 257: "This Code shall take effect one year after the completion of its publication in a newspaper of general circulation, as certified by the Executive Secretary, Office of the President." Publication was completed on August 4, 1987, and the Code took effect on August 3, 1988 (1988 being a leap year, the 365-day year ends a day "early") (Tolentino, citing Memorandum Circular No. 85 of the Executive Secretary).
      • For contrast, the Civil Code (RA 386) took effect on August 30, 1950 (Lara v. Del Rosario).
      Note ("year"): The August 3, 1988 date counts a year as 365 days (NCC 13). In CIR v. Primetown (2007), the SC held that the Administrative Code of 1987 (12 calendar months to a year) impliedly repealed NCC 13 on "years." Counted by calendar months under Primetown, the date would be August 4, 1988. The effectivity date of the Family Code, however, is settled as August 3, 1988 (Memorandum Circular No. 85, Tolentino, and Uribe). Use that date, and if asked, explain how it was computed. The difference never changes the answer to the usual problems.

      (Bar) The Family Code's publication was completed on August 4, 1987. On September 4, 1987, Junior and Gemma were married before a municipal mayor. Valid?

      Answer: Yes. The Family Code was not yet in force (effective August 3, 1988). The Civil Code then governed, and it authorized mayors to solemnize marriages. The marriage is valid if the other requisites were present.

      Amendments named in the syllabus

      LawWhat it did
      EO 227 (1987)Amended EO 209 before effectivity (incl. Art. 26 par. 2; Arts. 36, 39)
      RA 6809 (approved Dec. 13, 1989)Age of majority lowered to 18 (Art. 234); Arts. 235 and 237 repealed; Art. 236 amended (parental consent to marry until 21; NCC 2180 responsibility for those below 21 preserved); no retroactivity to the prejudice of minors (Sec. 4)
      RA 7160 (Local Government Code of 1991; effective January 1, 1992)Restored to municipal and city mayors the authority to solemnize marriages (Secs. 444 and 455), which the Family Code had omitted from FC 7
      Uribe (mayors): The mayor's authority to solemnize "was removed by the Family Code when it took effect on August 3, 1988. However, when the Local Government Code took effect..., such authority was smuggled in Sec. 444 as to municipal mayors and Sec. 455 as to city mayors." So from August 3, 1988 until the LGC took effect, mayors had no authority. A marriage they solemnized then is void (FC 35(2)), unless either or both parties believed in good faith that the mayor had authority. On "as of August 2, 1988" items, the Civil Code governs, and mayors could still solemnize.

      Later amendments (know they exist): RA 8533 (1998): Art. 39, the action or defense for nullity does not prescribe. RA 9255 (2004): Art. 176, an illegitimate child may use the father's surname. RA 9858 (2009): Art. 177, legitimation of children of parents below 18. RA 10572 (2013): Arts. 73 and 111. RA 11596 (2021): child marriage void and criminal.

      Repeal, separability and summary proceedings

      Art. 254, FC. Titles III, IV, V, VI, VIII, IX, XI, and XV of Book 1 of Republic Act No. 386, otherwise known as the Civil Code of the Philippines, as amended, and Articles 17, 18, 19, 27, 28, 29, 30, 31, 39, 40, 41, and 42 of Presidential Decree No. 603, otherwise known as the Child and Youth Welfare Code, as amended, and all laws, decrees, executive orders, proclamations, rules and regulations, or parts thereof, inconsistent herewith are hereby repealed.
      Art. 255, FC. If any provision of this Code is held invalid, all the other provisions not affected thereby shall remain valid.
      Art. 253, FC. The foregoing rules in Chapters 2 and 3 hereof shall likewise govern summary proceedings filed under Articles 41, 51, 69, 73, 96, 124 and 217, insofar as they are applicable.
      • Titles of the Civil Code repealed (Tolentino): III (Arts. 52–96, Marriage); IV (97–108, Legal Separation); V (109–117, Rights and Obligations Between Husband and Wife); VI (118–215, Property Relations); VIII (255–289, Paternity and Filiation); IX (290–304, Support); XI (311–355, Parental Authority); XV (397–406, Emancipation and Age of Majority). Not repealed: Arts. 1–51 (Preliminary Title, Civil Personality, Citizenship and Domicile), and the Civil Code titles on Funerals, Care and Education of Children (in part), Use of Surnames, Absence, Civil Register, etc.
      • Repealed PD 603 articles: 17–19, 27–31, 39–42.
      Note (syllabus "FC 253"): The syllabus lists "Repeal and Amendment: FC 253." The repealing clause is actually Art. 254. Art. 253 extends the summary-proceeding rules to Arts. 41, 51, 69, 73, 96, 124 and 217, which matters for FC 69: a disagreement on the family domicile is resolved in a summary proceeding. Know both articles. Tolentino's book also cites "Art. 255, F.C." for retroactivity. The correct article is 256.

      Retroactivity: FC 256

      Art. 256, FC. This Code shall have retroactive effect insofar as it does not prejudice or impair vested or acquired rights in accordance with the Civil Code or other laws.
      • Rule: the Family Code is retroactive, an express exception to NCC 4 ("Laws shall have no retroactive effect, unless the contrary is provided").
      • Limit: it cannot prejudice or impair vested or acquired rights under the Civil Code or other laws. A vested right is one that has become fixed and established and is no longer open to doubt or controversy, as opposed to a mere expectancy.
      • Validity of a marriage is determined by the law in force at the time of celebration. A pre-August 3, 1988 marriage is tested under the Civil Code impediments (e.g., NCC 80(7) step-siblings, void; NCC 80(6) killing a spouse requires a conviction). A marriage on or after that date is tested under the Family Code (Uribe: "it depends on when the marriage was celebrated").
      • Retroactive application illustrated: Art. 36 (psychological incapacity) applies to marriages celebrated before the Family Code, and since RA 8533 the action does not prescribe (Art. 39). Art. 40 (judicial declaration of nullity required for remarriage) applies to a remarriage contracted after August 3, 1988 even if the first marriage was earlier (Atienza v. Brillantes, 1995). Procedural rules apply to pending cases (cf. Pulido). Under FC 105 par. 2, the Family Code provisions on conjugal partnership apply to partnerships established before it, without prejudice to vested rights.
      Atienza v. Brillantes, Jr. (A.M. No. MTJ-92-706, March 29, 1995)

      Judge Brillantes married his first wife in 1965, before the Family Code, in a ceremony he later claimed lacked a marriage license. Without a judicial declaration of nullity, he married another woman in 1991, after the Family Code took effect. Charged administratively, he argued that the first marriage was void, so no judicial declaration was needed. Doctrine: Art. 40 applies to remarriages entered into after the effectivity of the Family Code, regardless of the date of the first marriage. Under Art. 256 it is given retroactive effect, since it does not prejudice vested rights; it is a procedural rule, and no one has a vested right in procedure.

      Bernabe v. Alejo (G.R. No. 140500, January 21, 2002)

      A child born in 1981, before the Family Code, sued after the father's death for recognition and a share in his estate. The defense invoked FC 172 and 175, which allow an illegitimate child to prove filiation after the father's death only in limited cases. Doctrine: Under NCC 285, the child had the right to sue for recognition within four years after attaining majority. That right had vested before the Family Code took effect, and FC 256 does not allow the Code to impair it. The action was timely.

      Tayag v. Court of Appeals (G.R. No. 95229, June 9, 1992)

      An action for recognition and partition was filed on behalf of a minor illegitimate child before the Family Code took effect. The defense argued that under FC 175 the action, based on open and continuous possession of status, should have been filed during the father's lifetime. Doctrine: The right of action vested when the complaint was filed under the Civil Code (which allowed the action within four years after the child's majority) and cannot be impaired by the Family Code's retroactive application.

      Candelario v. Candelario (B29 repository)

      A husband married before August 3, 1988 sued for nullity under Art. 36. Doctrine (per B29): Under Art. 256, the Family Code (including Art. 36) applies retroactively to marriages celebrated before its effectivity. If the respondent wife had a vested right that would be prejudiced, she should have raised it at the first opportunity, and she did not.

      (Uribe situationer) A and B, with no marriage settlement, married on August 1, 1988. X died at 9 A.M. on the wedding day, leaving A a parcel of land by will. After solemnization A died. Does the land form part of A's estate? Which property regime governs?

      Answer: The marriage preceded the Family Code (effective August 3, 1988), so the default regime is conjugal partnership of gains under the Civil Code (NCC 119), not absolute community. Uribe's key adds: "FC provisions will apply as long as vested rights are not impaired" (FC 256; FC 105 par. 2), so the CPG is administered and liquidated under the FC's CPG rules. Property acquired by gratuitous title (by will) is the acquiring spouse's exclusive property under CPG. Ownership vested in A at X's death (NCC 777), whether before or after the wedding, so the land forms part of A's estate as A's separate property. Uribe stresses the timing: under ACP "it does not matter when ownership was vested," but under CPG "it would matter."

      Quiz traps:
      • "The Family Code shall have retroactive effect" (standing alone): FALSE, because "insofar as it does not prejudice or impair vested or acquired rights" is missing.
      • "The Family Code took effect on August 4, 1988 / fifteen days after publication": FALSE. It took effect one year after the completion of publication in a newspaper of general circulation, on August 3, 1988.
      • "As of August 2, 1988, the following have authority to solemnize: ... city mayor" is TRUE, since the Civil Code still governed. For a date between August 3, 1988 and the effectivity of the LGC, mayors are excluded.
      • "Marriages between step-siblings are void": FALSE as a general statement. It was true under NCC 80(7), but the Family Code dropped this impediment, so validity depends on the date of celebration.

      Last-minute checklist

      • Art. 37: juridical capacity is the fitness to be the subject of legal relations; inherent; lost only through death. Capacity to act is the power to do acts with legal effect; acquired and may be lost. Juridical capacity can exist without capacity to act, never the reverse.
      • Art. 38 (six): minority, insanity or imbecility, deaf-mute, prodigality, civil interdiction. They are "mere restrictions" and do not exempt from certain obligations (from his acts, from property relations such as easements).
      • Art. 39 (eleven, "among others"): age, insanity, imbecility, deaf-mute, penalty, prodigality, family relations, alienage, absence, insolvency, trusteeship. Not limited by religious belief or political opinion. In "except" MCQs, the answer is usually none of the above.
      • Art. 40: birth determines personality. The conceived child is considered born for all purposes favorable to it, provided it be born later under Art. 41. Its personality is limited and provisional or conditional.
      • Art. 41: born if alive at complete delivery (umbilical cord cut). If intra-uterine life is less than 7 months, it must not die within 24 hours. Count intra-uterine life, not months since the father's death. Viability is not required.
      • Conception period: the first 120 of the 300 days before birth. Const. Art. II Sec. 12 protects the unborn from conception. PD 603 Art. 5 is the same as Art. 40.
      • Geluz: no indemnity "for death" of an aborted foetus, and no derivative action by the parents. Parents get only moral damages for their own distress and exemplary damages. Quimiguing: the unborn has a right to support. De Jesus v. Syquia: the unborn may be acknowledged. Roe was overruled by Dobbs (2022).
      • Art. 42: extinguished by death (natural only; no civil death). Effect on rights is by law, contract and will. The estate continues personality (Limjoco). A dead person cannot be sued (Dumlao). The corpse is a thing, and its custody goes to the lawful spouse, then relatives (Eugenio v. Velez).
      • Art. 43: persons called to succeed each other. Whoever alleges prior death proves it. Absent proof, presumed (disputable) simultaneous death and no transmission. It applies whatever the cause or place of death, even presumed death.
      • Rule 131 Sec. 3(jj): except for succession; same calamity; no inference possible. Both under 15: older. Both over 60: younger. Under 15 vs. over 60: under 15. Both 15–60: male, or if same sex, older. Under 15 or over 60 vs. between: the one between 15 and 60. (kk) = Art. 43. Joaquin v. Navarro: facts beat presumptions.
      • Arts. 44–47: (1) State and subdivisions; (2) public-interest entities created by law, whose personality begins "as soon as constituted according to law"; (3) private corporations, partnerships and associations. Nos. 1–2 are governed by the laws creating them; private corporations by laws of general application; partnerships by the Code. Juridical persons may bring civil or criminal actions. Art. 47 applies only to No. 2 entities, whose assets go to similar purposes for the benefit of the region, province, city or municipality that derived the principal benefits.
      • Smith Bell: a corporation is a "person" under due process and equal protection, but the alien-registry law is valid police power. Barlin: the Roman Catholic Church is a juridical person.
      • Presumption of capacity: Standard Oil v. Arenas. Monomania of wealth does not equal incapacity, and capacity continues until the contrary is proved.
      • Majority = 18 (RA 6809, Dec. 13, 1989). Parental consent to marry until 21, advice 21–25. Vote at 18. Will at 18 (797). Witness to a will at 18 (820).
      • Minor's contracts: one party incapable means voidable (1390); both means unenforceable (1403(3)). The capable party cannot invoke the other's incapacity (1397). Restitution only to the extent benefited (1399). Necessaries: reasonable price (1489). Arts. 1426–1427 (18–21) are practically inoperative after RA 6809.
      • Estoppel: active misrepresentation of age estops (Mercado; Sia Suan; later disclosure "of no moment"). Mere silence does not (Bambalan; Braganza). Braganza: restitution to the extent profited; minority raised as a defense is not barred by the 4-year period. Young v. Tecson (CA) is the contrary view.
      • Criminal liability: RA 9344 as amended. 15 and below: exempt. Above 15 to below 18: exempt unless with discernment (then privileged mitigating). Civil liability remains. (Syllabus RPC 12(2)–(3): under 9; 9–15 unless discernment. RPC 13(2): under 18 mitigating.)
      • Insanity: voidable marriage (FC 45(2)); no consent to contracts (1327(2)), but a lucid interval is valid (1328); exempting (RPC 12(1)) unless lucid interval. Presumption of sanity; burden on the one alleging; the relevant time is the time of the act (Vaquilar, Rafanan; Paña three-way test, clear and convincing evidence).
      • Deaf-mute: cannot consent only if he does not know how to write (1327(2)). May make a will (807). Cannot witness a will (820).
      • Prodigality: limits capacity only once he is under guardianship (Rule 92 Sec. 2; Tolentino).
      • Civil interdiction: accessory to reclusión temporal and perpetua (RPC 41). Loses parental authority, guardianship, marital authority, management, and disposition inter vivos (RPC 34). May dispose by will and may inherit (not accept personally). FC 79, 135(1), 142(3).
      • Family relations (FC 150): spouses; parents and children; other ascendants and descendants; siblings, full or half blood. FC 87 (donations between spouses void, except moderate gifts on family rejoicing; also common-law partners). NCC 1490 (sale between spouses). FC 151 (earnest efforts at compromise).
      • Alienage: aliens cannot acquire land except by hereditary succession (Uribe: "own and acquire are different"). They can own other real property.
      • Absence: declaration after 2 yrs (5 if he left an administrator); effective 6 months after publication. Presumed dead after 7 yrs except for succession; 10 yrs for succession (5 if he disappeared after 75); 4 yrs in danger of death (all purposes). FC 41: 4 / 2 years for remarriage. A reappearing absentee gets no fruits or rents.
      • Trusteeship: NCC 1491 (fiduciaries cannot buy). NCC 1381(1)–(2) (lesion of more than one-fourth makes it rescissible).
      • Art. 49: naturalization, loss and reacquisition of citizenship are governed by special laws.
      • Art. 50: domicile of natural persons is the place of habitual (not actual) residence. Art. 51: juridical persons: as fixed by law, else where their legal representation is established or where they exercise their principal functions.
      • Domicile = physical presence + animus manendi; one at a time; kept until a new one is acquired. Change requires (1) actual removal, (2) bona fide intent to abandon the old and establish the new, (3) definite corresponding acts (Romualdez-Marcos). No minimum period. Marriage does not automatically change the wife's domicile of origin. Abella: absence for study or business is not abandonment; abandonment must be proved by preponderance; Larrazabal lived in Ormoc with her husband, so she was not a Kananga resident. Election law: residence = domicile. Venue: residence = actual residence.
      • FC 69: H and W fix the family domicile; if they disagree, the court decides (summary, FC 253). The court may exempt a spouse if the other lives abroad or for valid and compelling reasons, but not if incompatible with family solidarity. Old NCC 110: the husband fixed it.
      • Family Code: EO 209 (July 6, 1987), amended by EO 227. Published Aug. 4, 1987. Effective Aug. 3, 1988 (FC 257: one year after completion of publication in a newspaper of general circulation). Civil Code effective Aug. 30, 1950.
      • FC 254 repeals NCC Titles III, IV, V, VI, VIII, IX, XI, XV of Book I and listed PD 603 articles. NCC 1–51 survive. FC 255 separability. FC 253 summary proceedings for Arts. 41, 51, 69, 73, 96, 124, 217.
      • FC 256: retroactive insofar as it does not prejudice or impair vested or acquired rights. Marriage validity is judged by the law at celebration. Art. 40 applies to post-FC remarriages (Atienza). Vested rights to sue for recognition are preserved (Bernabe v. Alejo; Tayag). Art. 36 applies to pre-FC marriages (Art. 39 per RA 8533).
      • RA 7160: mayors regained authority to solemnize (LGC Secs. 444, 455). Between Aug. 3, 1988 and the LGC's effectivity they had none.

      Marriage: Concept, Nature, Governing Law, Foreign Marriages & Foreign Divorce, Presumption of Marriage

      Syllabus VII.A (concept and nature; breach of promise to marry; not subject to stipulation), VII.B (law governing validity; lex loci celebrationis; foreign divorce), VII.D (presumption of marriage), and the cross-reference in VII.F.8 (marriage dissolved abroad). Provisions: FC 1, 2, 4, 10, 13, 21, 26; NCC 15, 17, 52, 71, 220, 221; 1987 Const. Art. II Secs. 12 & 14, Art. XV; PD 1083 Art. 14; Rule 131 Sec. 3(aa); NCC 19-21, 1403(2)(c). Reference reading: 1 Tolentino 217-231, 256-263.

      1. The governing provisions (memorize the exact words)

      Art. 1, FC. Marriage is a special contract of permanent union between a man and a woman entered into in accordance with law for the establishment of conjugal and family life. It is the foundation of the family and an inviolable social institution whose nature, consequences, and incidents are governed by law and not subject to stipulation, except that marriage settlements may fix the property relations during the marriage within the limits provided by this Code. (52a)
      Art. 52, NCC (source; repealed by FC 254). Marriage is not a mere contract but an inviolable social institution. Its nature, consequences and incidents are governed by law and not subject to stipulation, except that the marriage settlements may to a certain extent fix the property relations during the marriage.
      Art. XV, Sec. 1, 1987 Constitution. The State recognizes the Filipino family as the foundation of the nation. Accordingly, it shall strengthen its solidarity and actively promote its total development.
      Art. XV, Sec. 2, 1987 Constitution. Marriage, as an inviolable social institution, is the foundation of the family and shall be protected by the State.
      Art. II, Sec. 12, 1987 Constitution. The State recognizes the sanctity of family life and shall protect and strengthen the family as a basic autonomous social institution. It shall equally protect the life of the mother and the life of the unborn from conception. The natural and primary right and duty of parents in the rearing of the youth for civic efficiency and the development of moral character shall receive the support of the Government.
      Art. II, Sec. 14, 1987 Constitution. The State recognizes the role of women in nation-building, and shall ensure the fundamental equality before the law of women and men.
      Art. 149, FC. The family, being the foundation of the nation, is a basic social institution which public policy cherishes and protects. Consequently, family relations are governed by law and no custom, practice or agreement destructive of the family shall be recognized or given effect.
      Art. 14, PD 1083 (Code of Muslim Personal Laws; syllabus cites it as "MC Sec. 14"). Nature. – Marriage is not only a civil contract but a social institution. Its nature, consequences and incidents are governed by this Code and the Shari'a and not subject to stipulation, except that the marriage settlements may to a certain extent fix the property relations of the spouses.

      Compare the three "nature" provisions word by word

      PointFC 1NCC 52 (old)PD 1083 Art. 14
      What marriage is"a special contract of permanent union between a man and a woman""not a mere contract but an inviolable social institution""not only a civil contract but a social institution"
      Governed bylawlaw"this Code and the Shari'a"
      Exception to "not subject to stipulation"marriage settlements may fix property relations "within the limits provided by this Code"marriage settlements may "to a certain extent" fix property relationsmarriage settlements may "to a certain extent" fix property relations "of the spouses"
      Extra phrases"entered into in accordance with law"; "for the establishment of conjugal and family life"; "foundation of the family"nonenone
      Quiz trap: Uribe tests FC 1 by altering one phrase. Watch for: (a) "marriage settlements may fix the property relations during the marriage without any limitation" (FALSE: the codal says "within the limits provided by this Code"; quiz bank R-1); (b) "a special contract of union" with "permanent" dropped, or "between two persons"; (c) "Marriage is a mere contract" (FALSE; it is a special contract and an inviolable social institution); (d) "its nature, consequences and incidents are governed by the stipulation of the parties" (FALSE); (e) "marriage settlements may fix the property relations before the marriage" (the codal says "during the marriage"); (f) "foundation of the nation" (Art. 1 says foundation of the family; it is the family that is the foundation of the nation under Const. Art. XV Sec. 1 and FC 149).

      2. Concept of marriage: definition dissected

      Two senses of "marriage" (Tolentino)

      • Marriage as an act (the procedure/celebration): the procedure by which a man and a woman become husband and wife, whether by religious ceremony, civil ceremony or without ceremony. It inaugurates the relation: "that act by which a man and a woman unite for life, with the intent to discharge towards society and one another those duties which result from the relation of husband and wife."
      • Marriage as a status (the relation): the act produces a change of status, and the new status is also called marriage. As a status it involves duties and responsibilities that are no longer matters for private regulation but the concern of the State. In this aspect it is a civil or social institution, the foundation of the family and origin of domestic relations: "the civil status of one man and one woman, legally united for life, with rights and duties which, for the establishment of families and the multiplication of the species, are, or from time to time may thereafter be, assigned by law to matrimony."

      Elements of the FC 1 definition

      1. Special contract — a contract only in form; in essence an institution of public order (sui generis).
      2. Of permanent union — no term or condition; cannot be ended by agreement (see R-2 example below). Divorce is not available between Filipinos; the only exceptions are recognized by law (FC 26 par. 2; PD 1083 for Muslims).
      3. Between a man and a woman — heterosexual union (FC 2(1): "who must be a male and a female").
      4. Entered into in accordance with law — compliance with essential (FC 2) and formal (FC 3) requisites; absence makes it void (FC 4).
      5. For the establishment of conjugal and family life — the purpose; but the parties' private motive does not affect validity (Republic v. Albios).
      6. Foundation of the family and an inviolable social institution — hence the State's interest (Const. Art. XV Sec. 2).
      7. Nature, consequences and incidents governed by law, not by stipulation — with one exception: property relations, via marriage settlements, within the limits of the Code (FC 74-81).

      Purposes of marriage (Tolentino)

      • In general: (1) reproduction, (2) education of the offspring, (3) mutual help.
      • Immediate purpose: constitution of a complete and perfect community between two individuals of different sexes. Remote purpose: preservation of the human race.
      Tolentino: Kinds of marriage in older classifications: (1) firm, legal and consummated (canonical celebration not yet followed by carnal union; civil celebration not yet followed by copulation; marriage followed by sexual intercourse); (2) real, putative and presumed (a putative marriage is one celebrated between parties with an existing impediment, whether in good or bad faith; a presumed marriage, in Anglo-American law, is the common-law marriage); (3) public and secret (matrimonio de conciencia); (4) equal and morganatic; (5) valid, voidable and void, which is the only distinction under our present law.

      Constitutional overlay

      • Art. XV Sec. 2 constitutionalizes the "inviolable social institution" language: marriage "shall be protected by the State." This is why courts lean toward validity (NCC 220) and why the State, through the prosecutor/OSG, intervenes in nullity and annulment suits (FC 48).
      • Art. II Sec. 12: the family is a "basic autonomous social institution"; Art. XV Sec. 1: the family is the "foundation of the nation."
      • Art. II Sec. 14: fundamental equality of women and men, the policy basis for the FC's equalizing of spouses' rights; compare the equal-protection reasoning in Republic v. Manalo, which refused to treat the Filipino spouse unequally.

      3. Marriage as a "special contract": characteristics, distinctions, effects

      Tolentino: Marriage is a contract only in form; in essence it is an institution of public order, founded on custom and morality. It is a contract sui generis, a convention of a social character based on the consent of the parties, uniting a man and a woman in a juridical act for procreation and the other material and moral ends necessary for the development of personality. Because it is the foundation of the family, the State is deeply concerned in its maintenance in purity and integrity.

      Characteristics of marriage as an institution (Tolentino)

      1. Civil in character: established by the State independently of its religious aspect (cf. Tilar v. Tilar (2017): although a sacrament in the Church, marriage has civil and legal consequences governed by the Family Code, so a civil court may rule on the validity of a church wedding; separation of church and state is not violated).
      2. An institution of public order or policy: governed by rules established by law which cannot be made inoperative by the stipulation of the parties.
      3. An institution of natural character: one of its objects is the satisfaction of the intimate sentiments and needs of human beings for the organic perpetuation of man.

      Marriage vs. ordinary contracts (Tolentino; memorize the four)

      MarriageOrdinary contract
      Only one man and one womanAny number of persons, of the same or different sex
      The law fixes the duties and rights of the partiesThe agreement of the parties has the force of law between them (NCC 1159)
      Cannot be terminated by mutual agreement, nor even when one party becomes incapable of performing his partMay be terminated by mutual agreement (mutual dissent)
      Breach of marital obligations does not give rise to an action for damages; the law provides penal and civil sanctions instead (prosecution for adultery/concubinage, legal separation)Breach gives rise to an action for damages
      Both: based on the consent of the partiesSame

      Consequence (Tolentino): once a marriage has been properly solemnized and the obligations of married life undertaken, its validity cannot be affected by an antenuptial agreement not to live together, nor by an agreement that the marriage should not be valid and binding, nor because one or both parties did not intend it to be a permanent relation (citing Gregg v. Gregg, N.Y.: parties may not vary or diminish by private agreement the obligations the law attaches to the relationship).

      Principal effects of a valid marriage (Tolentino)

      1. Personal and economic relations between the spouses (rights and duties);
      2. Legitimacy of the sexual union and of the family;
      3. Personal and economic relations between parents and children;
      4. Family relationship (impediments to marriage, right to support, rights to inheritance);
      5. Emancipation of the spouses from parental authority;
      6. Incapacity of the spouses to make donations to each other (FC 87);
      7. Disqualification of the spouses to testify against each other (marital disqualification rule);
      8. Modification of criminal liability: exemption (e.g., one spouse defending the other from unlawful aggression, or being an accessory), mitigation (immediate vindication of a grave offense to the spouse), aggravation (relationship), or as an element (parricide).
      Uribe: Legal separation "is a kind of divorce which is relative" (a mensa et thoro: the spouses live apart but the bond is not severed), as opposed to absolute divorce (a vinculo matrimonii), which severs the bond. A divorce is relative when conditions are attached to remarriage or the bond subsists. Our law has no absolute divorce for Filipinos (except FC 26 par. 2 and Muslim divorce under PD 1083).

      A couple executes a prenuptial agreement providing that their marriage shall be valid for only 5 years, renewable by mutual consent negotiated at least 6 months before expiration. Is the agreement valid?

      Answer: No. FC 1: marriage is a special contract of permanent union whose nature, consequences and incidents are governed by law and not subject to stipulation. The only permissible stipulation concerns property relations (marriage settlements within the limits of the Code). A term on the marriage is void; the marriage itself, if all requisites are present, is valid and permanent (quiz bank R-2).

      4. "Between a man and a woman": same-sex unions

      Obergefell v. Hodges, Director, Ohio Department of Health (U.S. Supreme Court, 576 U.S. 644, June 26, 2015)

      Same-sex couples challenged Ohio and other states' refusal to license or recognize their marriages. Doctrine: The fundamental liberties protected by the Fourteenth Amendment's Due Process Clause extend to personal choices central to individual dignity and autonomy, including intimate choices defining personal identity and beliefs. The right to marry is a fundamental right inherent in the liberty of the person; under the Due Process and Equal Protection Clauses, same-sex couples may not be deprived of that right. States must license marriages between two people of the same sex and recognize such marriages lawfully performed out of state.

      Falcis v. Civil Registrar General (2019)

      Petitioner challenged FC 1 and 2 as unconstitutional for limiting marriage to opposite-sex couples (liberty, equal protection, due process, religious freedom). Doctrine: The Court dismissed the petition on procedural grounds (no actual case or controversy, lack of standing, disregard of the hierarchy of courts) and did not rule on the substantive question. The result is that marriage under the Family Code (Arts. 1 and 2) remains a union between a man and a woman; any change in that definition is a matter of policy for Congress, not the courts.

      Silverio v. Republic (2007)

      Doctrine: Sex reassignment is not among the acts or events recognized by law for correction of the civil register. Recognizing it would undermine the Family Code provisions on marriage, which restrict marriage to a union between a biological man and a woman.

      Tolentino: Difference in sex is an indispensable requisite dictated by biological law. Even under the Civil Code, which did not state it, it was understood as a natural element, because procreation cannot be realized by two persons of the same sex; the Family Code "merely states the obvious." If through deceit a marriage is celebrated between persons of the same sex (e.g., a hermaphrodite succeeds in marrying a man), the marriage is void and inexistent, producing no legal effect, without prejudice to liability for damages of the party who acted with fraud or deceit.
      Note: Obergefell is a U.S. decision; it is not binding here and was cited in Uribe's syllabus as comparative material. Application to Philippine problems: (1) Two Filipinos of the same sex who marry abroad where it is legal: the marriage is void here; their legal capacity (which includes the FC 2(1) requirement of "a male and a female") is governed by Philippine law even abroad (NCC 15), and FC 1, 2 and 4 make the union void. Answer "void." (2) Two foreigners of the same sex married abroad: there is no Philippine ruling. Their capacity is governed by their national law (NCC 15 applied to aliens; FC 21), and FC 26 par. 1's list of exceptions does not mention lack of sex difference; Tolentino argues the FC 26 exceptions should be limited to Filipinos. Present both views if asked: (a) recognized, because capacity follows national law and the marriage is valid where celebrated; (b) not recognized, because a same-sex union is contrary to a fundamental public policy of the forum (NCC 17 par. 3). (3) A Filipino and a foreigner of the same sex: void as to the Filipino's capacity (NCC 15).

      5. "Not subject to stipulation": NCC 221 and the cases

      Art. 221, NCC. The following shall be void and of no effect:
      (1) Any contract for personal separation between husband and wife;
      (2) Every extra-judicial agreement, during marriage, for the dissolution of the conjugal partnership of gains or of the absolute community of property between husband and wife;
      (3) Every collusion to obtain a decree of legal separation, or of annulment of marriage;
      (4) Any simulated alienation of property with intent to deprive the compulsory heirs of their legitime.
      Note: FC 254 expressly repeals Titles III, IV, V, VI, VIII, IX, XI and XV of Book I of the Civil Code. Title VII (The Family, where Arts. 220 and 221 are found) is not in that list, which is why Uribe's syllabus still cites NCC 220 and 221 by number; they survive to the extent not inconsistent with FC 149-151. (Tolentino's introductory list of repealed titles includes Title VII; the codal text of FC 254 does not. Cite the articles as Uribe does.)

      What NCC 221 and FC 1 allow and forbid

      Void agreements (no effect)What is allowed instead
      Contract for personal separation (spouses agree to live apart)Judicial legal separation (FC 55 ff.); spouses may in fact separate, but the agreement is unenforceable and does not change status or obligations (support, fidelity)
      Extrajudicial agreement during marriage dissolving CPG/ACPJudicial separation of property (FC 134-136); a property regime agreed upon in a marriage settlement executed before the marriage (FC 76, 77)
      Collusion to obtain legal separation or annulmentCollusion is a bar to legal separation (FC 56(5)); the prosecutor intervenes to prevent collusion, and no judgment may be based on a stipulation of facts or confession of judgment (FC 48, 60)
      Simulated alienation to defeat legitimesDisposition within the free portion
      Licenses to commit adultery/concubinage; authority to "remarry"None. Contrary to law, morals, public policy (NCC 1306, 1409)
      Panganiban v. Borromeo (58 Phil. 367, September 9, 1933)

      A lawyer prepared and notarized a contract between spouses which in effect permitted the husband to keep a concubine and the wife to commit adultery. Doctrine: Although the Revised Penal Code lets the offended spouse bar prosecution by consent or pardon, the legislature did not thereby legalize adultery and concubinage. A notarized contract permitting concubinage and adultery is not judicially recognizable: the acts remain contrary to good customs and morals and against the sanctity of marriage. The lawyer who drew it is administratively liable.

      In re Santiago (70 Phil. 66, June 21, 1940)

      A lawyer advised spouses Baniquit and Colares, who had been separated for years, to sign a document he prepared and notarized declaring that each was authorized to marry again and waiving any right of action against the one who remarried. Doctrine: The contract is contrary to law and morals and tends to subvert the vital foundation of the family. Marriage can be dissolved only by death or the causes provided by law; spouses cannot by contract authorize each other to remarry. Advising it, preparing it and notarizing it constitute malpractice justifying discipline of the lawyer.

      Selanova v. Mendoza (64 SCRA 69, May 19, 1975)

      A judge notarized/ratified a document by which spouses extrajudicially liquidated their conjugal partnership and allowed each other to commit acts of infidelity. Doctrine: Such a document is a void instrument because it contravenes NCC 221 declaring void contracts for the personal separation of husband and wife and for the extrajudicial dissolution of the conjugal partnership. A judge who lends his office to it is administratively liable.

      Lichauco-De Leon v. Court of Appeals (186 SCRA 345, June 6, 1990)

      The husband's family executed a letter-agreement to pay the estranged wife a sum and transfer property in exchange for her conformity to the separation of property and liquidation of the conjugal partnership. Doctrine: Marriage is not a mere contract but an inviolable social institution whose nature, consequences and incidents are governed by law and not subject to stipulation (NCC 52). An agreement whose object is to facilitate the separation of the spouses, the extrajudicial dissolution of the conjugal partnership, or the termination of the marriage is void for being contrary to law, morals and public policy (NCC 221, 1306).

      Quiz trap: "A contract for personal separation between husband and wife is voidable" (FALSE: void and of no effect). "Every extrajudicial agreement, before marriage, for the dissolution of the CPG is void" (FALSE: NCC 221(2) covers agreements during marriage; before marriage, the parties are free to choose any regime in a marriage settlement). "Collusion to obtain a decree of declaration of nullity" is not in NCC 221(3), which says legal separation or annulment; collusion in nullity cases is policed by FC 48 and A.M. 02-11-10-SC.

      H and W, separated in fact, sign a notarized "Agreement" that (1) they will live separately, (2) their ACP is dissolved and each keeps what he or she earns, and (3) each may live with another partner without objection. W later lives with X. H files a concubinage/adultery complaint; W invokes the agreement as consent. Effect?

      Answer: The agreement is void and of no effect (NCC 221(1) and (2); FC 1; Selanova; Panganiban). It does not dissolve the ACP (only a judicial separation of property can, FC 134-136) and does not license infidelity. However, for criminal purposes, a prior consent may still bar the prosecution under the RPC (the offended spouse cannot institute the case if he consented or pardoned). The civil rule (void agreement) and the penal rule (consent bars prosecution) are distinct; Panganiban stresses that the RPC rule does not legalize adultery. The notarizing lawyer is administratively liable (In re Santiago).

      6. Motive is immaterial; simulated and jest marriages

      Republic v. Albios (G.R. No. 198780, October 16, 2013)

      Liberty Albios (Filipina) married Daniel Lee Fringer (American) before a judge, under an arrangement that she would pay him US$2,000 so she could acquire American citizenship; they never lived together. She sued for nullity on the ground that the marriage was a sham for lack of consent. The RTC and CA declared it void. Doctrine: The SC reversed: the marriage is valid. Consent under FC 2(2) must be (a) freely given and (b) conscious or intelligent, the parties understanding the nature and consequences of their act. Both parties freely and willingly married each other precisely to obtain the benefit (citizenship), which requires a valid marriage; their consent was therefore real, not simulated. Unlike a marriage in jest (no genuine intent to be bound), a "marriage for convenience" or "limited purpose marriage" is valid: the motive for marrying is not among the grounds for nullity, and no law declares a marriage void because it was entered into for purposes other than those in FC 1 (e.g., to acquire foreign citizenship). Motives for marrying are varied and complex; the State does not and cannot dictate the kind of life a couple chooses to lead. So long as all essential and formal requisites are present and no ground for nullity exists, the marriage is valid. Marriage, an inviolable social institution protected by the Constitution, must be safeguarded from the whims and caprices of the contracting parties; courts will not allow it to be used as a tool to abuse the law or aid one who comes with unclean hands.

      Ado-an-Morimoto v. Morimoto (G.R. No. 247576, March 15, 2021)

      Rosario Ado-an agreed to a "fixed" marriage with Yoshio Morimoto (Japanese) to facilitate her Japanese visa. She signed a blank marriage certificate on the assurance that it would not be registered; no ceremony took place, but the certificate was later registered. She presented certifications that there was no record of the marriage license number stated in the certificate. The lower courts denied her petition. Doctrine: The SC declared the marriage void ab initio. Where no marriage ceremony actually took place and no license existed, the essential and formal requisites are utterly lacking; a simulated marriage used as a front for obtaining benefits is totally inexistent, the parties having no genuine intent to enter into marital relations. Albios does not apply: in Albios the parties actually appeared before a solemnizing officer, went through the ceremony and gave real consent; here there was only a signed and registered certificate. A certification from the local civil registrar that there is no record of the license is adequate proof of its absence. The marriage certificate is only evidence of a marriage; it cannot create one.

      Albios (valid)Morimoto (void)Marriage in jest (void)
      Real ceremony before a judge; license; parties declared they took each other as spousesNo ceremony; only a signed blank certificate later registered; license number not on recordCeremony performed but neither party intended to be bound, as both understood
      Consent real; motive (citizenship) irrelevantNo consent given in the presence of a solemnizing officer; no ceremony; no licenseNo real consent (FC 2(2)); a jest by one party alone, unknown to the other, does not invalidate
      Valid (no ground for nullity)Void ab initio (FC 4, 35(3); absence of FC 2(2) and 3(3))Void (no consent)
      Tolentino: Consent must be real (not vitiated by mistake, duress or fraud), conscious or intelligent (not affected by insanity, intoxication, drugs or hypnotism), given personally, and without any term or condition. A pretended marriage, legal in form but entered into in jest with no intention of entering into the actual marriage status and with a clear understanding that the parties are not to be bound, and not followed by conduct indicating a purpose to enter into such relation, is no marriage, even if the officiating person believed the parties were serious (McClurg v. Terry). But a lack of serious intention on the part of one party, unknown to the other, does not prevent the other from asserting validity, nor permit the insincere party to assert invalidity against the other.
      Uribe (recitation): "If the purpose of the other party in marrying is to get rich, what is the status of the marriage?" Answer: still valid. Motive does not affect validity (Albios).

      F, a Filipina, marries M, a Canadian, before the mayor, with a license, solely so she can immigrate; both agreed to divorce after she gets her residency. A year later she sues for nullity for "lack of consent," alleging the marriage was a sham. Will it prosper?

      Answer: No. Under Albios, a marriage for convenience is valid: the parties freely and intelligently consented to marry, which was precisely what was needed to secure the immigration benefit. Their agreement to divorce later is void (FC 1; NCC 221) and does not affect the marriage. Contrast: if no ceremony actually took place and they merely signed a certificate (Morimoto), the "marriage" would be void.

      7. Contract to marry and breach of promise to marry (VII.A.3)

      Art. 19, NCC. Every person must, in the exercise of his rights and in the performance of his duties, act with justice, give everyone his due, and observe honesty and good faith.
      Art. 20, NCC. Every person who, contrary to law, wilfully or negligently causes damage to another, shall indemnify the latter for the same.
      Art. 21, NCC. Any person who wilfully causes loss or injury to another in a manner that is contrary to morals, good customs or public policy shall compensate the latter for the damage.
      Art. 2176, NCC. Whoever by act or omission causes damage to another, there being fault or negligence, is obliged to pay for the damage done. Such fault or negligence, if there is no pre-existing contractual relation between the parties, is called a quasi-delict and is governed by the provisions of this Chapter.
      Art. 1403(2)(c), NCC. The following contracts are unenforceable, unless they are ratified: ... (2) Those that do not comply with the Statute of Frauds as set forth in this number. In the following cases an agreement hereafter made shall be unenforceable by action, unless the same, or some note or memorandum, thereof, be in writing, and subscribed by the party charged, or by his agent; evidence, therefore, of the agreement cannot be received without the writing, or a secondary evidence of its contents: ... (c) An agreement made in consideration of marriage, other than a mutual promise to marry;

      Rule, exceptions

      • Rule: A mere breach of promise to marry is not an actionable wrong. The Code Commission's draft chapter on "Promise of Marriage" (ten articles granting damages) was deliberately eliminated by Congress (Hermosisima, citing De Jesus v. Syquia: the action "has no standing in the civil law, apart from the right to recover money or property advanced by the plaintiff upon the faith of such promise"). The Family Code did not change this. Marriage cannot be compelled by specific performance; consent to the actual marriage must be purely voluntary.
      • Exceptions (damages recoverable, not for the breach itself but for an independent wrong):
        1. Walking out of a formally set, publicized and prepared wedding: contrary to good customs, Art. 21 (Wassmer v. Velez).
        2. Promise used as a deceptive device to obtain the woman's consent to sexual relations (moral seduction): Art. 21 for the fraud and deceit (Baksh v. CA). Mere sexual intercourse between consenting adults is not seduction (Tanjanco).
        3. Recovery of money or property advanced on the faith of the promise; return of gifts made in consideration of the marriage (unjust enrichment, NCC 22; Domalagan v. Bolifer).
        4. Quantifiable injury caused by the defendant's inducement, e.g., urging the woman to resign her job (Garcia v. Del Rosario, per Tolentino and B29).
      • Good faith required of the claimant: no recovery by one who acted in bad faith or is in pari delicto (Guevarra v. Banach (2022): the man who concealed a subsisting marriage could not recover the money he gave; Baksh held the woman's fault was not equal to the deceiver's). Voluntary intimacy between unmarried adults with no impediment and no deceit is not seduction (Abanag v. Mabute (2011), cf. Tanjanco).
      Wassmer v. Velez (12 SCRA 648, December 26, 1964)

      Two days before the wedding, after the license had been obtained, invitations sent, gown, reception and bridal showers arranged, the groom left a note postponing because his mother opposed; the next day he wired that "nothing changed," then never appeared. Doctrine: Mere breach of promise to marry is not an actionable wrong. But to formally set a wedding and go through all the preparation and publicity, only to walk out of it when the matrimony is about to be solemnized, is quite different. It is palpably and unjustifiably contrary to good customs, for which the defendant must be held answerable in damages under Art. 21 (actual, moral and exemplary).

      Hermosisima v. Court of Appeals (109 Phil. 629, 1960)

      A woman, about ten years older than the man, had intimate relations with him on his promise of marriage, became pregnant, and he married another. Doctrine: The action for breach of promise to marry has no standing in the civil law apart from the right to recover money or property advanced on the faith of the promise; moral damages for the breach itself cannot be recovered. Seduction was not present, given the woman's age relative to the man's; support for the child and actual damages may be awarded.

      Tanjanco v. Court of Appeals (18 SCRA 994, December 17, 1966)

      An adult woman maintained sexual relations with the man for about a year on his promise of marriage, became pregnant and resigned her job; he did not marry her. Doctrine: Seduction under Art. 21 connotes deceit, enticement, superior power or abuse of confidence that induces the woman to yield against her will. In an action by the woman, the enticement, persuasion or deception is the essence of the injury; mere proof of intercourse is insufficient. Repeated intercourse for a year between adults shows mutual passion, not seduction; no cause of action.

      Baksh v. Court of Appeals (G.R. No. 97336, February 19, 1993; the syllabus prints "97326")

      A foreign medical student courted a Filipina, promised to marry her, got her parents' consent to their living together preparatory to the wedding, deflowered her, then refused to marry her. Doctrine: Where the man's promise to marry is the proximate cause of the woman's acceptance of his love and of her giving herself to him in sexual congress, proof that he never intended to marry her and that the promise was only a subtle scheme or deceptive device to obtain her consent justifies damages under Art. 21, not because of the promise but because of the fraud and deceit behind it and the willful injury to her honor and reputation. Art. 21 applies where the woman is a victim of moral seduction. In pari delicto does not bar her because her fault was not equal to his.

      Cabague v. Auxilio (92 Phil. 294, November 26, 1952)

      The man and his father sued the woman and her father: the father had improved the bride's house and spent for the wedding in consideration of the promised marriage, which she refused. Doctrine: Two kinds of agreement were involved: (1) the mutual promise to marry between the lovers, which the Statute of Frauds expressly excepts, so oral evidence of it is admissible and the groom may sue for its breach (for the expenses advanced); and (2) the agreement between the fathers made in consideration of the marriage, which, being "other than a mutual promise to marry," cannot be proved by parol evidence (NCC 1403(2)(c)). The groom's father's action fails.

      Domalagan v. Bolifer (33 Phil. 471, February 8, 1916)

      Plaintiff paid the defendant a sum of money in consideration of the defendant's promise that his daughter would marry plaintiff's son; she married another. Doctrine: Verbal agreements made in consideration of marriage other than a mutual promise to marry are not invalid for not being in writing; the Statute of Frauds only makes them unprovable in court without a writing, and failure to object to oral evidence is a waiver. The defendant must return the money (Tolentino treats the basis as unjust enrichment).

      Estremos v. Ephan (CA, 83 O.G. 4022, No. 35)

      Doctrine: A mere breach of promise to marry is not an actionable wrong; Congress deliberately eliminated from the draft of the new Civil Code the provisions that would have made it so. The exception is the Wassmer situation, where the defendant's conduct is palpably contrary to good customs under Art. 21.

      Tolentino: A contract to marry (engagement) is a purely executory contract which cannot be enforced by court action because consent to the actual marriage must be voluntary. No ceremony is needed; a promise of marriage needs only to be made so that it may reasonably be believed by the injured party. A request to postpone for a reasonable cause is not repudiation (e.g., a party who develops a disease making it unsafe to marry). Tolentino believes that an action purely for breach of the contract to marry will not lie; but damages may be based on tort or quasi-delict, or on Arts. 19, 21 or 22: (a) seduction as a fact separate from the contract (he criticizes as too broad the pre-Code rule barring the woman's recovery because she participated in the carnal act); (b) abuse of right under Art. 19, as when a party capriciously breaks the engagement without reason, especially just before the wedding after a long engagement; (c) unjust enrichment under Art. 22 (Domalagan). Gifts made in contemplation of marriage are conditional and recoverable upon breach (e.g., the engagement ring), but absolute gifts (Christmas presents) are not. On the Statute of Frauds, he submits writing should not be required where the plaintiff already gave the consideration, and the Statute should apply only to actions to enforce the contract, not to actions for damages for breach.
      Quiz trap: (1) "A promise to marry has obligatory force; its breach is per se actionable" — FALSE. (2) "An agreement made in consideration of marriage, including a mutual promise to marry, is unenforceable unless in writing" — FALSE: the mutual promise to marry is the exception. (3) "Any person who wilfully or negligently causes loss or injury ... contrary to morals, good customs or public policy" — FALSE for Art. 21 (only "wilfully"; "wilfully or negligently" is Art. 20, which requires an act "contrary to law"). (4) In Baksh, damages are awarded "because of the fraud and deceit," not "because of the breach of the promise."

      8. Presumption of marriage and proof of marriage (VII.D)

      Art. 220, NCC. In case of doubt, all presumptions favor the solidarity of the family. Thus, every intendment of law or facts leans toward the validity of marriage, the indissolubility of the marriage bonds, the legitimacy of children, the community of property during marriage, the authority of parents over their children, and the validity of defense for any member of the family in case of unlawful aggression.
      Rule 131, Sec. 3(aa), Rules of Court. Disputable presumptions. – The following presumptions are satisfactory if uncontradicted, but may be contradicted and overcome by other evidence: ... (aa) That a man and woman deporting themselves as husband and wife have entered into a lawful contract of marriage;

      Related presumptions in the same section: (bb) property acquired by a man and a woman who are capacitated to marry each other and who live exclusively with each other as husband and wife without the benefit of marriage or under a void marriage has been obtained by their joint efforts, work or industry; (cc) in cohabitation by a man and a woman not capacitated to marry each other, contributions and corresponding shares are presumed equal (compare FC 147 and 148).

      The six things NCC 220 says every intendment leans toward (enumerate in order)

      1. validity of marriage;
      2. indissolubility of the marriage bonds;
      3. legitimacy of children;
      4. community of property during marriage;
      5. authority of parents over their children;
      6. validity of defense for any member of the family in case of unlawful aggression.
      Quiz trap: "A man and a woman deporting themselves as husband and wife are conclusively presumed to have entered into a lawful contract of marriage" — FALSE; the presumption is disputable (quiz bank R-3). "In case of doubt, all presumptions favor the individual rights of the spouses" — FALSE; they favor "the solidarity of the family." "Leans toward the separation of property" — FALSE; "the community of property during marriage."
      Perido v. Perido (63 SCRA 97, 1975)

      In a partition among descendants of a man's first and second marriages, the first set argued the second set were illegitimate; titles issued to the decedent in 1923 described him as "single/widower." Doctrine: A statement of civil status in certificates of title is not conclusive and is weak and insufficient to rebut the presumption that persons living together as husband and wife are married to each other. The presumption, especially where the legitimacy of the issue is involved, may be overcome only by cogent proof on the part of those who allege illegitimacy. In case of doubt, the law favors the validity of marriage.

      Fiel v. Banawa (CA, 76 O.G. 4619)

      Doctrine: Philippine law does not recognize common-law marriages. A man and woman not legally married who cohabit for years as husband and wife, represent themselves to the public as such, and are reputed to be spouses in their community may be considered "married" in common-law jurisdictions, but not here. Property of such relationships was governed by NCC 144 (co-ownership), which requires that (1) the couple not be incapacitated to marry, and (2) the property be acquired through the work or industry of either or both. (Now FC 147 and 148.)

      Note: Reconcile Perido and Fiel. The presumption of marriage (Rule 131 Sec. 3(aa)) is a rule of evidence that a ceremonial marriage took place; it does not make cohabitation itself a marriage. A common-law marriage (marriage by mere cohabitation and reputation, without ceremony) is not recognized (Fiel). So: cohabitation + reputation raises a disputable presumption that the couple were lawfully married; proof that no marriage was ever celebrated, or that one party had a subsisting prior marriage, rebuts it.

      Proof of marriage: the marriage certificate is the best, not the only, evidence

      Tolentino: The best proof of marriage is the marriage certificate, but it is not the only proof. Competent proof also includes: the declaration of one of the parties; testimony of persons present at the celebration; public and open cohabitation as husband and wife after the alleged marriage; birth and baptismal certificates of children naming the alleged spouses; statements of the marriage in subsequent documents. A marriage will be presumed valid and regular and will not be set aside because the priest and one of the parties cannot remember what was said during the ceremony, especially if followed by long cohabitation. A statement in a duly probated will that a woman is the testator's wife is admissible as an admission against pecuniary interest. There is a prima facie presumption that a man and woman living maritally under the same roof are married, because such is the common order of society; if they were not, they would be living in constant violation of decency and law. The presumption may be rebutted by evidence negating the fact of marriage or showing that one party is legally married to another; but after long cohabitation, during which the parties were generally known as husband and wife and their children bore the man's surname, the fact that the man abandoned the common home is not enough to overthrow it. It is rebuttable only by cogent proof. The failure of the priest to send a copy of the certificate to the civil registrar does not invalidate the marriage, since forwarding the certificate is not an essential requisite.
      Pugeda v. Trias (4 SCRA 849, March 31, 1962)

      Doctrine: The parish priest's failure to send a copy of the marriage certificate to the municipal secretary (in a marriage in articulo mortis) does not invalidate the marriage, where it does not appear that any requisite for validity was absent; forwarding the certificate is not a requisite of validity. The marriage may be proved by other evidence.

      Other cases on proof/presumption (from the B29 repository) (supplementary)

      Mariategui v. CA: the mere absence of a record of the marriage (certificate) does not invalidate it if all requisites were present; cohabitation and reputation raise the presumption. Macua Vda. de Avenido v. Avenido (2014): the fact of marriage may be proved by certifications on the loss/destruction of records and by testimony of witnesses to the ceremony; the presumption of a lawful marriage, so supported, is sufficient. Vda. de Jacob v. CA (1999) (cited in the quiz bank): the marriage certificate is the best but not the only evidence. Calimag v. Heirs of Macapaz (2016): persons dwelling together in apparent matrimony are presumed, absent counter-presumption or evidence special to the case, to be in fact married. People v. De la Cruz (2010): in parricide, the marital relationship may be proved by the accused's own admission in court (an admission against penal interest) even without a marriage certificate. Tambuyat v. Tambuyat (2015): "spouse" in the Civil Code means a lawfully wedded spouse; one with a subsisting prior marriage cannot claim the status.

      Quiz trap: "A marriage certificate is one of the formal requisites of marriage" — FALSE (samplex answer). The formal requisites under FC 3 are authority of the solemnizing officer, a valid marriage license (except FC 27-34), and a marriage ceremony with personal appearance and declaration before at least two witnesses of legal age. The certificate (FC 6, 22) is evidence, and failure to sign or register it is at most an irregularity. "Failure of the solemnizing officer to send copies within fifteen days invalidates the marriage" — FALSE (quiz bank R-68; FC 23; Pugeda).

      A and B lived together openly for thirty years, were known as husband and wife, and their children's birth certificates name them as married. No marriage certificate can be found. After B died, B's collateral relatives claim A is not the surviving spouse. Rule.

      Answer: A and B are disputably presumed to have been lawfully married (Rule 131 Sec. 3(aa); NCC 220; Perido). The certificate is the best but not the only proof; cohabitation, reputation, and the children's records are competent evidence (Tolentino). The relatives bear the burden of overcoming the presumption with cogent proof (e.g., that no marriage was ever celebrated, or that one had a subsisting prior marriage). A need not produce the certificate (quiz bank R-4).

      9. Law governing validity: general rules and the special rule for marriage (VII.B)

      General rules on contracts (syllabus VII.B.1)

      Art. 15, NCC. Laws relating to family rights and duties, or to the status, condition and legal capacity of persons are binding upon citizens of the Philippines, even though living abroad. (9a)
      Art. 17, NCC. The forms and solemnities of contracts, wills, and other public instruments shall be governed by the laws of the country in which they are executed.
      When the acts referred to are executed before the diplomatic or consular officials of the Republic of the Philippines in a foreign country, the solemnities established by Philippine laws shall be observed in their execution.
      Prohibitive laws concerning persons, their acts or property, and those which have for their object public order, public policy and good customs shall not be rendered ineffective by laws or judgments promulgated, or by determinations or conventions agreed upon in a foreign country.
      AspectGeneral rule (contracts)Marriage
      Form / solemnities (extrinsic)Lex loci celebrationis (NCC 17 par. 1); if before a Philippine consul abroad, Philippine law (NCC 17 par. 2)Lex loci celebrationis (FC 26 par. 1); consular marriage of Filipinos abroad follows Philippine law (FC 10; NCC 17 par. 2)
      Capacity / substantive (intrinsic)National law of the party (NCC 15, nationality principle); prohibitive laws and public policy cannot be defeated by foreign law (NCC 17 par. 3)Same: Filipinos carry Philippine law on capacity abroad; hence the exceptions in FC 26 par. 1; aliens' capacity follows their national law (FC 21)

      The special rule for marriage: lex loci celebrationis

      Art. 26, FC. All marriages solemnized outside the Philippines, in accordance with the laws in force in the country where they were solemnized, and valid there as such, shall also be valid in this country, except those prohibited under Articles 35 (1), (4), (5) and (6), 36, 37 and 38. (17a)
      Where a marriage between a Filipino citizen and a foreigner is validly celebrated and a divorce is thereafter validly obtained abroad by the alien spouse capacitating him or her to remarry, the Filipino spouse shall have capacity to remarry under Philippine law. (As amended by Executive Order 227)
      Art. 71, NCC (source of FC 26 par. 1, per Tolentino). All marriages performed outside the Philippines in accordance with the laws in force in the country where they were performed, and valid there as such, shall also be valid in this country, except bigamous, polygamous, or incestuous marriages as determined by Philippine law.

      Elements of FC 26 par. 1 (all must concur)

      1. Marriage solemnized outside the Philippines;
      2. in accordance with the laws in force in the country where solemnized; and
      3. valid there as such;
      4. → valid here, EXCEPT those prohibited under Arts. 35(1), (4), (5), (6), 36, 37 and 38.

      The exceptions (void here even if valid where celebrated)

      ArticleVoid marriageMnemonic
      35(1)Contracted by any party below eighteen years of age even with the consent of parents or guardiansAGE
      35(4)Bigamous or polygamous marriages not falling under Article 41BIGAMY
      35(5)Contracted through mistake of one contracting party as to the identity of the otherIDENTITY
      35(6)Subsequent marriages that are void under Article 53 (non-compliance with Art. 52 recording/partition/delivery of presumptive legitimes)ART. 53
      36Psychological incapacity existing at the time of celebrationPSYCH
      37Incestuous: ascendants and descendants of any degree; brothers and sisters, full or half blood (legitimate or illegitimate relationship)INCEST
      38Void for public policy: collateral blood relatives up to the fourth civil degree; step-parents and step-children; parents-in-law and children-in-law; adopter and adopted; surviving spouse of adopter and adopted; surviving spouse of adopted and adopter; adopted and legitimate child of adopter; adopted children of the same adopter; killing of a spouse with intent to marryPUBLIC POLICY

      NOT excepted (so lex loci governs): what is left out of the list

      • 35(2) lack of authority of the solemnizing officer: authority is a formal requisite, governed by the law of the place (e.g., a marriage solemnized by a ship captain, a notary, a mayor, or even the Prime Minister abroad, if authorized there, is valid here).
      • 35(3) absence of a marriage license: also formal, governed by lex loci (e.g., a country that does not require a license).
      • Personal appearance / proxy marriage: form of the ceremony (FC 3(3), 6), governed by lex loci. Uribe: valid if valid where celebrated, even between Filipinos.
      • Voidable marriages (FC 45): not in the list; a marriage abroad of a Filipino aged 18-21 without parental consent is merely voidable (governed by Philippine law on capacity, FC 45(1)), not void.
      • Art. 41 subsequent marriages: a bigamous marriage falling under Art. 41 (well-founded belief of death and judicial declaration of presumptive death) is excluded from 35(4), so it may be valid.
      • Relationships not prohibited by the FC: e.g., stepbrother and stepsister, brother-in-law and sister-in-law, guardian and ward (the FC dropped some NCC 82 impediments).
      Tolentino: As a rule the validity of a marriage is determined by the law of the place where it was entered into; a marriage valid where celebrated is valid everywhere. Thus a common-law marriage valid where contracted, or a proxy marriage contracted in a foreign country where good, is good in states where it is not allowed to be contracted.
