In private international law there are two general exceptions: (1) marriages deemed contrary to the law of nature and good morals as generally recognized in Christian countries (polygamous marriages; incestuous marriages in the direct line and between brothers and sisters), and (2) marriages which the local law-making power has declared shall not be allowed any validity (statutory prohibitions affecting morals or good order of society). FC 26 has expanded the exceptions by covering marriages void under Arts. 35, 36, 37 and 38. Tolentino believes the unqualified application of the exceptions should be limited to Filipinos. Where both spouses are foreigners and the validity of their marriage is questioned in Philippine courts, our courts must apply our law, but the judgment will have force only in Philippine territory; elsewhere, conflict rules govern. When Filipinos are involved, FC 26 must be read with NCC 15 and 17: their legal capacity to marry must still be tested by the criteria of our law; other requisites not affecting capacity may be governed by foreign law. Marriages between parties under the age of consent entered into in a foreign state have been held void in the state of their domicile, and the validity of a marriage contracted in a foreign state to evade the laws of the domicile may be questioned by the courts of the domicile.
      Tolentino (proof of foreign marriage): To uphold a foreign marriage, two facts must be proved: (1) the provisions of the foreign law, and (2) the celebration of the marriage in accordance with those provisions.
      Yao Kee v. Sy-Gonzales (1988)

      Doctrine: One who asserts a marriage celebrated abroad (there, a marriage in China under Chinese custom) must prove not only the fact of the marriage but also the foreign law or custom under which it was celebrated and its validity under that law. Philippine courts do not take judicial notice of foreign laws; absent proof, the foreign law is presumed to be the same as ours (processual presumption), and the marriage is tested by Philippine law.

      Board of Commissioners v. De la Rosa (1991); Ambrose v. Suque-Ambrose (2021) (B29 repository)

      Doctrine: Valid foreign marriages are recognized in the Philippines under lex loci celebrationis; but the party relying on a foreign marriage must prove the fact of marriage and its validity under the foreign law. Conversely, a marriage celebrated in the Philippines is governed by Philippine law (Ambrose).

      Uribe: In the Barcelona first-cousins problem, the marriage between A and B is void "not because of the general rule that such marriage is prohibited under Art. 38, but because it is an exception to the general rule that marriages validly celebrated in a foreign jurisdiction are valid in the Philippines (Art. 26[1]: EXCEPT those prohibited under Articles ... 38)." Cite FC 26 par. 1 first, then Art. 38. And on a proxy marriage abroad: valid under lex loci even if the parties are Filipinos, unless the case falls under the Art. 26 exceptions; there is no mistake as to identity because the absent party himself asked the brother to represent him.
      Uribe (on "may"): In the London series, when the choice says "the marriage is bigamous" and the stem asks what may leave the marriage valid, the answer is the bigamy choice, because a bigamous marriage falling under Art. 41 can be valid ("Even if bigamous, it can still be valid"). When the choice says "bigamous marriage not falling under Article 41," it is void (the qualifier "qualifies" it into 35(4)). Generally, "may" signals that exceptions are being entertained.
      Note (proxy marriages, conflicting views): Uribe's answer and the quiz bank (R-72, R-75, R-77): a proxy marriage valid where celebrated is valid here, because personal appearance is a matter of form governed by lex loci, and 35(2)/(3) and FC 6 are not in the FC 26 exceptions. Contrary view (some commentators): personal appearance goes to consent, an essential requisite, so a proxy marriage of Filipinos abroad would be void. Answer Uribe's way: valid. But a proxy marriage in the Philippines is void (FC 2(2), 3(3), 6: personal appearance required; Tolentino).
      Quiz trap: "All marriages solemnized outside the Philippines, in accordance with the laws in force in the country where they were solemnized, and valid there as such, shall also be valid in this country." — FALSE (it omits the exceptions; quiz bank R-71). Other alterations: "except those prohibited under Articles 35, 36, 37 and 38" (FALSE: only 35(1), (4), (5), (6)); "except those voidable under Art. 45" (FALSE); "valid in the place of celebration or under Philippine law" (FALSE); "solemnized outside the Philippines between Filipinos" (FC 26 par. 1 is not limited to Filipinos, though Tolentino would limit the exceptions to them).

      Application drill: the London series (Uribe's favorite)

      A and B, both Filipinos, were married in London in accordance with English law and valid there. The marriage is ALSO valid here even if: (a) A and B are first cousins; (b) B was only 17 and there was (or was no) parental consent; (c) it is a bigamous marriage not falling under Art. 41; (d) there was mistake as to the identity of the other party; (e) none of the above.

      Answer: (e). Each of (a)-(d) is an FC 26 par. 1 exception: (a) Art. 38(1); (b) Art. 35(1), void even with parental consent; (c) Art. 35(4); (d) Art. 35(5) (quiz bank R-73).

      Same facts. The marriage shall also be valid here even if: (a) first cousins; (b) B was 17 without parental consent; (c) C represented B during the marriage (proxy); (d) bigamous not falling under Art. 41; (e) none.

      Answer: (c). Proxy concerns form, governed by lex loci (quiz bank R-72; Uribe).

      Same facts. The marriage may be valid even if: (a) first cousins; (b) 17 without consent; (c) the marriage is bigamous; (d) mistake as to identity; (e) none.

      Answer: (c). A bigamous marriage may be valid if it falls under Art. 41; only bigamous marriages "not falling under Article 41" are excepted (quiz bank R-74; Uribe agreed with (c) because of "may").

      Same facts. The marriage shall be VOID here if: (a) A was 18 without parental consent; (b) it is a proxy marriage; (c) A and B are stepbrother and stepsister; (d) A and B are adopted children of the same adopter; (e) solemnized by the Prime Minister of the U.K.

      Answer: (d), Art. 38(8). (a) is merely voidable (FC 45(1)) and voidable marriages are not excepted; (b) form, lex loci; (c) step-siblings are not prohibited (FC 38(2) covers only step-parents and step-children); (e) authority is a formal requisite governed by lex loci (quiz bank R-76). If (d) is replaced by "none of the above," answer "none" (R-75).

      A (17) and B (16), Filipinos, marry in Hong Kong where the minimum age is 15. Later B sues for nullity. Will it prosper?

      Answer: Yes. Capacity of Filipinos is governed by Philippine law even abroad (NCC 15), and FC 35(1) is an express exception in FC 26 par. 1. Void even with parental consent; the action does not prescribe (FC 39); R.A. 11596 (2021) also declares child marriages void (quiz bank R-78).

      Gene and Jane, Filipinos, married in England. Jane obtained an English annulment for Gene's sterility (a ground in England). Is Gene free to remarry?

      Answer: No. The marriage was formally valid under lex loci, but as Filipinos, their status and family rights are governed by Philippine law even abroad (NCC 15; NCC 17 par. 3). Sterility is not a ground for annulment under FC 45 (physical incapacity to consummate is impotence, not sterility). The English decree has no effect here, and FC 26 par. 2 is irrelevant because neither spouse is an alien (quiz bank R-79; X-4). Alternative view noted by bar reviewers: voidability governed by lex loci. Answer "No."

      10. Marriages between Filipinos abroad; consular marriages (FC 10)

      Art. 10, FC. Marriages between Filipino citizens abroad may be solemnized by a consul-general, consul or vice-consul of the Republic of the Philippines. The issuance of the marriage license and the duties of the local civil registrar and of the solemnizing officer with regard to the celebration of marriage shall be performed by said consular official. (75a)
      Art. 7, FC (par. 5). Marriage may be solemnized by: ... (5) Any consul-general, consul or vice-consul in the case provided in Article 10. (56a)
      Art. 8, FC. The marriage shall be solemnized publicly in the chambers of the judge or in open court, in the church, chapel or temple, or in the office of the consul-general, consul or vice-consul, as the case may be, and not elsewhere, except in cases of marriages contracted on the point of death or in remote places in accordance with Article 29 of this Code, or where both of the parties request the solemnizing officer in writing in which case the marriage may be solemnized at a house or place designated by them in a sworn statement to that effect. (57a)

      Two routes for Filipinos marrying abroad

      Before a foreign officer (local law of the place)Before a Philippine consul (FC 10)
      Form governed byLaw of the place (FC 26 par. 1; NCC 17 par. 1)Philippine law (FC 10; NCC 17 par. 2)
      LicenseAs required by the foreign lawRequired; issued by the consular official acting as civil registrar (samplex: "a marriage license is required in ... between Filipino citizens abroad solemnized by a consul" — answer)
      CapacityPhilippine law (NCC 15), via the FC 26 exceptionsPhilippine law
      PartiesAnyBoth must be Filipino citizens
      PlaceAs local law allowsConsular office (FC 8), subject to FC 8 exceptions
      Tolentino: A marriage license is required for marriages of Filipinos abroad before Philippine consuls; the consular official issues it. The parties need not be permanent residents or immigrants of the foreign country; they may be there only temporarily. Philippine laws apply to marriages of Filipinos abroad under this article, so the marriage must comply with the requisites of the Family Code. A person must be designated consul-general, consul or vice-consul to have authority; an ambassador, even as head of the diplomatic mission, has no authority to solemnize marriages, because consuls (not ambassadors) take care of matters affecting Filipino citizens in their area.

      Limits of consular authority

      • Only marriages between Filipino citizens. A Philippine consul who marries a Filipino to a foreigner acts without authority: void under FC 35(2) unless either or both parties believed in good faith that he had authority (quiz bank R-35, Agay and Topacio: void; Australian law itself made the consular marriage's validity depend on the consul's own law, so lex loci gives no independent basis).
      • Only abroad. A consul-general on vacation in Manila has no authority to solemnize marriages here; an affidavit on venue cures only an irregularity of place, not lack of authority (quiz bank R-34).
      • Within his consular post ("in the case provided in Article 10").
      Quiz trap: "Marriages between Filipino citizens abroad shall be solemnized by a consul" (FC 10 says "may"; they may also marry before local officers). "The issuance of the marriage license ... shall be performed by the local civil registrar of the place where either party habitually resides" (FALSE for FC 10; the consular official performs it). "Ambassadors may solemnize marriages between Filipinos abroad" (FALSE).

      11. Marriages of foreigners in the Philippines; certificate of legal capacity (FC 21)

      Art. 21, FC. When either or both of the contracting parties are citizens of a foreign country, it shall be necessary for them before a marriage license can be obtained, to submit a certificate of legal capacity to contract marriage, issued by their respective diplomatic or consular officials.
      Stateless persons or refugees from other countries shall, in lieu of the certificate of legal capacity herein required, submit an affidavit stating the circumstances showing such capacity to contract marriage. (66a)

      Rules

      • A marriage celebrated in the Philippines, even between foreigners, follows Philippine law as to form (lex loci; FC 3, 6-8; license required unless exempt).
      • The foreigner's legal capacity is governed by his national law (nationality principle; NCC 15 applied to aliens; Garcia v. Recio). The certificate of legal capacity is the means of proving it before the license issues.
      • Stateless persons/refugees: affidavit in lieu of certificate; their capacity is determined by Philippine law (Tolentino: having no personal law, they are governed by the laws of the Philippines under which they enjoy temporary protection).
      • Absence of the certificate does not affect validity. It is a requirement for the issuance of the license, not an essential (FC 2) or formal (FC 3) requisite; at most there is an irregularity (FC 4 par. 3). Whether the alien in fact had capacity is a separate question governed by his national law.
      • A duly authenticated certificate is prima facie evidence of the alien's capacity (Garcia v. Recio).
      Uribe (class discussion on the T/F "The lack of certificate of legal capacity does not affect the validity of the marriage"): TRUE. "There will not necessarily be a defect, because he may have [capacity]. If he did not submit, it may be that he really has no legal capacity under his national law. But the mere fact that he was not able to submit — what is certain is there is an irregularity in the formal requisite. But there may not be a defect in the essential. He may have legal capacity but just did not submit." Also: "Stateless persons or refugees shall submit a certificate of legal capacity" — FALSE (affidavit in lieu).
      Tolentino: If the contracting party is a citizen of a country where the age of consent to marriage is 16 and he is given a certificate of legal capacity by his diplomatic or consular representative in the Philippines, a license can be issued to him even if he is only 16 or 17.
      Note (update): Tolentino's 16/17-year-old foreigner example predates R.A. 11596 (2021), which declares child marriages (a party below 18) void ab initio and penalizes those who facilitate or solemnize them. Since penal laws and laws of public security bind all who live or sojourn in the Philippines (NCC 14), a marriage celebrated in the Philippines involving a party below 18 should now be treated as void regardless of the foreigner's national law, and the solemnizing officer is criminally liable. If asked, state Tolentino's view, then the R.A. 11596 update.
      Quiz trap: FC 21 par. 1 says "either or both" of the contracting parties are foreign citizens; the certificate is issued by "their respective diplomatic or consular officials" (not the local civil registrar or the DFA); it must be submitted "before a marriage license can be obtained" (not before the ceremony). Par. 2: "stateless persons or refugees" submit an "affidavit stating the circumstances showing such capacity."

      12. Absolute divorce: the rule for Filipinos and the pre-1987 cases

      The baseline

      • There is no absolute divorce in the Philippines for non-Muslims. A marriage contracted in the Philippines cannot be dissolved except by death (Tolentino).
      • A divorce obtained abroad by Filipinos is void and not recognized here: NCC 15 (laws on family rights and duties, status and legal capacity bind Filipinos abroad) and NCC 17 par. 3 (prohibitive laws and public policy cannot be rendered ineffective by foreign judgments). If a Filipino divorcee then contracts a subsequent marriage, that marriage is void (bigamous) because the first is still subsisting (Tolentino).
      • Muslim divorce is governed by PD 1083 Arts. 45-55 (talaq, ila, zihar, li'an, khul', tafwid, faskh); PD 1083 applies where both parties are Muslims, or only the husband is Muslim and the marriage was solemnized under Muslim law (Art. 13, PD 1083). Conversion to Islam does not allow a party to a subsisting civil marriage to contract a second marriage; he remains liable for bigamy (Malaki v. People). A marriage solemnized under civil rites is governed by the Civil Code/FC, not PD 1083, so the RTC has jurisdiction over its nullity (Tamano v. Ortiz).
      • Divorce under special laws in force in the past (e.g., Act 2710; the Japanese occupation) is outside the scope of this section.
      Barretto-Gonzales v. Gonzales (58 Phil. 67, March 7, 1933)

      Filipino spouses obtained a Reno, Nevada divorce and asked Philippine courts to ratify it. Doctrine: Litigants by mutual agreement cannot compel the courts to approve their own actions or permit the personal relations of citizens of these Islands to be affected by decrees of foreign courts in a manner our Government believes contrary to public order and good morals. The conduct of the parties showed a purpose to circumvent our laws on divorce and secure a change of status for reasons and under conditions not authorized by our law.

      Tenchavez v. Escaño (15 SCRA 355, November 29, 1965)

      Vicenta Escaño secretly married Pastor Tenchavez before a Catholic chaplain in Cebu in 1948; she went to the U.S. and obtained a Nevada divorce on the ground of "extreme cruelty, entirely mental in character" while still a Filipino citizen; she later married an American and was naturalized. Doctrine: A foreign divorce between Filipino citizens, sought and decreed after the effectivity of the Civil Code, is not entitled to recognition as valid in this jurisdiction. Since Vicenta was still a Filipino when she obtained it, the decree gave her no right to remarry: at that time she was bound by Philippine law on family rights and duties and on status and legal capacity (NCC 15). To recognize it would be a patent violation of the declared public policy of the State (NCC 17 par. 3). Her marriage to Tenchavez subsisted, and her refusal to perform her wifely duties and her denial of consortium gave Tenchavez a right to damages.

      Van Dorn v. Romillo, Jr. (139 SCRA 139, October 8, 1985)

      Alice Reyes (Filipina) married Richard Upton (American) in Hong Kong in 1972; they were divorced in Nevada in 1982, both parties having appeared (Upton through counsel, stating that there was no community property). Alice remarried; Upton then sued her in Pasay for an accounting of her business as conjugal property. Doctrine: Owing to the nationality principle in NCC 15, only Philippine nationals are covered by the policy against absolute divorces. Aliens may obtain divorces abroad, which may be recognized in the Philippines provided they are valid according to their national law. Under his national law, Upton is no longer the husband; he has no standing to sue as husband or to exercise control over conjugal assets, and he is estopped by his representation before the Nevada court that there was no community property. The Filipina should not be obliged to live together with, observe respect and fidelity, and render support to a man who is no longer her husband under his own law; she should not be discriminated against in her own country if the ends of justice are to be served.

      Uribe (Aug 28, 2025 transcript): "In Van Dorn, who obtained the divorce decree?" Students say the foreign husband; Uribe: "In Van Dorn, it was not clear who filed for the divorce decree. Three reasons mentioned in the decision make it clear that it was the Filipina who filed": (1) statements in the special power of attorney showed it was the Filipina who initiated the divorce; (2) summons was served upon the foreign spouse; (3) the foreign spouse was the one who filed the answer (because he was the one served). So "even before Manalo, the SC had already given recognition to the divorce decree obtained by the Filipino spouse." If you read material saying pre-Manalo decisions recognized only divorces obtained by the foreign spouse, "that is NOT TRUE." In Pilapil, by contrast, the German spouse obtained the decree.
      Pilapil v. Ibay-Somera (174 SCRA 653, June 30, 1989)

      Imelda Pilapil (Filipina) married Erich Geiling (German) in Germany; Geiling obtained a divorce in Germany in 1986, then filed adultery complaints against her in Manila in 1987. Doctrine: Under RPC 344, adultery cannot be prosecuted except upon a sworn written complaint of the offended spouse. Since the German husband had obtained a valid divorce under his national law (recognized here by virtue of the nationality principle on status of persons), he was no longer her husband when he filed the complaint and had no standing to commence the case as the offended spouse. The status of the complainant vis-a-vis the accused must be determined as of the time the complaint was filed.

      Uribe: If the problem is the capacity of an heir to succeed, NCC 15 is not the basis ("Art. 15 does not have anything to do with succession. It is about persons: legal capacity to contract marriage, status of the child"). The correct basis is NCC 1039 (capacity to succeed is governed by the law of the nation of the decedent). And on the T/F "Laws relating to legal capacity of persons are binding upon citizens of the Philippines, even though living abroad": TRUE; "Are there any exceptions to this rule? WALA."

      Other foreign-divorce cases in the sources (B29 repository)

      • Quita v. CA (1998): a former Filipino who obtained a valid foreign divorce when already an alien is no longer a surviving spouse entitled to inherit from the former spouse (remanded to determine her citizenship at the time of the divorce).
      • Llorente v. CA (2000): the nationality principle applies to alien marriages so long as one spouse is an alien; a naturalized American's divorce, valid under his national law, is recognized.
      • Roehr v. Rodriguez (2003): even if the divorce decree is valid, its legal effects (custody, care and support of children) must still be determined by Philippine courts.
      • Diego v. Castillo (2004): foreign divorces are recognized only when one of the parties is an alien; a divorce between Filipinos does not bar a bigamy prosecution.
      • San Luis v. San Luis (2007): a Filipino divorced by his alien spouse abroad can validly remarry under Philippine law (Van Dorn applied; Art. 26 par. 2).
      • Bayot v. CA (2008): a foreign divorce is recognized if proven as a fact and as valid under the alien spouse's national law; citizenship is reckoned at the time the divorce is obtained.
      • Del Socorro v. Van Wilsem (2014): a foreign national divorced from a Filipina may still be compelled to support their child here; a foreign law not pleaded and proved is presumed the same as ours, and foreign law will not be applied when it works injustice to Filipinos.
      • Noveras v. Noveras (2014): a petition for liquidation filed without proof of the foreign divorce may be granted as one for judicial separation of property where the spouses have been separated in fact for at least one year.
      • Misalucha v. People: a foreign divorce has no automatic effect here; the party pleading it must prove it as a fact and its conformity to the foreign law; unproven, the bigamy charge stands.

      13. FC 26 par. 2: the mixed-marriage exception

      History

      • As originally promulgated by E.O. 209 (July 6, 1987), FC 26 had only one paragraph, excepting marriages prohibited under Arts. 35, 37 and 38.
      • E.O. 227 (July 17, 1987), issued before the FC took effect on August 3, 1988, amended FC 26 by (a) narrowing the exceptions to Arts. 35(1), (4), (5), (6) and adding Art. 36 (also inserted by E.O. 227), and (b) adding the second paragraph. Tolentino: the second paragraph "creates an exception to the foregoing rules" for mixed marriages, following Van Dorn.
      • Purpose: to avoid the absurd situation where the Filipino spouse remains married to the alien spouse who, after obtaining a divorce, is no longer married to the Filipino spouse (Orbecido; Manalo).
      • FC 13 confirms the Code contemplates foreign divorce: a previously married applicant for a license must furnish "the death certificate of the deceased spouse or the judicial decree of the absolute divorce, or the judicial decree of annulment or declaration of nullity of his or her previous marriage."

      Elements (Orbecido's "twin elements," as later read in Manalo)

      1. There is a valid marriage that has been celebrated between a Filipino citizen and a foreigner; and
      2. A valid divorce is obtained abroad (originally "by the alien spouse"; after Manalo, by either spouse) capacitating the alien spouse to remarry.

      Citizenship is reckoned at the time the valid divorce is obtained, not at the time of the celebration of the marriage (Orbecido). Result: "the Filipino spouse shall have capacity to remarry under Philippine law." Before the Filipino can remarry, the divorce must be judicially recognized, and the decree and the foreign law must be proved (Garcia v. Recio; Corpuz).

      Republic v. Orbecido III (472 SCRA 114, October 5, 2005)

      Cipriano Orbecido and Lady Myros Villanueva, both Filipinos, married in the Philippines in 1981; she later became a naturalized American and obtained a divorce in the U.S., then remarried. Cipriano petitioned for authority to remarry under FC 26 par. 2. Doctrine: FC 26 par. 2 should be interpreted to include cases involving parties who, at the time of the celebration of the marriage, were Filipino citizens, but later on one of them becomes naturalized as a foreign citizen and obtains a divorce decree. The reckoning point is not the citizenship of the parties at the time of the celebration of the marriage, but their citizenship at the time a valid divorce is obtained abroad by the alien spouse capacitating the latter to remarry. A contrary reading would sanction absurdity and injustice: the naturalized alien would be free while the Filipino stays bound. However, the party pleading the divorce must prove the divorce and the alien's naturalization and national law as facts; mere allegations are not enough (the SC set aside the RTC's grant for lack of such proof).

      Uribe (Sep 6, 2025, Quiz 3): On the T/F that the reckoning point is citizenship at the time a valid divorce is obtained: TRUE. "Before citing the case, cite first the provision that the SC is interpreting. By the letter of the law, it is a mixed marriage between a foreigner and a Filipino. Sempio-Diy [says] the decision is wrong. ... But it is the interpretation of the SC; cite Orbecido." Rationale: for Filipinos who were both Filipino when married, applying Art. 26 par. 2 avoids "an absurd situation": the alien spouse would no longer be married, but the Filipino would still be married.
      Note (conflicting views): Sempio-Diy (and Uribe's own textual observation): by its letter, FC 26 par. 2 covers only a marriage "between a Filipino citizen and a foreigner" at the time of celebration. The SC (Orbecido; reiterated in later cases) extends it to marriages that were Filipino-Filipino at celebration when one spouse is already an alien when the divorce is obtained. For Uribe's quiz, follow Orbecido: cite the provision, then the case.
      Republic v. Manalo (En Banc, G.R. No. 221029, April 24, 2018)

      Marelyn Manalo, a Filipina, filed a divorce case in Japan against her Japanese husband and obtained a divorce decree; she then petitioned for cancellation of the entry of marriage in the civil registry. The OSG argued that FC 26 par. 2 applies only when the alien spouse obtains the divorce. Doctrine: FC 26 par. 2 applies even if it was the Filipino spouse who initiated and obtained the divorce abroad. The provision only requires that there be a divorce "validly obtained abroad"; the word "obtained" does not demand that the alien spouse be the petitioner. The letter of the law should not be followed where it leads to absurdity and injustice; the purpose is to avoid the absurd situation where the Filipino remains married to an alien who is no longer married. Distinguishing between Filipino-initiated and alien-initiated divorces, where no substantial difference exists, would violate equal protection and unjustly discriminate against Filipinos. The divorce must still be valid under the national law of the alien spouse and capacitate the alien to remarry, and the foreign law and divorce must be proved (the case was remanded to receive evidence on Japanese law).

      Uribe (Aug 28, 2025): On the T/F "A divorce decree obtained abroad may only be recognized if it is obtained by a [foreigner]": FALSE; "the court has held that the word 'obtained' does not necessarily mean that it was the foreigner spouse who initiated, so even if it was the Filipino spouse who initiated the divorce decree abroad, it is binding" (Republic v. Manalo). Uribe insists on terminology: cite "the case of Republic v. Manalo," not "the jurisprudence"; a case is a decision, jurisprudence refers to the body of decisions or doctrines.
      Tolentino (outdated on this point): In case the parties to the marriage are a Filipino and a foreigner, if the foreigner obtains a valid foreign divorce the Filipino spouse has capacity to remarry under Philippine law; "but if it is the Filipino citizen who secures the divorce, the divorce will not be recognized in the Philippines, and he cannot remarry under our law." Tolentino himself criticizes this as placing the Filipino on a plane of inequality, though he adds that our law does not allow the Filipino to seek a foreign divorce and he remains subject to Philippine law on status wherever he goes. This view is superseded by Republic v. Manalo (2018). Answer per Manalo (quiz bank R-92).
      Racho v. Tanaka (G.R. No. 199515, June 25, 2018)

      A Filipina and a Japanese national, married in the Philippines, were divorced by agreement in Japan; she presented the Japanese certificate of acceptance of the report of divorce and sought a declaration of capacity to remarry. Doctrine: The Filipino spouse may be granted capacity to remarry once our courts find that the foreign divorce was validly obtained by the foreign spouse according to his or her national law, and that the foreign spouse's national law considers the dissolution of the marital relationship to be absolute. A divorce by agreement (mutual consent) valid under Japanese law may be recognized; a duly authenticated official certificate attesting to the divorce is competent proof of it.

      Dela Cruz Morisono v. Morisono (G.R. No. 226013, July 2, 2018)

      A Filipina and her Japanese husband obtained a divorce by agreement in Japan; the RTC refused recognition because the Filipina participated in obtaining it. Doctrine: Pursuant to Manalo, foreign divorce decrees obtained to dissolve marriages between a Filipino and an alien may be recognized in this jurisdiction regardless of who between the spouses initiated the divorce, provided that the party petitioning for recognition (presumably the Filipino) proves the divorce as a fact and demonstrates its conformity to the foreign law allowing it.

      Juego-Sakai v. Republic (G.R. No. 224015, July 23, 2018)

      A Filipina and her Japanese husband divorced by agreement in Japan; she sought recognition. Doctrine: Manalo applies to a divorce jointly obtained. But the starting point in any recognition of a foreign divorce judgment is that our courts do not take judicial notice of foreign judgments and laws: the foreign judgment and its authenticity must be proved as facts under our rules on evidence, together with the alien's applicable national law to show the effect of the judgment on the alien himself or herself. (Where the national law is not adequately proved, the case is remanded for reception of evidence.)

      Later decisions in the sources (B29 repository; doctrines as stated there)

      • Galapon v. Republic (2020): FC 26 par. 2 applies to mixed marriages where the divorce decree is (i) obtained by the foreign spouse, (ii) obtained jointly by the Filipino and foreign spouse, or (iii) obtained solely by the Filipino spouse.
      • Abel v. Rule (2021): FC 26 par. 2 does not require that the foreign spouse solely obtain the divorce; a divorce jointly obtained is recognized.
      • Basa-Egami v. Bersales; Octaviano v. Ruthe: FC 26 par. 2 only requires a divorce validly obtained abroad, without regard to who initiated it.
      • Republic v. Ng: a divorce by mutual agreement recorded in the Japanese family registry may be recognized if valid under the foreign spouse's national law, once the fact of divorce and the foreign law are duly proven (remanded for proper proof of Japanese law).
      • Takahashi v. Republic; Rivera v. Woo Namsun: recognition requires proof of both the fact of divorce and the applicable foreign law.
      • Republic v. Kikuchi: the foreign law must be proved from an official source; a translated photocopy of the Japanese Civil Code is not competent proof (remanded).
      • Anido v. Republic: the petitioner proves the law of the place where the divorce was obtained (there, Kentucky), not necessarily the law of the foreign spouse's nationality.
      • Kondo v. Civil Registrar; Tsutsumi v. Republic: courts should be liberal on procedural matters in recognition cases affecting Filipinos in mixed marriages; procedural rules secure, not override, substantial justice.
      • Johansen v. Office of the Civil Registrar: recognition may be joined with Rule 108 correction/annotation in one proceeding, but Rule 108's venue (where the civil registry is located) is jurisdictional.
      • Tesoro v. Landolt: a foreign public record is proved by an official publication or a copy attested by the officer with legal custody; if kept abroad, accompanied by a certificate of the proper Philippine diplomatic or consular officer and authenticated by his seal.
      Quiz trap: The exact words of FC 26 par. 2: "Where a marriage between a Filipino citizen and a foreigner is validly celebrated and a divorce is thereafter validly obtained abroad by the alien spouse capacitating him or her to remarry, the Filipino spouse shall have capacity to remarry under Philippine law." Some reviewers misquote it as "shall likewise have capacity"; the codal does not say "likewise." Other alterations: "obtained in the Philippines"; "capacitating the Filipino spouse to remarry" (the divorce must capacitate the alien); "the Filipino spouse shall automatically have capacity" (judicial recognition and proof are required); "the marriage is void" (it is dissolved, not void ab initio; it was valid until the divorce).

      14. Proving the foreign divorce and foreign law; judicial recognition

      Garcia-Recio v. Recio (366 SCRA 437, G.R. No. 138322, October 2, 2001)

      Rederick Recio, a Filipino, married an Australian in 1987; they were divorced in Australia in 1989; he became an Australian citizen in 1992 and in 1994 married Grace Garcia, a Filipina, in Cabanatuan, declaring himself "single" and Filipino. Grace sued for nullity on the ground of bigamy; Recio pleaded the Australian divorce (and, later, that the case was moot because he and Grace had themselves been divorced in Australia in 1998). Doctrine: (1) Philippine law does not provide for absolute divorce; a marriage between two Filipinos cannot be dissolved even by a divorce obtained abroad (NCC 15, 17). In mixed marriages, FC 26 allows the Filipino to remarry if the divorce is validly obtained abroad by the alien spouse capacitating him or her to remarry. A divorce obtained abroad by a couple who are both aliens may be recognized provided it is consistent with their respective national laws. (2) A divorce obtained abroad by an alien may be recognized provided the decree is valid according to the national law of the foreigner. However, the divorce decree and the governing personal law of the alien spouse must be alleged and proved; our courts do not take judicial notice of foreign laws and judgments. (3) The decree, a public document, must be proved under Rule 132 Secs. 24-25: an official publication, or a copy attested by the officer with legal custody, and, if the record is kept abroad, accompanied by a certificate of the Philippine diplomatic or consular officer stationed there, authenticated by his seal. (4) The burden of proof lies on the party who alleges the existence of the fact (here, the respondent who pleaded the divorce as a defense). (5) Divorces may be absolute or limited; the Australian decree might have been a "decree nisi" or have restrictions on remarriage, so Recio's capacity to marry Grace was not established. A duly authenticated certificate of legal capacity would have been prima facie evidence of capacity. Case remanded to receive evidence on Recio's legal capacity.

      Uribe (situationer on Garcia-Recio): Assuming the divorce decree is absolute, is the husband's second defense (the case is moot and academic because he and Grace were already divorced in Australia) tenable? No: "the argument that it is moot and academic is a weak defense since the validity of the [marriage] would give a number of effects such as the legitimacy of children and the like."
      Corpuz v. Sto. Tomas (G.R. No. 186571, August 11, 2010)

      Gerbert Corpuz, a former Filipino naturalized as Canadian, married Daisylyn Sto. Tomas (Filipina) in the Philippines in 2005, obtained a divorce in Canada later that year, and wanted to remarry here. The NSO told him the divorce could not be recorded without judicial recognition; the RTC denied his petition because only the Filipino spouse can invoke FC 26 par. 2. Doctrine: FC 26 par. 2 grants a substantive right only to the Filipino spouse; the alien spouse cannot invoke it to claim capacity. But the alien spouse is not without remedy: a foreign divorce decree, as a foreign judgment, may be recognized under Rule 39 Sec. 48(b) as presumptive evidence of a right, upon proof of the judgment and the alien's national law (Rule 132 Secs. 24-25). It may be repelled by evidence of want of jurisdiction, want of notice, collusion, fraud, or clear mistake of law or fact. The alien has a legal interest to petition for recognition (e.g., to remarry). A foreign divorce decree has no effect in the Philippines until judicially recognized; the civil registrar may not annotate it on the marriage certificate on the strength of the decree alone. Recognition may be sought in a Rule 108 proceeding for cancellation/correction of entries. Remanded to the RTC.

      Fujiki v. Marinay (G.R. No. 196049, June 26, 2013)

      Fujiki (Japanese) married Marinay (Filipina) in the Philippines; while that marriage subsisted, Marinay married Maekara (Japanese). Marinay obtained a Japanese family court judgment declaring the Maekara marriage void for bigamy. Fujiki petitioned the RTC for recognition of the Japanese judgment and annotation under Rule 108; the RTC dismissed under A.M. 02-11-10-SC (only the husband or wife of the questioned marriage may file). Doctrine: (1) A.M. No. 02-11-10-SC does not apply to a petition to recognize a foreign judgment relating to the status of a marriage where one party is a foreign citizen. (2) The petitioner need only prove the foreign judgment as a fact under the Rules of Court; Philippine courts do not relitigate the merits. The foreign judgment may be repelled only on the grounds in Rule 39 Sec. 48 (want of jurisdiction, notice, collusion, fraud, clear mistake of law or fact) and courts determine whether it is consistent with domestic public policy and other mandatory laws (e.g., a divorce between two Filipinos cannot be recognized). (3) The prior spouse is a real party in interest: the bigamous marriage threatens his property and financial interests and causes him emotional burden (Juliano-Llave), so he may petition to recognize a foreign judgment nullifying the bigamous marriage and have it annotated via Rule 108. (4) Recognition of a foreign judgment declaring a marriage void does not require a separate FC 26/nullity suit; it is consistent with FC 26 par. 2's policy of avoiding the absurdity of a marriage valid in one country and void in another.

      Uribe (situationer): "Who else can question validity [of a second, bigamous marriage]?" Answer: "Avenido or Fujiki: the spouse of the first marriage (where the second marriage is being assailed)."

      Requirements to prove a foreign divorce (checklist)

      What to proveHowAuthority
      1. Fact of the divorce (the decree or official record)Official publication, or copy attested by the officer having legal custody; if kept abroad, with certificate of the Philippine diplomatic/consular officer in that country, authenticated by his seal (or, for Apostille Convention states, an apostille, after the 2019 amendments to Rule 132)Rule 132 Secs. 24-25; Garcia v. Recio; Tesoro v. Landolt
      2. The foreign law allowing the divorceSame mode of proof (official publication or attested copy, authenticated); not judicially noticed; a mere photocopy/translation is insufficientGarcia v. Recio; Kikuchi; Juego-Sakai
      3. That the divorce capacitates the alien spouse to remarry (absolute, not limited/decree nisi)Through the foreign law and decreeFC 26 par. 2; Garcia v. Recio; Racho
      4. Citizenship of the spouse(s) at the time the divorce was obtainedProof of naturalization/foreign citizenshipOrbecido
      5. Judicial recognition by a Philippine courtPetition for recognition of foreign judgment (Rule 39 Sec. 48(b)), which may be joined with Rule 108 cancellation/annotation in the RTC where the civil registry is locatedCorpuz; Fujiki; Johansen
      Note: If the foreign law is not pleaded and proved, the processual presumption applies: the foreign law is presumed the same as Philippine law. Since Philippine law has no absolute divorce, the petition fails (and an unproven divorce is no defense in bigamy: Misalucha). The burden is on the party who pleads the divorce (Garcia v. Recio).

      15. Who may invoke what, and decision table

      Situation (citizenship when the divorce was obtained)Effect in the PhilippinesBasis
      Filipino + Filipino; divorce abroad (by either)Not recognized; marriage subsists; remarriage is bigamous and voidNCC 15, 17 par. 3; Tenchavez; Barretto-Gonzales; Garcia v. Recio
      Filipino + alien (mixed at celebration); divorce obtained by the alienRecognized; Filipino has capacity to remarry after judicial recognition and proofFC 26 par. 2; Van Dorn; Pilapil; Garcia v. Recio
      Filipino + alien; divorce obtained by the Filipino (or jointly)Recognized (same conditions)Manalo; Morisono; Juego-Sakai; Galapon; Abel
      Both Filipino at celebration; one later naturalized, then obtains divorceRecognized; FC 26 par. 2 appliesOrbecido
      Both Filipino; divorce obtained before naturalizationNot recognized; later naturalization does not validate it retroactivelyOrbecido (reckoning point); Tenchavez; quiz bank R-81, R-82
      Both aliensRecognized if valid under their respective national laws (proof required)Garcia v. Recio; NCC 15 (nationality principle)
      Alien spouse seeking to use FC 26 par. 2Cannot invoke FC 26 par. 2 (benefits only the Filipino), but may petition for recognition of the decree as a foreign judgmentCorpuz v. Sto. Tomas
      Prior spouse attacking a later bigamous marriage via a foreign nullity judgmentMay petition for recognition and Rule 108 annotationFujiki
      Muslim spouses under PD 1083Divorce under PD 1083 Arts. 45-55 (Shari'a courts)PD 1083

      Effects of a recognized foreign divorce

      • The marriage bond is dissolved as to both spouses; the Filipino spouse regains capacity to remarry (FC 26 par. 2).
      • The divorced alien is no longer a "spouse": no standing to manage conjugal/community property (Van Dorn), to file adultery as offended spouse (Pilapil), or to inherit as surviving spouse (Quita).
      • Effects on children (custody, support) are still determined by Philippine courts (Roehr v. Rodriguez); the alien parent may be compelled to support the child (Del Socorro v. Van Wilsem).
      • The decree must be annotated on the marriage record by court order (Corpuz; Rule 108).

      16. Application drill (Uribe-style)

      A and B, Filipinos, married in Tacloban in 1995. A went to New York, obtained a divorce there in 1998, and became a U.S. citizen in 2001. In 2002 A married C; in 2003 B married D in Tacloban. Is the B-D marriage valid? (a) Valid, the divorce capacitated B; (b) Void, because A and B were Filipinos at the time of the marriage, so Art. 26 par. 2 does not apply; (c) Valid, because when B married D, A was no longer Filipino; (d) Void, because A was still a Filipino when the divorce was obtained, thus it did not capacitate B to remarry D.

      Answer: (d). Under Orbecido, citizenship is reckoned when the divorce is obtained. In 1998 A was still a Filipino; a Filipino-Filipino divorce is not recognized (NCC 15). B's marriage to D is bigamous and void (FC 35(4)). (b) uses the wrong reckoning point; (c) the wrong time (quiz bank R-81; Uribe's class answer).

      Same, but A became a U.S. citizen in 1998 and obtained the divorce in 2001. Is the B-D marriage (2003) valid? Choices: (a) Void, A and B were Filipinos at the time of marriage; (b) Valid, A was no longer Filipino when B married D; (c) Void, A was still Filipino when the divorce was obtained; (d) Valid, a divorce decree was obtained by A, thus capacitating B to remarry.

      Answer: (d). A was already an alien when he obtained the divorce; FC 26 par. 2 applies (Orbecido), so B, the Filipino spouse, acquired capacity to remarry, subject to proof and judicial recognition (quiz bank R-83). (b) points to the wrong moment (B's remarriage).

      A and B, Filipinos, married in 2005. A obtained a New York divorce in 2009 and became a New York citizen only in 2011. B married D in 2013. Choices include (d) "Valid, because even if a Filipino was the one who obtained the divorce decree, it capacitated B to remarry D" and (e) "none of the above."

      Answer: (e). The B-D marriage is void, but no choice gives the right reason. (d) misreads Manalo: Manalo allows a Filipino-initiated divorce against an alien spouse; here both were Filipinos when the divorce was obtained (quiz bank R-82).

      In 1989 Maris (Filipina) married Johnson (American) in Tokyo under Japanese law. Johnson validly divorced her in Nevada. Maris married Pedro (Filipino) in Cebu. Pedro later became an American; Maris obtained a divorce in Maryland, then married Vincent (Filipino) in Cebu. (1) Was the Maris-Johnson marriage valid, and is it still existing? (2) Is the Maris-Vincent marriage valid; who is her lawful husband?

      Answer: (1) Valid when celebrated (FC 26 par. 1); dissolved by Johnson's valid divorce, which gave Maris capacity to remarry (FC 26 par. 2), subject to judicial recognition. (2) Valid; Vincent is her husband. Pedro was already an alien when the Maryland divorce was obtained (Orbecido), and it does not matter that Maris initiated it (Manalo), provided the divorce capacitated Pedro to remarry and is proved and recognized. (Older bar keys answered "void; Pedro remains husband" — outdated after Orbecido and Manalo; quiz bank R-84, R-85.)

      Eka (Filipina) and Du-guil (Korean) married in the Philippines and moved to Seoul. Du-guil agreed to a divorce only if Eka filed it on a "no fault" ground. After the divorce, the RTC denied recognition because Eka alone filed. Correct?

      Answer: No. FC 26 par. 2 requires only a divorce validly obtained abroad, whoever initiated it (Manalo; Galapon; Abel). Eka must prove the decree and Korean law; recognition is still required (quiz bank R-90).

      "Under Art. 26 of the Family Code, when a foreign spouse divorces his/her Filipino spouse, the latter may re-marry by proving only that the foreign spouse has obtained a divorce against her or him abroad." True or false?

      Answer: FALSE. The Filipino must also prove that the divorce is valid under the alien's national law and capacitated the alien to remarry; the foreign law must be alleged and proved (Garcia v. Recio), and the decree judicially recognized (Corpuz) (quiz bank R-93).

      Ted, a naturalized Canadian, obtained a Canadian divorce from Annie (Filipina) and wants to marry Corazon in the Philippines. The civil registrar refused to annotate the decree; the NSO told him to file for judicial recognition. Is that necessary?

      Answer: Yes. A foreign divorce decree has no effect here until judicially recognized upon proof of the decree and the foreign law (Corpuz v. Sto. Tomas; Rule 39 Sec. 48; Rule 108). Ted, as the alien, cannot invoke FC 26 par. 2 itself, but may petition for recognition of the decree as a foreign judgment (quiz bank R-94).

      Sonny and Lulu, Filipinos, married in 1985. In 1987 Sonny obtained a divorce in Canada (still a Filipino) and married Auring there in January 1988. In 1990 Lulu married Tirso. Sonny died in 1991. Status of the divorce, the Sonny-Auring and the Lulu-Tirso marriages?

      Answer: The divorce has no effect (both Filipinos; NCC 15; Tenchavez); the marriage subsisted. Sonny-Auring (before the FC): void as bigamous (NCC 83). Lulu-Tirso (1990, under the FC): void as bigamous (FC 35(4)); not under Art. 41 (no well-founded belief of death, no declaration of presumptive death, not even four years of absence). Sonny's death does not validate it (quiz bank R-88, V-74).

      Marvin (Filipino) and Shelley (American), residents of California, married there; Shelley later obtained a California divorce. Marvin then married Manel (Filipina) in Hong Kong. Valid?

      Answer: Valid. The first marriage was valid where celebrated (FC 26 par. 1); Shelley's divorce gave Marvin capacity (FC 26 par. 2); the Hong Kong marriage, valid there, is valid here (FC 26 par. 1). Marrying abroad to avoid publicity is immaterial. Marvin should have the divorce recognized for Philippine records (quiz bank R-89).

      Flor and Virgilio, Filipinos, married in 1980. Flor became Canadian in 1989 and obtained a Canadian divorce in 1990 after Virgilio was served summons; she remarried. Can Virgilio remarry in the Philippines?

      Answer: Yes, after judicial recognition and proof of the divorce and Canadian law: Flor was an alien when she obtained the divorce (Orbecido). The old bar key ("No, both were Filipinos at the time of marriage") is outdated (quiz bank R-86). Same for Harry and Wilma (R-87): Harry may marry Elizabeth only after judicial recognition; Wilma's remarriage alone does not free him.

      Agay (Filipina) and Topacio (Australian) married in the Philippine consular office in Australia; Australian law validates consular marriages only if valid under the consul's own law. Status?

      Answer: Void. Under FC 7(5) and 10, a Philippine consul may solemnize only marriages between Filipino citizens abroad; lack of authority makes the marriage void (FC 4, 35(2)), unless a party believed in good faith in the consul's authority (quiz bank R-35).

      Juan, a Filipino residing in Tokyo, marries a Japanese woman there. What law governs (a) his capacity to marry and (b) the form of the ceremony? If they marry instead before the Philippine consul in Tokyo, what follows?

      Answer: (a) Philippine law (NCC 15; quiz bank P-27). (b) Japanese law (lex loci; FC 26 par. 1; NCC 17 par. 1). Before the Philippine consul: void for lack of authority, since consular marriages are only between Filipino citizens (FC 10), subject to the good-faith exception of FC 35(2). (Contrast NCC 17 par. 2: a deed executed before the Philippine consul follows Philippine solemnities.)

      X and Y, Filipino first cousins, marry in Los Angeles with a license issued by the Philippine consul acting as civil registrar. X later marries Z in the Philippines without a judicial declaration of nullity. Status of X-Y and X-Z?

      Answer: X-Y is void (FC 38(1); excepted by FC 26 par. 1; and if solemnized by the consul, Philippine law governs anyway). X-Z is void under FC 40 and 35(6)/52-53 for lack of a prior final judgment declaring the first marriage void (Uribe's Barcelona situationer). On bigamy, the quiz bank (V-60) follows Pulido v. People (2021): no bigamy where the first marriage is void ab initio.

      Last-minute checklist

      • FC 1: "special contract of permanent union between a man and a woman entered into in accordance with law for the establishment of conjugal and family life"; "foundation of the family"; "inviolable social institution"; "nature, consequences, and incidents ... governed by law and not subject to stipulation"; exception: marriage settlements may fix the property relations during the marriage within the limits provided by this Code.
      • NCC 52: "not a mere contract"; settlements may "to a certain extent" fix property relations. PD 1083 Art. 14: "not only a civil contract but a social institution"; governed by "this Code and the Shari'a."
      • Const. Art. XV Sec. 2: marriage = inviolable social institution, foundation of the family, protected by the State. Art. XV Sec. 1: family = foundation of the nation. Art. II Sec. 12: family = basic autonomous social institution. Art. II Sec. 14: equality of women and men.
      • Marriage vs. ordinary contract (Tolentino): (1) one man + one woman; (2) law fixes rights/duties; (3) not terminable by agreement; (4) breach not actionable for damages (sanctions are penal and legal separation).
      • Three characteristics: civil, public order, natural. Eight principal effects (spouses' relations; legitimacy; parent-child; family relationship; emancipation; no donations; marital disqualification; criminal liability modified).
      • Same-sex: Obergefell (U.S., persuasive only); Falcis (dismissed on procedure; marriage remains man-woman; for Congress); Silverio (biological sex). Filipinos' same-sex marriage abroad: void here.
      • NCC 221: void — (1) contract for personal separation; (2) extrajudicial agreement during marriage dissolving CPG/ACP; (3) collusion to obtain legal separation or annulment; (4) simulated alienation to deprive heirs of legitimes. Cases: Panganiban v. Borromeo, In re Santiago, Selanova v. Mendoza (lawyer/judge liable), Lichauco-De Leon.
      • Albios: marriage for convenience (citizenship) valid; consent real; motive irrelevant. Morimoto: no ceremony + signed blank certificate + no license = void; Albios inapplicable. Marriage in jest by both = no consent, void.
      • Breach of promise: not actionable per se (Hermosisima; Estremos; Congress deleted the chapter). Damages if: Wassmer (walk-out after publicized preparations; Art. 21); Baksh (deceit/moral seduction; Art. 21); recovery of money advanced/gifts (Domalagan; Art. 22). Tanjanco: mutual passion is not seduction. Cabague: mutual promise to marry provable orally; other agreements in consideration of marriage need writing (NCC 1403(2)(c)).
      • NCC 220: in case of doubt, presumptions favor the solidarity of the family: validity of marriage, indissolubility, legitimacy, community of property, parental authority, validity of defense of family members.
      • Rule 131 Sec. 3(aa): man and woman deporting themselves as husband and wife are disputably (not conclusively) presumed married. Rebuttable only by cogent proof (Perido). Common-law marriage not recognized (Fiel v. Banawa).
      • Marriage certificate = best evidence, not the only evidence, and not a formal requisite. Failure to send copies within 15 days does not invalidate (Pugeda).
      • NCC 15 (status/capacity follow Filipinos abroad; "no exceptions" per Uribe); NCC 17 par. 1 (form = lex loci), par. 2 (before PH consul abroad = PH solemnities), par. 3 (prohibitive laws/public policy not defeated by foreign laws or judgments).
      • FC 26 par. 1 exceptions: 35(1), (4), (5), (6), 36, 37, 38. Not excepted: 35(2) authority, 35(3) license, proxy/form, voidable marriages, Art. 41 marriages. NCC 71's old exceptions: bigamous, polygamous, incestuous.
      • London drill: first cousins (38(1)) void; 17 years old, with or without consent (35(1)) void; bigamous not under Art. 41 (35(4)) void; mistake of identity (35(5)) void; adopted children of same adopter (38(8)) void; 18 without consent = voidable only; proxy = valid; step-siblings = valid; Prime Minister solemnizing = valid if authorized there.
      • FC 10: consul-general, consul or vice-consul; only between Filipino citizens abroad; consul issues the license and performs LCR duties; ambassador has no authority; consul cannot solemnize in the PH.
      • FC 21: foreigner ("either or both") submits certificate of legal capacity from "their respective diplomatic or consular officials" "before a marriage license can be obtained"; stateless/refugee: affidavit in lieu. Lack of certificate does not affect validity (irregularity only).
      • FC 26 par. 2 inserted by E.O. 227 (July 17, 1987); FC effective August 3, 1988. Text: "validly celebrated ... divorce is thereafter validly obtained abroad by the alien spouse capacitating him or her to remarry, the Filipino spouse shall have capacity to remarry under Philippine law" (no "likewise").
      • Pre-Code/early cases: Barretto-Gonzales (no ratification of Filipinos' Reno divorce); Tenchavez (Filipino divorce abroad void; damages); Van Dorn (alien bound by his divorce; estopped; Uribe: it was actually the Filipina who filed); Pilapil (divorced German no standing to file adultery; status at time of filing).
      • Orbecido (2005): reckon citizenship at the time the divorce is obtained; FC 26(2) covers originally Filipino-Filipino marriages if one is naturalized before divorcing; must prove divorce and naturalization. Uribe: cite the provision first, then the case; Sempio-Diy disagrees.
      • Manalo (2018, En Banc): FC 26(2) applies even if the Filipino obtained the divorce; "obtained" ≠ initiated by alien; equal protection; still must prove foreign law (remanded). Tolentino's contrary view is outdated.
      • Racho v. Tanaka, Morisono, Juego-Sakai (2018): divorce by agreement recognized; must prove decree and foreign law; dissolution must be absolute. Galapon (2020), Abel (2021): foreign spouse alone, jointly, or Filipino alone — all covered.
      • Garcia v. Recio (2001): divorce decree and alien's national law must be alleged and proved (Rule 132 Secs. 24-25); no judicial notice; burden on party pleading; decree may be limited (decree nisi); certificate of legal capacity = prima facie evidence of capacity. Uribe: "moot and academic" defense is weak.
      • Corpuz v. Sto. Tomas (2010): FC 26(2) benefits only the Filipino; alien may still seek recognition as foreign judgment (Rule 39 Sec. 48(b)); no annotation without court order; Rule 108 available.
      • Fujiki (2013): A.M. 02-11-10-SC inapplicable to recognition of foreign judgment; prior spouse is real party in interest; prove judgment as fact; no relitigation; Rule 108 annotation.
      • Foreign law unproven → processual presumption (same as ours) → no divorce → petition fails.
      • Divorce between two Filipinos: never recognized. Both aliens: recognized if valid under their national laws.

      Requisites of Marriage: Family Code Arts. 2–34

      Covers Arts. 2–25 and 27–34 of the Family Code: the essential requisites (Arts. 2, 5), the formal requisites (Arts. 3, 6–8), the effects of non-compliance (Art. 4), the solemnizing officers (Arts. 7, 10, 31, 32 and the LGC), the marriage license (Arts. 9–20), the certificate of legal capacity (Art. 21), the marriage certificate and registry (Arts. 22–25) and license-exempt marriages (Arts. 27–34). Art. 1, the presumption of marriage and Art. 26 appear only as cross-references for the quiz-bank points. Syllabus VII.C (1 Tolentino 222–269).

      Overview: kinds of requisites, kinds of non-compliance, effects

      Uribe's syllabus organizes this part in three steps: (1) kinds of requisites (FC 2, 3, 5; cf. NCC 53), (2) kinds of non-compliance and (3) effect of non-compliance (FC 4). Learn the map first, because nearly every quiz item comes down to which box a fact belongs in.

      RequisiteKindAbsenceDefect / irregularity
      Legal capacity: male and female; age 18+ (Art. 5)Essential (Art. 2(1))Void (Art. 4 par. 1; Art. 35(1) for age)Defect: party 18 to below 21 without parental consent, so voidable (Arts. 4 par. 2, 45(1))
      Consent freely given in the presence of the solemnizing officerEssential (Art. 2(2))Void: no consent at all (jest, simulation, play or movie, hypnosis), or mistake as to identity (Art. 35(5))Defect: vitiated consent (unsound mind, fraud, force, intimidation, undue influence; also Art. 45(5), (6) grounds), so voidable (Art. 45)
      Authority of the solemnizing officerFormal (Art. 3(1))Void, unless either or both parties believed in good faith that he had authority (Arts. 4, 35(2))Irregularity, e.g. a judge outside his territorial jurisdiction or the wrong venue: valid, with liability (Art. 4 par. 3)
      Valid marriage license, except in Chapter 2 casesFormal (Art. 3(2))Void (Art. 35(3)), except license-exempt marriages under Arts. 27–34Irregularity, e.g. wrong LCR, early issuance, no advice or counseling certificate: valid, with liability
      Ceremony: personal appearance, personal declaration, at least two witnesses of legal ageFormal (Art. 3(3); Art. 6)Void: no ceremony at all (e.g. merely signing forms)Irregularity, e.g. witnesses under age, unsigned certificate: valid, with liability
      Art. 53, NCC (repealed; for comparison). No marriage shall be solemnized unless all these requisites are complied with: (1) Legal capacity of the contracting parties; (2) Their consent, freely given; (3) Authority of the person performing the marriage; and (4) A marriage license, except in a marriage of exceptional character.

      What changed from the NCC. The Civil Code lumped four requisites together. The Family Code separates the essential requisites (Art. 2) from the formal ones (Art. 3), makes the ceremony an express formal requisite, writes the opposite-sex requirement into the text, and graduates the effect of non-compliance (Art. 4). Under NCC 80(2), a marriage by an unauthorized officer was void even if the parties were in good faith. The FC restored the good-faith rule of Act 3613 (Art. 35(2)).

      Tolentino: calling the Art. 3 requirements "formal" is only a convenient classification. They are essential to validity: without them, just as without capacity and consent, no valid marriage can exist, and their total absence makes the marriage void (Art. 4). A mere defect or irregularity in a formal requirement has no effect on the marriage if the essential requisites are present. The person responsible may be prosecuted or punished administratively.
      Uribe: asked whether a marriage is valid "if all the essential and formal requisites are present," the answer is not necessarily. The essential and formal requisites are only the minimum. A marriage with all of them may still be void under Art. 36 (psychological incapacity), Arts. 37–38 (incestuous and public-policy impediments), Art. 35(4) (bigamy), Arts. 40, 41, 44 or 53. He also faults answers that are not responsive: answer the exact question asked, and do not answer "will it be valid even if a requisite is lacking" when the question is the reverse.
      Uribe (a ground for nullity plus a ground for annulment): one marriage can have both a ground for nullity (e.g. no license) and a ground for annulment (e.g. no parental consent). Its status is then void ab initio. "Walang saysay ang voidable" if the marriage is void, just as a contract that is at once rescissible, unenforceable and void is treated as void.
      Pugeda v. Trias (4 SCRA 849, 1962)

      Listed at the head of syllabus VII.C. Doctrine (per Uribe's doctrines outline): a parish priest's failure to send a copy of the marriage certificate of an in articulo mortis marriage to the municipal secretary does not invalidate the marriage, because sending the certificate is not a requisite of validity and nothing showed that the requisites were absent. Tolentino also cites Pugeda for the rule that a marriage may be proved by competent evidence other than the certificate (see Proof of marriage below).

      Cross-reference: Art. 1 and the presumption of marriage (quiz-bank points)

      Art. 1, FC. Marriage is a special contract of permanent union between a man and a woman entered into in accordance with law for the establishment of conjugal and family life. It is the foundation of the family and an inviolable social institution whose nature, consequences, and incidents are governed by law and not subject to stipulation, except that marriage settlements may fix the property relations during the marriage within the limits provided by this Code.
      • A stipulation fixing the duration of the marriage (e.g. "valid for 5 years, renewable by mutual consent") is void. Only property relations may be stipulated, and only within the limits provided by this Code (Arts. 74–81), never "without any limitation".
      • Rule 131, Sec. 3(aa): a man and woman deporting themselves as husband and wife are disputably presumed to have entered into a lawful contract of marriage. The presumption is not conclusive.
      • NCC 220: "In case of doubt, all presumptions favor the solidarity of the family. Thus, every intendment of law or facts leans toward the validity of marriage, the indissolubility of the marriage bonds, the legitimacy of children…"
      Quiz trap: watch for "conclusively presumed" (false, it is disputable) and "without any limitation" (false, it is "within the limits provided by this Code").

      Art. 2: the essential requisites

      Art. 2, FC. No marriage shall be valid, unless these essential requisites are present:
      (1) Legal capacity of the contracting parties who must be a male and a female; and
      (2) Consent freely given in the presence of the solemnizing officer. (53a)

      Element 1: legal capacity, "who must be a male and a female"

      The syllabus breaks legal capacity into (1) gender (FC 2(1)), (2) age (FC 5, 35(1), RA 6809; NCC 54, 80(1)) and (3) parental consent (FC 14, 45; NCC 61, 85(1)). Tolentino adds that capacity requires the minimum age and also that no impediment exists between the parties, such as a relationship or a subsisting prior marriage. Uribe, however, separates capacity from impediment (see the next h3).

      Tolentino (difference in sex): an indispensable requisite "dictated by biological law," treated as a natural element even when the Civil Code did not state it, because procreation cannot be realized by two persons of the same sex. If, through deceit, a marriage is celebrated between persons of the same sex (e.g. a hermaphrodite succeeds in marrying a man), the marriage is void and inexistent, without prejudice to the deceived party's damages. Chapter 3: a marriage between persons of the same sex is one of the void marriages not enumerated in Arts. 35–38.
      Silverio v. Republic (G.R. No. 174689, Oct. 22, 2007)

      A male who underwent sex reassignment sought to change the name and sex entries in his birth certificate. Doctrine: no law allows the change of the entry of sex on the ground of sex reassignment. Sex is fixed at birth, and a person's "sex" for the purpose of marriage under Art. 2(1) remains the sex at birth. A post-surgery "female" therefore cannot marry a male; such a marriage lacks an essential requisite and is void (2014 Bar MCQ, bank R-5).

      Note: contrast Republic v. Cagandahan (2008), where a person with congenital adrenal hyperplasia (an intersex condition) was allowed to change the sex entry because the condition was natural, not surgically induced. Same-sex marriage is not recognized; Obergefell v. Hodges (2015) is US law, listed under Concept and Nature only for comparison. Fraud under Art. 46 does not fit a same-sex case: the answer is "void, absence of an essential requisite," not "voidable."

      Element 2: consent freely given in the presence of the solemnizing officer

      The syllabus lists, under consent: (1) mistake as to identity, FC 35(5); NCC 86(1); (2) unsound mind, FC 45(2); (3) fraud, FC 45(3), 46; NCC 1338–1344; (4) force, intimidation and undue influence, FC 45(4); NCC 1335–1337; (5) physical incapacity, FC 45(5); (6) affliction with STD, FC 45(6). Grounds (2) to (6) are treated in full in the voidable-marriages section. Here, the point is the classification: total absence of consent makes the marriage void; vitiated or defective consent makes it voidable.

      Tolentino (mutual consent): whether a man and a woman become husband and wife is for them to decide. Even a valid agreement to marry in the future cannot be specifically enforced, and either party may refuse consent up to the actual marriage. Consent must be (a) real, not vitiated by mistake, duress or fraud; (b) conscious or intelligent, not affected by insanity, intoxication, drugs or hypnotism; and (c) given personally by the parties, without any term or condition.
      • Marriage in jest. A pretended marriage, legal in form but entered into in jest with a clear understanding that the parties are not to be bound, and not followed by conduct showing an intent to enter the relation, is no marriage. Tolentino's illustration is McClurg v. Terry (N.J.): friends on an excursion "got married" by a justice of the peace on a dare and went home as if nothing had happened. Held, no marriage, since words without the corresponding intention do not make a marriage. A secret lack of serious intent by one party, unknown to the other, does not prevent the innocent party from asserting validity, and the jesting party cannot assert validity against the other's will. (Tolentino at one point says jest marriages are "subject to annulment at the suit of the parties"; in Chapter 3 he classes them as void for total want of consent. For Uribe's purposes, total absence of consent means void, per Art. 4 par. 1.)
      • Simulated marriages, such as one between actors in a play or film, are inexistent even if the person playing the officiant is really a priest (Tolentino, Chapter 3).
      • Mistake as to identity (Art. 35(5)): mistake as to the person himself, with another person substituted for the one desired, without the knowledge of the other party (e.g. X and Y are twins and Y substitutes for X; Jacob married Leah instead of Rachel). This is void. Mistake as to rank, fortune, character or health does not invalidate the marriage: "Nothing would be more dangerous than to allow those who have agreed to take each other for better or for worse to be permitted to say that one of the parties is worse than expected." Under NCC 86(1), misrepresentation as to identity was fraud making the marriage voidable. Under the FC it is a ground for nullity.
      • In the presence of the solemnizing officer. Consent outside the officer's presence is no consent for this purpose. That is why a mayor signing forms away from the parties produces a void marriage (2009 Bar, bank R-6).
      Sison v. Te Lay Li (CA, 48 O.G. No. 9)

      Listed in the syllabus as "Sison v. Te Jay Li"; same case. Doctrine: as a general rule the law will not look behind a clearly manifested appearance of consent to determine whether it was real. But mere words without the corresponding intention do not create the marriage relation, and even when the formalities indicating consent have been complied with, there is no valid marriage if the parties did not intend to marry. The policy of maintaining marriage ties does not apply where it is amply proved that the marriage was effected through duress and intimidation, against the will of a party. Then there are no ties to preserve and the marriage should be annulled.

      Republic v. Albios (G.R. No. 198780, Oct. 16, 2013)

      Albios, a Filipina, married Fringer, an American, for a fee so that she could acquire US citizenship, intending never to live together as spouses. The lower courts declared the marriage void as a sham. Doctrine (SC reversed): the marriage is valid. Consent under Art. 2(2) requires a conscious and intelligent act, and the parties here freely and knowingly consented to be married, because a real marriage was precisely what they needed to achieve their goal. Motives are immaterial: marriages for convenience, companionship, money, status, title or citizenship are valid if they comply with all the legal requisites. A "marriage for convenience" is not a jest marriage. The Court also refused to let Albios use the courts to escape a marriage she entered into for an illicit purpose.

      Quiz trap: "A marriage entered into solely to acquire foreign citizenship is void for lack of consent" is false (Albios). Do not confuse the parties' motive with the absence of consent.

      Art. 5: legal capacity by age; RA 6809 and RA 11596

      Art. 5, FC. Any male or female of the age of eighteen years or upwards not under any of the impediments mentioned in Articles 37 and 38, may contract marriage. (54a)
      Art. 35(1), FC. The following marriages shall be void from the beginning: (1) Those contracted by any party below eighteen years of age even with the consent of parents or guardians;
      Art. 54, NCC (repealed). Any male of the age of sixteen years or upwards, and any female of the age of fourteen years or upwards, not under any of the impediments mentioned in articles 80 to 84, may contract marriage.

      The age ladder (memorize)

      Age at solemnizationRequirementEffect if missing
      Below 18No capacityVoid, even with parental consent (Art. 35(1)); RA 11596 child marriage, void and criminal
      18 to below 21, not emancipated by a previous marriageParental consent (Art. 14) plus counseling (Art. 16)No consent: voidable (Art. 45(1)). No counseling certificate: license suspended 3 months; irregularity only
      21 to 25Parental advice (Art. 15) plus counseling (Art. 16)No or unfavorable advice: license not issued until 3 months after publication; validity unaffected
      Above 25Nothing additionaln/a
      • Reckoning point: the minimum age is reckoned on the date of the marriage, not the date of the license application (DOJ Opinion No. 146, s. 1991). A 17-year-old may apply if he turns 18 before the ceremony. The B29 reviewer notes that the LCR should not refuse to issue a license if the party will come of age within the 120-day validity period, but should note on the license that the marriage may not be celebrated until the party comes of age.
      • If a party lied about his age to get a license and married while still below 18, the marriage is void, because he lacked the age when he contracted it. A misrepresentation cannot supply capacity.
      • No maximum age and no required difference in ages. A big age gap is not an impediment, and marriages of persons of advanced age, entered for sentimental reasons, are respected (Tolentino).
      • RA 6809 (approved Dec. 13, 1989) lowered the age of majority to 18 but expressly provides that "contracting marriage shall require parental consent until the age of twenty-one."
      • RA 11596 (Dec. 10, 2021) prohibits child marriage (a party below 18). Such a marriage is void ab initio, and the action or defense for nullity does not prescribe (in line with FC 35 and 39). Arts. 50–54 govern support, property relations and custody after its termination. Those who facilitate, solemnize or arrange it, and the adult who cohabits with the child, are penalized. After a one-year transition period it also covers Muslim and indigenous cultural communities.
      Tolentino: under the old canonical and Civil Code systems the age of consent tracked puberty (14/12, later 16/14). The FC disregards puberty and adopts 18 for both sexes to prevent hasty and premature marriages, with consent (below 21), advice (below 25) and counseling as added safeguards. Below 18 a party "cannot give a binding valid consent." Between 18 and 21 consent is "insufficient," so the parents must give theirs, and for a perfect consent the parties should be 21. He also cites a sociological reason: a higher age is a legal check on population growth.
      Note (outdated Tolentino view): Tolentino submitted that a girl below 18 who was the victim of rape, seduction, abduction or acts of lasciviousness could validly marry the offender, as an exception tied to RPC 344 (marriage extinguishes criminal liability). This is no longer good law. Art. 35(1) voids the marriage even with parental consent, RA 11596 penalizes child marriage, and RPC 344 presupposes a valid marriage (bank R-10). Likewise, his discussion of a widow's 300-day waiting period (NCC 84) is history: the FC dropped it, and RA 10655 (2015) repealed RPC 351 on premature marriages.
      Quiz trap: "A and B were married on September 2, 1988, both 17": FC already in force (effective Aug. 3, 1988), so the answer is "void even if with parental consent" (bank R-11). Do not pick "voidable" or "valid if with parental consent." The date decides whether NCC 54 (16/14) or FC 5 (18) applies.

      Legal capacity vs. legal impediment (Uribe's recitation)

      Uribe (Aug. 30, 2018 recitation; repeated 2025): "One of the parties was 17 at the time of solemnization. Is this a legal impediment?" No, it goes to legal capacity, not impediment. Arts. 37 and 38 are the legal impediments (Art. 5 itself distinguishes "eighteen years or upwards" from "not under any of the impediments mentioned in Articles 37 and 38"). "Capacity is in the person (nasa tao); impediment is in relation to the other contracting party."

      Why the distinction matters (Uribe): legal impediment decides other questions, most notably legitimation. Under Art. 177 as amended by RA 9858, a child conceived and born outside wedlock of parents who, at the time of conception, were not disqualified by any impediment to marry each other, or were disqualified only because either or both were below 18, may be legitimated by their subsequent valid marriage. Minority is a matter of capacity, so it does not bar legitimation. An Art. 37–38 impediment does. Uribe also stressed that the law looks to the time of conception, not birth.

      Uribe (2025, first cousins): "A and B are first cousins; the marriage is void because they have no legal capacity." False as reasoned. The marriage is void, but because of a legal impediment (Art. 38(1), collateral blood relatives within the fourth civil degree), not lack of capacity. "If you have legal capacity, you can get married to anyone except your sibling, cousins and other legal impediments."

      A (17) and B (19) live together and have a child, C. When A turns 18 they marry. Is C legitimated?

      Answer: Yes. A's minority at conception is a lack of capacity, not an impediment, and RA 9858 expressly allows legitimation where the only disqualification was that either or both parents were below 18. Contrast: if B had been married to someone else at conception (a subsisting-marriage impediment), C could not be legitimated even if B later became free and married A.

      Art. 3: the formal requisites

      Art. 3, FC. The formal requisites of marriage are:
      (1) Authority of the solemnizing officer;
      (2) A valid marriage license except in the cases provided for in Chapter 2 of this Title; and
      (3) A marriage ceremony which takes place with the appearance of the contracting parties before the solemnizing officer and their personal declaration that they take each other as husband and wife in the presence of not less than two witnesses of legal age. (53a, 55a)
      Uribe: "There are only three formal requisites: authority of the solemnizing officer, marriage license, and marriage ceremony."
