Manresa would uphold one where the donor knew the other spouse could not expect to inherit (e.g., the stepson already has legitimate children).
      Tolentino (reason and status): Art. 87 covers donations inter vivos. It rests on the unity of the spouses and aims to prevent transfers driven by passion or avarice: the intimacy of marriage places "the weaker spouse under the will of the stronger, whatever the sex," who might extract property by abuse of affection or by threats. Such donations are a "patent nullity"; legally they do not exist (Uy Coque v. Navas, 45 Phil. 430). The nullity may be invoked at any time, by action or defense, by the donor, the donor's heirs, or anyone prejudiced (Manresa). On moderate gifts, the court weighs the family's social position, wealth, usages and circumstances. Scaevola would treat a gift above one-fifth of the giver's present property as immoderate (by analogy to Art. 84); Castan says the court's discretion controls. A husband may validly give his wife, as a manual gift, a car bought with community funds, and the car is then exempt from seizure for a later community debt (a Louisiana ruling Tolentino cites).
      Harding v. Commercial Union Assurance Co. (38 Phil. 464, 1918)

      (Digest from Tolentino.) With her husband's consent, the wife insured an automobile her husband had given her shortly before. The car was totally destroyed, and the insurer refused to pay, arguing that she had no insurable interest because the gift was void under the old Civil Code prohibition on donations between spouses (now Art. 87). Held: the insurer cannot raise the point. Citing Cook v. McMicking (27 Phil. 10), the Court said the prohibition may be invoked only by persons whose rights or interests are affected by the transfer; the insurer had no right or interest in the car when the transfer occurred. Even if it could invoke the article, it had the burden of showing that the gift was not a moderate one, and the Court could not say as a matter of law that a husband's gift of a car to his wife is not moderate.

      Matabuena v. Cervantes (38 SCRA 284, 1971)

      Felix Matabuena donated a parcel of land to Petronila Cervantes in 1956, while they were living together as husband and wife without the benefit of marriage. They married in 1962, and Felix died intestate soon after. His sister and only heir, Cornelia, sued to recover the land, invoking Art. 133 NCC, which voided donations between spouses during the marriage. The lower court upheld the donation because the parties were not yet married when it was made. Held: the donation is void. "While Art. 133 of the Civil Code considers as void a 'donation between the spouses during the marriage', policy considerations of the most exigent character as well as the dictates of morality require that the same prohibition should apply to a common-law relationship." If the law prohibits donations between spouses for fear of undue influence, "there is every reason to apply the same prohibitive policy to persons living together as husband and wife without benefit of nuptials," because such a connection "bespeaks greater influence of one party over the other." "So long as marriage remains the cornerstone of our family law, reason and morality alike demand that the disabilities attached to marriage should likewise attach to concubinage." Since the donation was void, the land passed by intestacy: Petronila, as surviving spouse, got one-half and Cornelia, as sister, got the other half.

      Uribe (situation 7, CivRev 2025): after the wedding, the husband gave his wife a Rolls-Royce worth ₱30 million (with the umbrella). He died, and his heirs question the donation. It is void under Art. 87 unless it is a moderate gift on the occasion of family rejoicing. Sir: "The operative word is moderate gifts. Baka for the Zobel-de Ayalas, moderate naman yan, or for Manny Pangilinan, what is ₱30M?" Moderation is measured against the spouses' means.
      Uribe (situation 8, from the 2025 bar): while his wife was abroad, the husband gave his paramour the rentals of a property he had inherited before the marriage, and the paramour lived with him in the conjugal home. Status? Void. One student cited Art. 739 NCC (donations between persons guilty of adultery or concubinage at the time of the donation). Another cited Art. 87 by analogy ("one cannot do indirectly what he cannot do directly"). Sir took Art. 87 as an argument by analogy. Then he raised the overlooked layer: classify the property. The rentals are fruits. In an ACP, the inherited-before-marriage property itself is community property (Art. 91), and so are its fruits. In a CPG, the fruits of exclusive property are conjugal (Art. 117(3)). Either way, the husband donated property that belonged to the community or partnership, without the wife's consent (Arts. 96, 98, 124, 125).
      Art. 739 NCC (also void): "(1) Those made between persons who were guilty of adultery or concubinage at the time of the donation; (2) Those made between persons found guilty of the same criminal offense, in consideration thereof; (3) Those made to a public officer or his wife, descendants and ascendants, by reason of his office." For (1), the guilt may be proved by preponderance of evidence in the same civil action. No criminal conviction is needed.

      UP BOC 2011 MCQ: Can common-law spouses donate properties of substantial value to one another? (A) No, they are only allowed to give moderate gifts to each other during family rejoicing. (B) No, they cannot give anything of value … (C) Yes, unlike legally married spouses … (D) Yes, as long as they leave sufficient property for themselves and their dependents.

      A (Art. 87, last sentence; Matabuena).

      UP BOC 2011 MCQ: May a spouse freely donate communal or conjugal property without the consent of the other? (A) Absolutely not, since the spouses co-own such property. (B) Yes, for properties the family may spare, regardless of value. (C) Yes, provided the donation is moderate and intended for charity or family rejoicing. (D) Yes, in a donation mortis causa that the donor may still revoke in his lifetime.

      C. This is a different rule: Art. 98 (ACP) and Art. 125 (CPG) bar a spouse from donating community or conjugal property without the other's consent, "except moderate donations for charity or on occasions of family rejoicing or family distress." Do not confuse it with Art. 87 (donations between the spouses).

      Art. 87Art. 98 (ACP) / Art. 125 (CPG)
      Who gives to whomOne spouse to the other (or common-law partner to partner)One spouse to a third person, out of community or conjugal property
      RuleVoidNot without the consent of the other spouse
      ExceptionModerate gifts on the occasion of any family rejoicingModerate donations for charity or on occasions of family rejoicing or family distress

      Checklist: Arts. 74–87 in one page

      1. Order: settlement (executed before the marriage) → Family Code → local custom.
      2. No settlement or void regime → ACP if married on or after August 3, 1988; CPG if married before.
      3. Settlement: writing + signed + executed before the celebration. Not a public instrument. Binds third persons only if registered in the LCR where the marriage is recorded and in the registries of property.
      4. Modifications: only before the celebration; after it, only through Arts. 66, 67, 128, 135, 136, all of which need the court.
      5. Minor (Art. 78): the persons who must consent to the marriage must be parties. RA 6809 took effect December 18, 1989. Civil interdiction or disability (Art. 79): the court-appointed guardian must be a party.
      6. Art. 80: Philippine law for Filipino spouses absent a contrary stipulation, regardless of place of celebration or residence; not if both are aliens; extrinsic validity of contracts over foreign property follows foreign formalities.
      7. Art. 81: no marriage → settlement stipulations in consideration of it, including donations between the prospective spouses made in it, are void, not revocable.
      8. DPN: before, in consideration, in favor of one or both future spouses. Any donor. Same form as ordinary donations (₱5,000 threshold for movables; public document for immovables).
      9. One-fifth of present property, only for regimes other than ACP, only between the future spouses in the settlement; only the excess is void. Future property → rules on wills.
      10. Encumbered property: the donee is not liable for the deficiency and is entitled to the excess.
      11. Art. 86: six grounds for the donor: not celebrated or declared void (except settlement donations); no parental consent; annulled and the donee in bad faith; legal separation and the donee guilty; resolutory condition fulfilled; ingratitude.
      12. Art. 87: donations between spouses during the marriage are void, except moderate gifts on family rejoicing. The rule also covers common-law partners (Matabuena).

      Absolute Community of Property

      Title IV, Chapter 3, Family Code, Arts. 88–104 (syllabus X.D). Covers commencement (Art. 88), waiver (Art. 89), suppletory co-ownership rules (Art. 90), what the community consists of and what it excludes (Arts. 91–92), the presumption (Art. 93), charges and obligations (Arts. 94–95), administration and disposition (Arts. 96–98), dissolution (Art. 99), separation in fact and abandonment (Arts. 100–101), liquidation (Arts. 102–103), and two or more marriages (Art. 104). Cases: Ko v. Aramburo, Abrenica v. Law Firm of Abrenica, Delizo v. Delizo.

      The two-step method Uribe wants on every property problem

      1. Find the regime. Is there a valid marriage settlement (in writing, signed, executed before the wedding, with the Art. 78–79 parties)? If yes, follow it. If not, when was the marriage celebrated? On or after August 3, 1988 → ACP (Art. 75). Before → CPG (NCC 119). Remarried without liquidating a prior regime → complete separation (Arts. 103, 130). Void marriage → Art. 147 or 148 co-ownership, not ACP or CPG.
      2. Classify the property within that regime. Owned at the celebration or acquired after? Gratuitous or onerous? Fruits? Exclusive use? Jewelry? Does the spouse have legitimate descendants by a former marriage?
      Uribe (essay B, CivRev midterms): "This needs a three-/four-level discussion." To know the nature of the rentals, you must know the nature of the property itself, and to know that, you must know the regime. In the Bong–Liza–Rudy problem, most of the class wrongly applied the Civil Code because Liza's first marriage was in 1987. The property question was about her second marriage to Rudy, which took place after Bong died in 1989, so the Family Code applies. The oral CPG agreement is void, so the regime is ACP. The land Liza inherited before marrying Rudy would ordinarily become community property, but Liza has a legitimate daughter (Imee) by her former marriage, so Art. 92(3) excludes the land and its fruits. The rentals are therefore her separate property and form part of her estate.
      Uribe (situation 9, CivRev 2025): "I did not ask you to whom the property should belong. I asked you the nature of the property." Answer the question asked: exclusive, community, or conjugal. If the question asks who is entitled, then the answer is the community or partnership, not "the spouses".

      Arts. 88–90: commencement, waiver and suppletory rules

      Tolentino (what the ACP is): In the ACP the husband and wife are joint owners of all the property of the marriage. What each brings in and what they acquire form one common mass, which is divided on dissolution equally (or in the agreed proportion) "irrespective of the value each one may have originally owned." In the CPG only the profits are divided; in the ACP the entire mass is divided, so each spouse loses ownership of what he or she brought in. The Civil Code Commission noted that Filipino couples in practice treat everything as co-owned, but kept the CPG as the legal regime because making the ACP the default "would be looked upon as revolutionary." Where the spouses adopt the ACP, their stipulations prevail over the Code, which is only suppletory.
      Tolentino (his criticism of the ACP as the default): He calls the switch "a radical change" from a regime that had prevailed for almost a century. The argument that couples can always opt out ignores reality: "I am sure not even one out of a hundred couples has marriage settlements." The ACP and complete separation are both extremes; the Civil Code chose the CPG as the middle ground, and "it is neither just nor logical to adopt one of the extremes in the absence of express selection." The ACP can transfer wealth from the richer spouse to the poorer ("an aid to fortune hunters"), restricts the circulation of property, takes from an owner (perhaps unknowingly) what was always his or hers, and, being unchangeable, may become a source of friction. He doubts that "what is yours is mine" is really Filipino custom beyond small personal items. Critics also call it an indirect way around the limits on donations propter nuptias; its defenders say it best fits the nature of marriage (Bevilaqua).
      Art. 88, FC. The absolute community of property between spouses shall commence at the precise moment that the marriage is celebrated. Any stipulation, express or implied, for the commencement of the community regime at any other time shall be void. (145a)
      • "Precise moment": property owned by a spouse at 10:00 a.m. becomes community property at 5:00 p.m., when the marriage is celebrated.
      • Any stipulation that the regime starts earlier (e.g., on the date of the settlement) or later (e.g., one year after the wedding) is void. The rest of the settlement survives.
      • Tolentino: the Civil Code said the partnership begins on "the date" of the celebration; the Family Code clarified it to the "precise moment" (following Art. 1261 of the Argentine Civil Code). The ACP as the legal regime applies only to marriages after the Family Code took effect (or to earlier marriages whose settlement adopted it). A pre-FC marriage stays under the CPG it started with: applying the ACP retroactively would impair vested rights (Art. 256), and Art. 105 confirms this. Most writers reject a suspensive condition on the regime, since the property relations cannot be left uncertain even briefly.

      CivRev midterms MCQ #25 (Uribe): In the will of X, a parcel of land was validly bequeathed to A, who was married to B at 5 PM on June 1, 2019. A and B orally agreed on a conjugal partnership of gains. At 10 AM on June 1, 2019, X died. The land will form part of the: (a) conjugal partnership property; (b) community property; (c) separate property of A; (d) estate of X; (e) property of the State.

      B (community property). Successional rights are transmitted at death (Art. 777, NCC), so A owned the land at 10 AM. The oral settlement is void (Art. 77), so the regime is ACP (Art. 75). The ACP commenced at 5 PM (Art. 88) and consists of all property owned by the spouses at the time of the celebration (Art. 91). The land is not excluded under Art. 92(1), because it was acquired before the marriage, not during it. Sir: "Even before the solemnization, A being the owner, under the FC in an ACP regime, properties owned before become community property."

      Compare situation 9 (CivRev 2025): same facts, but the spouses executed a valid settlement adopting CPG. Nature of the land?

      Exclusive property of A, because it was brought to the marriage as his own (Art. 109(1)). The difference is entirely in the regime. And the 2018 situationer: a CPG settlement stipulated that the regime would commence on the date of the settlement, 15 days before the wedding. That stipulation is void (Arts. 88, 107). The CPG begins only at the precise moment of the celebration, so the land inherited at 9 AM that day remains A's exclusive property "entirely".

      Art. 89, FC. No waiver of rights, shares and effects of the absolute community of property during the marriage can be made except in case of judicial separation of property.
      When the waiver takes place upon a judicial separation of property, or after the marriage has been dissolved or annulled, the same shall appear in a public instrument and shall be recorded as provided in Article 77. The creditors of the spouse who made such waiver may petition the court to rescind the waiver to the extent of the amount sufficient to cover the amount of their credits. (146a)
      • During the marriage: no waiver, except in a judicial separation of property.
      • Upon judicial separation, or after dissolution or annulment: the waiver must be in a public instrument and recorded as in Art. 77 (LCR and registries of property).
      • The waiving spouse's creditors may ask the court to rescind the waiver to the extent of their credits (an accion pauliana).
      • A valid waiver affects the division of net assets (Art. 102(4): "unless there has been a voluntary waiver of such share provided in this Code").
      • Tolentino (waiver of the community vs. waiver of its benefits): a waiver of the community itself is valid only in a marriage settlement before the wedding; a waiver of its benefits is valid only after dissolution (or upon judicial separation). Any contract renouncing the community during the marriage is void and inexistent, whatever its consideration (Quintana v. Lerma, 24 Phil. 285). Art. 221(2) NCC said so expressly; the Family Code omits it, but the rule stands because renunciation can be made only in a pre-nuptial settlement. After dissolution, a waiver in favor of a particular person is really an assignment of rights; a waiver in general terms makes the share accrue to the other spouse or his or her heirs. The renouncing spouse keeps his or her separate property and remains bound by his or her personal obligations.
      Quiz trap: contrast with the marriage settlement itself. A settlement needs only a writing (Art. 77). A waiver of the ACP share needs a public instrument (Art. 89). Also, "no waiver … during the marriage can be made" is true only with the exception: "except in case of judicial separation of property."
      Art. 90, FC. The provisions on co-ownership shall apply to the absolute community of property between the spouses in all matters not provided for in this Chapter. (n)
      Quiz trap (pairs with Art. 108): ACP → suppletory rules on co-ownership (Art. 90). CPG → suppletory rules on the contract of partnership (Art. 108). His TF item "The conjugal partnership shall be governed by the rules of co-ownership in all that is not in conflict …" is False.

      Art. 91: what the community consists of

      Art. 91, FC. Unless otherwise provided in this Chapter or in the marriage settlements, the community property shall consist of all the property owned by the spouses at the time of the celebration of the marriage or acquired thereafter. (197a)

      The general rule covers everything: property owned at the moment of the wedding, however acquired (onerous or gratuitous, inherited or bought), plus everything acquired afterward, including winnings from gambling (Art. 95), hidden treasure, and salaries. Exceptions: Art. 92 ("otherwise provided in this Chapter") and the marriage settlement.

      Tolentino (automatic conversion; third persons): Art. 91 comes from Art. 1108 of the Portuguese Code and Art. 215 of the Swiss Code. Each spouse's patrimony at the wedding becomes common property automatically, without any juridical act transferring ownership of the individual items, and the same is true of later acquisitions. Title should then be put in both names, which can be done by registering the settlement. Until that is done, third persons acting in good faith may rely on a title in the name of one spouse and are protected.
      Quiz trap (his most repeated ACP item; Quiz 4 #8; Quiz #3 pair 5; Quiz comp TF9; Quiz 3 key #13): "The community property shall consist of all the property owned by the spouses at the time of the celebration of the marriage or acquired thereafter." False: it omits "Unless otherwise provided in this Chapter or in the marriage settlements". Some property owned at the celebration (Art. 92(3)) and some acquired after (Art. 92(1)–(2)) are excluded.
      Uribe (Quiz 4 #8 discussion): a student cited only the exclusions for property acquired during the marriage. Sir: "He did not say what about the properties acquired at the time of the celebration of the marriage." The exclusion for those is Art. 92(3): property of a spouse with legitimate descendants by a former marriage. He also corrected another student: "Just because it is by gratuitous title does not mean na CP na siya," and vice versa. Property acquired by gratuitous title is excluded unless the donor, testator or grantor provides that it shall form part of the community.

      CivRev midterms essay C(1) (Uribe): A inherited a parcel of land from his grandfather in 1989. Thereafter, A married B without a marriage settlement. In 1995, A died intestate, survived by B; C, their son; D and E, his children with his girlfriend Y before his marriage to B; and F and G, his parents. Is the land separate property of A?

      No, it is community property. The marriage was after 1989 and there is no settlement, so the regime is ACP (Art. 75). The land was owned at the time of the celebration, so it is community property (Art. 91). The manner of acquisition (inheritance) does not matter, because Art. 92(1) excludes only property acquired during the marriage by gratuitous title. Art. 92(3) does not apply, because D and E are illegitimate children, not legitimate descendants by a former marriage. Sir: "90% got it wrong." Part (2): the land is first divided in two. B gets one-half as her share of the community (Art. 102(4)). Only the other half is A's estate, which is divided among C (legitimate child: ½ of the estate), B (surviving spouse: ¼), and D and E (illegitimate children: the remaining ¼, or ⅛ each, because the legitime of the illegitimate children cannot exceed the free portion). B practically holds ⅝ of the land.

      Art. 92: what is excluded from the community

      Art. 92, FC. The following shall be excluded from the community property:
      (1) Property acquired during the marriage by gratuitous title by either spouse, and the fruits as well as the income thereof, if any, unless it is expressly provided by the donor, testator or grantor that they shall form part of the community property;
      (2) Property for personal and exclusive use of either spouse. However, jewelry shall form part of the community property;
      (3) Property acquired before the marriage by either spouse who has legitimate descendants by a former marriage, and the fruits as well as the income, if any, of such property. (201a)
      ExclusionElementsWhat about the fruits?Exception
      (1) Gratuitous acquisitionsduring the marriage; by gratuitous title (donation, inheritance, legacy, devise); by either spouseAlso excludedThe donor, testator or grantor expressly provides that they shall form part of the community
      (2) Personal and exclusive useclothes, personal effects, tools of one spouse—Jewelry is always community property, even if for personal and exclusive use
      (3) Prior-family propertyacquired before the marriage; the spouse has legitimate descendants; by a former marriageAlso excluded—
      Marriage settlementproperty the settlement excludes (Art. 91: "unless otherwise provided … in the marriage settlements")per the settlement—
      Tolentino ("reserved property"): The excluded properties are called reserved property. The spouses may agree to bring any of them into the community, or to reserve other property not listed; absent agreement, all three classes are reserved.

      Art. 92(1): gratuitous title during the marriage

      • The exclusion is limited to acquisitions during the marriage. Property inherited or donated before the wedding is community property under Art. 91 (unless Art. 92(3) applies).
      • The donor or testator can override the exclusion by expressly providing that the property shall form part of the community. A statement such as "inherited by A" means A alone inherited.
      • When both spouses inherit (e.g., from their own child), each spouse's share is that spouse's separate property. Sir (2018): "Is it possible that this is not conjugal or community property pero silang dalawa ang magmamana? Yes, if the one who died is their child."
      • Tolentino: property received by donation or inheritance is presumed reserved; to become community property, the deed or will must say so expressly. Property inherited by intestate succession is always separate, because it passes by operation of law and there is no expression of the decedent's will. If the reserved property is later sold or exchanged, the Family Code is silent, but Tolentino applies the Portuguese rule that the substitute keeps the separate character (real subrogation): "The mere alienation of separate property of a spouse does not make it community property."

      CivRev midterms pair #1, Statement 2 (Uribe): "In the absence of a marriage settlement, a parcel of land inherited by A during his marriage to B in 1989 will be his separate property."

      True per Sir (his answer to #1 was A, both true). The class answered False, arguing that the testator may have provided that the land would be community property. Sir: "The statement is true. Kaya lang ang argument is false because the testator may have provided in the will that it should be a community property. Ang mali dun is inherited by A … Siya lang nagmana. Otherwise, dapat nakalagay inherited by the spouses or pertains to the absolute community." The facts say A inherited it during a 1989 marriage (ACP), so Art. 92(1) applies.

      CivRev midterms pair #2, Statement 2 (Uribe): "The rentals from a building inherited by B during her marriage to A in 1989 will be a community property in the absence of a marriage settlement."

      False (Sir: both false, B). Under ACP, Art. 92(1) excludes property inherited during the marriage and its fruits and income. Rentals are civil fruits, so they follow the building and are B's separate property. (In a CPG, the rentals would be conjugal under Art. 117(3).)

      Art. 92(2): personal and exclusive use, but jewelry is community

      Tolentino (what counts as personal use; which jewelry): Personal-use property includes clothing, toilet articles, books, eyeglasses, hearing aids and the like, and (following Russian decisions he finds applicable) the tools of a spouse's trade or profession, unless they are luxury items or of special value. The jewelry that falls into the community is expensive or luxurious jewelry reserved for special occasions. Minor or inexpensive jewelry worn daily (costume jewelry, rings or necklaces of small value) should be treated as separate property, judged by the spouse's financial and social position. For Uribe's quizzes, the codal is absolute: "jewelry shall form part of the community property."
      Quiz trap (CivRev 2025 Quiz 4 #12; midterms #34 and #48; Quiz comp #18; Quiz #3 MCQ 10): "Jewelry for personal and exclusive use" is not excluded, so an option that names it is wrong. The law's own exception is that jewelry "shall form part of the community property" even when it is for one spouse's personal and exclusive use.

      Art. 92(3): property of a spouse with legitimate descendants by a former marriage

      • Three elements: (a) property acquired before the marriage; (b) the spouse has legitimate descendants; (c) by a former marriage. The fruits and income of that property are also excluded.
      • Rationale: to protect the legitimes and inheritance of the children of the first marriage, so that their parent's property does not pass into a new community with a stranger. Sir (situation 5): "If the spouse has legitimate descendants by a prior marriage … they are separate properties of the spouse, kasi para sa legitimate descendants niya yon."
      • Illegitimate children, or legitimate descendants not "by a former marriage", do not trigger the exclusion.
      • Tolentino: under the Civil Code, only the presumptive legitimes of the descendants were reserved; the Family Code reserves all the property the spouse owned before the marriage, so only his or her acquisitions during the marriage enter the community. The property is not reserved for the descendants. It simply stays the separate property of the remarried spouse, who may alienate it freely, and the proceeds remain separate.
      Spouses Abrenica v. Law Firm of Abrenica, Tungol and Tibayan (G.R. No. 180572, June 18, 2012)

      In execution proceedings against Atty. Abrenica, his second wife, Joena, claimed that two motor vehicles (bought in 1992 and 1997) and a house and lot were community property of their marriage and could not be levied for his obligation. Held: Art. 92(3) excludes from the community property acquired before the marriage by a spouse who has legitimate descendants by a former marriage, together with its fruits and income. "Neither these two vehicles nor the house and lot belong to the second marriage." The properties were therefore not community property of Joena's marriage and could answer for Atty. Abrenica's liability.

      CivRev midterms MCQ #34 (Uribe): This shall be excluded from the community property: (a) property acquired during the marriage by onerous title by either spouse; (b) property acquired before the marriage by either spouse who has a child by a prior marriage; (c) property acquired before the marriage by gratuitous title by either spouse; (d) jewelry for personal and exclusive use; (e) none of the above.

      B per Sir. The class split between B and E because the codal says "legitimate descendants". Sir: "pero kung may kasal edi legit. Therefore the child is legit. So covered siya ng exclusion." A child by a prior marriage is presumptively legitimate (Art. 164). Contrast the older quiz variant: "… who has a child before the marriage." A child born before the marriage may be illegitimate, so that option is not absolutely an exclusion (answer E).

      Uribe (2018 situationer): A inherited land from his grandfather before marrying B in 1988, and A had a child with X born after the marriage to B. Status of the land? If the marriage was on or after August 3, 1988, it is community property (Art. 91). The child is illegitimate and not "by a former marriage", so Art. 92(3) does not apply. "The fact that A inherited such land prior to the marriage does not affect [the answer], because the mode of acquisition does not affect its inclusion in the community property."

      Art. 93: the presumption of community

      Art. 93, FC. Property acquired during the marriage is presumed to belong to the community, unless it is proved that it is one of those excluded therefrom. (160)
      • Trigger: acquisition during the marriage. The presumption does not depend on the title (onerous or gratuitous) or on whose name the property is registered in. The burden is on the party claiming exclusive ownership.
      • Condition sine qua non: the party invoking the presumption must first prove that the property was acquired during the marriage (Dela Peña v. Avila; Andrade v. Tan; Go v. Yamane; these CPG cases on NCC 160 and FC 116 apply equally to Art. 93).
      • The presumption is disputable. It yields to proof that the property falls under Art. 92 or the settlement.
      Quiz trap (CivRev 2025 Quiz 4 #20; Quiz #3 MCQ 6): "A parcel of land is presumed to belong to the community property if: (a) acquired by gratuitous title; (b) acquired by onerous title; (c) acquired before the marriage; (d) registered during the marriage; (e) none of the above." E, because the correct trigger, "acquired during the marriage", is not among the options. Registration is not acquisition: "malay mo it was registered during the marriage" but acquired before. (In the older version, where "acquired during the marriage" was an option, that option is the answer.)
      Ko v. Aramburo (G.R. No. 190995, August 9, 2017)

      Listed in the syllabus under "Presumption of ACP, FC 93 cf. NCC 160". The dispute was between the heirs of two siblings over seven parcels in Tabaco City, Albay, all titled in the name of Corazon. The plaintiffs alleged that Virginia and her husband Simeon, together with Corazon and her husband Felix, acquired the properties from the Spouses Casaul through a Deed of Cession dated April 10, 1970. Corazon countered that the properties were her parents', that Simeon sold his entire one-half share to her on December 14, 1974, and that the action had prescribed. The syllabus places the case under the presumption that property acquired during the marriage belongs to the community or partnership, and that the presumption must be overcome by proof. Verify the holding against the full text before relying on details: the case was not digested in your materials, and the case sites could not be reached to confirm the Court's reasoning.

      Under the Civil Code (NCC 160): "All property of the marriage is presumed to belong to the conjugal partnership, unless it be proved that it pertains exclusively to the husband or to the wife." The cases in the CPG section apply here too: the presumption needs proof of acquisition during the marriage (Torela, Dela Peña, Andrade); it does not apply when there is no showing of when the property was acquired (Maramba, Magallon, Cuenca); and "married to" in a title is merely descriptive (Magallon, Go-Bangayan).

      Arts. 94–95: charges upon and obligations of the community

      Art. 94, FC. The absolute community of property shall be liable for:
      (1) The support of the spouses, their common children, and legitimate children of either spouse; however, the support of illegitimate children shall be governed by the provisions of this Code on Support;
      (2) All debts and obligations contracted during the marriage by the designated administrator-spouse for the benefit of the community, or by both spouses, or by one spouse with the consent of the other;
      (3) Debts and obligations contracted by either spouse without the consent of the other to the extent that the family may have been benefited;
      (4) All taxes, liens, charges and expenses, including major or minor repairs, upon the community property;
      (5) All taxes and expenses for mere preservation made during marriage upon the separate property of either spouse used by the family;
      (6) Expenses to enable either spouse to commence or complete a professional or vocational course, or other activity for self-improvement;
      (7) Ante-nuptial debts of either spouse insofar as they have redounded to the benefit of the family;
      (8) The value of what is donated or promised by both spouses in favor of their common legitimate children for the exclusive purpose of commencing or completing a professional or vocational course or other activity for self-improvement;
      (9) Ante-nuptial debts of either spouse other than those falling under paragraph (7) of this Article, the support of illegitimate children of either spouse, and liabilities incurred by either spouse by reason of a crime or a quasi-delict, in case of absence or insufficiency of the exclusive property of the debtor-spouse, the payment of which shall be considered as advances to be deducted from the share of the debtor-spouse upon liquidation of the community; and
      (10) Expenses of litigation between the spouses unless the suit is found to be groundless.
      If the community property is insufficient to cover the foregoing liabilities, except those falling under paragraph (9), the spouses shall be solidarily liable for the unpaid balance with their separate properties. (161a, 162a, 163a, 202a-205a)

      Breakdown: four groups

      • Family needs: (1) support; (6) self-improvement of a spouse; (8) donations by both spouses to common legitimate children for education.
      • Debts: (2) debts with consent or by the administrator for the benefit of the community (no benefit test if both consented); (3) debts without consent, to the extent the family benefited; (7) ante-nuptial debts that redounded to the family.
      • Property: (4) taxes, liens, charges and repairs (major or minor) upon community property; (5) taxes and expenses for mere preservation of separate property used by the family.
      • Advances (par. 9): personal ante-nuptial debts, support of a spouse's illegitimate children, and crime or quasi-delict liabilities. These are paid by the community only if the debtor-spouse's exclusive property is absent or insufficient, and only as advances deducted from that spouse's share on liquidation.
      • Last paragraph: if the community is insufficient, the spouses are solidarily liable with their separate properties, except for par. (9) items.
      Quiz trap (CivRev midterms pair #3, Statement 2): "The absolute community of property shall be liable for all expenses for mere preservation made during marriage upon the separate property of either spouse." False: it omits "used by the family" (Art. 94(5)). Sir corrected a student who said the requirement is that the expense "redounds to the benefit of the family": "Her term was to benefit the fam. That is not required. Who cares kung may benefit o wala. Ang term is 'used'. Basta ginagamit." The same student confused (5) with (7): "these are for preservation, not ante-nuptial debts."
      Uribe (situation 10, CivRev 2025; 2018 situationer): before the marriage, A inherited a building. After the wedding, ₱5M was spent to retrofit it (or ₱2M for preservation). Chargeable to whom? It depends on the regime. ACP: the building is community property unless Art. 92(3) applies. If it is A's separate property, the expense is chargeable to the community only if the building is used by the family (Art. 94(5)); otherwise it is A's. CPG: the building is A's exclusive property (brought to the marriage), and preservation expenses are chargeable to the partnership whether or not used by the family (Art. 121(5) has no such qualifier). Why the difference? In the CPG, the fruits of the exclusive property go to the partnership (Art. 117(3)), so the partnership bears the preservation costs. In the ACP, the fruits of separate property are excluded (Art. 92(1), (3)), so the community pays only when the family uses the property.
      Uribe (2018 situationer, Art. 94(9)): "Is there any other expense chargeable to ACP but not to CPG?" The support of a spouse's illegitimate children. In an ACP, whatever a spouse owns usually becomes community property, so the spouse with illegitimate children often has no separate property from which to support them. Art. 94(9) lets the community advance the support, deducted from that spouse's share upon liquidation. (In a CPG, the spouse keeps exclusive property for this purpose, and Art. 122 lets the partnership answer only after the Art. 121 responsibilities are covered.)

      UP BOC 2007 TF: "An individual, while single, purchases a house and lot in 1990, and borrows money in 1992 to repair it. In 1995, such individual gets married while the debt is still being paid. After the marriage, the debt is still the responsibility of such individual."

      False. The ACP is liable for ante-nuptial debts "insofar as they have redounded to the benefit of the family" (Art. 94(7)). Alternatively, the house and lot itself became community property in 1995 (Art. 91), and the debt for its repair is a charge on community property (Art. 94(4)).

      Art. 95, FC. Whatever may be lost during the marriage in any game of chance, betting, sweepstakes, or any other kind of gambling, whether permitted or prohibited by law, shall be borne by the loser and shall not be charged to the community but any winnings therefrom shall form part of the community property. (164a)
      Quiz trap: losses → borne by the loser, whether the gambling is legal or illegal; winnings → community. In the CPG, Art. 117(7) puts winnings in the partnership ("acquired by chance"), and Art. 123 has the same rule on losses.
      Tolentino (charges, Arts. 94–95): (1) The ACP supports the spouses, their common children and the legitimate children of either; a spouse's illegitimate children are supported by that spouse, with the community advancing the cost if his or her exclusive property is insufficient, chargeable to his or her share on liquidation. (2) Taxes on community property and on separate property used by the community, all repairs on community property, and minor repairs on separate property used by the community are community charges. Major repairs on separate property (used by the family or not), and taxes on separate property not used by the family, are borne by the owner. (3) Litigation between the spouses: both sides' expenses come from the community, except that a plaintiff whose suit is groundless bears his or her own. Tolentino points out the inequality: a defendant who gave cause for a successful suit still charges the community. Equal treatment would make that defendant pay too, "but this is not the law, which creates only one exception." (4) Subsidiary liability: except for the par. (9) advances, if the community is insufficient, the separate properties are solidarily liable; the creditor may sue either spouse for the whole, and the spouse who pays is reimbursed the other's share on liquidation (see Santos v. IAC, 145 SCRA 238). (5) Crime and quasi-delict liabilities: Art. 205 NCC charged them to the community without reimbursement, which Tolentino criticized as inconsistent with the benefit rule and with the Portuguese source. "The Family Code has changed the rule in line with the suggestion in our observation": they are now only advances under par. (9). (6) Gambling: the law punishes the gambler-spouse. If he loses, he bears the loss alone; if he wins, the winnings go to the community. "In relation to the community, he never wins."

      Arts. 96–98: administration, disposition, wills and donations

      Art. 96, FC. The administration and enjoyment of the community property shall belong to both spouses jointly. In case of disagreement, the husband's decision shall prevail, subject to recourse to the court by the wife for proper remedy, which must be availed of within five years from the date of the contract implementing such decision.
      In the event that one spouse is incapacitated or otherwise unable to participate in the administration of the common properties, the other spouse may assume sole powers of administration. These powers do not include disposition or encumbrance without authority of the court or the written consent of the other spouse. In the absence of such authority or consent, the disposition or encumbrance shall be void. However, the transaction shall be construed as a continuing offer on the part of the consenting spouse and the third person, and may be perfected as a binding contract upon the acceptance by the other spouse or authorization by the court before the offer is withdrawn by either or both offerors. (206a)

      Breakdown of Art. 96

      1. Joint administration and enjoyment.
      2. Disagreement: the husband's decision prevails, but the wife may go to court within five years from the date of the contract implementing the decision.
      3. Sole administration by one spouse if the other is incapacitated or otherwise unable to participate. Sole administration does not include disposition or encumbrance.
      4. Disposition or encumbrance needs the court's authority or the other spouse's written consent. Without either, it is void, but it is construed as a continuing offer by the consenting spouse and the third person, perfected upon the other spouse's acceptance or the court's authorization before the offer is withdrawn.
      The "husband's decision prevails" clause and equal protection. Art. 96 still reads this way and is quoted verbatim on quizzes. Commentators note that it is in tension with the equality clause (Art. II, Sec. 14; Art. XIII, Sec. 14, 1987 Constitution) and with RA 9710 (Magna Carta of Women), which mandates review of discriminatory provisions. For quiz items, answer according to the text of Art. 96.

      2017 / 2015 Bar (Danny–Elsa / Marco–Gina): The spouses married in 2002 (1989), without a settlement. Years later the wife left the conjugal home and the children to live with another man. The husband, needing money for the children's tuition, sold a parcel of land registered in his name, which he had bought before the marriage, without her consent. Valid, void or voidable?

      Void. The regime is ACP (Art. 75), so the land became community property when the marriage was celebrated even though it is registered in his name alone (Art. 91), and no Art. 92 exclusion applies. Disposition of community property needs the other spouse's written consent or court authority (Art. 96). Her abandonment does not dispense with it. Under Art. 100(2), in a separation in fact, the required consent is replaced by judicial authorization in a summary proceeding, which he did not obtain. Good motive (tuition) does not cure the defect.

      2025 Bar: A and B married in 1991 without a prenuptial agreement. In 1997, A forged B's signature on a promissory note and on a real estate mortgage over three parcels acquired during the marriage. PCB foreclosed and bought the lands. B sued to nullify the mortgage and the certificate of sale. Is B correct?

      Yes. The parcels are presumed community property (Arts. 75, 93). An encumbrance without the other spouse's consent is void under Art. 96. It remains only a continuing offer that B never accepted. The foreclosure and sale built on the void mortgage are likewise void (UPLC suggested answer, citing PNB v. Reyes, Jr., G.R. No. 212483, October 5, 2016).

      UP BOC 2011 MCQ: The husband assumed sole administration of the family's mango plantation since his wife worked abroad. Without her knowledge, he entered into an antichretic transaction giving a company possession of the plantation with power to harvest and sell the fruits to pay his loan. Standing of the contract?

      D: a continuing offer, perfected only upon the wife's acceptance or the court's authorization (Art. 96 2nd par.; Art. 124 2nd par. has the same text). Antichresis is an encumbrance, which a sole administrator cannot make alone.

      Art. 97, FC. Either spouse may dispose by will of his or her interest in the community property. (n)
      Art. 98, FC. Neither spouse may donate any community property without the consent of the other. However, either spouse may, without the consent of the other, make moderate donations from the community property for charity or on occasions of family rejoicing or family distress. (n)
      • Art. 97: a will takes effect only at death, which dissolves the community, so a spouse may bequeath his or her interest (his or her eventual share in the net assets). The spouse cannot will specific community property as if it were wholly his or her own.
      • Art. 98: donation of community property requires the other spouse's consent, except moderate donations for charity or on occasions of family rejoicing or family distress. Compare Art. 87 (between spouses: family rejoicing only).
      • Tolentino (joint ownership): Art. 206 NCC said ownership, administration, possession and enjoyment belong to both spouses jointly; Art. 96 mentions only administration and enjoyment, but joint ownership and possession follow from the nature of the ACP. Hence neither spouse may alienate or encumber community property without the other's written consent or court authority. The transaction is void, but until either or both parties withdraw it, the other spouse's approval or the court's authorization can perfect it. Either spouse may question an alienation by the other; third persons are protected as in other cases, but less so, because the husband has no right to freely dispose of common property.
      • Tolentino (no inter vivos sale of one's share): the spouses' rights in the community and in each item are "united permanently." Neither spouse may dispose inter vivos of his or her share, and such a disposition is void even with the other spouse's consent. If the husband transfers to X a one-half interest in community land with the wife's consent, the remaining half is still community property, and the price received is also community property. A disposition by will is valid under Art. 97: the heir receives what is allotted to the testator-spouse in the liquidation.
      • Tolentino (what "joint" administration means): each spouse may validly perform acts of administration alone; the court intervenes only if the other spouse objects before the act is done, by analogy to partnerships with two or more managers (Art. 1801 NCC). Art. 96's sole-administration rule supports this. He expects few conflicts, since mutual love encourages give-and-take, and a deadlock is unlikely because the husband's decision prevails, subject to the wife's recourse to court. A "moderate" donation under Art. 98 depends on the couple's financial and social circumstances.

      Arts. 100–101: separation in fact and abandonment

      Art. 100, FC. The separation in fact between husband and wife shall not affect the regime of absolute community except that:
      (1) The spouse who leaves the conjugal home or refuses to live therein, without just cause, shall not have the right to be supported;
      (2) When the consent of one spouse to any transaction of the other is required by law, judicial authorization shall be obtained in a summary proceeding;
      (3) In the absence of sufficient community property, the separate property of both spouses shall be solidarily liable for the support of the family. The spouse present shall, upon proper petition in a summary proceeding, be given judicial authority to administer or encumber any specific separate property of the other spouse and use the fruits or proceeds thereof to satisfy the latter's share. (178a)
      Art. 101, FC. If a spouse without just cause abandons the other or fails to comply with his or her obligations to the family, the aggrieved spouse may petition the court for receivership, for judicial separation of property or for authority to be the sole administrator of the absolute community, subject to such precautionary conditions as the court may impose.
      The obligations to the family mentioned in the preceding paragraph refer to marital, parental or property relations.
      A spouse is deemed to have abandoned the other when her or she has left the conjugal dwelling without intention of returning. The spouse who has left the conjugal dwelling for a period of three months or has failed within the same period to give any information as to his or her whereabouts shall be prima facie presumed to have no intention of returning to the conjugal dwelling. (178a)
      Separation in fact (Art. 100 / 127)Abandonment (Art. 101 / 128)
      Does not affect the regime, with three exceptionsGives the aggrieved spouse three remedies: receivership, judicial separation of property, or sole administration
      The spouse who leaves without just cause loses the right to supportAbandonment = leaving the conjugal dwelling without intention of returning; the presumption arises after three months away or without information on whereabouts
      Consent required by law → judicial authorization in a summary proceeding (Arts. 238–253)"Obligations to the family" = marital, parental or property relations
      Insufficient community property → separate properties solidarily liable for family support; the present spouse may get court authority to administer or encumber the other's separate propertyAbandonment for more than one year is a ground for legal separation (Art. 55(10)); abandonment, or failure to comply with obligations to the family as provided in Art. 101, is a sufficient cause for judicial separation of property (Art. 135(4))
      Quiz traps: (1) "The spouse who has left the conjugal dwelling for a period of three months … shall be deemed to have no intention of returning" is False: it is only "prima facie presumed" (a disputable presumption). (2) "Shall be prima facie presumed to have no intention of returning: (a) after 90 days …" is the keyed answer to that old MCQ (three months = 90 days). (3) Separation in fact does not dispense with the other spouse's consent. It replaces the consent with judicial authorization in a summary proceeding.
      Tolentino (separation in fact, Art. 100): Separation in fact is the actual, definite separation of the spouses that ends cohabitation without a court order. There is none while the spouses remain intimate and friendly even though business keeps them in separate residences (Seva v. Nolan). An agreement to live apart cannot be enforced, and courts will not compel cohabitation under pain of contempt (Arroyo v. Vazquez de Arroyo, 42 Phil. 54). The spouse who leaves without justification and refuses to return loses the right to be supported but is still bound to support the other. Judicial authorization substitutes for the absent spouse's consent only when that consent cannot be obtained; it cannot override a separated spouse who is ready and willing to consent. On support, the present spouse may be authorized to administer the absent spouse's separate property and use its fruits; Tolentino adds that if there are no fruits, the property itself may be sold with court approval. If only one spouse has separate property, that spouse may be made to bear the entire family support, which is the effect of solidarity.
      Tolentino (abandonment, Art. 101): Art. 101 requires real abandonment, not mere separation: departure with the avowed intent never to return, followed by prolonged absence without just cause and without providing for the family although able to do so, an absolute cessation of marital relations, duties and rights with intent of perpetual separation (De la Cruz v. De la Cruz, 22 SCRA 333). No abandonment where the husband leaves but keeps supplying the family with all its needs while he sets up a separate domicile pending a legal separation suit, or where he leaves because the wife's affection has permanently changed; and a wife who refuses without just cause to follow the husband to a new domicile cannot claim she was abandoned. The same remedies are available when a spouse, without leaving, fails without just cause to meet his or her obligations as spouse or parent. Justified separation: a wife may live apart if the husband maltreats her, brings a concubine into the conjugal home, forces her to live with persons whose habits and language offend her dignity, or makes her a mere subordinate of his mother; the husband must then pay her separate maintenance.

      Art. 99: when the absolute community terminates

      Art. 99, FC. The absolute community terminates:
      (1) Upon the death of either spouse;
      (2) When there is a decree of legal separation;
      (3) When the marriage is annulled or declared void; or
      (4) In case of judicial separation of property during the marriage under Articles 134 to 138. (175a)
      Tolentino (effects of dissolution): After dissolution by death, what the survivor acquires is his or her own; after dissolution for other causes, what either spouse acquires is his or her own. Those acquisitions answer for community debts only if the community is insufficient (solidary liability of separate property). Debts incurred by a spouse after dissolution are his or her own, except those incurred to administer, care for, protect and preserve the community property. If the survivor and the heirs leave the community unliquidated, they impliedly form a co-ownership; the community no longer exists, so fruits are divided by shares. Pending liquidation, a party can sell only his or her undivided interest, not a specific property or physical portion; the buyer gets what is adjudicated to the seller in the partition. The dissolution must be registered to affect third persons in good faith. Buyers in connivance with a surviving husband's fraud get nothing, but a buyer in good faith gets a valid title and the heirs must sue the husband (Nable Jose v. Nable Jose, 41 Phil. 713). Tolentino says this holds under the Torrens system: if the title is in the husband's name or the community's and no estate proceeding is annotated, a good-faith buyer prevails over the heirs when the sale would have been within the husband's power had the community existed.
      Quiz traps: "The absolute community terminates when there is a decree of legal separation" is True (TF compilation #4), and so is "The conjugal partnership terminates when there is a decree of legal separation" (Quiz 3 key #16; Art. 126(2)). Legal separation dissolves the regime but not the marriage. The old MCQ "The following will dissolve both the absolute community and the marriage, except:" turns on this: only death, annulment and nullity end the marriage.
      Uribe (2018 situationer): "The declaration of nullity, annulment, legal separation: there will be a dissolution of property relations. Do you agree?" No. With annulment and legal separation, yes. When the marriage is void, there was never an ACP or CPG to dissolve. The property relations were governed all along by Art. 147 or 148 co-ownership. "Kapag void, co-ownership ang magogovern. There is nothing to dissolve." (Art. 99(3) speaks of "declared void" because, in practice, a void marriage's property relations are settled in the same proceeding; Arts. 50 and 43(2) apply to Art. 40 and Art. 45 cases.)

      Art. 102: liquidation after dissolution (other than by death)

      Art. 102, FC. Upon dissolution of the absolute community regime, the following procedure shall apply:
      (1) An inventory shall be prepared, listing separately all the properties of the absolute community and the exclusive properties of each spouse.
      (2) The debts and obligations of the absolute community shall be paid out of its assets. In case of insufficiency of said assets, the spouses shall be solidarily liable for the unpaid balance with their separate properties in accordance with the provisions of the second paragraph of Article 94.
      (3) Whatever remains of the exclusive properties of the spouses shall thereafter be delivered to each of them.
      (4) The net remainder of the properties of the absolute community shall constitute its net assets, which shall be divided equally between husband and wife, unless a different proportion or division was agreed upon in the marriage settlements, or unless there has been a voluntary waiver of such share provided in this Code. For purpose of computing the net profits subject to forfeiture in accordance with Articles 43, No. (2) and 63, No. (2), the said profits shall be the increase in value between the market value of the community property at the time of the celebration of the marriage and the market value at the time of its dissolution.
      (5) The presumptive legitimes of the common children shall be delivered upon partition, in accordance with Article 51.
      (6) Unless otherwise agreed upon by the parties, in the partition of the properties, the conjugal dwelling and the lot on which it is situated shall be adjudicated to the spouse with whom the majority of the common children choose to remain. Children below the age of seven years are deemed to have chosen the mother, unless the court has decided otherwise. In case there in no such majority, the court shall decide, taking into consideration the best interests of said children. (n)

      Steps in order

      1. Inventory: community property and each spouse's exclusive property, listed separately.
      2. Pay community debts from community assets; if insufficient, the spouses are solidarily liable with their separate property (Art. 94, 2nd par.).
      3. Deliver the remaining exclusive properties to each spouse.
      4. Divide the net assets equally, unless the settlement provides another proportion or a spouse validly waived his or her share. For forfeiture (Arts. 43(2), 63(2)), "net profits" = market value of community property at dissolution minus market value at the celebration.
      5. Deliver the presumptive legitimes of the common children (Art. 51).
      6. Conjugal dwelling and lot → to the spouse with whom the majority of the common children choose to remain; children below seven are deemed to have chosen the mother unless the court decides otherwise; no majority → the court decides on the children's best interests.
      Tolentino (liquidation details): (1) If a spouse's own creditors and unpaid community creditors together exceed that spouse's separate property, Tolentino submits that the spouse's own creditors should be preferred: the spouse is primarily liable to them and only subsidiarily liable to community creditors. (2) Personal creditors who remain unpaid may reach the debtor-spouse's share in the net remainder after community creditors are paid. (3) The forfeiture under Arts. 43(2) and 63(2) goes to the common children; if none, to the guilty spouse's children by a previous marriage; failing those, to the innocent spouse. (4) Presumptive legitimes (Art. 51) come from both spouses, computed on all the property allotted to each (separate property plus share in the net remainder). These deductions are not made when the community is dissolved by death. (5) Other ways to liquidate (alternative, not cumulative): an extrajudicial agreement (all parties of age, no debts), an ordinary action for partition (no debts, no agreement), or, only if a spouse died, the testate or intestate proceeding.
      Tolentino's criticism of the "net profits" formula. Art. 102(4) defines net profits as the increase in market value from the wedding to dissolution, ignoring debts. His illustration: market value at dissolution ₱225,000; at the wedding ₱75,000; the formula gives ₱150,000. But if ₱125,000 of community debts are paid, the net assets are only ₱100,000. "How can there be net profits of ₱150,000?" He would compute net profits as net assets at dissolution minus the value at the wedding: ₱100,000 − ₱75,000 = ₱25,000; and if the net remainder is less than the starting value, there is a loss and nothing to forfeit. For Uribe's quizzes, follow the codal formula (increase in market value), as in the trap below.
      Quiz trap (forfeiture): in an ACP, the forfeitable "net profits" are not the whole share. They are only the increase in market value of the community property between the celebration and the dissolution (Art. 102(4)). In legal separation, the guilty spouse's share in the net profits is forfeited in favor of the common children, or, if none, the children of the guilty spouse by a previous marriage, or, in default, the innocent spouse (Art. 63(2) in relation to Art. 43(2)).

      Art. 103: liquidation upon death, and the mandatory separation rule

      Art. 103, FC. Upon the termination of the marriage by death, the community property shall be liquidated in the same proceeding for the settlement of the estate of the deceased.
      If no judicial settlement proceeding is instituted, the surviving spouse shall liquidate the community property either judicially or extra-judicially within one year from the death of the deceased spouse. If upon the lapse of the said period, no liquidation is made, any disposition or encumbrance involving the community property of the terminated marriage shall be void.
      Should the surviving spouse contract a subsequent marriage without compliance with the foregoing requirements, a mandatory regime of complete separation of property shall govern the property relations of the subsequent marriage. (n)
      • Liquidate in the estate proceedings. If none, the surviving spouse liquidates judicially or extra-judicially within one year from the death.
      • After the period lapses without liquidation, any disposition or encumbrance of community property of the terminated marriage is void.
      • If the survivor remarries without liquidating, the subsequent marriage is governed by a mandatory regime of complete separation of property, whatever the new settlement says.
      • Rationale (Quiz 4 #13 discussion): liquidation is needed to deliver the legitimes of the heirs and to pay the debts of the deceased. Mandatory separation protects the heirs of the first marriage from having that property mixed into a new regime.
      • Tolentino: the one-year period applies to any of the three methods (estate proceeding, partition action, extrajudicial agreement). A disposition after the period is void and may be attacked by the deceased spouse's heirs, but it stands to the extent the property is finally allotted to the seller or mortgagor in the partition, and it is fully valid if the survivor is the deceased's only heir. On mandatory separation, Tolentino sees "no logical reason" for it: if the heirs later obtain a partition of the first marriage's property, why should separation continue for the second marriage? The new spouses may want a community, but by then it is too late for a settlement.
      Quiz trap (ACP vs CPG period): Art. 103 (ACP) gives one year. Art. 130 (CPG) gives six months ("within six months from the death … If upon the lapse of the six-month period …"). The rest of the two articles is parallel. Expect a swapped period.
      Tolentino's text of Art. 130. The 1990 Tolentino commentary prints Art. 130 with "within one year" and says it is the "same as Article 103." The Family Code text in Sir's codal and in the class materials says six months for the CPG. Answer with six months for Art. 130 and one year for Art. 103.
      Compare Art. 40 and Art. 53. Art. 53 makes a subsequent marriage void if the former spouses failed to comply with Art. 52 (recording of the judgment of annulment or nullity, the partition and distribution of the properties, and the delivery of the children's presumptive legitimes). Art. 103 deals with a marriage terminated by death: the subsequent marriage is valid, but it falls under mandatory separation of property. Do not mix them up.

      Art. 104: two or more marriages liquidated together; Delizo v. Delizo

      Art. 104, FC. Whenever the liquidation of the community properties of two or more marriages contracted by the same person before the effectivity of this Code is carried out simultaneously, the respective capital, fruits and income of each community shall be determined upon such proof as may be considered according to the rules of evidence. In case of doubt as to which community the existing properties belong, the same shall be divided between the different communities in proportion to the capital and duration of each. (189a)
      Delizo v. Delizo (69 SCRA 216, 1976)

      Nicolas Delizo married twice. His first conjugal partnership (with Rosa Villasfer, three children) and his second (with Dorotea de Ocampo, nine children) were liquidated together after his death, and the evidence did not clearly show which partnership acquired which properties. Applying NCC 189 (the source of FC 104), the Court divided the total mass between the two partnerships in proportion to the duration of each: 18/64 to the first and 46/64 to the second. Each partnership's net remainder was then divided equally between the spouses (NCC 185). Nicolas's half of both partnerships formed his estate, distributed equally among his twelve children, with his widow taking a share equal to one child's. In the digest's computation, Rosa's share was 9/64 and Dorotea's 23/64, plus Dorotea's share as heir. Doctrine: in case of doubt about which of several communities or partnerships owns existing properties, divide them in proportion to the capital and the duration of each (FC 104 adds capital to the NCC's duration).

      Tolentino (Art. 104 beyond pre-FC marriages): The article literally covers only marriages "contracted by the same person before the effectivity of this Code." Tolentino sees no reason for the limitation: the same rules should apply if one or both marriages came after the Family Code, or if the two regimes differ (taking each regime into account). With proof, liquidate the first marriage (what was brought in vs. what existed at dissolution), deliver the shares, then liquidate the second; the remarried spouse's capital in the second marriage may be his share from the first liquidation, or less or more depending on what he disposed of or acquired as a widower. Without proof, divide what remains between the marriages in proportion to capital (if known) and duration. His illustration: Pedro brought ₱50,000 and Rosa ₱20,000 to the first marriage (₱70,000); Pedro brought ₱40,000 and Alicia ₱10,000 to the second (₱50,000). At Pedro's death the assets are ₱100,000. If both marriages lasted equally long: first marriage 70/120 × ₱100,000 = ₱58,333.33; second marriage 50/120 × ₱100,000 = ₱41,666.67. Under ACP in both, Pedro's heirs get ₱50,000, Rosa's heirs ₱29,166.67, and Alicia ₱20,833.33. If the capitals are unknown and the marriages lasted 5 and 10 years: ₱33,333.33 and ₱66,666.67, so Rosa's heirs get ₱16,666.67, Alicia ₱33,333.33, and Pedro's heirs ₱50,000. (Compare the CPG "double proportion" under Art. 131.)

      Checklist: ACP in one page

      1. Commences at the precise moment of the celebration; any stipulation otherwise is void (Art. 88).
      2. No waiver during the marriage, except upon judicial separation; a waiver then or after dissolution must be in a public instrument, recorded, and is rescissible by creditors (Art. 89).
      3. Suppletory: co-ownership (Art. 90).
      4. Consists of all property owned at the celebration or acquired after, unless otherwise provided by the Chapter or the settlement (Art. 91).
      5. Excluded: (1) gratuitous acquisitions during the marriage, with their fruits, unless the giver says otherwise; (2) personal and exclusive use, except jewelry; (3) property before the marriage of a spouse with legitimate descendants by a former marriage, with its fruits (Art. 92).
      6. Presumption: acquired during the marriage → community, unless proved excluded (Art. 93).
      7. Charges (Art. 94): note (5) "used by the family", (3) and (7) "benefit / redounded", (9) advances, and solidary liability except (9).
      8. Gambling: losses → loser; winnings → community (Art. 95).
      9. Joint administration; disagreement → husband prevails, wife's recourse within five years from the contract; disposition or encumbrance without written consent or court authority → void but a continuing offer (Art. 96).
      10. Either spouse may will his or her interest (Art. 97); no donation of community property without consent, except moderate donations for charity, family rejoicing or family distress (Art. 98).
      11. Terminates: death, legal separation decree, annulment or nullity, judicial separation of property (Art. 99).
      12. Separation in fact: regime unaffected except no support for the spouse who left without just cause, judicial authorization in place of consent, and solidary liability of separate property for support (Art. 100). Abandonment: receivership, judicial separation, or sole administration; three months → prima facie presumption (Art. 101).
      13. Liquidation (Art. 102): inventory → debts → exclusive property returned → net assets equally (forfeitable profits = increase in market value) → presumptive legitimes → conjugal dwelling to the majority's choice (below 7 → mother).
      14. Death: liquidate in the estate proceeding or within one year; otherwise dispositions are void; remarriage without liquidation → mandatory complete separation (Art. 103). CPG: six months (Art. 130).

      Conjugal Partnership of Gains

      Title IV, Chapter 4, Family Code, Arts. 105–133 (syllabus X.E). Covers when the CPG applies (Arts. 105–108), exclusive property and its administration (Arts. 109–115), the presumption and what is conjugal (Arts. 116–120), charges (Arts. 121–123), administration (Arts. 124–125), dissolution (Art. 126), separation in fact and abandonment (Arts. 127–128), liquidation (Arts. 129–133), and the syllabus cases decided mostly under the Civil Code (NCC 142–189).

      The CPG in one paragraph, and how it differs from the ACP

      In the CPG, each spouse keeps what he or she owned before the marriage and what he or she later receives gratuitously. What goes into the common fund is the gains: the fruits and income of everything (including the exclusive properties), the products of each spouse's work, and acquisitions by onerous title at the common fund's expense. Upon dissolution, the net gains are divided equally (Art. 106). The ACP is the opposite starting point: everything is common, with a short list of exclusions (Arts. 91–92).

      IssueACPCPG
      Default regimeMarriages on or after Aug. 3, 1988 (Art. 75)Marriages before Aug. 3, 1988 (NCC 119); afterward, only by settlement
      Property owned at the celebrationCommunity (Art. 91), unless Art. 92(3)Exclusive: "brought to the marriage as his or her own" (Art. 109(1))
      Gratuitous acquisitions during the marriageExcluded, with their fruits, unless the giver provides otherwise (Art. 92(1))Exclusive (Art. 109(2)); but their fruits are conjugal (Art. 117(3))
      Fruits of exclusive propertySeparate, if the property is excluded under Art. 92(1) or (3)Conjugal: "net fruits from the exclusive property of each spouse" (Art. 117(3))
      JewelryCommunity, even if for personal use (Art. 92(2))No special rule; follows the source of funds or title
      PresumptionArt. 93 (acquired during the marriage)Art. 116 (acquired during the marriage, whatever the name in the title)
      Suppletory rulesCo-ownership (Art. 90)Contract of partnership (Art. 108)
      Preservation expenses on separate propertyOnly if used by the family (Art. 94(5))Always (Art. 121(5))
      Personal debts, fines, support of illegitimate childrenAdvances (Art. 94(9))After the Art. 121 charges are covered, if no or insufficient exclusive property; charged at liquidation (Art. 122)
      Improvements on separate propertyProperty is community anyway, except excluded propertyArt. 120 (reverse accession test)
      What is divided equallyNet assets (Art. 102(4))Net profits (Art. 129(7))
      Liquidation after death without estate proceedingsWithin one year (Art. 103)Within six months (Art. 130)

      Arts. 105–108: when the CPG applies; nature; suppletory rules

      Art. 105, FC. In case the future spouses agree in the marriage settlements that the regime of conjugal partnership gains shall govern their property relations during marriage, the provisions in this Chapter shall be of supplementary application.
      The provisions of this Chapter shall also apply to conjugal partnerships of gains already established between spouses before the effectivity of this Code, without prejudice to vested rights already acquired in accordance with the Civil Code or other laws, as provided in Article 256. (n)
      Art. 106, FC. Under the regime of conjugal partnership of gains, the husband and wife place in a common fund the proceeds, products, fruits and income from their separate properties and those acquired by either or both spouses through their efforts or by chance, and, upon dissolution of the marriage or of the partnership, the net gains or benefits obtained by either or both spouses shall be divided equally between them, unless otherwise agreed in the marriage settlements. (142a)
      Art. 107, FC. The rules provided in Articles 88 and 89 shall also apply to conjugal partnership of gains. (n)
      Art. 108, FC. The conjugal partnership shall be governed by the rules on the contract of partnership in all that is not in conflict with what is expressly determined in this Chapter or by the spouses in their marriage settlements. (147a)
      • Art. 105: two situations, (1) chosen in a settlement under the Family Code, and (2) pre-Family Code CPGs, to which the Family Code chapter applies without prejudice to vested rights.
      • Art. 107: the CPG, like the ACP, commences at the precise moment of the celebration (any contrary stipulation is void), and no waiver is allowed during the marriage except upon judicial separation of property. UP BOC 2011 MCQ: "When does the CPG begin to exist?" A: at the moment the parties take and declare each other as husband and wife.
      • Art. 108: suppletory rules are those on the contract of partnership, not co-ownership.
      Tolentino (concept of the partnership of gains): Following Manresa, it is a partnership formed by the marriage, by which the spouses put into a common fund the fruits of their separate properties and of their work, and divide equally on dissolution the profits "indiscriminately obtained by either of the spouses." Each spouse keeps his or her own property and debts. The law intends no merger of them: it keeps the capital account completely separate from the account of gains, which is "an insurmountable obstacle to the presumption of solidarity between the spouses" (PNB v. Quintos, 46 Phil. 370). Under the Civil Code the CPG was the legal regime; under the Family Code it is optional and must be adopted in a settlement, whose rules prevail over the Code. Marriages before the Family Code that were under the CPG stay under it, because the regime vested at the celebration.
      Tolentino (CPG vs. ordinary partnership): (1) The CPG arises from the mere fact of marriage, even independently of the parties' will; an ordinary partnership arises from agreement. (2) Its purpose, duration and rules are fixed by law; an ordinary partnership's are fixed by the partners. (3) Profits are divided equally regardless of the capital each spouse brought; in an ordinary partnership they follow the capital or the agreement. (4) Under the Civil Code the husband had predominance in management, while partners generally have equal rights. (Point (4) no longer holds under Art. 124's joint administration.)
      Tolentino (three patrimonies; nature of each spouse's interest): There are three patrimonies, the husband's, the wife's and the partnership's, each with its own assets and liabilities, and the spouses cannot change them by agreement: separate property cannot be made conjugal, conjugal property cannot be made separate, and one patrimony's debts cannot be charged to another. Value may pass from one to another (one may pay the other's debts), but any transfer must be balanced by an indemnity from the patrimony that benefited. Unlike in the ACP, there is no co-ownership between the spouses in conjugal property during the marriage. Neither spouse may alienate his or her interest in the partnership or in any of its property, or ask for partition before dissolution. Each has only an inchoate right, "a mere expectancy, which constitutes neither a legal nor an equitable estate," that ripens into title only if there are assets left after liquidation; the right is to one-half of the net remainder (Madrigal v. Rafferty, 38 Phil. 414; Nable Jose v. Nable Jose, 41 Phil. 713; Quintos de Ansaldo v. Sheriff, below).
      Tolentino (spouses separated in fact): Is there still a partnership in gains acquired after a definite separation? The Argentine high court said a separated wife has no share in property her husband accumulated after the separation, because one who contributes neither property nor industry should not share in the profits, and "when the reason for the law ceases, the law also ceases."
