Liquidation after the partnership is dissolved differs from separation of property during the marriage, which does need a court decree; and under Rule 74 the parties may partition extrajudicially, which implies the liquidation.

      Art. 130, FC. Upon the termination of the marriage by death, the conjugal partnership property shall be liquidated in the same proceeding for the settlement of the estate of the deceased.
      If no judicial settlement proceeding is instituted, the surviving spouse shall liquidate the conjugal partnership property either judicially or extra-judicially within six months from the death of the deceased spouse. If upon the lapse of the six-month period no liquidation is made, any disposition or encumbrance involving the conjugal partnership property of the terminated marriage shall be void.
      Should the surviving spouse contract a subsequent marriage without compliance with the foregoing requirements, a mandatory regime of complete separation of property shall govern the property relations of the subsequent marriage. (n)
      Quiz trap: CPG → six months; ACP → one year (Art. 103).
      Art. 131, FC. Whenever the liquidation of the conjugal partnership properties of two or more marriages contracted by the same person before the effectivity of this Code is carried out simultaneously, the respective capital, fruits and income of each partnership shall be determined upon such proof as may be considered according to the rules of evidence. In case of doubt as to which partnership the existing properties belong, the same shall be divided between the different partnerships in proportion to the capital and duration of each. (189a)
      Tolentino (two partnerships; double proportion): When a man dies leaving children of two marriages and a widow, liquidate the first partnership (the first wife's half goes to her children; the husband's half to his estate), then the second (half to the widow, half to his estate); his halves from both form his estate. Each partnership owns what was acquired during its existence: where 11 parcels were acquired during the first marriage and 20 during the second, it is "preposterous," absent very convincing proof, to claim the 20 came from the products of the 11. Without proof, divide the total mass between the partnerships by a double proportion, duration and capital. His illustration: Emilio's first wife Marcela brought ₱5,000 and his second wife Eva ₱3,000; the total mass at Emilio's death is ₱10,000, so after returning the ₱8,000 capital, ₱2,000 is conjugal in both marriages. If the marriages lasted equally: Marcela's partnership 5/8 × ₱2,000 = ₱1,250; Eva's 3/8 × ₱2,000 = ₱750. If Marcela's lasted 4 years and Eva's 7: ₱5,000 × 4 = 20,000 and ₱3,000 × 7 = 21,000, total 41,000, so Marcela's partnership gets 20/41 × ₱2,000 = ₱975.61 and Eva's 21/41 × ₱2,000 = ₱1,024.39. Each partnership's share is then divided equally, and the capitals go back to Marcela and Eva or their heirs.
      Art. 132, FC. The Rules of Court on the administration of estates of deceased persons shall be observed in the appraisal and sale of property of the conjugal partnership, and other matters which are not expressly determined in this Chapter. (187a)
      Art. 133, FC. From the common mass of property support shall be given to the surviving spouse and to the children during the liquidation of the inventoried property and until what belongs to them is delivered; but from this shall be deducted that amount received for support which exceeds the fruits or rents pertaining to them. (188a)
      Beumer v. Amores (G.R. No. 195670, December 3, 2012)

      A Dutch national, after the nullity of his marriage to a Filipina, sought reimbursement for half of the lots bought during the marriage, claiming he paid for them with his own money. Held: no reimbursement. He knowingly violated the constitutional prohibition on aliens owning land, so "he acquired no right whatsoever over the subject properties by virtue of its unconstitutional purchase." "[E]quity as a rule will follow the law and will not permit that to be done indirectly which, because of public policy, cannot be done directly" (NCC 1412: the law leaves the parties where it finds them). His inconsistent statements about the source of funds also meant he came to court with unclean hands.

      Santero v. CFI of Cavite (153 SCRA 728, 1987)

      Under NCC 188 (now FC 133), support during liquidation goes to the surviving spouse and the children "without distinction". That the children "are of age, gainfully employed, or married is of no moment." The Rules of Court limit allowances to the widow and the minor or incapacitated children, but this procedural rule cannot impair the substantive right in the Civil Code. The allowances are advances from their shares. "Spouse" means the legitimate spouse, not a common-law spouse.

      Tolentino (support during liquidation, Art. 133): The Code's grant of support to the surviving spouse and the children prevails over Rule 83 §3, which limits allowances to the "widow" and "minor or incapacitated children": Art. 132 makes the Rules apply only to matters the Code does not expressly settle, and the right is substantive (Santero). So the widower and children who are of age, married or employed also qualify. Grandchildren do not (Babao v. Villanueva, 44 Phil. 921), but absent legitimate children, parents may receive support as an advance on their legitime. Whatever exceeds the fruits of a recipient's share is an advance on that share, both in the partnership and in the inheritance. So the right depends on the recipient having some share: in Moore & Sons Mercantile Co. v. Wagner (62 Phil. 128), the estate realized ₱899.79 against approved claims of ₱2,457.99, and a ₱80 monthly allowance to the widow and daughter could not be ordered, because the estate was insolvent and they could expect no share. Tolentino adds that a widow needs no allowance from her own paraphernal property, since she owns and manages it and its fruits.

      Checklist: CPG in one page

      1. Applies by settlement (Family Code) or by default (pre-August 3, 1988 marriages). The Family Code chapter applies to old CPGs without prejudice to vested rights.
      2. Commences at the celebration; no waiver during the marriage except upon judicial separation (Art. 107). Suppletory rules: partnership (Art. 108).
      3. Exclusive (Art. 109): brought to the marriage; gratuitous during the marriage; redemption, barter or exchange with exclusive property; bought with exclusive money.
      4. Conjugal (Art. 117): onerous acquisitions at the common fund's expense; labor and profession; fruits of everything, including net fruits of exclusive property; hidden treasure shares; occupation; excess livestock; winnings.
      5. Presumption (Art. 116): acquired during the marriage → conjugal, whatever the name in the title. Proof of acquisition during the marriage comes first; the source of funds need not be shown; "married to" is descriptive; innocent third parties are protected.
      6. Installments (Art. 118): when full ownership vested. Credits (Art. 119): principal → spouse; interest → partnership.
      7. Improvements (Art. 120): cost + increase vs. value of the property; ownership vests upon reimbursement at liquidation.
      8. Charges (Art. 121): note "legitimate children of either spouse" and preservation of separate property without the "used by the family" condition; solidary liability for any balance. Art. 122: personal debts only if they benefited the family; fines and support of illegitimate children are subsidiary, charged at liquidation.
      9. Joint administration; disposition without written consent or court authority → void (NCC: voidable within 10 years); continuing offer (Art. 124). Donations need consent except moderate ones (Art. 125).
      10. Termination (Art. 126) and separation in fact or abandonment (Arts. 127–128) mirror the ACP.
      11. Liquidation (Art. 129): inventory → credit advances → reimburse spouses → pay debts → return exclusive property → indemnify movables → divide profits equally → presumptive legitimes → conjugal dwelling.
      12. Death: estate proceeding or six months, otherwise dispositions are void; remarriage without liquidation → mandatory separation (Art. 130). Support from the common mass during liquidation (Art. 133; Santero).

      Separation of Property During the Marriage and the Regime of Separation of Property

      Title IV, Chapters 5–6, Family Code, Arts. 134–146 (syllabus X.F–G). Covers judicial separation of property, voluntary or for sufficient cause (Arts. 134–136), its effects (Arts. 137–140), revival of the former regime (Art. 141), court transfer of the administration of exclusive property (Art. 142), and the regime of separation of property, whether by settlement or by mandate of law (Arts. 143–146; Arts. 103, 130, 66, 63). Cases: Garcia v. Manzano; Lacson v. San Jose-Lacson.

      When the spouses' property is separate: the four routes

      RouteBasisNotes
      1. Marriage settlement adopting separationArts. 75, 143–146Total or partial, present or future property (Art. 144)
      2. Mandatory by lawArts. 103 and 130 (survivor remarries without liquidating)Overrides any settlement for the subsequent marriage
      3. Legal separation and reconciliationArt. 63(2) (dissolution and liquidation); Art. 66(2) (separation subsists after reconciliation unless the spouses agree to revive)Revival only by a sworn agreement filed in court (Art. 67)
      4. Judicial separation of propertyArts. 134–138: voluntary (Art. 136) or for sufficient cause (Art. 135); also Arts. 101, 128 (abandonment)After dissolution, complete separation applies (Art. 138)
      Uribe (2018 situationer): "There can be regime of separation of property if so agreed upon by parties in marriage settlements. Do you agree?" No, if the point is that the settlement is the only way. Separation also arises by mandate of law (Arts. 103, 130), after legal separation, and by judicial decree.
      Tolentino (five sources of separation): Separation of property may be (1) agreed in a marriage settlement, (2) ordered by the court on one spouse's petition, (3) adopted by voluntary agreement of the spouses approved by the court, (4) a result of legal separation, or (5) compulsory, when a surviving spouse remarries without liquidating the property of the prior marriage (Arts. 103, 130). It is the only regime that may begin during the marriage rather than at the celebration.

      Art. 134: separation during the marriage needs a judicial order

      Art. 134, FC. In the absence of an express declaration in the marriage settlements, the separation of property between spouses during the marriage shall not take place except by judicial order. Such judicial separation of property may either be voluntary or for sufficient cause. (190a)
      Tolentino (Art. 134): The article is "deficient" because it ignores the compulsory separation that the law itself imposes under Arts. 103 and 130. A contract of separation of property signed by the spouses during the marriage without court approval is non-existent, whatever its consideration (Quintana v. Lerma; Garcia v. Manzano), and separation in fact does not create a separation regime (Arts. 100, 127). The agreement may be submitted to the court, but the separation is effected by the court's decree approving it, not by the contract, and it takes effect only upon approval (Brugi; In re Bermas, 14 SCRA 327; Lacson v. San Jose-Lacson, 24 SCRA 837). Likewise, the mere existence of an Art. 135 ground does not separate the property: a spouse must petition, and the court's order effects the separation.
      Quiz traps: (1) UP BOC 2012 MCQ: "Separation of property between spouses during the marriage may take place only: (a) by agreement of the spouses; (b) if one spouse has given ground for legal separation; (c) upon order of the court; (d) if one spouse has abandoned the other." C. Agreement alone is insufficient, and grounds and abandonment still require a court order. (2) 2005 Bar (Gabby and Mila): a private document dissolving the CPG and adopting separation mid-marriage is void. The CPG subsists. (3) 2018 situationer: "If a petition for separation of property was filed, for this petition to prosper, the petitioner must allege and thereafter prove a sufficient cause." No. Separation may be voluntary (Art. 136), with no cause needed. Creditors are protected because they must be listed and notified.

      Art. 135: sufficient causes for judicial separation

      Art. 135, FC. Any of the following shall be considered sufficient cause for judicial separation of property:
      (1) That the spouse of the petitioner has been sentenced to a penalty which carries with it civil interdiction;
      (2) That the spouse of the petitioner has been judicially declared an absentee;
      (3) That loss of parental authority of the spouse of petitioner has been decreed by the court;
      (4) That the spouse of the petitioner has abandoned the latter or failed to comply with his or her obligations to the family as provided for in Article 101;
      (5) That the spouse granted the power of administration in the marriage settlements has abused that power; and
      (6) That at the time of the petition, the spouses have been separated in fact for at least one year and reconciliation is highly improbable.
      In the cases provided for in Numbers (1), (2), and (3), the presentation of the final judgment against the guilty or absent spouse shall be enough basis for the grant of the decree of judicial separation of property. (191a)

      Breakdown

      • Judgment-based grounds (1)–(3): civil interdiction, judicial declaration of absence, loss of parental authority. The final judgment alone suffices; nothing else need be proved.
      • Fact-based grounds (4)–(6): abandonment or failure to comply with obligations to the family (Art. 101: marital, parental or property); abuse of the power of administration granted in the settlement; separation in fact for at least one year with reconciliation highly improbable.
      • Compare with legal separation (Art. 55(10)): abandonment without justifiable cause for more than one year. For judicial separation of property, any abandonment under Art. 101 suffices (the three-month presumption helps prove it).
      Number traps: separation in fact "for at least one year" (Art. 135(6)); abandonment presumption after "three months" (Arts. 101, 128); legal separation for abandonment "for more than one year" (Art. 55(10)). His legal separation key: "Abandonment of petitioner by respondent for more than one year is a ground for legal separation" is False (it omits "without justifiable cause").
      De la Cruz v. De la Cruz (22 SCRA 333, 1968)

      (Also in the CPG section.) A husband who leaves the conjugal home but keeps managing the conjugal properties diligently and supports his family has not "abandoned" his wife in the sense that justifies separation of property. The remedies exist "to protect the conjugal partnership from waste and shield the wife from want."

      Art. 136: voluntary separation of property

      Art. 136, FC. The spouses may jointly file a verified petition with the court for the voluntary dissolution of the absolute community or the conjugal partnership of gains, and for the separation of their common properties.
      All creditors of the absolute community or of the conjugal partnership of gains, as well as the personal creditors of the spouse, shall be listed in the petition and notified of the filing thereof. The court shall take measures to protect the creditors and other persons with pecuniary interest. (191a)
      • Joint, verified petition by both spouses. No cause needs to be alleged or proved.
      • All creditors (of the regime and the personal creditors of each spouse) must be listed and notified. The court takes protective measures.
      • Only one voluntary separation is allowed after a revival: once a voluntary separation is revived under Art. 141(7), "no voluntary separation of property may thereafter be granted."
      Tolentino (grounds for approving a voluntary separation): The law does not state the reasons that justify approval; it leaves their sufficiency to the court's sound discretion. An agreement with no reason at all should be disapproved. Any ground that would lessen friction and misunderstanding over the property or its administration, or that is for the mutual benefit of the spouses and the family, justifies approval.
      Garcia v. Manzano (103 Phil. 798)

      "The husband and the wife may agree upon the dissolution of the conjugal partnership during the marriage, subject to judicial approval. All the creditors of the husband and of the wife, as well as of the conjugal partnership, shall be notified of any petition for judicial approval of the voluntary dissolution of the conjugal partnership, so that any such creditors may appear at the hearing to safeguard his interests. Upon approval of the petition for dissolution of the conjugal partnership, the court shall take such measures as may protect the creditors and other third persons." (Uribe's syllabus places it under "For sufficient cause, FC 135, cf. FC 55(10)"; its doctrine is on judicial approval and protection of creditors.)

      Lacson v. San Jose-Lacson (24 SCRA 837, 1968)

      The spouses, separated in fact, executed a compromise agreement on the separation of their property and the dissolution of their conjugal partnership, which the court approved. Held: "The law allows separation of property of the spouses and the dissolution of their conjugal partnership provided judicial sanction is secured beforehand." Here "the spouses obtained judicial imprimatur of their separation of property and the dissolution of their conjugal partnership," and no creditors would be prejudiced, so the separation of property was valid. (The same compromise also dealt with the custody of the children; the case is more often cited under parental authority for the rule that a child under seven should not be separated from the mother by mere agreement.)

      Arts. 137–140: effects of judicial separation

      Art. 137, FC. Once the separation of property has been decreed, the absolute community or the conjugal partnership of gains shall be liquidated in conformity with this Code.
      During the pendency of the proceedings for separation of property, the absolute community or the conjugal partnership shall pay for the support of the spouses and their children. (192a)
      Art. 138, FC. After dissolution of the absolute community or of the conjugal partnership, the provisions on complete separation of property shall apply. (191a)
      Art. 139, FC. The petition for separation of property and the final judgment granting the same shall be recorded in the proper local civil registries and registries of property. (193a)
      Art. 140, FC. The separation of property shall not prejudice the rights previously acquired by creditors. (194a)
      1. Liquidation under Art. 102 (ACP) or Art. 129 (CPG).
      2. Support pendente lite from the common property while the case is pending.
      3. Complete separation of property thereafter (Arts. 143–146).
      4. Recording of both the petition and the final judgment in the LCR and the registries of property.
      5. Creditors' prior rights are unaffected.
      6. A waiver of the ACP or CPG share is allowed only upon judicial separation, in a public instrument, recorded, and subject to the creditors' action to rescind (Arts. 89, 107).
      Tolentino (effects of the decree): (1) the ACP or CPG is dissolved and liquidated; (2) each spouse thereafter owns exclusively his or her earnings and the fruits of his or her separate property; (3) the duty to support the children continues, each spouse contributing in proportion to his or her income or property; (4) the spouses' mutual duty of support continues. Contributions are based on the income from their property, not its value, and on market value only if the income is insufficient. A spouse who paid all the children's expenses because the other had no means cannot later recover a proportionate share when the other's means improve: he or she was paying his or her own legal obligation.

      Art. 141: revival of the former regime

      Art. 141, FC. The spouses may, in the same proceedings where separation of property was decreed, file a motion in court for a decree reviving the property regime, in the following instances:
      (1) When the civil interdiction terminates;
      (2) When the absentee spouse reappears;
      (3) When the court, being satisfied that the spouse granted the power of administration in the marriage settlements will not again abuse that power, authorizes the resumption of said administration;
      (4) When the spouse who has left the conjugal home without a decree of legal separation resumes common life with the other;
      (5) When parental authority is judicially restored to the spouse previously deprived thereof;
      (6) When the spouses who have separated in fact for at least one year, reconcile and resume common life; or
      (7) When after voluntary dissolution of the absolute community of property or conjugal partnership has been judicially decreed upon the joint petition of the spouses, they agree to the revival of the former property regime. No voluntary separation of property may thereafter be granted.
      The revival of the former property regime shall be governed by Article 67. (195a)

      Each ground in Art. 141 mirrors a cause in Art. 135 (or the voluntary separation in Art. 136) that has ceased. The revival is by motion in the same proceeding, and the procedure follows Art. 67.

      Tolentino (who files the motion): Revival is not automatic when the cause ends; the court must grant a motion. Tolentino says the motion must be filed by both spouses: Art. 141 does not give the right to only one, and Art. 67, which governs the revival, requires an agreement of both.
      Art. 67, FC. The agreement to revive the former property regime referred to in the preceding Article shall be executed under oath and shall specify:
      (1) The properties to be contributed anew to the restored regime;
      (2) Those to be retained as separated properties of each spouse; and
      (3) The names of all their known creditors, their addresses and the amounts owing to each.
      The agreement of revival and the motion for its approval shall be filed with the court in the same proceeding for legal separation, with copies of both furnished to the creditors named therein. After due hearing, the court shall, in its order, take measure to protect the interest of creditors and such order shall be recorded in the proper registries of properties.
      The recording of the ordering in the registries of property shall not prejudice any creditor not listed or not notified, unless the debtor-spouse has sufficient separate properties to satisfy the creditor's claim. (195a, 108a)
      Quiz trap: the revival agreement must be under oath (not merely in writing) and filed in court. Compare the original settlement (a private writing is enough, Art. 77), the waiver of a share (a public instrument, Art. 89), and the transfer of administration of exclusive property (a public instrument, recorded, Art. 110).

      Art. 142: court transfer of the administration of exclusive property

      Art. 142, FC. The administration of all classes of exclusive property of either spouse may be transferred by the court to the other spouse:
      (1) When one spouse becomes the guardian of the other;
      (2) When one spouse is judicially declared an absentee;
      (3) When one spouse is sentenced to a penalty which carries with it civil interdiction; or
      (4) When one spouse becomes a fugitive from justice or is in hiding as an accused in a criminal case.
      If the other spouse is not qualified by reason of incompetence, conflict of interest, or any other just cause, the court shall appoint a suitable person to be the administrator. (n)

      Compare Art. 110 (2nd par.): the owner-spouse may voluntarily transfer administration of his or her exclusive property to the other by a recorded public instrument. Art. 142 is the judicial transfer.

      Tolentino (Art. 142): Art. 196 NCC let the court transfer the administration of "all classes of property in the marriage"; Art. 142 covers only the exclusive property of either spouse. The section heading still speaks of "Administration of Common Property by One Spouse", which Tolentino treats as an error in phrasing. For common property, Arts. 96 and 124 let the capable spouse assume sole administration without court intervention; for exclusive property, the court makes the transfer. If the other spouse is unfit (incompetence, conflict of interest or other just cause), the court appoints a suitable person. The administrator is only a trustee: ownership does not pass, and he or she cannot alienate or encumber the property without court authority, and the court may impose conditions to protect the owner. When the cause ends, the owner may petition to end the administration, recover the property, and demand an accounting.

      Arts. 143–146: the regime of separation of property

      Tolentino (the separation regime): Under separation of property, the spouses' interests are completely independent; there is separation not only of assets but also of liabilities. Each spouse has full ownership, enjoyment and administration of his or her own property, its fruits, and the products of his or her work. Its advantage is simplicity (no complicated liquidation). Its disadvantages: it runs contrary to the community of life and interest that marriage creates, and it may cause constant friction over family expenses. Conventional vs. judicial separation: conventional separation (by settlement) takes effect at the celebration, is permanent and immutable, may be partial, and is governed first by the settlement; judicial separation (by decree) takes effect during the marriage, is provisional (it ends when its cause ends, Art. 141), covers the whole patrimony of both spouses with no exceptions, and is governed by Arts. 135–141.
      Art. 143, FC. Should the future spouses agree in the marriage settlements that their property relations during marriage shall be governed by the regime of separation of property, the provisions of this Chapter shall be suppletory. (212a)
      Art. 144, FC. Separation of property may refer to present or future property or both. It may be total or partial. In the latter case, the property not agreed upon as separate shall pertain to the absolute community. (213a)
      Art. 145, FC. Each spouse shall own, dispose of, possess, administer and enjoy his or her own separate estate, without need of the consent of the other. To each spouse shall belong all earnings from his or her profession, business or industry and all fruits, natural, industrial or civil, due or received during the marriage from his or her separate property. (214a)
      Art. 146, FC. Both spouses shall bear the family expenses in proportion to their income, or, in case of insufficiency or default thereof, to the current market value of their separate properties.
      The liabilities of the spouses to creditors for family expenses shall, however, be solidary. (215a)
      • Scope (Art. 144): present property, future property, or both; total or partial.
      • Partial separation: what is not agreed upon as separate goes to the absolute community, not the CPG.
      • Tolentino (partial separation): partial separation means separation and the ACP (or the CPG, if agreed) exist side by side. If the settlement says nothing about the spouses' earnings from work during the marriage, those earnings go to the community or partnership; property acquired for value during the marriage is presumed common; accessions to property under separation belong to its owner. In total separation, nothing is common: fruits and earnings belong to each spouse.
      • Ownership and administration (Art. 145): each spouse owns, disposes of, possesses, administers and enjoys his or her own estate without the other's consent. Each keeps his or her own earnings and the fruits of his or her separate property.
      • Tolentino (Art. 145): (1) A wife under separation may transfer the management of her property to her husband, as Art. 110 allows in the CPG. This is not an amendment of the settlement; it is an agency, revocable at will (the Swiss Code makes a waiver of the right to take back management void). (2) Property belongs to the spouse who appears as buyer or grantee, without prejudice to creditors or heirs proving that he or she acted only for the other. In case of doubt, real property belongs to the spouse in whose name it is registered or was acquired, and personal property to the spouse in possession. Personal property possessed jointly may be attached by either spouse's creditor, leaving the other spouse to prove exclusive ownership; between the spouses or their heirs, it is presumed to belong to the spouse who owns or leases the building where it is found, and personal effects belong to their user. (3) Liabilities are separate: one spouse's creditors cannot levy on the other's property, except when the debtor acted as the other's authorized agent, or the other spouse benefited (liable to the extent of the unjust enrichment). (4) Each spouse may recover from the other any credit or advance even during the marriage, and damages caused by the other's fraud, fault or negligence; but neither may charge for personal services, advice or help, which are part of the duty of mutual help.
      • Family expenses (Art. 146): borne in proportion to income, or, if income is insufficient or lacking, to the current market value of their separate properties. As to creditors, the spouses are solidarily liable for family expenses.
      • Tolentino (Art. 146): for family expenses it does not matter which spouse contracted the debt; both are liable in proportion. If one spouse has income but no property and the other has property but no income, the proportion is based on the amount of the income and the value of the property, respectively. A spouse who paid all the family expenses because the other had neither property nor income cannot seek reimbursement, because the obligation was his or her own, and the same is true if a creditor enforced the solidary liability against one spouse.
      Quiz traps: (1) partial separation → the rest goes to the absolute community (Art. 144), not "the conjugal partnership". (2) Family expenses are borne "in proportion to their income", not "equally", and the fallback is "current market value" of separate properties. (3) Liability to creditors for family expenses is solidary, even though the sharing between the spouses is proportional.
      Uribe (Quiz 4 #13 discussion on the mandatory regime): under Arts. 103 and 130, liquidation is needed to deliver the legitimes to the heirs and to pay the debts of the deceased. If the surviving spouse remarries without doing so, a mandatory regime of complete separation of property governs the new marriage "in order to protect the rights of the heirs left by the deceased."

      Checklist: Arts. 134–146

      1. Separation during the marriage: only by judicial order, unless the settlement expressly provides otherwise. It may be voluntary or for sufficient cause (Art. 134).
      2. Causes (Art. 135): civil interdiction, judicial absence, loss of parental authority (the final judgment is enough); abandonment or failure of obligations (Art. 101); abuse of administration granted in the settlement; separation in fact for at least one year with reconciliation highly improbable.
      3. Voluntary (Art. 136): joint verified petition; list and notify all creditors.
      4. Effects: liquidation; support pendente lite from the common property; complete separation thereafter; recording in the LCR and registries of property; creditors' prior rights preserved (Arts. 137–140).
      5. Revival (Art. 141): by motion in the same proceeding, on seven grounds; procedure under Art. 67 (sworn agreement listing properties and creditors). No further voluntary separation after reviving a voluntary one.
      6. Judicial transfer of the administration of exclusive property (Art. 142): guardian, absentee, civil interdiction, fugitive or accused in hiding.
      7. Regime of separation (Arts. 143–146): present or future, total or partial (residue → ACP); each spouse administers and disposes of his or her own property without consent; family expenses in proportion to income, then market value; solidary liability to creditors for family expenses.

      Property Regimes of Unions Without Marriage

      Title IV, Chapter 8, Family Code, Arts. 147–148 (syllabus X.H; review FC 35–38, 41, 44, 45, 50, 53). Covers the special co-ownership of parties capacitated to marry each other (Art. 147), the limited co-ownership of parties who are not (Art. 148), forfeiture, and the cases: Maxey, Salas v. Aguila, Juaniza v. Jose, Gomez v. Lipana, Vda. de Consuegra v. GSIS, Yap v. CA, Cariño v. Cariño, Go-Bangayan v. Bangayan, Ventura v. Abuda. Sir flagged this chapter for emphasis: "focus really on property regimes on unions without marriage … last year tinanong sa bar."

      147 or 148? The threshold question

      Arts. 147 and 148 apply only where there is no valid marriage: either (a) a man and a woman live together as husband and wife without marrying, or (b) they are parties to a void marriage. They do not apply to voidable marriages, which are valid until annulled, so the ACP or CPG governs and is liquidated under Arts. 50 and 43. There is never an ACP or CPG to "dissolve" in a void marriage.

      Art. 147Art. 148
      WhoA man and a woman capacitated to marry each other, living exclusively with each other as husband and wife, without marriage or under a void marriage"Cohabitation not falling under the preceding Article": parties with a legal impediment to marry each other (bigamous or adulterous unions, concubinage, either or both married to others, under-age parties, and so on)
      Wages and salariesOwned in equal sharesBelong to the earner exclusively (and, if he or she is validly married to another, to that marriage's ACP or CPG)
      Property acquired during cohabitationCo-ownership; presumed acquired by joint efforts and owned in equal sharesCo-owned only if acquired through actual joint contribution of money, property or industry, in proportion to the contributions. Once actual joint contribution is shown, the contributions and shares are presumed equal.
      Care and maintenance of the family and householdCounts as a joint contributionDoes not count
      Disposition of one's share during cohabitationNot without the other's consent, until after the cohabitation endsNo such rule in the article (ordinary co-ownership rules apply)
      Forfeiture of the bad-faith party's shareOnly in a void marriage where one party is in good faith → to the common children → their descendants → the innocent party; upon termination of the cohabitationIf the bad-faith party is validly married to another → share accrues to that marriage's ACP or CPG; otherwise forfeited as in Art. 147; applies even if both are in bad faith
      SourceNCC 144 (expanded)New (codifies Juaniza and related cases)
      Uribe's rule of thumb (CivRev 2025): "If one of them or both of them is or are married to other persons, a third person will be affected by the cohabitation or marriage (bigamous or adulterous in character): 148 will apply. All other grounds that will make a marriage void, as long as no third person will be affected, 147 will apply." Asked whether first cousins who married fall under 147 or 148, the class answered 147 (the marriage is void for public policy, but no third person is affected), and Sir's rule of thumb supports that.
      Conflict with the text and with commentators. Art. 147 requires parties "capacitated to marry each other". Many commentators and bar reviewers treat any legal impediment between the parties themselves (e.g., first cousins under Art. 38(1), step-relations, or a party below 18) as falling under Art. 148, which covers "cohabitation not falling under the preceding Article". Cariño lists Art. 148's coverage as "bigamous marriages, adulterous relationships, relationships in a state of concubine, relationships where both man and woman are married to other persons, multiple alliances of the same married man". On Sir's exam, apply his rule of thumb and say why (no third person is affected). If the item is a bar-style MCQ, note that the textual test is capacity to marry each other.
      Tolentino (coverage of Arts. 147 and 148): Art. 147 covers void marriages, whether the parties were in good or bad faith, and a man and a woman, both unmarried and without impediment to marry each other, who live together as husband and wife. Art. 148 covers (1) parties with no legal capacity to marry each other who live together without marrying, e.g., persons below 18, those whose marriage would be incestuous, and those whose marriage would be against public policy (Arts. 35–38); and (2) cohabitation where one or both parties are validly married to others. This supports the textual reading in the note above. Both articles require cohabitation: living together as husband and wife, shown by sexual relations together with a common household, holding out as spouses to third persons, correspondence and documents, mutual financial help, and raising children together. Occasional secret meetings for sex are not enough; a man who repeatedly visited a woman at night for five months, had intercourse and left did not live with her as husband and wife.
      Tolentino (comparing Arts. 147 and 148): Similarities: (1) cohabitation as husband and wife; (2) no ACP or CPG is formed; (3) the common property is governed by co-ownership; (4) property that is not co-owned (bought with money each had before living together, or from the fruits of separate property) belongs to each exclusively; (5) bad faith forfeits a party's share. Differences: (1) capacity to marry each other vs. incapacity or impediment; (2) exclusive cohabitation vs. one or both may have a valid existing marriage; (3) wages and work-acquired property co-owned in equal shares vs. co-ownership only by actual joint contribution of money, property or industry, in proportion; (4) a presumption that property acquired during cohabitation came from joint efforts vs. no such presumption; (5) care of the family and household counts as a contribution vs. it does not; (6) Art. 147 presumes the acquisition by joint effort (and equal shares), while Art. 148 presumes only the equality of contributions. "Under Art. 148, if the actual contribution by one party is not proved, there will be no co-ownership and no presumption of equal shares."
      Uribe (2018 situationer): the marriage of A and B was declared void. During the cohabitation, A saved ₱1M in BDO, and a condominium unit was bought from A's income and registered in his name. B inherited a parcel of land from her grandmother. Who owns what? "It depends on why the marriage was declared void" (147 vs. 148). Under 147, the savings from wages are shared equally, and the condo is presumed acquired by joint efforts and owned equally (B's care of the household counts). Under 148, both belong to A unless B proves actual contribution. Under either article, the inherited land is B's alone, because it was not acquired through work or industry. Follow-up: "What if they were minors but obtained the consent of the parents? 147 or 148?" Under the Family Code, a party below 18 cannot marry even with consent (Art. 35(1)), so the parties are not "capacitated", which points to 148.

      Art. 147: the special co-ownership

      Art. 147, FC. When a man and a woman who are capacitated to marry each other, live exclusively with each other as husband and wife without the benefit of marriage or under a void marriage, their wages and salaries shall be owned by them in equal shares and the property acquired by both of them through their work or industry shall be governed by the rules on co-ownership.
      In the absence of proof to the contrary, properties acquired while they lived together shall be presumed to have been obtained by their joint efforts, work or industry, and shall be owned by them in equal shares. For purposes of this Article, a party who did not participate in the acquisition by the other party of any property shall be deemed to have contributed jointly in the acquisition thereof if the former's efforts consisted in the care and maintenance of the family and of the household.
      Neither party can encumber or dispose by acts inter vivos of his or her share in the property acquired during cohabitation and owned in common, without the consent of the other, until after the termination of their cohabitation.
      When only one of the parties to a void marriage is in good faith, the share of the party in bad faith in the co-ownership shall be forfeited in favor of their common children. In case of default of or waiver by any or all of the common children or their descendants, each vacant share shall belong to the respective surviving descendants. In the absence of descendants, such share shall belong to the innocent party. In all cases, the forfeiture shall take place upon termination of the cohabitation. (144a)

      Requisites

      1. A man and a woman. (2015 Bar: Bert and Joe, both men, cannot invoke Art. 147, because they are not a man and a woman capacitated to marry each other under Arts. 1 and 2.)
      2. Capacitated to marry each other: no legal impediment between them.
      3. Living exclusively with each other.
      4. As husband and wife.
      5. Without the benefit of marriage, or under a void marriage (e.g., no license, Art. 36 psychological incapacity, absence of authority with both parties in bad faith).

      Rules on property

      • Wages and salaries → equal shares, regardless of who earned them. Sir: "Regardless of actual monetary contribution? Yes … kahit yung asawa nagsusugal lang araw-araw at gabi-gabi? Yes, it does not matter."
      • Property acquired through work or industry → co-ownership. In the absence of proof to the contrary, it is presumed acquired by joint efforts and owned equally. A party whose efforts consisted in the care and maintenance of the family and household is deemed to have contributed jointly.
      • Not covered: property acquired by gratuitous title (inheritance, donation), property acquired before the cohabitation, and property acquired by chance (lottery winnings), because none of these came from "work or industry". They remain the acquiring party's own.
      • No disposition inter vivos of one's share in the common property without the other's consent until the cohabitation ends.
      • Tolentino: in ordinary co-ownership a co-owner may sell his or her undivided share without the others' consent; Art. 147 makes an exception while the cohabitation lasts. After one party dies, the survivor cannot validly sell the common property without the consent of the deceased partner's heirs, who may recover their half from the buyer. A disposition by will is valid, because death ends the relationship and the common property becomes subject to partition.
      • Tolentino (what is covered; shares): the co-ownership covers property acquired through work or industry, wages and salaries, and purchases made with them (substitution), but not the fruits of either party's own property. Under the Civil Code (Art. 144), shares followed each party's contribution, presumed equal absent proof, and a woman who helped maritally and contributed to the prosperity of the union shared at least in proportion to the value of her work. (The Family Code now treats care of the family and household as a joint contribution.)
      • Tolentino (debts and expenses): with no partnership between them, each party is personally liable for his or her own debts, except expenses to preserve the common property, which they bear proportionately (Arts. 485, 488 NCC), enforceable against each one's share. But where the woman buys household necessities and the man usually pays, a tacit agency arises and he is liable to sellers who relied on it. The cohabitants may validly form an ordinary partnership by following the law on partnerships. If they later marry each other, the Court of Appeals once held that what they acquired before becomes conjugal (Woodfine v. Woodfine), but Tolentino finds the contrary view (Ceniza v. Gella: each one's share in the co-ownership is exclusive property brought to the marriage) "more acceptable."
      • Forfeiture (void marriage, one party in good faith): the bad-faith party's share goes to the common children → if they default or waive, to their respective surviving descendants → if none, to the innocent party. Forfeiture takes effect upon termination of the cohabitation.
      Uribe (CivRev 2025): "In 147, as far as salaries and wages are concerned, will this be shared proportionately?" No: equal shares under Art. 147. "However, as to the property that may be acquired during this cohabitation or marriage (void), the rules on co-ownership will apply. So if there is no proof, then equal share; if there is proof of contribution, it will follow. Except if the contribution is for the maintenance of the household or family; she or he can claim 50% of the property during cohabitation. This is not applicable to 148."
      Maxey v. CA (129 SCRA 187, 1984; under NCC 144)

      Melbourne Maxey and Regina Morales lived together as husband and wife, with children, in a union that began before the Civil Code. Properties acquired during the cohabitation were later sold by Maxey, and Regina's children sued to recover their mother's share. Before the Civil Code took effect on August 30, 1950, the courts recognized an informal civil partnership in which common-law spouses had an equal share in property acquired through their joint efforts. Article 144 codified this, "but with the modification that the property governed by the rules on co-ownership may be acquired by either or both of them through their work or industry. Even if it is only the man who works, the property acquired during the man and wife relationship belongs through a fifty-fifty sharing to the two of them." The "real contribution" of a woman includes not only her earnings "but also her contribution to the family's material and spiritual goods through caring for the children, administering the household, husbanding scarce resources, freeing her husband from household tasks, and otherwise performing the traditional duties of a housewife." Held: the properties acquired during the union were co-owned by the partners in equal shares.

      Tolentino's summary of Maxey: the partners lived together from 1903 and married in 1919; after the woman's death, the survivor sold, in 1953, land acquired before their legal marriage. The children were entitled to recover one-half from the buyer, and a co-ownership arises "even if common-law wife does not work or is not gainfully employed."
      Tolentino on Art. 147 vs. Arts. 43 and 50 in void marriages. Art. 147 sets up a special co-ownership in void marriages, implying no ACP or CPG; but Art. 50, with Art. 43(2), expressly recognizes an ACP or CPG in certain void marriages (those under Art. 40). "It is extremely difficult to offer a solution to this inconsistency." Courts should choose the more equitable rule in each case, and forfeitures should be strictly construed. Forfeiture under Art. 43(2) reaches the guilty party's share in the net profits (which may include fruits and all acquisitions), while forfeiture under Art. 147 reaches only the share in property acquired through work or industry; Tolentino prefers the latter because it deprives less. (Compare Valdes, which applies Art. 147 to Art. 36 nullity and reserves Arts. 50–52 for Arts. 40 and 45.)
      Salas, Jr. v. Aguila (G.R. No. 202370, September 23, 2013)

      The marriage of Juan Sevilla Salas, Jr. and Eden Aguila was declared void for psychological incapacity. Eden later found properties (the "Discovered Properties") registered in Salas's name and in the name of "Juan S. Salas, married to Rubina C. Salas", and asked for their partition. Held: the regime is co-ownership under Art. 147, not a conjugal partnership. "Under this property regime, property acquired during the marriage is prima facie presumed to have been obtained through the couple's joint efforts and governed by the rules on co-ownership." Salas did not rebut the presumption, and Rubina, who claimed the properties as her own, failed to prove she had bought them with her own money (the words "married to Rubina" are merely descriptive). The partition was sustained, "but on the basis of co-ownership and not on the regime of conjugal partnership of gains."

      Valdes v. RTC, Quezon City (G.R. No. 122749, July 31, 1996; cited in the bar answers)

      In a marriage declared void under Art. 36, the property relations are governed by Art. 147, and the properties are liquidated under the rules on co-ownership, not Arts. 102 or 129. Arts. 50–52 (liquidation, presumptive legitimes, recording) apply only to marriages declared void under Art. 40 and to annulled marriages. Diño v. Diño (G.R. No. 178044, January 19, 2011) applied this: for an Art. 36 void marriage under Art. 147, delivery of the presumptive legitime is not a precondition to the issuance of the decree. This is the basis of the 2018 bar answer that Shalimar is not entitled to presumptive legitime in the Sancho–Sandy liquidation.

      2016 Bar: Bernard and Dorothy, both capacitated to marry, lived together as common-law spouses. Dorothy worked in Dubai and sent money to Bernard, who used it to buy a lot and later sold it without her consent. (a) Will her suit to nullify the sale prosper? (b) Same, if she was jobless and only cared for the family and household?

      (a) Yes, unless the buyer bought in good faith and for value. Under Art. 147, neither party may dispose of his or her share in the property acquired during the cohabitation without the other's consent until the cohabitation ends. (b) Yes, still. Her care and maintenance of the family and household is deemed a joint contribution, so the lot is co-owned equally, and her consent remains necessary. (The UP BOC note gives credit to examinees who reasoned that Art. 147 does not apply because they were not living together as husband and wife while she was abroad.)

      2023 Bar: Santiago and Lucia lived together as common-law spouses from 2000. They acquired several properties, mainly from Lucia's salon and water-refilling business. The purchase records were destroyed by Typhoon Ondoy. In 2023 Lucia sued, claiming all the properties. Is she correct?

      No, assuming they were capacitated to marry each other. Under Art. 147, properties acquired during the cohabitation are presumed obtained by joint efforts and owned equally, and a party who cared for the household is deemed to have contributed (Paterno v. Paterno, 2020; Barrido v. Nonato, 2014). The burden of proving otherwise is on Lucia, and she has no records. (If they were not capacitated, Art. 148 would require proof of Santiago's actual contribution.)

      2010 Bar: G and B married on July 3, 1989. In 2001, the marriage was declared void under Art. 36. They had (1) a house and lot bought by B on installment on August 3, 1988 (one-third down payment from B; one-third paid by G in 1990 from a cash gift her parents gave her at graduation in 1989; the rest from their joint income) and (2) an apartment unit donated to B by an uncle in 1987. Who owns them?

      No ACP or CPG ever existed. Art. 147 governs (they were capacitated). If B acquired ownership of the house and lot on August 3, 1988, before the marriage, it is his, subject to reimbursing G for her payment and her half of the payments from joint income. If ownership was acquired during the cohabitation, it is co-owned: one-third is B's (his premarital down payment), one-third is G's (her gift money, which is not wages), and one-third is co-owned equally (joint income). Altogether they hold it in equal shares. The apartment is B's alone (acquired before the cohabitation, and by gratuitous title). If they had married in 1987, the result would be the same: NCC 144 is substantially identical, and Art. 147 applies retroactively under Art. 256 because no vested right is impaired.

      1997 Bar: Luis and Rizza, both 26 and single, lived together for 20 years. Luis worked, and Rizza kept house. They have (a) ₱200,000 of Luis's savings from his salary; (b) a house and lot worth ₱500,000 bought with ₱200,000 from the sale of palay harvested from Luis's hacienda and ₱300,000 from the rentals of Rizza's building; (c) a car worth ₱100,000 donated to Rizza by her parents. Allocation?

      (a) Salary: equal shares (Art. 147). (b) Acquired through the fruits of their separate properties, so co-owned in proportion to contributions: Luis two-fifths, Rizza three-fifths (UPLC answer). (c) Car: Rizza's alone (gratuitous title). Had they been validly married 20 years earlier (under the NCC), the CPG would apply, and the salary, the house and lot (bought from fruits) would be conjugal and divided equally, while the car would be Rizza's exclusive property.

      Art. 148: co-ownership limited to actual joint contribution

      Art. 148, FC. In cases of cohabitation not falling under the preceding Article, only the properties acquired by both of the parties through their actual joint contribution of money, property, or industry shall be owned by them in common in proportion to their respective contributions. In the absence of proof to the contrary, their contributions and corresponding shares are presumed to be equal. The same rule and presumption shall apply to joint deposits of money and evidences of credit.
      If one of the parties is validly married to another, his or her share in the co-ownership shall accrue to the absolute community or conjugal partnership existing in such valid marriage. If the party who acted in bad faith is not validly married to another, his or her share shall be forfeited in the manner provided in the last paragraph of the preceding Article.
      The foregoing rules on forfeiture shall likewise apply even if both parties are in bad faith. (144a)

      Rules

      • Co-ownership arises only over property acquired through actual joint contribution of money, property or industry, owned in proportion to the contributions.
      • The presumption of equal shares arises only once the fact of actual joint contribution is shown, and it covers the extent of each contribution. There is no presumption that property was acquired jointly (Ventura; Go-Bangayan; Borromeo v. Descallar).
      • Care of the home, children and household, and "spiritual or moral inspiration", are not contributions (Cariño).
      • Wages and salaries belong to the earner (Cariño). If the earner is validly married to someone else, they belong to that marriage's ACP or CPG (2009 Bar).
      • Share of a party validly married to another → accrues to the ACP or CPG of the valid marriage. Share of a bad-faith party not validly married to another → forfeited as in Art. 147. The forfeiture rules apply even if both are in bad faith.
      • Tolentino (bad faith in adulterous cohabitation): the share of the party who is not married to another stays with him or her if he or she did not know of the other's marriage. If he or she knew when the cohabitation began, the share is forfeited to the common children or descendants. If there are none, Art. 147 would give it to the innocent party, but under Art. 148 there is no "innocent" party, since the other is married. The last paragraph (forfeiture "even if both parties are in bad faith") should apply, Tolentino says, only when there are common children or descendants. Without them, the bad-faith unmarried party's share should stay with him or her: "to forfeit it in favor of the married party would be rewarding infidelity."
      • Tolentino (adulterous relations and the legal spouse): Art. 147 does not cover adulterous cohabitation. The legal spouses' ACP or CPG continues, so no co-ownership can exist between a spouse and the paramour over that spouse's earnings or work; Art. 148's second paragraph allows co-ownership only of what the two acquired by actual joint contribution. In Layson v. Oliquino (CA, 47 O.G. 4216), a husband bought a lot and built a house with his earnings, titled in his mistress's name; they were conjugal property of the legal marriage, and the "gift" to the mistress could not prejudice the wife.
      Juaniza v. Jose (89 SCRA 306, 1979)

      Eugenio Jose, a married man, lived with Rosalia Arroyo. His jeepney, registered in his name, figured in a collision, and the victims sued both. Held: the co-ownership under NCC 144 "requires that the man and the woman living together must not in any way be incapacitated to contract marriage." Since Jose was legally married to Socorro Ramos, "Arroyo cannot be a co-owner of the jeepney. The jeepney belongs to the conjugal partnership of Jose and his legal wife." There was therefore no basis to hold Arroyo liable for damages as a co-owner. (This is the rule now codified in Art. 148.)

      Gomez v. Lipana (33 SCRA 615, 1970)

      The husband married a second wife (1935) while his first marriage subsisted. (1) A bigamous marriage, void under the Marriage Law, may be collaterally attacked in the intestate proceedings. (2) The party invoking the exceptions under Sec. 29 of the Marriage Law (absence of the first spouse) bears the burden of proving them. (3) The second wife could not invoke Art. 1417 of the Spanish Civil Code to forfeit the husband's share, because that partnership terminated on his death in 1958, when the Spanish Code was no longer in force. The Court divided the property acquired during the second union: the second wife's half was recognized as hers, and the husband's half pertained to the conjugal partnership of the first, subsisting marriage (as summarized in Consuegra).

      Vda. de Consuegra v. GSIS (37 SCRA 315, 1971)

      Jose Consuegra married Rosario Diaz and later, while the first marriage subsisted, married Basilia Berdin in good faith. The GSIS divided his retirement insurance proceeds equally between the first wife and the second wife with her children. Held: correct. Citing Gomez v. Lipana, the first marriage was never dissolved, so its conjugal partnership never ceased. As to the second wife, although the second marriage was void, "the only just and equitable solution in this case would be to recognize the right of the second wife to her share of one-half in the property acquired by her and her husband and consider the other half as pertaining to the conjugal partnership of the first marriage."

      Yap v. CA (145 SCRA 229, 1986)

      Maning Yap's first marriage, to Talina Bianong, was valid. His second marriage, to Nancy Yap, was void under the Marriage Law (Act 3613). Held: the second "wife" got no share in the estate of the husband; only the legal wife did. (A bigamous "spouse" is not an heir and has no share in property she did not help acquire.)

      Cariño v. Cariño (351 SCRA 127, February 2, 2001)

      SPO4 Santiago Cariño married Susan Nicdao (1969, with no marriage license) and then Susan Yee (1992) while the first marriage had not been judicially declared void. Both "wives" claimed his death benefits. (1) A judicial declaration of nullity of the prior marriage is required before remarriage (Art. 40), so the second marriage is also void. "Considering that the two marriages are void ab initio, the applicable property regime would not be absolute community or conjugal partnership of property, but rather, be governed by the provisions of Articles 147 and 148." (2) Under Art. 148, which covers "bigamous marriages, adulterous relationships, relationships in a state of concubine, relationships where both man and woman are married to other persons, multiple alliances of the same married man," the properties acquired through actual joint contribution belong to the co-ownership. "Wages and salaries earned by each party belong to him or her exclusively. Then too, contributions in the form of care of the home, children and household, or spiritual or moral inspiration, are excluded in this regime." Susan Yee, having made no contribution, had no share in the benefits. (3) The first marriage, void for lack of a license, falls under Art. 147, so the death benefits from his salary were owned equally by Nicdao and Santiago. His half passed to his legal heirs, his children with Nicdao, not to Nicdao herself, since she was not his legal spouse.

      Go-Bangayan v. Bangayan (G.R. No. 201061, July 3, 2013)

      Benjamin Bangayan, married to Azucena, lived with Sally Go and signed a purported marriage contract with her. The marriage was void (and, the Court found, inexistent, the supposed license being fictitious). Several properties were titled in the name of "Benjamin, married to Sally". Held: "the words 'married to' preceding the name of a spouse are merely descriptive of the civil status of the registered owner. Such words do not prove co-ownership. Without proof of actual contribution from either or both spouses, there can be no co-ownership under Article 148."

      Ventura, Jr. v. Spouses Abuda (G.R. No. 202932, October 23, 2013)

      Socorro married Esteban Abuda while her prior marriage subsisted, so the union fell under Art. 148. The petitioner, Edilberto, claimed shares in the properties through that union. Held: as Edilberto himself admitted, quoting Borromeo v. Descallar, "it is necessary for each of the partners to prove his or her actual contributions to the acquisition of property in order to be able to lay claim to any portion of it. Presumptions of co-ownership and equal contribution do not apply." Without proof of Socorro's actual contribution, no co-ownership arose.

      2024 Bar (and CivRev 2025 slide): In 2021, Jesse and Celeste got married. After a year, Jesse took all their savings and abandoned Celeste for his paramour, Diana. Jesse asked Diana to quit her job. Diana hesitated because she had no money and was drowning in debt, but Jesse promised to provide for all her needs. They lived together, and the next day they bought a brand-new car registered exclusively in Diana's name. Celeste sued to recover the car, claiming it is part of her community property. Diana countered that she and Jesse are co-owners. Can Celeste recover the car?

      Yes. Jesse is not capacitated to marry Diana (he is married to Celeste), so Art. 148 governs. Diana, jobless and in debt, could not have contributed to the purchase. Her claim of co-ownership fails, and registration in her name does not prove ownership. The money came from Jesse's and Celeste's savings, which are community property (Arts. 91, 93, 75). In any case, Jesse's share in any co-ownership with Diana would accrue to the ACP (Art. 148, 2nd par.). Sir in class: argue from the facts and the law, not by conclusion ("the money used was the salary only of the husband … Diana has no money and she is drowning in debts"). Would it matter if Diana cooked and kept house for Jesse? No. "Art. 148, contribution by way of maintenance of the household does not matter. It is only available if it would fall under 147."

      UP BOC 2011 MCQ: Venecio and Ester lived as common-law spouses, both still married to others from whom they had been separated in fact for years. Each earned income from their own profession and enterprise. Nature of their incomes?

      B: separate, since their property relations with their legal spouses are still subsisting. Each income belongs to the earner's ACP or CPG with his or her lawful spouse (Art. 148).

      UP BOC 2009 TF: "If there is no marriage settlement, the salary of a 'spouse' in an adulterous marriage belongs to the conjugal partnership of gains."

      False. The salary of a married partner belongs to the ACP or CPG of his or her lawful marriage. The paramour is deemed not to have contributed to earning it (Art. 148).

      2000 / 1997 / 1992 Bar: In 1989, Rico (a widower, 40) cohabited with Cora (a widow, 30), and they bought rice land from their combined earnings. They separated, and Rico lived with Mabel (16), who kept house while Rico bought coconut land from his savings. They separated a year later, and Rico married Letty, who bought a mango orchard from her own earnings during the marriage. Who owns each, under what regime?

      Rice land: Rico and Cora as co-owners (Art. 147; both capacitated). After Rico married Letty, his half became ACP property of Rico and Letty. Coconut land: Rico alone. Mabel, at 16, was not capacitated to marry, so Art. 148 applies, and her housekeeping is not a contribution. It later became ACP property of Rico and Letty (owned at the celebration). Mango orchard: ACP of Rico and Letty (acquired during the marriage; Arts. 75, 91).

      2000 Bar: Tony (a bank vice-president) and Susan (an entertainer who stopped working and kept house) lived together for five years from 1989, both capacitated to marry, and Tony bought a house and lot. (a) Who is entitled to it? (b) Would it differ if Tony could not marry Susan because he was legally separated from his wife, Alice?

      (a) Tony and Susan are co-owners in equal shares (Art. 147; her care of the household counts). (b) Yes. A legally separated spouse is still married, so Art. 148 applies, Susan's housekeeping is not a contribution, and she gets nothing. If Tony cohabited with Susan after the decree of legal separation, the house and lot is his exclusive property (the ACP or CPG with Alice having been dissolved). If before, it belongs to his community or partnership with Alice.

      1991 Bar: In June 1985, James married Mary. In September 1988, he also married Ophelia, and they had two children and acquired a residential lot. Mary died in July 1989. In July 1990, James married Shirley. What regime governed James and Ophelia?

      Art. 148. The marriage to Ophelia was bigamous and void, and James was not capacitated to marry her. Only property acquired through their actual joint contribution is co-owned in proportion to their contributions, and James's share accrued to his CPG with Mary while that marriage subsisted.

      Checklist: Arts. 147–148

      1. No valid marriage, or a void marriage. Voidable marriages use the ACP or CPG.
      2. Art. 147: a man and a woman, capacitated to marry each other, living exclusively as husband and wife. Wages and salaries → equal. Property acquired through work or industry → co-owned, presumed joint and equal; care of the household counts. No disposition of one's share without consent until the cohabitation ends. Forfeiture of the bad-faith party's share → common children → descendants → innocent party, upon termination of the cohabitation.
      3. Art. 148: all other cohabitations. Co-ownership only over what was acquired by actual joint contribution, in proportion; equal shares are presumed only as to the amount once contribution is shown; household care does not count; wages belong to the earner; the share of a party validly married to another → that marriage's ACP or CPG; forfeiture rules apply even if both are in bad faith.
      4. Sir's rule of thumb: a third person affected (either party married to another) → 148; otherwise → 147.
      5. Gratuitous acquisitions and premarital property are never part of either co-ownership. "Married to" in a title is descriptive only (Go-Bangayan; Salas).
      6. Art. 147 liquidation of a void Art. 36 marriage follows co-ownership; no presumptive legitimes are required (Valdes; Diño).

      The Family

      Title V, Chapter 1, Family Code, Arts. 149–151 (syllabus XI), with NCC 2035 and the rule on condition precedents in the Rules of Court. Covers the policy declaration (Art. 149), the closed list of family relations (Art. 150), and the earnest-efforts requirement for suits between family members (Art. 151). Cases: Alavado, Arroyo, Gayon, Wainwright-Versoza, Heirs of Favis and Salazar v. Felias (the syllabus lists Salazar here, but its doctrine is on the family home, so it is digested in the next section).

      Art. 149: the family as a basic social institution

      Art. 149, FC. The family, being the foundation of the nation, is a basic social institution which public policy cherishes and protects. Consequently, family relations are governed by law and no custom, practice or agreement destructive of the family shall be recognized or given effect. (216a, 218a)
      • Family relations are governed by law, not by the parties' will. Rights and duties within the family are generally inalienable, non-transferable, imprescriptible and not subject to waiver.
      • A custom, practice or agreement destructive of the family is not recognized. Examples: an agreement between spouses to live separately or to "free" each other to cohabit with others; a stipulation renouncing future support; a waiver of future legitime (NCC 905, 2035).
      • Cf. Const. Art. XV, Sec. 1 (the State recognizes the Filipino family as the foundation of the nation) and Art. II, Sec. 12.
      Tolentino (Art. 149): the Spanish Civil Code had no declaration of policy; the Code Commission added principles that sustain family solidarity, as guidance for the courts and for their "wholesome influence". "The vitality and strength of the State depends upon the solidarity of its nucleus, the family." The family has two aspects. The internal aspect (the spouses' intimate relations, the career parents choose for a child, domestic practices) is natural and moral and is beyond the reach of law. The external aspect is regulated by law only where third persons or the public interest are involved, or to protect the wife and children from abuse (support, parental authority). Family law is marked by (1) increasing State intervention and (2) its obligatory character: its rules are of public order and cannot be set aside by agreement except in very exceptional cases, and family rights and duties cannot be performed through agents.
      Alavado v. City Government of Tacloban (139 SCRA 230, 1985)

      The claimant's status as the deceased Alavado's lawful wife (and so her right to what was due the family) was contested by the city. Held: the presumption that a man and a woman deporting themselves as husband and wife are legally married stands. "Public and open cohabitation as husband and wife, birth and baptismal certificates of children born unto them after the celebration of the questioned marriage, and a statement of such marriage in subsequent document were held to be competent evidence as proof of said marriage." Nothing in the records overthrew the presumption in favor of the claimant's marriage to the deceased. (The case illustrates the law's leaning toward the validity of marriage and the solidarity of the family, which Art. 149 protects.)

      Arroyo, Jr. v. CA (203 SCRA 750, 1991)

      Dr. Jorge Neri filed a complaint for adultery against his wife, Ruby Vera-Neri, and Eduardo Arroyo, who were convicted. The wife later executed an affidavit that she had been pardoned, and the husband filed a manifestation that he was no longer interested in prosecuting. Held: the conviction stands. Pardon must be given before the institution of the criminal action, and the husband's later desistance does not bind the State: "while Article 344 of the Revised Penal Code provides that the crime of adultery cannot be prosecuted without the offended spouse's complaint, once the complaint has been filed, the control of the case passes to the public prosecutor. Enforcement of our law on adultery is not exclusively, nor even principally, a matter of vindication of the private honor of the offended spouse … Such enforcement relates, more importantly, to protection of the basic social institutions of marriage and the family in the preservation of which the State has the strongest interest; the public policy here involved is of the most fundamental kind."

      Quiz traps (Art. 149): "Family relations are governed by custom and by the agreement of the parties" → false: by law. "A custom destructive of the family is valid if long practiced in the locality" → false: no custom, practice or agreement destructive of the family is recognized. "Adultery is a private crime, so the offended spouse controls the case until judgment" → false (Arroyo): control passes to the public prosecutor once the complaint is filed.

      Art. 150: who are members of the family

      Art. 150, FC. Family relations include those: (1) Between husband and wife; (2) Between parents and children; (3) Among other ascendants and descendants; and (4) Among brothers and sisters, whether of the full or half-blood. (217a)
      Count the items: there are four. Some student reviewers (including the B29 provisions file and some notes) print only three items and drop "(3) Among other ascendants and descendants". The official text, which Tolentino reproduces (p. 504), has four. So grandparents and grandchildren are family under Art. 150, and a suit between them requires earnest efforts.
      • The list is exclusive and strictly construed, because Art. 151 is an exception to the general right to sue (Gayon).
      • Brothers and sisters are included "whether of the full or half-blood", and the text does not distinguish legitimate from illegitimate.
      • Not included: relatives by affinity (brothers- and sisters-in-law, parents-in-law, stepparents and stepchildren), uncles and aunts, nephews and nieces, and cousins.
      Tolentino (Art. 150): relationship may be natural (consanguinity, legitimate or illegitimate; and affinity), civil (adoption) or religious (from baptism or confirmation). For Art. 150, religious relationship and affinity are given no legal effect. Family relations in the broad sense are not limited to this list: civil relationship (adoption) and collateral consanguinity up to the fifth degree are recognized elsewhere in the law, e.g., in intestate succession.

      Art. 151: earnest efforts toward a compromise

      Art. 151, FC. No suit between members of the same family shall prosper unless it should appear from the verified complaint or petition that earnest efforts toward a compromise have been made, but that the same have failed. If it is shown that no such efforts were in fact made, the same case must be dismissed.
      This rule shall not apply to cases which may not be the subject of compromise under the Civil Code. (222a)
      Art. 2035, NCC. No compromise upon the following questions shall be valid: (1) The civil status of persons; (2) The validity of a marriage or a legal separation; (3) Any ground for legal separation; (4) Future support; (5) The jurisdiction of courts; (6) Future legitime.

      Requisites and nature

      1. The suit is between members of the same family as enumerated in Art. 150, and all the parties are family; if a stranger is a co-party, Art. 151 does not apply.
      2. The subject is compromisable.
      3. The verified complaint or petition must allege that earnest efforts toward a compromise were made and failed.
      4. The requirement is a condition precedent, not a jurisdictional requirement. Non-compliance is a ground to dismiss (Rule 16, Sec. 1(j), 1997 Rules: "a condition precedent for filing the claim has not been complied with"; now an affirmative defense under Rule 8, Sec. 12 of the 2019 amendments). It is waived if not raised in a motion to dismiss or the answer, and the court cannot dismiss on that ground motu proprio (Heirs of Favis).
      Gayon v. Gayon (36 SCRA 104, 1970)

      Pedro Gayon sued the spouses Silvestre Gayon and Genoveva de Gayon over land. Silvestre had died before the complaint was filed, and the suit was in substance against his widow and heirs. The trial court dismissed for failure to allege earnest efforts under NCC 222 (now Art. 151), since the plaintiff and the deceased were brothers. Held: dismissal reversed. The defendants were Silvestre's surviving spouse and children, and "inasmuch as a sister-in-law, nephew or niece is not included in the enumeration contained in Article 217 [now Art. 150], … which should be construed strictly, it being an exception to the general rule, it follows that the same does not come within the purview of Art. 222, and plaintiff's failure to seek a compromise before filing the complaint does not bar the same."

      Wainwright-Versoza v. Versoza (26 SCRA 78, 1968)

      A wife (with her child) sued her husband for support. The husband moved to dismiss for failure to allege earnest efforts toward a compromise under NCC 222. Held: the action may proceed. "Since the present action also revolves on the right to future support and because compromise on future support is prescribed, then the conclusion is irresistible that an attempt at compromise of future support and failure thereof is not a condition precedent to the filing of the present suit. It need not be alleged in the complaint." (Art. 151, last paragraph, with NCC 2035(4).)

      Heirs of Favis, Sr. v. Gonzales (G.R. No. 185922, January 15, 2014)

      The children of Dr. Mariano Favis, Sr. by his first marriage sued his second wife, Juana Gonzales, their son Mariano, Jr., and Mariano Jr.'s wife and children, to annul a deed of donation Dr. Favis had executed in favor of those grandchildren. The RTC ruled for the plaintiffs; the CA motu proprio dismissed the complaint because it did not allege earnest efforts toward a compromise. Held: CA reversed. Failure to allege earnest efforts is not a jurisdictional defect; it is a condition precedent whose non-fulfillment is a ground for a motion to dismiss. "No motion to dismiss the complaint based on the failure to comply with a condition precedent was filed in the trial court and neither was such failure assigned as error in the appeal that respondent brought before the Court of Appeals. Therefore the rule on deemed waiver of the non-jurisdictional defense or objection is wholly applicable to respondent." Under Rule 9, Sec. 1, the court may dismiss on its own only for lack of jurisdiction over the subject matter, litis pendentia, res judicata or prescription.

      Other cases often cited (not in Sir's syllabus)

      Gonzales v. Lopez (160 SCRA 346, 1988), cited by Tolentino: Art. 151 does not apply where the defendants include strangers to the family. Hontiveros v. RTC (G.R. No. 125465, June 29, 1999): a suit by spouses against the husband's brother and the brother's wife is not covered, because the sisters-in-law are not "members of the same family"; the inclusion of a stranger takes the case out of the article. Mendoza v. CA (19 SCRA 756, 1967): an action involving a non-compromisable question (there, support) needs no allegation of earnest efforts.

      Tolentino (Art. 151): the Code Commission's reason: "It is difficult to imagine a sadder and more tragic spectacle than a litigation between members of the same family"; a suit between close relatives "generates deeper bitterness than between strangers". The article does not apply where the defendants are strangers to the principal parties, is limited to the members listed in Art. 150 (Gayon), and does not cover non-compromisable questions.
