"Once filiation is established, whether legitimate or illegitimate, the child is entitled to recognition and support as a matter of legal obligation" (B29 reviewer's summary). (Facts from the reviewer and general knowledge; the full text was not among the sources.)

      Perla v. Baring (G.R. No. 172471, November 12, 2012)

      Mirasol Baring and her son Randy sued Antonio Perla for support, claiming he was Randy's father. Their evidence included a birth certificate naming Antonio as father, which he did not sign, a baptismal certificate, and testimony. Held: complaint dismissed. "An order for support must be issued only if paternity or filiation is established by clear and convincing evidence. Just like in a birth certificate, the lack of participation of the supposed father in the preparation of a baptismal certificate renders this document incompetent to prove paternity." To prove open and continuous possession of status, "there must be evidence of the manifestation of the permanent intention of the supposed father to consider the child as his, by continuous and clear manifestations of parental affection and care, which cannot be attributed to pure charity." (Doctrine from the B29 reviewer; facts from general knowledge.)

      Heirs of Roldan v. Heirs of Roldan (G.R. No. 202578, September 27, 2017)

      Not found in any of your sources. Sir lists it under Proof of Filiation (general). From general recollection (verify before relying on it): in a partition case between two sets of Roldan heirs, the Court held that the filiation of a party claiming to be an heir may be passed upon in the partition case itself, without a separate action to establish filiation. Read the full text if this case comes up in recitation.

      Reyes v. CA (135 SCRA 439, 1985)

      Irene Delgado claimed to be the recognized natural child of the late Francisco Delgado, relying on certificates of birth he had not signed. Held: not recognized. "The birth certificate, to be sufficient recognition, must be signed by the father and mother jointly, or by the mother alone if the father refuses, otherwise she may be penalized; and if the alleged father did not sign in the birth certificate, the placing of his name by the mother, or doctor or registrar, is incompetent evidence of paternity of said child." Nor can such a birth certificate be taken as recognition in a public instrument.

      Castro v. CA (173 SCRA 656, 1989; the syllabus prints 658)

      Benita claimed to be the natural child of Eustaquio Castro, born in 1919. Eustaquio himself had reported and registered her birth, but he did not sign the birth certificate, and the record was not preserved. Her status was contested some 60 years later. Held: the omissions were not held against her. "Strictly speaking, a birth certificate to be sufficient for purposes of recognizing a child must be signed by the father and mother jointly and if the father refuses, by the mother alone otherwise she may be penalized. It was Eustaquio himself who had the birth of Benita reported and registered. There is no indication in the records that Eustaquio should have known in 1919 that apart from reporting the birth of a child, he should also have signed the certificate and seen to it that it was preserved for 60 years." (Contrast Reyes: here the father himself caused the registration.)

      Mendoza v. IAC (152 SCRA 445, 1987; caption as in the syllabus)

      Modesta Gabuya claimed to have been recognized as a natural child by her mother, Nicolasa Gabuya. Her only document was a certificate of birth and baptism signed by the assistant parish priest of Pardo, Cebu City, stating that she was Nicolasa's illegitimate daughter. Held: not enough. "Recognition or acknowledgment of a natural child under said Code must be made in a record of birth, a will, a statement before a court of record, or in some other public document. … Philippine jurisprudence is consistent and uniform in ruling that the canonical certificate of baptism is not sufficient to prove recognition." (Uribe's Doctrines prints these facts under this caption; the parties' names do not match it, so the caption may be off.)

      Uribe (2018 situationer): "If the only evidence presented as proof of filiation is a birth certificate with the name of the putative father. Is that a sufficient basis that the child is the child of that person?" No. "You can actually put Gokongwei's name." The father must have signed or otherwise taken part in the registration (Reyes; Vda. de Alberto; Baluyut).

      Cases: final judgment, admissions, possession of status

      Ramos v. Ramos (61 SCRA 284, 1974)

      The plaintiffs claimed to be natural children of Martin Ramos and sued for their shares in his estate; the legitimate heirs pleaded res judicata based on the 1913 intestate proceeding (Civil Case No. 217). Held (on status): "It is true that the acknowledgment of the plaintiffs is not evidenced by a record of birth, will or other public document (Art. 131, Old Civil Code). But the record of Civil Case No. 217 … indubitably shows that the plaintiffs were treated as acknowledged natural children of Martin Ramos. The reasonable inference is that they were in the continuous possession of the status of natural children of Martin Ramos, as evidenced by his direct acts and the acts of his family." (Per the case digest, their claim to recover their shares was, however, held barred by prescription and laches; verify if asked.)

      Lim v. CA (65 SCRA 160, 1975)

      Felisa Lim offered her marriage contract, which named the alleged father, as a public document of recognition. Held: insufficient. "The marriage contract presented by Felisa Lim does not satisfy the requirements of solemnity prescribed by article 131 of the Civil Code of 1889. Such contract is not a written act with the intervention of a notary; it is not an instrument executed in due form before a notary and certified by him. The marriage contract is a mere declaration by the contracting parties, in the presence of the person solemnizing the marriage and of two witnesses of legal age, that they take each other as husband and wife … The marriage contract does not possess the requisites of a public document of recognition. Be it remembered that recognition, under the Civil Code of 1889, 'must be precise, express and solemn.'"

      Ranas v. Ranas (cited by Tolentino as 134 SCRA 260; the syllabus prints 64 SCRA 260)

      Listed under "signed and handwritten private instrument". Your sources give no facts. Tolentino cites it for two propositions: in an admission of filiation in a document, "the intent to recognize the child must be sufficiently apparent"; and family pictures, relatives' affidavits, the claimant's biodata, unsigned marriage contracts, school records and other writings not signed by the alleged father do not constitute evidence of filiation. Related modern rule (Dela Cruz v. Gracia, G.R. No. 177728, July 31, 2009): a private handwritten instrument must be signed by the parent if it is the only evidence; if other evidence corroborates it, it is enough that the parent wrote it.

      Mendoza v. CA (201 SCRA 675, September 24, 1991)

      Teopista Toring Tuñacao sued Casimiro Mendoza for recognition as his illegitimate daughter. She lived with her mother, not with Casimiro, although all lived in Omapad, Mandaue City; Casimiro and his wife were childless, yet another alleged illegitimate child, Vicente Toring, lived with them. Teopista did not use Casimiro's surname, and his giving of money through relatives was "off-and-on". Held: open and continuous possession was not shown. "'Continuous' does not mean that the concession of status shall continue forever but only that it shall not be of an intermittent character while it continues. The possession of such status means that the father has treated the child as his own, directly and not through others, spontaneously and without concealment though without publicity (since the relation is illegitimate). There must be a showing of the permanent intention of the supposed father to consider the child as his own, by continuous and clear manifestation of paternal affection and care." Her filiation was nonetheless upheld under "other means allowed by the Rules of Court": the testimony of Mendoza relatives on pedigree and family reputation (Rule 130).

      When the action may be brought (Arts. 173, 175)

      Art. 173, FC. The action to claim legitimacy may be brought by the child during his or her lifetime and shall be transmitted to the heirs should the child die during minority or in a state of insanity. In these cases, the heirs shall have a period of five years within which to institute the action.
      The action already commenced by the child shall survive notwithstanding the death of either or both of the parties. (268a)
      Art. 175, FC. Illegitimate children may establish their illegitimate filiation in the same way and on the same evidence as legitimate children.
      The action must be brought within the same period specified in Article 173, except when the action is based on the second paragraph of Article 172, in which case the action may be brought during the lifetime of the alleged parent. (289a)
      Tolentino (Arts. 173, 175): a disputed legitimacy can be resolved only in a direct action by the proper parties within the period (Rosales v. Castillo, 132 SCRA 132). The child's action does not prescribe while he lives and cannot be renounced: "rights which emanate or are derived from blood are not subject either to prescription or waiver." It passes to his heirs only if he dies during minority or insanity, and then for five years. An illegitimate child uses the same evidence, period and parties; if the evidence is secondary, the action must be brought during the alleged parent's lifetime, so that "the supposed parent is given the chance to dispute personally the evidence of the paternity attributed to him". An illegitimate child "should be allowed that status if the evidence presented satisfies the judicial mind" (Dempsey).
      Ara and Garcia v. Pizarro and Rossi (G.R. No. 187273, February 15, 2017)

      The petitioners claimed to be children of the late Josefa A. Ara, mother of the respondents, and sought shares in her estate. For at least one petitioner, there was no record of birth, final judgment or signed admission by Josefa; the claim rested on secondary evidence, and the action was filed after her death. Held: that claim fails. "Even without a record of birth appearing in the civil register or a final judgement, filiation may still be established after the death of a putative parent through an admission of filiation in a public document or a private handwritten instrument, signed by the parent concerned. Absent such admission, a deceased person will have no opportunity to contest a claim of filiation." (Doctrine from the B29 reviewer.)

      Uribe (Quiz 1, item 10, and Quiz 5): "The filiation of illegitimate children may be established by open and continuous possession of status of a child after the death of the alleged parent." In the Quiz 1 discussion, the class said the action must be brought during the parent's lifetime: possession of status is enjoyed "nung buhay pa siya". Sir pushed back: "Di naman mandatory siguro na during the lifetime dahil 'may'." He then pointed to Art. 172's "any other means allowed by the Rules of Court and special laws": "Ano kayang proof diyan? DNA testing. Even patay na ang alleged parent, pwede pa maprove ang filiation by 2nd paragraph of Art. 172. See Aquino v. Aquino and Yap v. Yap → remanded to trial court to prove filiation kahit na patay na ang parent." In Quiz 5 he asked the reverse question ("Is it not clear under the last paragraph of 175 that … the 2nd paragraph of Art. 172 can only be used during the lifetime of the putative father?"), and the posted answer was "D or E". On DNA: "Yung recent decisions ng SC, assuming sumunod sa protocols, DNA testing is 99.99%."
      Conflict: secondary proof after the alleged parent's death. The text, Tolentino and Ara v. Pizarro: an illegitimate child relying on Art. 172's second paragraph (possession of status or other means) must sue during the alleged parent's lifetime; after death, only primary evidence (a record of birth, final judgment or signed admission) will do. Sir reads "may be brought during the lifetime" as permissive, and cites Aquino and Yap for allowing DNA evidence after death. Sir's past keys follow the codal: "After the death of the alleged parent, the filiation of an illegitimate child may be established by any of the following except: … (d) the open and continuous possession of the status of an illegitimate child" was keyed (d), with his note: "That's because the law says 'may.' … Sir doesn't think this is good law because technology has already improved. Even if the person is already dead, you can still get his DNA to prove filiation. So it's like the law is regressing." The T/F "The filiation of illegitimate children may be established by the open and continuous possession of the status of a child after the death of the alleged parent" was keyed false in the older quiz. In the 2025 version, the old answer was replaced by "any other means allowed by the Rules of Court and special laws", and the class notes record "D or E". On a written quiz: answer with Art. 175 (secondary proof only during the parent's lifetime), and if there is room, add that Sir and Aquino/Yap would allow DNA after death. Note also: for a legitimate child (Art. 173), the parent's death does not bar any kind of proof (Uribe midterm #45, keyed "none of the above").

      Cases: proof of illegitimate filiation

      Vda. de Alberto v. CA (173 SCRA 436, 1989)

      A claimant sought recognition as the illegitimate child of the deceased Alberto, against the widow, relying in part on a birth certificate naming the alleged father, which he had not signed. Held: "A birth certificate not signed by the alleged father therein indicated, like in the instant case, is not competent evidence of paternity."

      Baluyut v. Baluyut (186 SCRA 506, 1990; the syllabus prints "Baluyot, 166 SCRA 606")

      The petitioners claimed to be spurious children of the late Enrique Baluyut and sought to share in his estate. Their birth records were in his name but not signed by him, and they presented no authentic writing or statement in a court of record. Held: not recognized. "There is no evidence as required by Article 278 which proves that the petitioners were recognized by the deceased during his lifetime as his spurious children. The petitioners' records of birth, although in the name of Enrique Baluyut, were not signed by the latter. There was no authentic writing presented nor any statement in a court of record which would prove that the petitioners were recognized by the deceased."

      Paterno v. Paterno (186 SCRA 630, 1990; not the 2020 property-relations case of the same name)

      The private respondents claimed to be illegitimate children of the late Dr. Paterno; his widow, Jacoba T. Paterno, denied it. Their witnesses testified, with some inconsistencies, that Dr. Paterno had treated them as his children from birth. Held: filiation proved. "True, certain inconsistencies may be noted in the testimony given by the witnesses for the private respondents, but it is on the whole unanimous and consistent as to the really crucial fact that Dr. Paterno treated and acted towards said respondents, from their birth onward, in a manner only a real father would and leaving little doubt that he recognized and considered them as in truth his children. The simple denials of the widow, petitioner Jacoba T. Paterno, do not suffice to refute such proof."

      Compulsory recognition in criminal cases (RPC 345)

      Art. 345, RPC. Persons guilty of rape, seduction or abduction, shall also be sentenced: 1. To indemnify the offended woman. 2. To acknowledge the offspring, unless the law should prevent him from so doing. 3. In every case to support the offspring. …
      People v. Rafanan (182 SCRA 811, 1990)

      The accused was convicted of raping Filomena, and a child was born of the rape; the record did not show the child's identity. Held: the trial court correctly sentenced him "to acknowledge and support her off-spring", under RPC 345 and NCC 283(1) (the father must recognize the child "in cases of rape, abduction or seduction, when the period of the offense coincides more or less with that of the conception").

      People v. Rizo (189 SCRA 265, 1990)

      The trial court ordered a married man convicted of rape to recognize the child born of it, John Paul Valencia, as his legitimate son. Held: that portion is eliminated. "The rule is that if the rapist is a married man, he cannot be compelled to recognize the offspring of the crime, should there be any, as his child, whether legitimate or illegitimate."

      Dempsey v. RTC (164 SCRA 384, 1988; the syllabus prints "Demsey, 164 SCRA 364")

      The accused pleaded guilty to criminal charges concerning the child Christina Marie (under P.D. 603, for failure to give support), and the court ordered him, as part of the civil liability, to recognize her as his natural child. Held: error. "The recognition of a child by her father is provided for in the Civil Code and now in the new Family Code. In this criminal prosecution, where the accused pleaded guilty to criminal charges and the issue of recognition was not specifically and fully heard and tried, the trial court committed reversible error when it ordered recognition of a natural child as part of the civil liability in the criminal case."

      People v. Barranco (177 SCRA 103, 1989; decided in Filipino)

      A married man convicted of rape was ordered to acknowledge the child. Held: "Subalit mayroong pagkakamali ang mababang hukuman ng ipag-utos nito na kilalanin ng nahahabla bilang anak ang bunga ng kanyang kasalanan. Ang nahahabla ay may asawa. Hindi maaari na kilalanin ang batang bunga ng kasalanan na anak ng isang may-asawa. Subalit may katungkulan siyang sustentuhan ang bata ayon sa batas." (The lower court erred in ordering the married accused to acknowledge the child of his crime; but he must support the child.)

      Gapusan-Chua v. CA (183 SCRA 160, 1990; the syllabus prints "Gapusan v. CA, 185 SCRA 160")

      Ligaya Gapusan-Chua had been voluntarily recognized by her mother, Prudencia Gapusan, as her natural child; the recognition was questioned in the settlement of the mother's estate. Held: valid. "Voluntary recognition … 'is an admission of the fact of paternity or maternity by the presumed parent, expressed in the form prescribed by the Civil Code'", i.e., "in the record of birth, a will, a statement before a court of record, or in any authentic writing." If Ligaya was of age, she consented, impliedly by never impugning it during her mother's life and expressly by asserting it in the estate proceeding. If she was a minor, the lack of judicial approval "was cured by her ratification of that recognition, after having reached the age of majority, by her initiation of the proceedings for the settlement of her deceased mother's estate". (Listed under "compulsory recognition" in the syllabus, but it is a voluntary-recognition case.)

      Legitimated children (Arts. 177–182; R.A. No. 9858)

      Art. 177, FC (as amended by R.A. No. 9858). Children conceived and born outside of wedlock of parents who, at the time of conception of the former, were not disqualified by any impediment to marry each other, or were so disqualified only because either or both of them were below eighteen (18) years of age, may be legitimated. (269a)
      Art. 178, FC. Legitimation shall take place by a subsequent valid marriage between parents. The annulment of a voidable marriage shall not affect the legitimation. (270a)
      Art. 179, FC. Legitimated children shall enjoy the same rights as legitimate children. (272a)
      Art. 180, FC. The effects of legitimation shall retroact to the time of the child's birth. (273a)
      Art. 181, FC. The legitimation of children who died before the celebration of the marriage shall benefit their descendants. (274)
      Art. 182, FC. Legitimation may be impugned only by those who are prejudiced in their rights, within five years from the time their cause of action accrues. (275a)
      Uribe (Quiz 5, CivRev 2025, situationers): "What is important is at the time of the conception, not conception and birth: no legal impediment to marry. Age is not a legal impediment but capacity, so if the parents are 16 years old and thereafter, when 18, they marry, may the child be legitimated? Of course, being less than 18 is not a legal impediment, so long as the marriage is a valid marriage." Situationer: "C is the child of A and B. When A and B were both 25, only live-in, the child was conceived. Before the birth of C, B married X. The child was born during this marriage between B and X; thereafter X died. A and B got married. Was C legitimated? Is it not required by law that this was conceived AND born?" Answer: "Law only requires that the child was CONCEIVED during the time when there was no legal impediment to marriage. No issue as to impediments during the birth. 38, 37: legal impediments. This is not the same as capacity." In Quiz 5, a statement that a child born when the parents had no impediment "will be legitimated" was attacked: the law says may be legitimated, because a subsequent valid marriage is still required.
      Uribe (CivRev midterm essay, with Sir's discussion): "While A's girlfriend (B) was pregnant, A married C. B gave birth to X 6 months after the solemnization of the marriage of A and C. During the subsistence of the marriage of A and C, B gave birth to Y, A's second child with B. When Y was already 5 years old, C died. Three months after the death of C, A and B were married. B is the great-granddaughter of the brother of [A]. What is the status of Y?" Sir's structure: (1) first establish the status: Y was conceived and born outside wedlock, with no exception (no Art. 36, no Art. 53), so Y is illegitimate; "hindi ka pwede pumunta sa legitimation" before that. (2) Then legitimation: not legitimated, because when Y was conceived A was married to C. "Ang common na mali … there was legal impediment when Y was conceived AND born. Hindi required yan ng batas. As long as conceived with legal impediment, di na pwede legitimated." (3) The A–B marriage is not void for public policy: B is A's grandniece's daughter, related in the fifth degree, beyond the fourth. (4) The issue is legal impediment, not legal capacity. (5) If you raise a side issue (no liquidation after C's death), state both sides. Also, in another midterm item Sir faulted "at the time of the birth" in a restatement of Art. 177, and added that "may be" legitimated still requires a subsequent valid marriage. In a later succession recitation, Sir corrected a student who named legitimated children as compulsory heirs "not related by blood": legitimated children are blood relatives; the correct example is a child of artificial insemination with donor sperm.
      Watch the Uribe situationer on C. On the given facts C was born during B's valid marriage to X, so under Art. 164 C would be presumed X's legitimate child unless X (or his heirs) impugned it. Sir's answer focuses only on Art. 177's conception test. If this comes up, give Sir's answer (impediment tested at conception, so C is legitimable) and add that C must first be shown not to be X's child (Arts. 164, 166, 170).
      Tolentino (Arts. 177–182): legitimation is a remedy by which children not born in lawful wedlock are, by fiction, considered legitimate, as if born when their parents were validly married. It is "a product of nature and law": unlike adoption, which creates by fiction a relation that does not exist, legitimation makes legal what exists by nature, and needs no prior judicial approval (Colorado v. CA, 135 SCRA 47). Only children formerly classed as "natural" can be legitimated. A child of a married father and a single mother cannot be legitimated even if the father is later widowed and marries the mother (but see Tongay v. CA, 123 SCRA 99, a liberal ruling under the NCC). Tolentino criticizes the inconsistency: had the same parents contracted a void (bigamous) marriage, the child would be legitimate under Art. 54, so the law favors children of prohibited marriages over children of parents who respected the prohibition. Art. 178: the NCC required acknowledgment by both parents; the FC requires only the marriage, but filiation must still be established, if disputed, under Arts. 172, 173 and 175 (e.g., a seduced young mother gave the child away at birth and later married the father). If the subsequent marriage is void, there is no legitimation; if voidable and annulled, the legitimation stands. Art. 179: legitimation creates a relationship with all the parents' relatives (De los Santos v. Luciano, 60 Phil. 328: a legitimated daughter is the legitimate sister of her parents' legitimate son, so her child inherits from him as a legitimate niece). Art. 180: most codes date legitimation from the marriage; ours dates it from birth to protect the child, since the parents may marry long afterwards. Example: Z born in 1945 to X and Y, both capacitated; X's father dies intestate in 1951; X repudiates and X's brother B takes everything; X marries Y in 1953. Z, legitimated retroactively to 1945, was a legitimate grandchild in 1951 and takes the estate from B. Art. 181: a logical consequence: a child who died before the wedding transmits the rights of a legitimate child to his descendants, who inherit by representation. Art. 182: legitimation may be attacked when the child was not legitimable or is not the child of the persons who married. Who may sue: Sánchez Román and Burón say only those who suffer economic or material injury (testate or intestate heirs); Castán would include those with a moral interest. Tolentino sides with Sánchez Román: "rights" means rights recognized and enforceable by law.
      Tolentino's text of Art. 177 is outdated. His 1990 commentary quotes the original Art. 177, which had no clause on parents below 18. R.A. No. 9858 (2009) added "or were so disqualified only because either or both of them were below eighteen (18) years of age". Quote the amended text. (Some reviewers also describe the original wording as "conceived and born outside of wedlock of parents who, at the time of the conception of the former, were not disqualified by any impediment to marry each other".)
      Quiz traps (legitimation): "Children conceived and born outside of wedlock will be legitimated if their parents had no impediment" → false: may, upon a subsequent valid marriage. "The impediment is tested at the time of the birth" or "at the wedding" → false: at conception. "Legitimation takes effect from the date of the marriage" → false: it retroacts to birth (Art. 180). "Legitimation requires acknowledgment by both parents" → false under the FC. "Anyone may impugn legitimation at any time" → false: only those prejudiced in their rights, within 5 years from accrual (Art. 182). "Children of parents who were 17 at conception cannot be legitimated" → false (R.A. 9858). Syllabus misprint: it lists "Action to impugn, FC 162"; the article is 182.

      1990 Bar (cleaned up): B and G, college students, both single, had an affair, and G became pregnant. B then married C in Cebu; two weeks after the wedding, G gave birth to E. B and C had two children, X and Y. During the last five years of that marriage, B renewed his relationship with G, and F was born to them two years before C died. B later married G. What is the status of each child?

      X and Y: legitimate children of B and C (Art. 164). E: legitimated by the marriage of B and G, because when E was conceived both were single and not disqualified; that B was already married when E was born does not matter (Art. 177; Uribe). E has the same rights as X and Y (Art. 179). F: illegitimate and cannot be legitimated, because B was married to C when F was conceived. F uses G's surname (or B's if he expressly recognized F), and F's legitime is one-half of that of each legitimate (or legitimated) child (Art. 176).

      Practice (after Tolentino's example): X and Y, both 17 and single, had a child, Z, in 2018. In 2022, X's father F died intestate, leaving X as his only child and a brother, B. X repudiated the inheritance, and B took the whole estate. In 2024, X and Y, now of age, married each other. May Z claim F's estate from B?

      Yes. Z was legitimable even though X and Y were below 18 at conception (Art. 177, as amended by R.A. 9858: minority is not an impediment), and the subsequent valid marriage legitimated him (Art. 178). Legitimation retroacts to Z's birth in 2018 (Art. 180), so when F died in 2022 Z already had the rights of a legitimate grandchild. With X repudiating, Z, a legitimate descendant, excludes F's brother B, a collateral relative, so the estate must go to Z. Had the effect dated only from the 2024 wedding (the Spanish rule), Z would have had no claim.

      Adoption

      Syllabus XIV. The syllabus still cites the Family Code (Arts. 183–193) and the Domestic Adoption Act (R.A. 8552, Secs. 7–22); both are now repealed by the Domestic Administrative Adoption and Alternative Child Care Act (R.A. 11642, approved January 6, 2022), and simulated births are rectified under R.A. 11222 (2019). Sir's rule: the law in force when the petition was filed governs, so know all three. Cases: Lazatin, Cervantes, Republic v. CA (1996), Republic v. CA & Bobiles, Lim, Santos v. Aranzanso, Daoang, Nieto, Duncan, Cang, Bobanovic, Pardo de Tavera, Edwin Villa; from the class reviewer and the group report, Landingin, Toledano, Bartolome, Stephanie Garcia, Lahom, Tamargo, Sayson, Bagcat-Gullas.

      Which law governs

      Uribe (CivRev, adoption discussion): asked whether students still need to study the Domestic Adoption Act since R.A. 11642 repealed it, Sir said yes: "If the petition was filed during the effectivity of those laws, those laws will apply whether or not that petition should be granted. Fair lang naman kasi kung qualified ka at that time of the filing, pag nabago na ang batas edi di na pwede di na igrant ang petition? Parang di naman tama yun." Same idea as the property regime of a marriage solemnized in 1985. "It is possible in a case, the adoption took place in 1982 kaso ngayon lang nagkaproblem kasi sa mamanahin. The law governing is the law at the time the adoption is filed, so hindi totoo na aaralin lang ang batas ngayon." Also: under R.A. 8552, "18 pwede na but under 11642 hindi na pwede kasi 25 na."
      Old answer keys vs. R.A. 11642: a past Uribe quiz keyed "Domestic adoption is essentially judicial" as true; under R.A. 11642 it is now administrative (an Order of Adoption from the NACC, appealable to the Court of Appeals). Inter-country adoption remains under R.A. 8043, with the NACC replacing the ICAB.
      Republic v. CA and Bobiles (G.R. No. 92326, January 24, 1992)

      Zenaida Bobiles filed alone, under P.D. 603 (which allowed it), a petition to adopt Jason Condat. The Family Code took effect while the case was pending and required spouses to adopt jointly. Held: the petition was properly granted. The law in force at the filing governs, and the petitioner acquired a vested right that the FC could not impair. In any case, "the affidavit of consent attached by the husband showed that he actually joined his wife in adopting Jayson. His declarations and subsequent confirmatory testimony in open court was sufficient to make him a co-petitioner. Future of an innocent child must not be compromised by arbitrary insistence of rigid adherence to procedural rules on the form of the pleadings." (Applied in Republic v. Miller, G.R. No. 125932, April 21, 1999: a German couple who filed under P.D. 603 kept their right to adopt after the FC disqualified aliens; 2001 Bar.)

      Lazatin v. Campos (92 SCRA 250, 1979)

      Renato Lazatin sought to intervene in the settlement of the estate of Margarita de Asis, claiming to be her adopted son, and offered evidence of acts and declarations of the deceased treating him as such, but no decree. Held: no adoption shown. "Only an adoption made through the court, or in pursuance with the procedure laid down under Rule 99 of the Rules of Court is valid in this jurisdiction. Withal, the attempts of petitioner to prove his adoption by acts and declarations of the deceased do not discharge the mandatory presentation of the judicial decree of adoption." (Today, the Order of Adoption issued by the NACC under R.A. 11642.)

      Who may adopt (R.A. 11642, Sec. 21)

      Sec. 21, R.A. 11642. Who May Adopt. – The following may adopt:
      (a) Any Filipino citizen at least twenty-five (25) years of age, who is in possession of full civil capacity and legal rights; has not been convicted of any crime involving moral turpitude; is of good moral character and can model the same; is emotionally and psychologically capable of caring for children; at least sixteen (16) years older than the adoptee; and who is in a position to support and care for adopted children in keeping with the means of the family: Provided, That the requirement of sixteen (16)-years difference between the age of the adopter and the adoptee may be waived when the adopter is the biological parent of the adoptee, or is the spouse of the adoptee's parent;
      (b) The legal guardian with respect to the ward after the termination of the guardianship and clearance of financial accountabilities;
      (c) The legal guardians with respect to the foster child;
      (d) Philippine government officials and employees deployed or stationed abroad: Provided, That they are able to bring the child with them; and
      (e) Foreign nationals who are permanent or habitual residents of the Philippines for at least five (5) years possessing the same qualifications as above stated for Filipino nationals prior to filing of the petition: Provided, That they come from a country with diplomatic relations with the Republic of the Philippines and that the laws of the adopter's country will acknowledge the Certificate of Adoption as valid, acknowledge the child as a legal child of the adopters, and allow entry of the child into such country as an adoptee: Provided, further, That requirements of residency may be waived for the following: (1) A former Filipino citizen, habitually residing in the Philippines, who seeks to adopt a relative within fourth (4th) civil degree of consanguinity or affinity; or (2) One who seeks to adopt the legitimate child of the Filipino spouse; or (3) One who is married to a Filipino citizen and seeks to adopt jointly with the spouse a relative within the fourth (4th) degree of consanguinity or affinity of the Filipino spouse.
      Spouses shall jointly adopt, except in the following cases: (a) If one spouse seeks to adopt the legitimate child of the other; or (b) If one spouse seeks to adopt own illegitimate child: Provided, That the other spouse has signified consent thereto; or (c) If the spouses are legally separated from each other.
      Uribe (Quiz, with class discussion): "The adopter must be at least sixteen years older than the adoptee." False: the gap may be waived when the adopter is the biological parent or the spouse of the adoptee's parent. Another item: a statement that the adopter need only be "of legal age" is false under R.A. 11642: "kung sinabi mong at least of legal age, pwede na 19 or 18. But when the law requires 25, kung 24 palang siya, di pa siya pwedeng mag-adopt." On the MC "Following are necessary for a Filipino to be able to adopt, except: (a) of legal age …", Sir's basis was (a), because R.A. 11642 requires 25. (In the same item, "not been convicted of a crime with penalty of more than 6 years" is not the statutory test either; the law says a crime involving moral turpitude.) On aliens: "before, the requirement is 3 years residency … pareho pa rin ang instances where that requirement will be waived" (former Filipino adopting a relative within the 4th degree, etc.).
      Uribe (CivRev Quiz 2, item 7): "Husband and wife must jointly adopt if one seeks to adopt his own illegitimate child." False: "The law provides that consent is only needed and not adopt jointly. Consent ≠ Joint Adoption." In class Sir pressed: "When will the spouses have joint authority when only one of them is the petitioner?" Answer: when one spouse adopts the legitimate child of the other. "Aside from that scenario, any other scenario where a petition for adoption will prosper even if the spouses did not jointly file? … If the spouses are legally separated. … Alamin niyo ang exemptions." Samplex MC: "In case of adoption, husband and wife shall exercise joint parental authority in the following cases, except: (a) if husband and wife jointly adopt; (b) one spouse adopts the [legitimate] child of the other; (c) one spouse seeks to adopt his own illegitimate child …" → (c): "the adopting spouse needs the consent of the other, but this doesn't mean that they must jointly adopt. Consent does not lead to parental authority."
      In re Adoption of Michelle P. Lim and Michael Jude P. Lim (G.R. Nos. 168992–93, May 21, 2009)

      Monina and Primo Lim, childless, were entrusted with two infants of unknown parents and registered them as their own. After Primo died, Monina married Angel Olario, an American, and, availing herself of the amnesty in R.A. 8552, Sec. 22, filed petitions alone to adopt Michelle (then 25) and Michael (18), with Olario's affidavit of consent. Held: denied. "Husband and wife shall jointly adopt except in 3 instances", none present. "The use of the word 'shall' signifies that joint adoption of husband and wife is mandatory. This is in consonance with the concept of joint parental authority since the child to be adopted is elevated to the level of a legitimate child." Olario's consent does not suffice: as an alien he must himself meet Sec. 7(b), and the residency and certification requirements cannot be waived. That the adoptees were already emancipated does not matter: "Parental authority is merely just one of the effects of legal adoption."

      Republic v. Toledano (G.R. No. 94147, June 8, 1994; class reviewer)

      Alvin Clouse, an American, and his wife Evelyn, a former Filipino who had become an American citizen, jointly petitioned to adopt Evelyn's minor brother. Held: denied. Alvin was not qualified (not a former Filipino, not adopting his Filipino spouse's legitimate child); Evelyn alone was, but she could not adopt alone because spouses must adopt jointly. "As the child to be adopted is elevated to the level of a legitimate child, it is but natural to require the spouses to adopt jointly." (Same answer in the 2000, 2003 and 2005 Bar questions on Sarah and Tom, Lina, and Eva and Paul.)

      Nieto v. Magat (136 SCRA 533, 1985)

      Filipino spouses temporarily residing in Guam (the husband was employed there) petitioned to adopt a minor; the trial court dismissed it on the ground that they were non-residents. Held: they may adopt. "The fact that the petitioners reside temporarily in Guam does not disqualify them from adopting the minor child." Arts. 27 and 28 of P.D. 603 did not disqualify Filipinos temporarily abroad.

      Daoang v. Municipal Judge of San Nicolas (159 SCRA 369, 1988)

      The spouses Agonoy petitioned to adopt two minors; relatives opposed because the spouses had a legitimate daughter (since deceased) and grandchildren, invoking the old NCC 335 disqualification of persons with legitimate descendants. Held: the adoption may proceed. "Under the law now in force, having legitimate, legitimated, acknowledged natural children, or children by legal fiction, is no longer a ground for disqualification to adopt. Adoption used to be for the benefit of the adoptor … The present tendency, however, is geared more towards the promotion of the welfare of the child and the enhancement of his opportunities for a useful and happy life."

      Bobanovic v. Montes (142 SCRA 485, 1986)

      Foreign spouses who had been granted the adoption of the infant Adam Christopher could not take him abroad because the MSSD refused a travel clearance, insisting that only the MSSD could make the case study (the court had relied on its own social worker's report). Held: the MSSD must issue the clearance. It did not appeal the decree and never claimed the social worker's report was wrong; "absent any proof that prejudice would be caused to the Adam Christopher if he joins his adoptive parents, the MSSD should be faulted for declining to issue the travel clearance."

      Pardo de Tavera v. Cacdac (167 SCRA 636, 1988)

      An American couple, the Gordons, adopted a Filipino child on the strength of a case study by the court's social worker; the MSSD objected that the case study was its exclusive prerogative. Held: the adoption stands. Before E.O. 91, the MSSD had no exclusive authority to make the case study; the court found its social worker's report based on "very honest insight and opinion based on personal interviews and home study painstakingly made", and the MSSD never alleged it was faulty. "The objective of trial custody had been substantially achieved."

      Tolentino (FC Arts. 183–186): adoption statutes are liberally construed to carry out their beneficent purpose; the proceedings are in rem. Under the FC, aliens were generally disqualified, except a former Filipino adopting a relative by consanguinity, one adopting the legitimate child of his Filipino spouse, and one married to a Filipino adopting jointly a relative of the Filipino spouse. Tolentino read the old Code as allowing one spouse to adopt alone with the other's consent (to prevent dissension), and the consent as unnecessary after legal separation; the FC and later laws made joint adoption mandatory, keeping legal separation as an exception.

      Who may be adopted (R.A. 11642, Sec. 22)

      Sec. 22, R.A. 11642. Who May Be Adopted. – The following may be adopted:
      (a) Any child who has been issued a CDCLAA;
      (b) The legitimate child of one spouse by the other spouse;
      (c) An illegitimate child by a qualified adopter to improve status of legitimacy;
      (d) A Filipino of legal age if, prior to the adoption, said person has been consistently considered and treated by the adopters as their own child for a period of at least three (3) years;
      (e) A foster child;
      (f) A child whose adoption has been previously rescinded;
      (g) A child whose biological or adoptive parents have died: Provided, That no proceedings shall be initiated within six (6) months from the time of death of said parents; or
      (h) A relative of the adopter.
      In re Adoption of Edwin Villa (21 SCRA 399, 1967)

      The spouses Luis Santos, Jr. and Edipola Villa Santos petitioned to adopt Edwin Villa, Edipola's younger brother, whom they had cared for since infancy. The Solicitor General opposed, arguing that adoption between siblings would create confusing relationships. Held: granted. "The fact alone that petitioner wife and minor are siblings should not prevent the adoption. There is no express provision in law that disallows relatives by blood or affinity from adopting one another."

      Samplex (Uribe quizzes; Civ Rev Samplex #46): "Only minors may be adopted." False: "Illegitimate child may be adopted by parent regardless of age" (FC 183, 2nd par., and 187(1); now Sec. 22(c), (d)).

      Whose consent is needed (Sec. 23)

      Sec. 23, R.A. 11642. Whose Consent is Necessary to the Adoption. – After being properly counseled and informed of the right to give or withhold approval of the adoption, the written consent of the following to the adoption are hereby required:
      (a) The adoptee, if ten (10) years of age or over;
      (b) The biological parents of the child, if known, or the legal guardian, or the proper government instrumentality which has legal custody of the child, except in the case of a Filipino of legal age if, prior to the adoption, said person has been consistently considered and treated as their own child by the adopters for at least three (3) years;
      (c) The legitimate and adopted children, ten (10) years of age or over, of the adopters, if any;
      (d) The illegitimate children, ten (10) years of age or over, of the adopter if living with said adopter or over whom the adopter exercises parental authority and the latter's spouse, if any; and
      (e) The spouse, if any, of the person adopting or to be adopted.
      Provided, That children under ten (10) years of age shall be counseled and consulted, but shall not be required to execute within consent.
      Uribe (Quiz, with class discussion): "The consent of the following is required to the adoption, except: … (d) parents of the adopter" → (d), not provided in the law. Sir then asked why: "Pag walang anak at namatay, at least intestate succession, sino ang magmamana? … parents. Bakit di kailangan ang consent ng parents? … As a matter of policy, baka kailangan ng consent ng parents. But the point is more important in Domestic Administrative Adoption: sa letter of the law, magmamana na ang adoptee sa parents of adopter" (Sec. 41 extends legitimate filiation to them), "pero walang kailangan ng consent sa parents tapos magmamana na sa kanila?" A variant: "The consent of the following is not required except: (a) adoptee if 7 years or over; (b) siblings of adoptee, if known; (c) spouse of adoptee …; (d) parents of adopter" → (c): the adoptee's spouse must consent (an adult may be adopted, so he may be married); 10, not 7, is the age.
      Cang v. CA (296 SCRA 128, September 25, 1998)

      Herbert Cang and Anna Marie Clavano separated; he went to the U.S., divorced her there, and became an American. Anna Marie's brother Ronald and his wife petitioned to adopt the couple's three children, with Anna Marie's consent, alleging that Herbert had abandoned them. The lower courts granted it. Held: reversed. "The written consent of the natural parent is indispensable for the validity of the decree of adoption. Nevertheless, the requirement of written consent can be dispensed with if the parent has abandoned the child or that such parent is insane or hopelessly intemperate. The court may acquire jurisdiction over the case even without the written consent of the parents or one of the parents provided that the petition for adoption alleges facts sufficient to warrant exemption from compliance therewith." But there was no abandonment: Herbert had sent money, gifts and letters and kept in touch. Abandonment means "neglect or refusal to perform the natural and legal obligations of care and support which parents owe their children"; mere physical estrangement is not enough.

      Duncan v. CFI of Rizal (69 SCRA 298, 1976)

      An unwed mother gave her three-day-old child, through a lawyer (Atty. Corazon Velasco), to the Duncan spouses, asking that her identity be kept secret; she never saw the child again. The Duncans petitioned to adopt with the lawyer's consent as de facto guardian. Held: granted. "The parental consent required by law in adoption proceedings refers to parents who have not abandoned their child. Thus, where the natural and unwed mother turned over her three-day old child to another person and from that date on to the time of the adoption proceedings in court, she is considered to have abandoned her child and her consent to the adoption is no longer necessary."

      Santos v. Aranzanso (16 SCRA 344, 1966)

      The adoption of Paulina and Aurora Santos by Simplicio Santos and Juliana Reyes was attacked collaterally in the settlement of Juliana's estate, by her relatives, for lack of the natural parents' consent. Held: the decree stands. "Consent by the parents to the adoption is not an absolute requisite. If the natural parents have abandoned their children, consent by the guardian ad litem suffices." The decree cannot be attacked collaterally.

      Landingin v. Republic (G.R. No. 164948, June 27, 2006; class reviewer)

      Diwata Landingin, a U.S. citizen of Filipino parentage, petitioned to adopt her three minor nephews and niece, children of her deceased brother; their mother had gone to Italy and remarried. Only a social worker's report said the mother consented. Held: denied. "Written consent of the biological parent/s is necessary—indispensable—for the adoption to proceed." Abandonment was not proved: the mother kept in touch and sent money. Also, "it is the financial capacity of the adopter that should be considered, not the biological parent", and Landingin, relying on her children's help, had not shown she could support the adoptees.

      Bagcat-Gullas v. Gullas (class reviewer)

      The spouses Gullas adopted a minor, Jo Anne, whose mother had abandoned her. Jose Gullas's adult legitimate children later attacked the decree: they had not been impleaded or served summons, and the "affidavit of consent" in the record was not genuine. Held: the decree is void. "The written consent of the adopter's legitimate children aged ten or older is a mandatory jurisdictional requirement in adoption proceedings, and failure to implead and serve summons upon them renders the judgment void." Lack of jurisdiction defeats immutability of judgments.

      Tolentino (FC Art. 188): parental consent is essential to confer jurisdiction; the parent's testimony in court, beyond the written consent, is not required. Where a parent survives, grandparents with actual custody cannot consent. Consent cannot be required from an insane parent, one under civil interdiction or declared absent, or one judicially deprived of parental authority. Until the court approves the adoption, the parents still have parental authority and may withdraw consent with court approval.

      Effects of adoption (Secs. 41–43)

      Sec. 41, R.A. 11642. Legitimacy. – The adoptee shall be considered the legitimate child of the adopter for all intents and purposes and as such is entitled to all the rights and obligations provided by law to legitimate children born to them without discrimination of any kind. To this end, the adoptee is entitled to love, guidance, and support in keeping with the means of the family. The legitimate filiation that is created between the adopter and adoptee shall be extended to the adopter's parents, adopter's legitimate siblings, and legitimate descendants.
      The adopter is also given the right to choose the name by which the child is to be known, consistent with the best interest of the child.
      Sec. 42, R.A. 11642. Parental Authority. – Upon issuances of the Order of Adoption, adoption shall cease as alternative care and becomes parental care. Adoptive parents shall now have full parental authority over the child. Except in cases where the biological parent is the spouse of the adopter, all legal ties between the biological parents and the adoptee shall be severed and the same shall then be vested on the adopters.
      In case spouses jointly adopt or one spouse adopts the legitimate child of the other, joint parental authority shall be exercised by the spouses.
      Sec. 43, R.A. 11642. Succession. – In testate and intestate succession, the adopters and the adoptee shall have reciprocal rights of succession without distinction from legitimate filiations. However, if the adoptees and their biological parents have left a will, the law on testamentary succession shall govern.
      Art. 190, FC (repealed; still asked). Legal or intestate succession to the estate of the adopted shall be governed by the following rules: (1) Legitimate and illegitimate children and descendants and the surviving spouse of the adopted shall inherit from the adopted, in accordance with the ordinary rules of legal or intestate succession; (2) When the parents, legitimate or illegitimate, or the legitimate ascendants of the adopted concur with the adopter, they shall divide the entire estate, one-half to be inherited by the parents or ascendants and the other half, by the adopters; (3) When the surviving spouse or the illegitimate children of the adopted concur with the adopters, they shall divide the entire estate in equal shares, one-half to be inherited by the spouse or the illegitimate children of the adopted and the other half, by the adopters; (4) When the adopters concur with the illegitimate children and the surviving spouse of the adopted, they shall divide the entire estate in equal shares, one-third to be inherited by the illegitimate children, one-third by the surviving spouse, and one-third by the adopters; (5) When only the adopters survive, they shall inherit the entire estate; and (6) When only collateral blood relatives of the adopted survive, then the ordinary rules of legal or intestate succession shall apply.
      Samplex (Civ Rev Samplex #47; Uribe Quiz #4, T/F 7): the verbatim Art. 190(1) and 190(3) statements were keyed true ("This is a verbatim provision"). Under R.A. 8552 and 11642, Art. 190 no longer exists; Sir still tests the text.
      Cervantes v. Fajardo (In re Habeas Corpus of Angelie Anne Cervantes) (169 SCRA 575, 1989)

      Conrado Fajardo and Gina Carreon, common-law partners, gave their daughter Angelie Anne to the Cervantes spouses, who adopted her with the natural parents' consent. Later the natural mother took the child back and demanded money. Held: custody to the adopters. "A decree of adoption has the effect, among others, of dissolving the authority vested in natural parents over the adopted child, except where the adopting parent is the spouse of the natural parent of the adopted, in which case, parental authority over the adopted shall be exercised jointly by both spouses. The adopting parents have the right to the care and custody of the adopted child and exercise parental authority and responsibility over him." Moreover, "in all controversies regarding the custody of minors, the foremost consideration is the moral, physical and social welfare of the child", and the natural mother's common-law situation weighed against her.

      Bartolome v. SSS (G.R. No. 192531, November 12, 2014; class reviewer)

      John Colcol, adopted as a child by his great-grandfather Cornelio (who died in 1987, when John was four), died in a work accident, childless and single. His biological mother, Bernardina, with whom he had lived since Cornelio's death and whom he had named as his beneficiary, claimed death benefits as a "dependent parent". The ECC denied it, holding that the adoption severed her status. Held: she is entitled. "Parents" in the Labor Code is not limited to legitimate parents. Applying by analogy the rule that parental authority of the biological parents is restored when an adoption is rescinded during minority, the Court held that "the biological parents retain their rights of succession to the estate of their child who was the subject of adoption … [which] include the exercise of parental authority, in the event of the untimely passing of their minor offspring's adoptive parent."

      In re Adoption of Stephanie Nathy Astorga Garcia (G.R. No. 148311, March 31, 2005)

      Honorato Catindig adopted his illegitimate daughter, Stephanie, and asked that her middle name be changed from "Astorga" to "Garcia", her mother's surname, and her surname to "Catindig". Held: allowed. "There is no law prohibiting an illegitimate child adopted by her natural father … to use, as middle name her mother's surname"; what is not prohibited is allowed. Being now a legitimate child, she has the right to bear the surnames of both her father and her mother; it preserves her maternal lineage and her right to inherit from her mother, and follows Filipino custom. (1996, 2006, 2012 Bar.)

      Republic v. CA and Caranto (255 SCRA 99, March 15, 1996)

      The Carantos petitioned to adopt a minor and, in the same petition, to correct his first name in his birth record from "Midael" to "Michael". Notice was published only of the adoption. Held: the adoption is valid, but the correction is void. The published notice "only the prayer for adoption of the minor was stated. Nothing was mentioned that in addition the correction of his name in the civil registry was also being sought. The local civil registrar was thus deprived of notice and, consequently, of the opportunity to be heard." Failure to implead the civil registrar as an indispensable party and to publish the petition for correction made that part "null and void for lack of jurisdiction both as to party and as to the subject matter." (See Civil Register: Rule 108; today R.A. 9048 for a clerical change of first name.)

      2007 Bar: Ramon married Dessa in 1970. Before the marriage, Ramon had an illegitimate child, Anna. Ramon and Dessa adopted Cherry (1971) and Michelle (1972). Dessa died in 1973 giving birth to Larry. Anna had an illegitimate child, Lia. Cherry adopted Shelly. Larry had twins, Hans and Gretel, with his girlfriend Fiona. In 2005 Anna, Larry and Cherry died in an accident; in 2007 Ramon died. Who may inherit from Ramon?

      Michelle (adopted, inherits as a legitimate child) and Lia (by representation of Anna; Art. 992 does not bar her because Anna herself was illegitimate). Not Shelly: under the law then in force, adoption created a personal relation only between Cherry and Shelly, so Shelly cannot represent Cherry in Ramon's estate. Not Hans and Gretel: illegitimate children of a legitimate child are barred by Art. 992. Under R.A. 11642, the legitimate filiation of an adoptee extends to the adopter's parents, so a Shelly adopted under it would arguably be Ramon's legitimate granddaughter and could represent Cherry (a point to raise, not settled).

      2009 Bar: Rafael, a bachelor, petitioned to adopt Dolly, a one-year-old foundling. He died while the case was pending. (a) Should it be dismissed? (b) What if Dolly died instead?

      (a) Under R.A. 8552, Sec. 13, if the petitioner dies after the petition has been submitted for decision, the court may still issue the decree, which retroacts to the date of filing; otherwise the case is terminated. (b) The adoptee's death terminates the proceedings.

      2010 Bar: Rex and Lea have two children, 14 and 8. Rex fathered a child, now 10, with another woman; Lea obtained a decree of legal separation. Rex wants to adopt his illegitimate child. Whose consent is needed? What if there had been no legal separation?

      The 14-year-old legitimate child, the 10-year-old adoptee, and the adoptee's biological mother. The 8-year-old is only counseled and consulted. Lea's consent is not needed after legal separation. Without legal separation, Rex may still adopt alone, his own illegitimate child being an exception to joint adoption, but with Lea's consent as well.

      Rescission (Secs. 47–53; FC 191–193; R.A. 8552, Secs. 19–20)

      Sec. 47, R.A. 11642. Grounds for Rescission of Administrative Adoption. – The adoption may be rescinded only upon the petition of the adoptee with the NACC, or with the assistance of the SWDO if the adoptee is a minor, or if the adoptee is eighteen (18) years of age or over but who is incapacitated or by his or her guardian on any of the following grounds committed by the adopter(s): (a) Repeated physical or verbal maltreatment by the adopter despite having undergone counseling; (b) Attempt on the life of the adoptee; (c) Abandonment and failure to comply with parental obligations.
      Adoption, being in the best interest of the child, shall not be subject to rescission by the adopter. However, the adopter may disinherit the adoptee for causes provided in Article 919 of the Civil Code of the Philippines.
      Lahom v. Sibulo (G.R. No. 143989, July 14, 2003)

      Dr. Diosdado Lahom and his wife Isabelita adopted Isabelita's nephew, Jose Melvin Sibulo, in 1972. In 1999, after R.A. 8552 took effect, Isabelita petitioned to rescind the adoption: Jose Melvin refused to use the surname Lahom, Diosdado had wanted to revoke the adoption before he died, and Jose Melvin neglected her. Held: dismissed. R.A. 8552 deleted the adopter's right to rescind. Even assuming a right to rescind had vested under the law in force when she adopted, it was "an action that should be exercised within the period allowed by" the Rules (five years from the minor's majority), which had long lapsed. "While R.A. No. 8552 has unqualifiedly withdrawn from an adopter a consequential right to rescind the adoption decree even in cases where the adoption might clearly turn out to be undesirable, it remains, nevertheless, the bounden duty of the Court to apply the law…. [T]he adopter may, for valid reasons, cause the forfeiture of certain benefits otherwise accruing to an undeserving child", e.g., by disinheritance or by excluding him from the free portion.

      Tolentino (FC 191–193): a decree of adoption cannot be attacked collaterally in a settlement proceeding; a separate action is required. Grounds for the adopted differed by age: a minor or incapacitated adoptee could rescind on the grounds for loss or suspension of parental authority (Arts. 229–232); an adult, on the grounds for disinheriting an ascendant (NCC 920). On rescission while the adopted is a minor, the court reinstates the parental authority of the natural parents unless they are disqualified, or appoints a guardian; the adopted loses the adopter's surname.

      Bar (1994–1995, adapted): Carol consented to the adoption of her illegitimate daughter Bing by Norma and Manuel in 1990. In 1991 she learned they ran a call-girl ring from their house; Bing wanted to return to her. Who has the better right to custody, and what legal actions may be taken?

      Carol, because the child's welfare is paramount and Bing's stay in a house used for prostitution is harmful (though if Bing is already of age, custody is moot). The remedies: an action to deprive the adopters of parental authority (Art. 231(2): corrupting example), or rescission of the adoption, which under the law then in force was available to the adoptee on the same grounds (FC 191). Under R.A. 11642 the adoptee would petition the NACC on the grounds of Sec. 47, and corrupting the child would be argued as maltreatment or failure to comply with parental obligations.

      Rectification of simulated birth (R.A. 11222; R.A. 8552, Sec. 22)

      Sec. 4, R.A. 11222. Rectification of Simulated Birth Record. – Notwithstanding any provision of law to the contrary, a person or persons who, prior to the effectivity of this Act, simulated the birth of a child, and those who cooperated in the execution of such simulation, shall not be criminally, civilly, or administratively liable for such act: Provided, That the simulation of birth was made for the best interest of the child and that the child has been consistently considered and treated by such person or persons as her, his, or their own daughter or son: Provided, further, That such person or persons has or have filed a petition for adoption with an application for the rectification of the simulated birth record within ten (10) years from the effectivity of this Act: Provided, finally, That all the benefits of this Act shall also apply to adult adoptees.
      Sec. 5, R.A. 11222. Administrative Adoption and Rectification. – A person or persons who simulated the birth of a child under the conditions provided under Section 4 of this Act may avail of administrative proceedings for the adoption and rectification of the simulated birth record of such child: Provided, That the child has been living with the person for at least three (3) years before the effectivity of this Act: Provided, further, That a certificate declaring the child legally available for adoption (CDCLAA) is issued by the DSWD in favor of such child.
      Simulation of birth is "the tampering of the civil registry to make it appear in the record of birth that a child was born to a person who is not such child's biological mother, causing the loss of the true identity and status of such child" (R.A. 11222, Sec. 3). Before these laws, a simulated birth certificate could be cancelled at the instance of an interested relative (Babiera v. Catotal, G.R. No. 138493, June 15, 2000: a sister may sue to cancel a birth certificate falsely showing their mother, aged 54 at the alleged birth, as the mother of another), and simulated "parents" were exposed to prosecution under RPC 347. R.A. 8552, Sec. 22 gave a five-year amnesty (used in Lim); R.A. 11222 replaced it.
      Quiz traps (adoption): "A Filipino of legal age may adopt" → false under R.A. 11642 (25). "The adopter must in all cases be at least 16 years older" → false (waivable). "Only minors may be adopted" → false. "Spouses must adopt jointly when one adopts his own illegitimate child" → false (consent only). "The adopter may rescind the adoption for causes for disinheritance" → false since R.A. 8552 (disinherit only). "The adopter's parents must consent" → false. "An adoption decree retroacts to make the adopters liable for the child's torts before they had custody" → false (Tamargo). "A foster child or ward may not be adopted by his guardian" → false (Sec. 21(b), (c); Sec. 22(e)). "Proceedings to adopt an orphan may begin a month after the parents' death" → false: six months (Sec. 22(g)).

      Support

      Title VIII, Family Code, Arts. 194–208 (syllabus XV). What support covers, who must give it and in what order, which property answers for it, how much and when it is paid, support pendente lite, and how the right ends. Cases: Pelayo v. Lauron, Sanchez v. Zulueta, Reyes v. Ines-Luciano, Lerma v. CA, Abella v. Cabañero, Melgar v. People, Canonizado v. Benitez; from the class reviewer, Mangonon, Lim v. Lim, De Asis, Perkins, Altobano-Ruiz, Otamias.

      What support comprises (Art. 194)

      Art. 194, FC. Support comprises everything indispensable for sustenance, dwelling, clothing, medical attendance, education and transportation, in keeping with the financial capacity of the family.
      The education of the person entitled to be supported referred to in the preceding paragraph shall include his schooling or training for some profession, trade or vocation, even beyond the age of majority. Transportation shall include expenses in going to and from school, or to and from place of work. (290a)
      Tolentino (Art. 194): natural support is what is absolutely indispensable for subsistence; civil support is what the recipient needs to live according to his social position. The Civil Code kept the distinction; the Family Code erased it. Support does not include a simple loan of money to the wife (Perkins v. Perkins, 57 Phil. 223). The obligation has a permanent aspect (physical needs, for the recipient's lifetime unless it ceases) and a temporary aspect (intellectual development, only while acquiring a profession, trade or vocation). If the recipient began a course while still a minor, the obligor must keep paying until it is finished, even after the recipient comes of age.
      Quiz trap: "Education as part of support ends when the child reaches majority" → false: it includes schooling or training "even beyond the age of majority". 2010 Bar: children aged 18 and 19 who squandered a ₱3 million education fund may still ask for support for their schooling; squandering the fund does not extinguish the parents' obligation.

      Who must support whom (Arts. 195–196)

      Art. 195, FC. Subject to the provisions of the succeeding articles, the following are obliged to support each other to the whole extent set forth in the preceding article:
      (1) The spouses;
      (2) Legitimate ascendants and descendants;
      (3) Parents and their legitimate children and the legitimate and illegitimate children of the latter;
      (4) Parents and their illegitimate children and the legitimate and illegitimate children of the latter; and
      (5) Legitimate brothers and sisters, whether of full or half-blood. (291a)
      Art. 196, FC. Brothers and sisters not legitimately related, whether of the full or half-blood, are likewise bound to support each other to the full extent set forth in Article 194, except only when the need for support of the brother or sister, being of age, is due to a cause imputable to the claimant's fault or negligence. (291a)
      Uribe (CivRev Quiz 2, item 5; also Samplex T/F 9 and the PFR Quiz 3 key): "Brothers and sisters not legitimately related, whether of the full or half-blood, are likewise bound to support each other." False, because Art. 196 has an exception (claimant of age whose need is due to his own fault or negligence). Sir's warning: do not attack the premise ("brothers and sisters not legitimately related, whether of the full or half-blood" is correct as written); what is wrong is the unqualified conclusion. "Huwag niyo palitan ang premise or rule unless it is misleading." And: "Do not say 'should,' unless it should be tomorrow." Asked whether Art. 196's exception applies to ascendants and descendants, the answer was no: it applies only to siblings not legitimately related.
      Tolentino (Arts. 195–196): the FC corrected an inequality in the Civil Code (Art. 291), under which illegitimate descendants of legitimate children could not claim support from their grandparents; now descendants, legitimate or illegitimate, of children legitimate or illegitimate, are on equal footing. Under the Civil Code, siblings were entitled only to natural support; the FC gives them civil support "to the full extent set forth in Article 194". Art. 196 is ambiguous: does the exception deny all support, or only the "full extent"? Tolentino: the intention is the same as under the old Code; the right to support ceases. Between spouses, the right depends on the wife's status as such: once the marriage is annulled she is not entitled to support, even pending the liquidation (Mendoza v. Parungao, 49 Phil. 271). A wife forced to sue for support is entitled to the expenses of litigation, including attorney's fees, as part of support; the same holds where the wife is rich and the husband poor. A mother who gave away her two-year-old child and never cared for her cannot later claim support from the child.
      Pelayo v. Lauron (12 Phil. 453, 1909)

      A physician was called one night by the defendants, husband and wife, to attend their daughter-in-law, who was giving birth in their house. She lived with her husband (the defendants' son) independently of them and was only accidentally in their house that night. The physician charged ₱500 and sued the parents-in-law, who had called him. Held: they are not liable. "The rendering of medical assistance in case of illness is comprised among the mutual obligations to which the spouses are bound by way of mutual support." The person bound to pay is the husband of the patient, not her father- and mother-in-law, who are strangers to that obligation; it is immaterial that he was not the one who called the doctor.

      De Asis v. CA (G.R. No. 127578, February 15, 1999; class reviewer)

      The mother of a minor sued the alleged father for support; she later moved to dismiss, manifesting that the defendant denied paternity, and the case was dismissed with prejudice. A second action for support was filed in the child's name. Held: not barred. "In order to claim support, filiation and/or paternity must first be shown between the claimant and the parent. However, paternity and filiation or the lack of the same is a relationship that must be judicially established and it is for the court to declare its existence or absence. It cannot be left to the will or agreement of the parties." The earlier dismissal amounted to a renunciation of future support, which is void (NCC 2035).

      Abella v. Cabañero (G.R. No. 206647, August 9, 2017)

      Not in your sources in full; from general recollection (verify). Richelle Abella sued Policarpio Cabañero for support of her minor daughter, alleging that he had sexually abused her while she was a minor and was the child's father. The lower courts dismissed the complaint for failure to state a cause of action, reasoning that the child's filiation had not first been established in a separate action. Held: reversed. Filiation may be proved, and support adjudged, in the same action; an illegitimate child need not file a separate action for recognition before suing for support. The case was remanded for trial on filiation and support.

      Melgar v. People (G.R. No. 223477, February 14, 2018)

      Not in your sources in full; from general recollection (verify). Melgar was charged under R.A. No. 9262, Sec. 5(i), for psychological violence through denial of financial support to his illegitimate son with AAA. He entered into a compromise on the civil aspect. Held: the compromise does not extinguish criminal liability. Deprivation or denial of financial support to the child is itself a form of economic abuse punished by Sec. 5(e); since the mental or emotional anguish required by Sec. 5(i) was not proved, but the denial of support was, he was convicted under Sec. 5(e) under the variance doctrine, the offense charged including the offense proved.

      Altobano-Ruiz v. Atty. Ruiz (class reviewer)

      A wife sought the disbarment of her husband, a lawyer convicted under R.A. 9262 for, among others, depriving her and their child of support, who even tried to hide his assets through an agreement with his mistress. Held: he must support their son Jarren, who is legitimate despite the declaration of nullity of the marriage under Art. 36 (Art. 54). "While one spouse is no longer obligated to legally support the other because their marriage was nullified, his obligation to provide support to his minor child does not cease even if care and custody are no longer with the second spouse."

      Which property answers for support (Arts. 197–198)

      Art. 197, FC. In case of legitimate ascendants; descendants, whether legitimate or illegitimate; and brothers and sisters, whether legitimately or illegitimately related, only the separate property of the person obliged to give support shall be answerable provided that in case the obligor has no separate property, the absolute community or the conjugal partnership, if financially capable, shall advance the support, which shall be deducted from the share of the spouse obliged upon the liquidation of the absolute community or of the conjugal partnership. (n)
      Art. 198, FC. During the proceedings for legal separation or for annulment of marriage, and for declaration of nullity of marriage, the spouses and their children shall be supported from the properties of the absolute community or the conjugal partnership. After the final judgment granting the petition, the obligation of mutual support between the spouses ceases. However, in case of legal separation, the court may order that the guilty spouse shall give support to the innocent one, specifying the terms of such order. (292a)
      Tolentino (Art. 198): if there is common property, support pendente lite from it is mandatory. If there is none, may one spouse demand it from the other? In an annulment, yes: the marriage subsists until the decree. In legal separation, a ground committed by the plaintiff would end his or her right. After a final judgment of annulment, the wife may not ask support from the husband even while the liquidation is pending, but the court may order an advance on her share in the conjugal property. In legal separation, support of the innocent spouse by the guilty one is discretionary with the court, not a matter of right.
      Lerma v. CA (61 SCRA 440, December 20, 1974)

      Teodoro Lerma filed a complaint for adultery against his wife, Concepcion Diaz, and her paramour. She then sued him for legal separation and/or separation of property, custody of the children and support, with an urgent petition for support pendente lite for herself and their youngest son. The trial court granted it. Held: she is not entitled to it. "The right to separate support or maintenance, even from the conjugal partnership property, presupposes the existence of a justifiable cause for the spouse claiming such right to live separately." A petition in bad faith, filed by one who is herself guilty of an act constituting a ground for legal separation, is not within the law granting separate support. Under NCC 303, support ceases when the recipient commits an act giving rise to disinheritance, and under NCC 921 one such cause is "when the spouse has given cause for legal separation." "The loss of the substantive right to support in such a situation is incompatible with any claim for support pendente lite." (The criminal case for adultery against her was then pending in the Court of Appeals; the Court said its ruling did not prejudge it.)

      Order of obligors and division (Arts. 199–200)

      Art. 199, FC. Whenever two or more persons are obliged to give support, the liability shall devolve upon the following persons in the order herein provided:
      (1) The spouse;
      (2) The descendants in the nearest degree;
      (3) The ascendants in the nearest degree; and
      (4) The brothers and sisters. (294a)
      Art. 200, FC. When the obligation to give support falls upon two or more persons, the payment of the same shall be divided between them in proportion to the resources of each.
      However, in case of urgent need and by special circumstances, the judge may order only one of them to furnish the support provisionally, without prejudice to his right to claim from the other obligors the share due from them.
      When two or more recipients at the same time claim support from one and the same person legally obliged to give it, should the latter not have sufficient means to satisfy all claims, the order established in the preceding article shall be followed, unless the concurrent obligees should be the spouse and a child subject to parental authority, in which case the child shall be preferred. (295a)
      Uribe (CivRev Quiz 2 continuation): "If the spouse has no capacity to support or may be dead already, the children are required to give support equally, correct?" No. A student answered that it goes automatically to the brothers and sisters, which is also wrong: the next in line are the descendants, and among co-obligors the payment is divided "in proportion to the resources of each" (Art. 200), not equally.
      Tolentino (Arts. 199–200): the order follows the closeness of the relationship; remoter relatives are called only in default of nearer ones. The NCC said the descendants and ascendants are liable in the order they would succeed ab intestato; the FC dropped that clause, but Tolentino would still apply it, "as support follows succession": (1) legitimate children and descendants, (2) legitimate parents and ascendants, (3) illegitimate children and their descendants. The action may be brought against any obligor, but the plaintiff must show that those ahead of the defendant have no means; a rich brother is not liable if he proves that the father can give the support. Co-obligors in the same grade are liable jointly, not solidarily, each in proportion to his means; in urgent cases one may be made to give all of it provisionally, with recourse against the others. Among recipients, children under parental authority (legitimate, legitimated, illegitimate or adopted) are preferred over everyone, including the spouse.
