But that preference applies only when the support comes from the obligor's separate property; if it comes from the ACP or CPG, there is no preference, because it is a charge on the community itself.
      Mangonon v. CA (G.R. No. 125041, June 30, 2006; class reviewer)

      Ma. Belen Mangonon sought support for her twin daughters, Rica and Rina, then in college in the United States, from their father Federico Delgado and their paternal grandfather Francisco Delgado. The mother herself was financially incapable, relying on loans. Held: Francisco must give the support pendente lite. Federico's claimed inability had no evidence behind it, and the mother could not; "the obligation to give support rests principally on those more closely related to the recipient. However, the more remote relatives may be held to shoulder the responsibility should the claimant prove that those who are called upon to provide support do not have the means to do so." Francisco, owner and director of several corporations, had ample means.

      Spouses Lim v. Lim (G.R. No. 163209, October 30, 2009; class reviewer)

      A mother sued her husband and his parents for the support of their three children. Held: the paternal grandparents are liable for the deficiency. "The obligation to provide legal support passes on to ascendants not only upon default of the parents but also for the latter's inability to provide sufficient support." But "only descendants by a direct line are entitled to such support": the grandparents had no obligation to support the mother, their daughter-in-law.

      Amount, time and manner of payment (Arts. 201–204)

      Art. 201, FC. The amount of support, in the cases referred to in Articles 195 and 196, shall be in proportion to the resources or means of the giver and to the necessities of the recipient. (296a)
      Art. 202, FC. Support in the cases referred to in the preceding article shall be reduced or increased proportionately, according to the reduction or increase of the necessities of the recipient and the resources or means of the person obliged to furnish the same. (297a)
      Art. 203, FC. The obligation to give support shall be demandable from the time the person who has a right to receive the same needs it for maintenance, but it shall not be paid except from the date of judicial or extra-judicial demand.
      Support pendente lite may be claimed in accordance with the Rules of Court.
      Payment shall be made within the first five days of each corresponding month or when the recipient dies, his heirs shall not be obliged to return what he has received in advance. (298a)
      Art. 204, FC. The person obliged to give support shall have the option to fulfill the obligation either by paying the allowance fixed, or by receiving and maintaining in the family dwelling the person who has a right to receive support. The latter alternative cannot be availed of in case there is a moral or legal obstacle thereto. (299a)
      Samplex (Uribe quizzes, several versions): "Payment for support shall be made within the first 15 days of each corresponding month" → false: five days (Art. 203). "Payment shall be made within the first five days of each corresponding month" → true. "The person obliged to give support shall fulfill the obligation by paying the allowance fixed" → false: he has the option to pay the allowance or to receive and maintain the recipient in the family dwelling (Art. 204). Its mirror, "shall fulfill the obligation by receiving and maintaining in the family dwelling", is also false; in the class discussion, the point was that "the person obliged to give support has an option", and the second alternative is unavailable when there is a moral or legal obstacle.
      Tolentino (Arts. 202–204): a judgment for support is never final; it may always be modified as the obligor's means and the recipient's needs change (Canonizado). A change has no retroactive effect: no refund of what was paid, and arrears are not condoned by a later reduction. A support judgment does not lapse after five years like ordinary judgments; it lasts until the children come of age, though unpaid installments more than ten years old are uncollectible (Florendo v. Organo). It may be enforced by contempt (only for willful disobedience), or by attachment and execution (on mere failure to pay), or both. Art. 204 option has two requisites: the obligor has his own home, and there is no moral or legal obstacle. Obstacles recognized: a husband who abducted the girl and married her to avoid prosecution but never lived with her; a natural father who never supported the child and has since married another woman; a married daughter, who must live with her husband; a wife driven out by the husband's demands for unchaste acts (Goitia v. Campos Rueda), by his tolerance of his son's seduction of her daughter, by repeated infidelity, or by abuse. Emancipated children cannot be compelled to live with the parent to be supported. Where the wife leaves without sufficient cause (e.g., mere jealousy), the husband may insist on supporting her at home, but the court will not order her to live with him. The option may be waived, e.g., by a contract giving the wife custody and promising a pension.
      Canonizado v. Benitez (127 SCRA 610, 1984)

      A wife had a final judgment for monthly support against her husband. Later he moved to stop paying current support, arguing that she no longer needed it, so that under NCC 303(3) his obligation had ceased. (Facts simplified; your sources give only the doctrine.) Held: NCC 303 "provides that the obligation to give support shall also cease 'when the recipient may engage in a trade, profession, or industry, or has obtained work, or has improved his fortune in such a way that he no longer needs the allowance for his subsistence'. … It does not mean, however, that the obligation to give or the right to ask for support also ceases permanently because the lack of a need for it may only be temporary. In other words, the above circumstances do not affect the right to support between spouses but only the action to make it demandable, such right being born from the law and created as such by the marriage tie." "A judgment for support is never final in the sense that not only can its amount be subject to increase or decrease but its demandability may also be suspended or re-enforced when appropriate circumstances exist." No separate action is needed to suspend current support; the court that rendered the judgment decides it on evidence.

      Perkins v. Perkins (57 Phil. 223, 1932; class reviewer)

      A wife sued for separate maintenance and claimed reimbursement of expenses long before the suit. Held: "The obligation to provide support only becomes enforceable and payable from the date of the filing of the complaint for separate maintenance. Items of expense that long precede the date of the filing of the suit are generally outside the allowable claims for support." A simple loan of money to the wife is not support.

      Exemption, strangers who give support, contractual support (Arts. 205–208)

      Art. 205, FC. The right to receive support under this Title as well as any money or property obtained as such support shall not be levied upon on attachment or execution. (302a)
      Art. 206, FC. When, without the knowledge of the person obliged to give support, it is given by a stranger, the latter shall have a right to claim the same from the former, unless it appears that he gave it without intention of being reimbursed. (2164a)
      Art. 207, FC. When the person obliged to support another unjustly refuses or fails to give support when urgently needed by the latter, any third person may furnish support to the needy individual, with right of reimbursement from the person obliged to give support. This Article shall particularly apply when the father or mother of a child under the age of majority unjustly refuses to support or fails to give support to the child when urgently needed. (2166a)
      Art. 208, FC. In case of contractual support or that given by will, the excess in amount beyond that required for legal support shall be subject to levy on attachment or execution.
      Furthermore, contractual support shall be subject to adjustment whenever modification is necessary due to changes of circumstances manifestly beyond the contemplation of the parties. (n)
      Samplex (Uribe Civil Law Reviewer, Quiz #4, T/F 10): "When, without the knowledge of the person obliged to give support, it is given by a stranger, the latter shall have a right to claim the same from the former." Keyed false: the statement drops the "unless" clause ("unless it appears that he gave it without intention of being reimbursed").
      Tolentino (Arts. 205–208): exemption from execution protects the recipient "against want and misery"; but the excess of contractual or testamentary support over legal support may be levied (Art. 208). Requisites under Art. 206: (1) support was furnished to a dependent of one bound to give it who fails to do so, (2) by a stranger, (3) without the obligor's knowledge, (4) not without expectation of recovering it. The obligor must first be given a chance: a sister-in-law who sent money to a wife whose husband had merely reduced his allowance abroad could not recover (Ramirez v. Redfern, 49 Phil. 849). "Stranger" means one with no obligation to support; a relative lower in the Art. 199 order who gives support when a nearer one fails is not a stranger under Art. 206.
      Otamias v. Republic (G.R. No. 189516, June 8, 2016; class reviewer)

      A retired AFP officer executed a deed assigning 50% of his retirement benefits to his wife and children for their support, then stopped. The RTC ordered automatic deduction; the CA set it aside, citing the exemption of pensions from execution (P.D. 1638) and the AFP's non-party status. Held: the deduction may be enforced. The exemption of pension benefits from execution is a personal statutory right that may be waived, "especially in order to comply with a husband's duty to support" under the Constitution and the Family Code; the deed of assignment was such a waiver.

      Support pendente lite and defenses

      Rule 61, Sec. 1, Rules of Court. At the commencement of the proper action or proceeding, or at any time prior to the judgment or final order, a verified application for support pendente lite may be filed by any party stating the grounds for the claim and the financial conditions of both parties, and accompanied by affidavits, depositions or other authentic documents in support thereof. (Secs. 2–6: three days to answer; hearing; provisional order considering the applicant's needs, the adverse party's means and the probable outcome; enforcement by execution or contempt.)
      Sanchez v. Zulueta (68 Phil. 110, 1939)

      A wife sued her husband for support for herself and her child, and asked for support pendente lite. The husband alleged that she had committed adultery and that the child was not his, and asked to present evidence; the lower courts granted support pendente lite without letting him prove it. Held: error. "Adultery on the part of the wife is a valid defense against an action for support (Quintana v. Lerma, 24 Phil. 285). Consequently, as to the child, it is also a defense that it is the fruit of such adulterous relations, for in that case, it would not be the child of the defendant and, hence, would not be entitled to support as such. But as this defense should be established, and not merely alleged, it would be unavailing if proof thereof is not permitted. It is not of course necessary to go fully into the merits of the case, it being sufficient that the court ascertain the kind and amount of evidence which it may deem sufficient to enable it to justly resolve the application, one way or the other, in view of the merely provisional character of the resolution to be entered."

      Reyes v. Ines-Luciano (88 SCRA 803, 1979)

      Celia Ilustre-Reyes sued her husband Manuel J. C. Reyes for legal separation, alleging that he had twice tried to kill her, and asked for support pendente lite for herself and their three children. He opposed, alleging that she had committed adultery with her physician. The trial court granted ₱5,000 a month, reduced to ₱4,000. Held: affirmed. Adultery is a good defense, but "the alleged adultery must be established by competent evidence"; the husband offered only allegations. The Court also doubted whether adultery would bar support pendente lite here, since the wife sought it from the conjugal property, not from Manuel's personal funds.

      Tolentino (pendente lite): if the defendant's answer denies the marriage, thus putting the plaintiff's very status in issue, alimony pendente lite should not be allowed until the marriage is established; nor where the defense is that the plaintiff wife committed adultery. In an action by a child, the defense that he is the fruit of adulterous relations must likewise be established, not merely alleged. The court has no jurisdiction to award support pendente lite to one claiming to be the defendant's son if paternity is denied, and the defendant's lawyer's consent does not confer it. The husband cannot defend by saying he has other persons to support: the wife's claim is preferred, second only to that of children under parental authority. Support pendente lite cannot be ordered in an action for recovery of property against persons with no legal duty of support.

      2011 Bar: Is the wife who leaves her husband without just cause entitled to support? (A) No, because the wife must always be submissive and respectful to the husband. (B) Yes, the marriage not having been dissolved, the husband continues to have an obligation to support his wife. (C) No, because in leaving the conjugal home without just cause, she forfeits her right to support. (D) Yes, since the right to receive support is not subject to any condition.

      (C). A spouse who leaves without just cause has no right to separate maintenance; at most the husband may exercise his Art. 204 option to support her in the family home. Compare Tolentino: the right to separate maintenance presupposes a cause justifying a separate domicile (Goitia v. Campos Rueda; Lerma).

      Renunciation and termination

      Tolentino (cessation): under old NCC 303(4), when the recipient is not a compulsory heir (e.g., a brother), the grounds are those of unworthiness found among the causes of disinheritance: an attempt on the life of the obligor or his family; a groundless accusation of a crime punished by six years or more; conviction of adultery or concubinage with the obligor's spouse; and fraud, violence, intimidation or undue influence regarding a will. When support from one obligor ends because of the recipient's act, he may turn to the next in line, unless the cause bars that too: a husband who forced his wife to make a will loses support from her but may ask his children; a daughter who loses support from her parents through prostitution cannot turn to her brothers.
      Quiz traps (support): "Support between spouses ceases upon the filing of a petition for legal separation" → false: upon the final judgment (Art. 198); during the case they are supported from the common property. "Future support may be the subject of a compromise" → false (NCC 2035). "The amount of support fixed in a final judgment can no longer be changed" → false (Art. 202; Canonizado). "Co-obligors share equally" → false: in proportion to their resources (Art. 200). "When the spouse and a minor child both claim support from one person who cannot satisfy both, the spouse is preferred" → false: the child under parental authority is preferred (Art. 200). "Arrears in support can never be waived" → false: only future support cannot.

      2011 Bar: Spouses X and Y have a minor daughter, Z, who needs support for her education. Both X and Y are financially distressed and cannot give it. Z's other relatives are financially capable. From whom may Z first rightfully demand support? (A) Grandfather. (B) Brother. (C) Uncle. (D) First cousin.

      (A) Grandfather. After the parents come the ascendants in the nearest degree, before brothers and sisters (Art. 199); uncles and cousins are not obliged at all (Art. 195). Lim v. Lim: the obligation passes to the grandparents on the parents' inability, not only on their default.

      2018 Bar (adapted): Sofia and Semuel, both unmarried, lived together and had three children. Semuel became a naturalized German citizen. Must he support the minor children?

      Yes. Parents must support their illegitimate children (Art. 195(4)), with everything indispensable for sustenance, dwelling, clothing, medical attendance, education and transportation (Art. 194). Even if German law did not require it, his refusal to support them while in the Philippines is punishable under R.A. No. 9262 by the territoriality principle (Del Socorro v. Van Wilsem, G.R. No. 193707, December 10, 2014). Compare the 2023 Bar on an American father: his duty to support is governed by his national law, which he must plead and prove, failing which it is presumed to be the same as ours.

      Parental Authority

      Title IX, Family Code, Arts. 209–233 (syllabus XVI), with NCC 2180, Rule 130, Sec. 25 and P.D. 603. Who exercises parental authority, substitute and special parental authority and the liability that comes with it, the filial privilege, authority over the child's person and property, and suspension, termination and revival. Cases: Hontiveros, Unson, Exconde, Palisoc, Amadora, Salvosa, St. Mary's, Medina, Luna, Lindain, Chua v. Cabangbang; from the class reviewer, Eslao, Santos Sr., Briones, Vancil, Cuadra, Tamargo, Lee.

      Concept; cannot be renounced (Arts. 209–210)

      Art. 209, FC. Pursuant to the natural right and duty of parents over the person and property of their unemancipated children, parental authority and responsibility shall include the caring for and rearing them for civic consciousness and efficiency and the development of their moral, mental and physical character and well-being. (n)
      Art. 210, FC. Parental authority and responsibility may not be renounced or transferred except in the cases authorized by law. (313a)
      Eslao v. CA (G.R. No. 116773, January 16, 1997; class reviewer)

      After her husband Reynaldo died, Maria Paz Cordero-Ouye left her daughter Angelica with her mother-in-law, Teresita Sagala-Eslao, who begged to keep the child to ease her grief. Maria Paz later married an American and returned to take Angelica with her; Teresita refused, claiming abandonment. Held: custody goes to the mother. Leaving the child with her grandmother was temporary and was not a renunciation. "Parental authority and responsibility are inalienable and may not be transferred or renounced except in cases authorized by law. The right attached to parental authority, being purely personal, the law allows a waiver of parental authority only in cases of adoption, guardianship and surrender to a children's home or an orphan institution."

      Who exercises it (Arts. 211–213)

      Art. 211, FC. The father and the mother shall jointly exercise parental authority over the persons of their common children. In case of disagreement, the father's decision shall prevail, unless there is a judicial order to the contrary.
      Children shall always observe respect and reverence towards their parents and are obliged to obey them as long as the children are under parental authority. (311a)
      Art. 212, FC. In case of absence or death of either parent, the parent present shall continue exercising parental authority. The remarriage of the surviving parent shall not affect the parental authority over the children, unless the court appoints another person to be the guardian of the person or property of the children. (n)
      Art. 213, FC. In case of separation of the parents, parental authority shall be exercised by the parent designated by the Court. The Court shall take into account all relevant considerations, especially the choice of the child over seven years of age, unless the parent chosen is unfit.
      No child under seven years of age shall be separated from the mother unless the court finds compelling reasons to order otherwise. (n)
      Art. 176, FC (as amended by R.A. 9255, first sentence). Illegitimate children shall use the surname and shall be under the parental authority of their mother, and shall be entitled to support in conformity with this Code. …
      Bar traps (custody): A mother's lesbian relationship (2024 Bar) or her work as an entertainer in a men's club (2023 Bar) is not, by itself, a compelling reason: there must be proof that it harms the child. The illegitimate child stays with the mother (Art. 176), and the tender-age rule adds to it. A biological father's offer to support mother and child if they live with him does not give him custody. Contrast Unson, where the mother's situation was an "obviously unwholesome, not to say immoral influence" on a girl at an impressionable age.
      Unson v. Navarro (101 SCRA 183, 1980)

      Edgar Unson and Edita Araneta separated; their daughter Maria Teresa stayed with her mother, who was then living with Agustin Uy, the husband of her own sister, by whom she had children. The father sought custody when the girl reached school age. Held: custody to the father; the mother gets visitorial rights only. "In all controversies regarding the custody of minors, the sole and foremost consideration is the physical, education, social and moral welfare of the child concerned, taking into account the respective resources and social and moral situations of the contending parents." The girl should be "freed from the obviously unwholesome, not to say immoral influence, that the situation in which private respondent has placed herself … might create in the moral and social outlook of Teresa who is now in her formative and most impressionable stage." "Decisions even of this Supreme Court on the custody of minor children are always open to adjustment as the circumstances relevant to the matter may demand."

      Hontiveros v. IAC (132 SCRA 745, 1984)

      A father contested the mother's custody of their minor child, claiming before the Supreme Court that she was unfit, after his own custody case below had been dismissed for his lack of interest. Held: the mother keeps custody. Unfitness is a question of fact that cannot be raised for the first time in a Rule 45 petition; "it is just too bad that the case for custody was dismissed for lack of interest on the part of the petitioner. Clearly, the private respondent has a clear legal right under Article 17 of P.D. 603 to the custody of her minor child, there being no compelling reason to the contrary."

      Briones v. Miguel (G.R. No. 156343, October 18, 2004; class reviewer)

      Joey Briones and Loreta Miguel, never married, had a son, Michael. Loreta worked in Japan and married a Japanese national; Joey sought custody by habeas corpus, arguing that he had recognized the child and could support him. Held: custody to the mother, visitation for the father. Under Art. 176, illegitimate children are under the parental authority of their mother; "the recognition of an illegitimate child by the father could be a ground for ordering the latter to give support to, but not custody of, the child." Rule 99, Sec. 6 (choice of a child over seven between separated parents) applies only to married parents, so it was deleted from the CA's ruling.

      Tolentino (Arts. 211–213): Art. 211 formalized Filipino practice. The mother's authority is "subordinated, although not subsidiary" to the father's: in private, internal matters (education, moral guidance) they share equally, but in a conflict the father's decision prevails subject to a court order; in external, juridical matters the law itself prefers the father (administration of the child's property, Art. 225; liability for quasi-delicts under NCC 2180). The duty of obedience lasts only while the child is under parental authority; the duty of respect and reverence lasts for life, though after emancipation it has no sanction except, in grave cases, disinheritance. Other ascendants have no authority while the parents live and have not lost it; an aunt, by that relationship alone, is not entitled to custody (Ortiz v. Del Villar). Parental authority follows the parent abroad (national law). On separation, the welfare of the child controls (Perkins v. Perkins, 57 Phil. 217: custody of a girl over ten awarded to the father despite her preference for the mother, who had poisoned her mind against him and kept her in court hearings).
      "Choice of the child over seven": Art. 213 says "over seven years of age"; Art. 102(6) and 129(9) (adjudication of the family dwelling) say "children below the age of seven years are deemed to have chosen the mother". A child of exactly seven is outside both the tender-age presumption and, on a strict reading, the "over seven" choice. On a quiz, quote the text.

      Substitute parental authority (Arts. 214, 216, 217, 233)

      Art. 214, FC. In case of death, absence or unsuitability of the parents, substitute parental authority shall be exercised by the surviving grandparent. In case several survive, the one designated by the court, taking into account the same consideration mentioned in the preceding article, shall exercise the authority. (355a)
      Art. 216, FC. In default of parents or a judicially appointed guardian, the following persons shall exercise substitute parental authority over the child in the order indicated:
      (1) The surviving grandparent, as provided in Art. 214;
      (2) The oldest brother or sister, over twenty-one years of age, unless unfit or disqualified; and
      (3) The child's actual custodian, over twenty-one years of age, unless unfit or disqualified.
      Whenever the appointment of a judicial guardian over the property of the child becomes necessary, the same order of preference shall be observed. (349a, 351a, 354a)
      Art. 217, FC. In case of foundlings, abandoned, neglected or abused children and other children similarly situated, parental authority shall be entrusted in summary judicial proceedings to heads of children's homes, orphanages and similar institutions duly accredited by the proper government agency. (314a)
      Art. 233, FC. The person exercising substitute parental authority shall have the same authority over the person of the child as the parents.
      In no case shall the school administrator, teacher or individual engaged in child care exercising special parental authority inflict corporal punishment upon the child. (n)
      Uribe (CivRev Quiz 2, item 6; PFR Quiz 3, item 20; Samplex T/F 10): "In case of death, absence or unsuitability of the parents, special parental authority shall be exercised by the surviving grandparent." False: that is substitute parental authority (Arts. 214, 216). Special parental authority belongs to "teachers, administrators, the school" (Art. 218). A second version: "… substitute parental authority shall be exercised by the surviving grandparents." Also false: the law says "the surviving grandparent", and if several survive, the one designated by the court. Watch every letter.
      Vancil v. Belmes (G.R. No. 132223, June 19, 2001; class reviewer)

      Bonifacia Vancil, the paternal grandmother and an American citizen in Colorado, sought guardianship of her grandson Vincent against his mother, Helen Belmes, whom she called unfit because Vincent's sister had been abused by Helen's live-in partner. Held: the mother prevails. "The natural parents of the child have preferential natural and legal rights to the custody of the child"; substitute parental authority of the grandparent under Art. 214 arises only if the mother is first proved dead, absent or unsuitable, which was not shown. The grandmother's age, foreign residence and a prior conviction also made her an impractical guardian.

      Santos, Sr. v. CA (G.R. No. 113054, March 16, 1995; class reviewer)

      The maternal grandparents, who had cared for the boy since birth, resisted the father's claim to custody. Held: custody to the father. "Parental authority is primarily and exclusively vested in the parents, and substitute parental authority of grandparents may arise only when statutory conditions are met, namely, the death, absence, incapacity, or unfitness of both parents." The grandparents' greater means and affection are not enough.

      Tolentino (Arts. 216–217): including grandparents and the oldest sibling conforms to Filipino custom. The Art. 216 order is mandatory unless special circumstances require otherwise: if the child's welfare is better served with the maternal grandparents, they prevail over the paternal grandparents. An "abandoned" child is one with no parental care or guardianship, or whose parents or guardians have deserted him for at least six months. Teachers have no power of corporal punishment; it belonged only to parents.
      "Over twenty-one" in Art. 216: R.A. 6809 lowered the age of majority to 18 but did not amend Art. 216, which still says "over twenty-one years of age" for the oldest sibling and the actual custodian. Quote 21.

      Special parental authority and liability for the minor's acts (Arts. 218–219, 221; NCC 2180)

      Art. 218, FC. The school, its administrators and teachers, or the individual, entity or institution engaged in child care shall have special parental authority and responsibility over the minor child while under their supervision, instruction or custody.
      Authority and responsibility shall apply to all authorized activities whether inside or outside the premises of the school, entity or institution. (349a)
      Art. 219, FC. Those given the authority and responsibility under the preceding Article shall be principally and solidarily liable for damages caused by the acts or omissions of the unemancipated minor. The parents, judicial guardians or the persons exercising substitute parental authority over said minor shall be subsidiarily liable.
      The respective liabilities of those referred to in the preceding paragraph shall not apply if it is proved that they exercised the proper diligence required under the particular circumstances.
      All other cases not covered by this and the preceding articles shall be governed by the provisions of the Civil Code on quasi-delicts. (n)
      Art. 221, FC. Parents and other persons exercising parental authority shall be civilly liable for the injuries and damages caused by the acts or omissions of their unemancipated children living in their company and under their parental authority subject to the appropriate defenses provided by law. (2180(2)a and (4)a)
      Art. 2180, NCC (pars. 2, 3, 7, 8). The father and, in case of his death or incapacity, the mother, are responsible for the damages caused by the minor children who live in their company. Guardians are liable for damages caused by the minors or incapacitated persons who are under their authority and live in their company. … Lastly, teachers or heads of establishments of arts and trades shall be liable for damages caused by their pupils and students or apprentices, so long as they remain in their custody. The responsibility treated of in this article shall cease when the persons herein mentioned prove that they observed all the diligence of a good father of a family to prevent damage.
      Exconde v. Capuno (101 Phil. 843, 1957)

      Dante Capuno, 15, a student of Balintawak Elementary School, joined a school-ordered parade in honor of Dr. Jose Rizal. On the way he boarded a jeep, took the wheel, and the jeep turned over, killing two passengers, including Isidoro Caperiña. His father, Delfin Capuno, was sued with him. Held: the father is solidarily liable with his son; the school is not, because NCC 2180 then applied only to teachers or heads of "establishments of arts and trades", not academic schools. "The civil liability which the law imposes upon the father, and, in case of his death or incapacity, the mother, for any damages that may be caused by the minor children who live with them, is obvious. This is a necessary consequence of the parental authority they exercise over them…. The only way by which they can relieve themselves of this liability is if they prove that they exercised all the diligence of a good father of a family to prevent the damage", which Delfin failed to prove.

      Palisoc v. Brillantes (41 SCRA 548, 1971)

      Dominador Palisoc, 16, a student of the Manila Technical Institute, was fatally punched in the school laboratory by a classmate, Virgilio Daffon, during a quarrel, while their instructor was nearby. Held: the head of the school (Valenton), the instructor (Quibulue) and Daffon are solidarily liable. They "could have avoided the unfortunate death … had said defendants but complied with their duty of providing adequate supervision over the activities of the students in the school premises to protect their students from harm, whether at the hands of fellow students or other parties." "There is nothing in the law which prescribes that a student must be living and boarding with his teacher or in the school before heads and teachers of the school may be held liable for the tortious acts of their students." (Abandoning the contrary dictum in Mercado v. CA.)

      Amadora v. CA (160 SCRA 315, 1988)

      Alfredo Amadora, 17, a graduating student of Colegio de San Jose-Recoletos, went to the school auditorium a few days before graduation to submit his physics report, though classes had formally ended. A classmate, Pablito Daffon, shot and killed him there. Held: NCC 2180 now applies to all schools, academic or not; the teacher-in-charge of an academic school, and the head of a school of arts and trades, are liable. Alfredo "was in the custody of the authorities of the school notwithstanding classes had formally ended when the incident happened. It was immaterial if he was in the school auditorium to finish his physics requirement. What was important is that he was there for a legitimate purpose." But the rector, principal and dean of boys were not liable, "because none of them was the teacher-in-charge … Each was exercising only a general authority over the students and not direct control and influence," and no teacher-in-charge was shown negligent. The school itself is not directly liable under NCC 2180.

      Salvosa v. IAC (166 SCRA 274, 1988)

      Jimmy Abon, a commerce student and ROTC armorer of Baguio Colleges Foundation (a school of arts and trades), shot Napoleon Castro on the campus with a rifle he had taken from the armory, after school hours, when he was supposed to be at home. Held: the school and its officers are not liable. The rationale of NCC 2180 is that a student in the teacher's custody is one over whom the teacher "stands, to a certain extent, in loco parentis." "So long as (the students) remain in their custody" means "the protective and supervisory custody that the school and its heads and teachers exercise over the pupils and students for as long as they are at attendance in the school, including recess time." Abon "cannot be considered to have been 'at attendance in the school,' or in the custody of BCF, when he shot Napoleon Castro."

      St. Mary's Academy v. Carpitanos (G.R. No. 143363, February 6, 2002)

      During an enrollment drive organized by St. Mary's Academy, student Sherwin Carpitanos rode a jeep driven by another minor student, James Daniel II, 15; the jeep turned over and Sherwin died. The trial court held the school liable under Arts. 218–219. Held: the school is not liable. "Considering that the negligence of the minor driver or the detachment of the steering wheel guide of the jeep owned by respondent Villanueva was an event over which petitioner St. Mary's Academy had no control, and which was the proximate cause of the accident, petitioner may not be held liable for the death resulting from such accident." Liability under Art. 219 still requires that the school's negligence be the proximate cause of the injury.

      Cuadra v. Monfort (35 SCRA 160, 1970; class reviewer)

      Two Grade 6 girls were weeding a school garden as instructed by their teacher. Maria Teresa Monfort, in jest, tossed a piece of headband she said was a worm; it hit Maria Teresa Cuadra in the eye, which she rubbed, and she lost the sight of her right eye. Her parents sued Monfort's father. Held: complaint dismissed. The parents' responsibility under NCC 2180 ceases on proof of the diligence of a good father of a family; the act happened in school, outside the father's company, and was an innocent prank whose consequences no parent could anticipate.

      Tamargo v. CA (G.R. No. 85044, June 3, 1992; class reviewer)

      Adelberto Bundoc, 10, shot Jennifer Tamargo with an air rifle while living with his natural parents. A petition for his adoption by the Rapisura spouses had been filed before the shooting and was granted after it. The natural parents argued that, since a decree of adoption retroacts to the filing of the petition, parental authority and liability had passed to the adopters. Held: the natural parents are liable. The retroactive effect of an adoption decree is meant to benefit the child; it cannot impose liability on adopters "accruing at a time when adopting parents had no actual or physical custody over the adopted child." Parental liability rests on those who actually exercise custody and control.

      Tolentino (Arts. 218–221): liability of parents rests on a presumption that they failed in their duty of vigilance and guidance; they may rebut it by proving the diligence of a good father of a family. The old rule (Bagajo v. Marave) that only teachers, not the head of an academic school, are answerable for their students' torts was modified by Arts. 219 and 221, which have a much broader application. A head of family who keeps a car for the family's general use is liable for its negligent operation by a child he permits to drive it (Gutierrez v. Gutierrez, 56 Phil. 177).

      2003 Bar: During class hours, while the teacher was chatting with other teachers in the corridor, a 7-year-old pupil stabbed another boy in the eye with a ball pen during a fight, causing permanent blindness. Who may be liable: the teacher, the school authorities, or the guilty boy's parents?

      The teacher and the school authorities, principally and solidarily, because the pupil was under their special parental authority (Art. 218) and they were negligent: the teacher was out of the classroom chatting during class time (Art. 219). The boy's parents are subsidiarily liable (Art. 219, 1st par.).

      2010 Bar: On May 5, 1989, Rozanno, 16, drove his car on a school field trip at his teacher's request, carrying four classmates; he made a wrong maneuver, and one classmate died. (a) Who is liable? (b) Same facts, but the accident happened in mid-1994.

      (a) Rozanno was a minor on an authorized activity outside the premises, so the school, its administrators and teachers are liable under Arts. 218–219, with his parents subsidiarily liable (and principally under Art. 221 if negligent). (b) By mid-1994 Rozanno was 21; R.A. 6809 (majority at 18) took effect in December 1989. Arts. 218, 219 and 221 no longer apply; Rozanno alone is liable, unless the school or his parents were themselves negligent, in which case they answer under the general rules on quasi-delict. (Compare Art. 236, 3rd par.: parents remain responsible under NCC 2180 for children below 21; see Emancipation.)

      Filial privilege (Art. 215; Rule 130, Sec. 25)

      Art. 215, FC. No descendant shall be compelled, in a criminal case, to testify against his parents and grandparents, except when such testimony is indispensable in a crime against the descendant or by one parent against the other. (315a)
      Rule 130, Sec. 25, Rules of Court. Parental and filial privilege. — No person may be compelled to testify against his parents, other direct ascendants, children or other direct descendants, except when such testimony is indispensable in a crime against that person or by one parent against the other.
      Lee v. CA (G.R. No. 177861, July 13, 2010; class reviewer)

      In a Rule 108 case over the birth records of the children of Lee Tek Sheng (registered as children of his wife, Keh Shiok Cheng, though allegedly borne by his concubine, Tiu Chuan), Tiu Chuan was called to testify. The filial privilege was invoked on the ground that she would be testifying against Emma Lee, whose stepmother she was claimed to be. Held: the privilege "only applies to 'direct' ascendants and descendants, a family tie connected by a common ancestry. A stepdaughter has no common ancestry by her stepmother." She may be compelled to testify.

      Authority over the child's person (Arts. 220–224)

      Art. 220, FC. The parents and those exercising parental authority shall have with respect to their unemancipated children or wards the following rights and duties:
      (1) To keep them in their company, to support, educate and instruct them by right precept and good example, and to provide for their upbringing in keeping with their means;
      (2) To give them love and affection, advice and counsel, companionship and understanding;
      (3) To provide them with moral and spiritual guidance, inculcate in them honesty, integrity, self-discipline, self-reliance, industry and thrift, stimulate their interest in civic affairs, and inspire in them compliance with the duties of citizenship;
      (4) To enhance, protect, preserve and maintain their physical and mental health at all times;
      (5) To furnish them with good and wholesome educational materials, supervise their activities, recreation and association with others, protect them from bad company, and prevent them from acquiring habits detrimental to their health, studies and morals;
      (6) To represent them in all matters affecting their interests;
      (7) To demand from them respect and obedience;
      (8) To impose discipline on them as may be required under the circumstances; and
      (9) To perform such other duties as are imposed by law upon parents and guardians. (316a)
      Art. 222, FC. The courts may appoint a guardian of the child's property or a guardian ad litem when the best interests of the child so requires. (317)
      Arts. 223–224, FC (summary). The parents (or, in their absence or incapacity, whoever exercises parental authority) may petition the court of the child's residence for disciplinary measures; the child is entitled to counsel and a summary hearing. If the court finds the petitioner at fault, it may instead suspend or deprive him of parental authority. The measures may include commitment of the child for not more than thirty days in an accredited child-care institution; the parent may not interfere but must support the child.
      Nine items, not eight: some class reviewers drop item (4) ("to enhance, protect, preserve and maintain their physical and mental health at all times") and list eight rights and duties. The official text, as Tolentino prints it, has nine.
      Medina v. Makabali (27 SCRA 602, 1969)

      Zenaida Medina gave birth to Joseph in Dra. Venancia Makabali's clinic and left him there. Dra. Makabali raised him as her own, had him treated for polio and sent him to school; Zenaida never visited or paid anything for over five years, then sought custody by habeas corpus. Asked whom he preferred, the boy pointed to Dra. Makabali: "She is the one rearing me." Held: custody stays with Dra. Makabali. "While our law recognizes the right of a parent to the custody of her child, Courts must not lose sight of the basic principle that 'in all questions on the care, custody, education and property of children, the latter's welfare shall be paramount' (Civil Code, Art. 363), and that for compelling reasons, even a child under seven may be ordered separated from the mother." "The right of parents to the company and custody of their children is but ancillary to the proper discharge of parental duties to provide the children with adequate support, education, moral, intellectual and civic training and development."

      Luna v. IAC (137 SCRA 7, 1985; the syllabus prints 167 SCRA 7)

      The natural parents of a girl, Shirley, who had been raised since infancy by the Lunas, obtained a final judgment awarding them custody. During the execution proceedings, the girl, then about ten, manifested that she would kill herself or run away if taken from the Lunas. Held: execution of the final judgment is stayed and the child stays with the Lunas. "In child custody cases, execution of final judgment of appellate courts awarding custody to child's biological parents may be stayed where during hearings on execution the child manifests that she will kill herself and escape if given to custody of her biological parents." "The best interest of the minor can override procedural rules and even the rights of parents to the custody of their children."

      Tolentino (Art. 220): rights of parents: custody; representation in all matters affecting the child; respect, obedience and discipline; administration of the child's property and use of its fruits for the child and the family; consent to marriage, settlements, donations propter nuptias, adoption and employment; disinheritance for cause. Duties: support and upbringing; education, guidance, love; defense; answering for the child's damages; leaving the legitime. Parental support of an unemancipated child depends only on the parent's means, not the child's needs, and is not lost by the child's misconduct. A third person who could give a better home will not get custody if the parents' home is decent. Parents may open the child's correspondence and forbid unwholesome associations, but not his dealings with his grandparents. They may not force a child to marry (Salvaña v. Gaela: refusing consent to the child's marriage is not ground for deprivation), nor impose forced labor. They may now represent the child in court. Correction must be moderate; parents cannot confine children in "private prisons".

      Authority over the child's property (Arts. 225–227)

      Art. 225, FC. The father and the mother shall jointly exercise legal guardianship over the property of the unemancipated common child without the necessity of a court appointment. In case of disagreement, the father's decision shall prevail, unless there is a judicial order to the contrary.
      Where the market value of the property or the annual income of the child exceeds P50,000, the parent concerned shall be required to furnish a bond in such amount as the court may determine, but not less than ten per centum (10%) of the value of the property or annual income, to guarantee the performance of the obligations prescribed for general guardians. … The ordinary rules on guardianship shall be merely suppletory except when the child is under substitute parental authority, or the guardian is a stranger, or a parent has remarried, in which case the ordinary rules on guardianship shall apply. (320a)
      Art. 226, FC. The property of the unemancipated child earned or acquired with his work or industry or by onerous or gratuitous title shall belong to the child in ownership and shall be devoted exclusively to the latter's support and education, unless the title or transfer provides otherwise.
      The right of the parents over the fruits and income of the child's property shall be limited primarily to the child's support and secondarily to the collective daily needs of the family. (321a, 323a)
      Art. 227, FC. If the parents entrust the management or administration of any of their properties to an unemancipated child, the net proceeds of such property shall belong to the owner. The child shall be given a reasonable monthly allowance in an amount not less than that which the owner would have paid if the administrator were a stranger, unless the owner, grants the entire proceeds to the child. In any case, the proceeds thus given in whole or in part shall not be charged to the child's legitime. (322a)
      Lindain v. CA (G.R. No. 95305, August 20, 1992; 212 SCRA 725)

      The widowed mother of the Lindain minors, as their legal administrator, sold their land without court approval to the spouses Apostol, who knew the sale had no judicial approval. Years later the children sued for annulment and reconveyance. Held: the sale is void as to the children. "Under Art. 320 (NCC), a parent acting merely as a legal administrator of the property of his minor children does not have the power to dispose of or alienate the property of the said child without judicial approval." The powers of a legal administrator are "merely powers of possession and management"; the power to sell, mortgage, encumber or dispose "must proceed from the court". The buyers were not in good faith, and the action had not prescribed.

      Tolentino (Arts. 225–227): administration covers acts of preservation and the receipt of fruits; any act of disposition, alienation or reduction of the child's patrimony exceeds it, so parents cannot dispose of the child's property without express judicial authority, nor compromise the child's rights. The legal guardianship cannot be renounced or delegated (to the child or a stranger). A minor parent cannot administer his child's property; a guardian should be appointed. The parents' right over the fruits is a limited usufruct, an attribute of parental authority for the family's benefit; it is inalienable and, Tolentino believes, cannot be renounced. A donor or testator may exclude it. The child's salary is not "fruits" but property, so it cannot be attached for the parent's debts. The usufruct ends with emancipation, the child's death, judicial loss of parental authority, consent to the child's living independently, and disinheritance or unworthiness of the parent (NCC 923, 1035). Under Art. 227, the child's allowance is compensation for his services, not support; the parents still owe support.
      Hebron v. Loyola (G.R. No. 168960, July 5, 2010; class reviewer)

      In a partition among the heirs of Remigia Baylon, the administrator's successor claimed that the shares of certain grandchildren had been waived or paid by their mother. Held: the grandchildren keep their shares. "The powers given to the mother by the laws as the natural guardian covers only matters of administration and cannot include the power of disposition"; she could not relinquish her children's inheritance.

      Termination, suspension and revival (Arts. 228–232)

      Art. 228, FC. Parental authority terminates permanently:
      (1) Upon the death of the parents;
      (2) Upon the death of the child; or
      (3) Upon emancipation of the child. (327a)
      Art. 229, FC. Unless subsequently revived by a final judgment, parental authority also terminates:
      (1) Upon adoption of the child;
      (2) Upon appointment of a general guardian;
      (3) Upon judicial declaration of abandonment of the child in a case filed for the purpose;
      (4) Upon final judgment of a competent court divesting the party concerned of parental authority; or
      (5) Upon judicial declaration of absence or incapacity of the person exercising parental authority. (327a)
      Art. 230, FC. Parental authority is suspended upon conviction of the parent or the person exercising the same of a crime which carries with it the penalty of civil interdiction. The authority is automatically reinstated upon service of the penalty or upon pardon or amnesty of the offender. (330a)
      Art. 231, FC. The court in an action filed for the purpose or in a related case may also suspend parental authority if the parent or the person exercising the same:
      (1) Treats the child with excessive harshness or cruelty;
      (2) Gives the child corrupting orders, counsel or example;
      (3) Compels the child to beg; or
      (4) Subjects the child or allows him to be subjected to acts of lasciviousness.
      The grounds enumerated above are deemed to include cases which have resulted from culpable negligence of the parent or the person exercising parental authority.
      If the degree of seriousness so warrants, or the welfare of the child so demands, the court shall deprive the guilty party of parental authority or adopt such other measures as may be proper under the circumstances.
      The suspension or deprivation may be revoked and the parental authority revived in a case filed for the purpose or in the same proceeding if the court finds that the cause therefor has ceased and will not be repeated. (332a)
      Art. 232, FC. If the person exercising parental authority has subjected the child or allowed him to be subjected to sexual abuse, such person shall be permanently deprived by the court of such authority. (n)
      Chua v. Cabangbang (27 SCRA 791, March 28, 1969)

      Pacita Chua, a cabaret hostess, left her infant daughter with the Cabangbang spouses and did nothing for five years to recover her, claiming the Cabangbangs were powerful and influential. Held: the child stays with the Cabangbangs. "A mother who really loves her child would go to any extent to be reunited with her. The natural and normal reaction of the petitioner … should have been to move heaven and earth … in order to recover her. Yet she lifted not a finger." "Abandonment is one of the grounds for depriving parents of parental authority over their children." In certain cases, custody may be awarded even to strangers, as against either parent or both.

      Tolentino (Arts. 228–232): except for emancipation and the child's death, termination is "not absolute": on the parents' death, substitute parental authority follows; on adoption, the adopter takes over; on abandonment, absence, incapacity or a divesting judgment, a guardian. Remarriage of a widowed parent no longer ends parental authority (as it did for widows under NCC 328), though the court may appoint a guardian for cause. The causes in the Code are not exclusive: a child maltreated by a stepmother whom the remarried father does not stop may be given a guardian (Cortes v. Castillo: a mother convicted of adultery was denied custody, which stayed with the paternal grandmother). "Sexual abuse" (Art. 232, permanent deprivation) is more serious than "acts of lasciviousness" (Art. 231, suspension), but even serious lasciviousness may justify deprivation.
      Quiz traps (parental authority): "Remarriage of the surviving parent terminates parental authority" → false (Art. 212). "Parental authority may be renounced by a notarized agreement" → false (Art. 210). "In a disagreement between the parents, the court decides" → false: the father's decision prevails unless there is a judicial order to the contrary (Arts. 211, 225). "Teachers may impose reasonable corporal punishment" → false (Art. 233). "Parents need no court approval to sell the child's land as legal guardians" → false (Lindain). "The school is subsidiarily liable" → false: the school is principally and solidarily liable; the parents are subsidiarily liable (Art. 219). "Parental authority over an illegitimate child is exercised jointly if the father recognized the child" → false (Art. 176; Briones).

      Emancipation; Care and Education of Children; Summary Judicial Proceedings

      Family Code, Titles X and XI, Arts. 234–253 (syllabus XVII–XVIII), as amended by R.A. 6809, with NCC 356–363 on the care and education of children. Emancipation at 18 and what still follows the child to 21; and the summary procedure the Family Code uses for spousal consent, parental-authority incidents, presumptive death and other matters.

      Emancipation (Arts. 234–237, as amended by R.A. 6809)

      Art. 234, FC (as amended by R.A. 6809, approved December 13, 1989). Emancipation takes place by the attainment of majority. Unless otherwise provided, majority commences at the age of eighteen years.
      Art. 236, FC (as amended by R.A. 6809). Emancipation shall terminate parental authority over the person and property of the child who shall then be qualified and responsible for all acts of civil life, save the exceptions established by existing laws in special cases.
      Contracting marriage shall require parental consent until the age of twenty-one.
      Nothing in this Code shall be construed to derogate from the duty or responsibility of parents and guardians for children and wards below twenty-one years of age mentioned in the second and third paragraphs of Article 2180 of the Civil Code.
      Arts. 235 and 237, FC. Repealed by R.A. 6809.
      Uribe (CivRev Quiz 2, item 3): "Any contracting party between the age of twenty-one and twenty-five shall be obliged to ask their parents or guardian for consent." False: advice, not consent (Art. 15). Consent is required for parties between 18 and 21 (Art. 14). Sir then asked: if a 19-year-old who was previously married marries again, is parental consent needed? No: Art. 14 requires consent only from parties "not having been emancipated by a previous marriage". "Will you maintain that [consent] is for the specific person or for the FACT that their child is getting married? If unemancipated, then parental consent is needed; therefore a 19-year-old previously married does not need consent … because the child had already got married. This is a better view." (The same point was keyed in the CivRev midterm: a 19-year-old widow did not need parental consent.)
      Tolentino (Arts. 234–237): R.A. 6809 protects existing wills, bequests, donations, insurance policies and similar instruments favorable to minors from prejudicial retroactivity. Requiring parental consent for the marriage of an emancipated 18-to-21-year-old is "an anomalous situation": he may enter any contract but not marry without consent. Keeping the parents' liability for torts of children below 21 is "more anomalous": "upon emancipation … parental authority ceases, and yet responsibility for his torts continues until he reaches 21 years of age. This is a case of responsibility without authority." If both parents are dead and the child is released from guardianship at 18, no one else answers; the child is personally liable. On marriage: a person below 18 whose marriage is declared void reverts to parental authority as a legal consequence of the marriage's nonexistence, despite the repeal of Art. 237; but a voidable marriage annulled on any ground involves someone already over 18 and emancipated by age, so there is nothing to revert to.

      1993 Bar: Julio, 18 and living with his parents, shot and killed Jake at a party with his father's .38-calibre revolver, taken from an unlocked drawer in his father's bedroom. Jake's parents sued Julio's parents for damages based on quasi-delict. They moved to dismiss, saying Julio was already of age. (a) Should the motion be granted? (b) What is the parents' liability?

      (a) No. Art. 236, 3rd par., as amended by R.A. 6809: "Nothing in this Code shall be construed to derogate from the duty or responsibility of parents and guardians for children and wards below twenty-one years of age mentioned in the second and third paragraphs of Article 2180." Julio was below 21 and living in their company. (b) Liability for quasi-delict: indemnity for death, loss of earning capacity, and moral damages; they may escape only by proving the diligence of a good father of a family, which the unlocked gun drawer belies.

      Art. 236 vs. the 2010 Rozanno answer: the suggested answer to the 2010 Bar (see Parental Authority) said that at 21 Rozanno alone is liable and Arts. 218, 219 and 221 no longer apply. That is consistent: Arts. 218–221 cover unemancipated minors; Art. 236's 21-year line preserves only the NCC 2180 liability of parents and guardians for children below 21. Between 18 and 21, the school's special parental authority is gone but the parents' NCC 2180 liability remains.

      Care and education of children (NCC 356–363)

      Art. 356, NCC. Every child: (1) Is entitled to parental care; (2) Shall receive at least elementary education; (3) Shall be given moral and civic training by the parents or guardian; (4) Has a right to live in an atmosphere conducive to his physical, moral and intellectual development.
      Art. 357, NCC. Every child shall: (1) Obey and honor his parents or guardian; (2) Respect his grandparents, old relatives, and persons holding substitute parental authority; (3) Exert his utmost for his education and training; (4) Cooperate with the family in all matters that make for the good of the same.
      Art. 363, NCC. In all questions on the care, custody, education and property of children, the latter's welfare shall be paramount. No mother shall be separated from her child under seven years of age, unless the court finds compelling reasons for such measure.

      Summary judicial proceedings (Arts. 238–253)

      Art. 238, FC. Until modified by the Supreme Court, the procedural rules provided for in this Title shall apply as regards separation in fact between husband and wife, abandonment by one of the other, and incidents involving parental authority. (n)
      Art. 239, FC. When a husband and wife are separated in fact, or one has abandoned the other and one of them seeks judicial authorization for a transaction where the consent of the other spouse is required by law but such consent is withheld or cannot be obtained, a verified petition may be filed in court alleging the foregoing facts.
      The petition shall attach the proposed deed, if any, embodying the transaction, and, if none, shall describe in detail the said transaction and state the reason why the required consent thereto cannot be secured. In any case, the final deed duly executed by the parties shall be submitted to and approved by the court. (n)
      Arts. 240–248, FC (summary). Claims for damages by either spouse, except costs, only in a separate action (240). Jurisdiction, upon proof of notice to the other spouse, in the family court or the RTC where either spouse resides (241). The court notifies the other spouse to show cause on or before the initial conference; notice with a copy of the petition, served at the last known address (242). The preliminary conference is conducted by the judge personally, without counsel; counsel may assist afterwards (243). Non-appearance: the court inquires and requires appearance if possible (244); if still not secured, it may proceed ex parte, protecting the absent spouse's interests (245). If unresolved at the initial conference, a summary hearing on affidavits, documents or oral testimony (246). The judgment is immediately final and executory (247). The same rules govern a petition to administer or encumber the separate property of the abandoning spouse for the family's support (248).
      Arts. 249–253, FC (summary). Petitions under Arts. 223, 225 and 235 involving parental authority shall be verified (249) and filed where the child resides (250); the court notifies the parents or those exercising parental authority (251); Chapter 2 rules apply (252). "The foregoing rules in Chapters 2 and 3 hereof shall likewise govern summary proceedings filed under Articles 41, 51, 69, 73, 96, 124 and 217, insofar as they are applicable." (253)
      Tolentino (Arts. 238–253): the rules are procedural and the Supreme Court may modify any of them under its rule-making power. Tolentino prints Art. 238 in a broader form, applying the Title "in all cases provided for in this Code requiring summary court proceedings", to be "decided in an expeditious manner, without regard to technical rules"; the official text limits it to separation in fact, abandonment, and parental-authority incidents, with Art. 253 extending it to the listed articles.
      Consent first, court second (class reviewer, under Arts. 100 and 127): judicial authorization cannot take the place of the separated spouse's consent if that spouse is willing to give it; it is subsidiary, available only when consent is withheld or cannot be obtained.
      Republic v. Bermudez-Lorino (G.R. No. 160258, January 19, 2005; not in your sources)

      A wife obtained a declaration of the presumptive death of her husband under Art. 41; the Republic appealed to the CA by notice of appeal. Held: the appeal should not have been entertained. "In Summary Judicial Proceedings under the Family Code, there is no reglementary period within which to perfect an appeal, precisely because judgments rendered thereunder, by express provision of Article 247, Family Code, … are 'immediately final and executory'." The remedy is a petition for certiorari under Rule 65. (Reaffirmed in Republic v. Granada, G.R. No. 187512, June 13, 2012.)

      Quiz traps (summary proceedings): "The parties must be assisted by counsel at the preliminary conference" → false: without counsel; counsel may assist afterwards (Art. 243). "Damages may be claimed in the summary petition" → false: separate action, except costs (Art. 240). "The judgment may be appealed within 15 days" → false: immediately final and executory (Art. 247); certiorari. "If the other spouse does not appear, the petition is dismissed" → false: the court may proceed ex parte (Art. 245). "Venue is where the petitioner resides" → incomplete: where either spouse resides (Art. 241); parental-authority petitions, where the child resides (Art. 250).

      Use of Surnames

      Civil Code, Title XIII, Arts. 364–380 (syllabus XIX), with FC 176 as amended by R.A. 9255, C.A. 142 as amended by R.A. 6085 (aliases), and R.A. 9048 (administrative change of first name; see Civil Register). Which surname each kind of child and a married woman uses, identical names, judicial change of name, usurpation, pen names and aliases. Cases: Naldoza, Johnston, Llaneta, Tolentino v. CA, Legamia; from the class reviewer, Telmo, Wang, Ursua, Dapar, People v. Estrada, Santos v. Republic.

      What a name is

      Surnames of children (NCC 364–369; FC 176)

      Art. 364, NCC. Legitimate and legitimated children shall principally use the surname of the father.
      Art. 365, NCC. An adopted child shall bear the surname of the adopter.
      Arts. 366–368, NCC (now read with FC 176). A natural child acknowledged by both parents shall principally use the surname of the father; if recognized by only one, the surname of the recognizing parent (366). Natural children by legal fiction shall principally employ the surname of the father (367). Illegitimate children referred to in article 287 shall bear the surname of the mother (368).
      Art. 369, NCC. Children conceived before the decree annulling a voidable marriage shall principally use the surname of the father.
      Art. 176, FC (as amended by R.A. 9255). Illegitimate children shall use the surname and shall be under the parental authority of their mother, and shall be entitled to support in conformity with this Code. However, illegitimate children may use the surname of their father if their filiation has been expressly recognized by the father through the record of birth appearing in the civil register, or when an admission in a public document or private handwritten instrument is made by the father. Provided, the father has the right to institute an action before the regular courts to prove non-filiation during his lifetime. The legitime of each illegitimate child shall consist of one-half of the legitime of a legitimate child.
      Children of void marriages: they are illegitimate and use the mother's surname (FC 165, 176), except children of marriages void under Art. 36 (psychological incapacity) and of subsequent marriages void under Art. 53, who are legitimate (Art. 54) and use the father's surname. (Class reviewer note.)
      Grande v. Antonio (G.R. No. 206248, February 18, 2014; class reviewer)

      Grace Grande and Patricio Antonio, not married, had two sons, whom Antonio later acknowledged. He sued for custody and to have the boys' surname changed to Antonio; the lower courts ordered the change. Held: reversed on the surname. Under Art. 176 as amended by R.A. 9255, the illegitimate child "may" use the father's surname: the word is permissive, so the father has no right to compel it, and the choice belongs to the child (through the mother while a minor). The IRR provision making the use of the father's surname mandatory once recognized is void. Parental authority and custody remain with the mother unless she is unfit.

      Johnston v. Republic (7 SCRA 1040, 1963)

      A married woman adopted a minor alone, her husband (Johnston) merely consenting, and the child was to bear the surname "Johnston". Held: the child bears the adopter's maiden surname, not the husband's. The adopter's surname in NCC 341 (now 365) "refers to the adopter's own original family surname and not to her surname acquired by virtue of marriage. As petitioner-appellant made the adoption without concurrence of her husband, her name as adopter was her maiden name." Using the husband's surname "would mislead the public into believing that the child has also been adopted by the husband, and, later, if questions of successional rights arise, the husband's consent to the adoption might be presented to prove that he had actually joined in the adoption."

      Naldoza v. Republic (112 SCRA 568, 1982; see also Paternity)

      A mother whose husband had abandoned the family sought to change her legitimate sons' surname to her own. Held: denied. Using only the mother's surname "might create the impression that the minors are illegitimate". "The child should, and in the course of time must, know of his parentage. If, when he fully appreciates the circumstances and is capable of selecting a name for himself, he wants to use his mother's surname only and to avoid using his father's surname, then he should be the one to apply for a change of surname."

      Tolentino (Arts. 364–369): a legitimate child has the right to bear the surnames of both parents, but the father's is principally used; the law does not forbid adding the surnames of other ascendants. When both parents recognize a natural child, the father's surname is principally used, even if the mother recognized first, because it hides the illegitimacy; with the FC's abolition of "natural children", this should apply to all illegitimate children. Illegitimate children cannot be restrained from using what may be their father's surname: the legitimate children have a right to it, but not "monopolistic proprietary control" (Osmeña de Valencia). Children of an annulled voidable marriage, being legitimate, may also use the mother's surname.

      Married women, widows, and after annulment or legal separation (NCC 370–373)

      Art. 370, NCC. A married woman may use:
      (1) Her maiden first name and surname and add her husband's surname, or
      (2) Her maiden first name and her husband's surname, or
      (3) Her husband's full name, but prefixing a word indicating that she is his wife, such as "Mrs."
      Art. 371, NCC. In case of annulment of marriage, and the wife is the guilty party, she shall resume her maiden name and surname. If she is the innocent spouse, she may resume her maiden name and surname. However, she may choose to continue employing her former husband's surname, unless:
      (1) The court decrees otherwise, or
      (2) She or the former husband is married again to another person.
      Art. 372, NCC. When legal separation has been granted, the wife shall continue using her name and surname employed before the legal separation.
      Art. 373, NCC. A widow may use the deceased husband's surname as though he were still living, in accordance with article 370.
      Tolentino v. CA (162 SCRA 66, 1988)

      Arturo Tolentino's first wife, Consuelo David, obtained a divorce from him in 1943 under the law then in force during the Japanese occupation, but kept using the surname "Tolentino". His second wife, Constancia, sued to enjoin her. Held: no injunction. The action had prescribed, and in any case "the use of the surname Tolentino does not impinge on the rights of the petitioner." Considering the respondent's age, the burden of reconstituting documents, and that "while still not remarried, [she] will have to use a surname different from the surnames of her own children", the Court found it "just and equitable to leave things as they are, there being no actual legal injury to the petitioner save a deep hurt to her feelings which is not a basis for injunctive relief." The wife's right to the husband's surname is not exclusive; mere use of the surname is not usurpation of the status of wife (distinguishing Silva v. Peralta, where the defendant held herself out as the man's wife).

      Telmo v. Republic (class reviewer)

      Milagros Llerena Telmo petitioned to change her husband's surname, as she used it, from "Telmo" to "Thelmo"; the husband only executed an affidavit of no objection. Held: denied. A married woman uses her husband's surname by virtue of the marriage; a judicial change of its spelling must be initiated by the husband, the real party in interest, and her reasons were insufficient.

      Remo v. Secretary of Foreign Affairs (G.R. No. 169202, March 5, 2010; not in your sources)

      A married woman whose passport bore her husband's surname wanted to revert to her maiden name in her renewed passport while the marriage subsisted. Held: denied. Under Art. 370 the use of the husband's surname is optional, so she could have kept her maiden name from the start; but having used his surname in her passport, she may revert only in the cases allowed by the Philippine Passport Act (death of the husband, divorce, annulment or nullity).

      Tolentino (Arts. 370–373): in some countries the wife must take the husband's family name; ours says "may", so it is permissive, in line with the principle that surnames indicate descent. The wife cannot be prevented from using the husband's surname, but she cannot restrain others from using it either (Baumann v. Baumann, N.Y.: the second "wife" in a void marriage could keep calling herself Mrs. Baumann; the first wife's hurt feelings are not ground for an injunction). After legal separation she must continue using her married name, because the vinculum is not severed; a widow's use is optional because there is no more vinculum.

      Identical names (NCC 374–375)

      Art. 374, NCC. In case of identity of names and surnames, the younger person shall be obliged to use such additional name or surname as will avoid confusion.
      Art. 375, NCC. In case of identity of names and surnames between ascendants and descendants, the word "Junior" can be used only by a son. Grandsons and other direct male descendants shall either:
      (1) Add a middle name or the mother's surname, or
      (2) Add the Roman numerals II, III, and so on.
      Quiz traps: "A grandson with the same name as his grandfather may use 'Junior'" → false: only a son; grandsons add a middle name or the mother's surname, or Roman numerals. "The older of two persons with identical names must add a name" → false: the younger.

      Change of name (NCC 376; Rule 103; R.A. 9048)

      Art. 376, NCC. No person can change his name or surname without judicial authority.
      Llaneta v. Agrava (57 SCRA 29, 1974)

      Teresita Llaneta was born to Atanacia Llaneta after the death of Atanacia's husband, Serafin Ferrer, so she could not be his child; but she was raised by the Ferrers and known all her life as "Teresita Ferrer". She petitioned to change her surname to Ferrer; the judge denied it because it would give the false impression of a family relationship. Held: granted. "The principle that disallows change of name as would give the false impression of family relationship … remains valid but only to the extent that the proposed change of name would in great probability cause prejudice or future mischief to the family whose surname it is that is involved or to the community in general." She had always used "Ferrer"; her records bore it; Serafin's nearest kin approved. "A sudden shift at this time … would result in confusion among the persons and entities she deals with and entail endless and vexatious explanations."

      In re Change of Name of Julian Lin Carulasan Wang (G.R. No. 159966, March 30, 2005; class reviewer)

      Parents of a minor born to a Filipino mother and a Chinese father, planning to move to Singapore, sought to drop his middle name "Carulasan" because Singaporeans do not use middle names and he would be teased. Held: denied. The reason is not compelling; the middle name identifies his maternal lineage, and the request was a matter of convenience. The Court restated the five characteristics of a name.

      Santos v. Republic (2021; class reviewer)

      Francis Luigi G. Santos, the illegitimate son of Bong Revilla, was adopted by his stepfather and became a Santos; he petitioned under Rule 103 to change his surname to "Revilla", citing his desire to associate with his biological father's family, his "true identity", and his screen name. Held: denied. "Rule 103 is an action to change a person's whole name, while Rule 108 is to correct errors or cancel entries in the Civil Register." A change of name is a privilege addressed to the court's discretion; it needs a proper and compelling reason, and these reasons do not override the legal effect of the adoption.

      Tolentino (Art. 376): sufficient causes: (1) the name is ridiculous, dishonorable or very hard to write or pronounce; (2) the change follows a change of status; (3) it avoids confusion; (4) a sincere desire to adopt a Filipino name. Not enough: mere whim, a condition in a will or donation, or merely having been known by another name. A change of name does not alter family relations, status, capacity or citizenship; it changes only the label. It is a proceeding in rem; strict compliance with publication is jurisdictional, and an error in spelling the petitioner's name in the publication is substantial. When a father changes his name, his children's names are unaffected: adults must petition themselves; minors' names may be changed on the father's petition if the same justification exists.

      Usurpation, unauthorized use, pen names, aliases (NCC 377–380; C.A. 142)

      Art. 377, NCC. Usurpation of a name and surname may be the subject of an action for damages and other relief.
      Art. 378, NCC. The unauthorized or unlawful use of another person's surname gives a right of action to the latter.
      Art. 379, NCC. The employment of pen names or stage names is permitted, provided it is done in good faith and there is no injury to third persons. Pen names and stage names cannot be usurped.
      Art. 380, NCC. Except as provided in the preceding article, no person shall use different names and surnames.
      C.A. 142, Sec. 1 (as amended by R.A. 6085). Except as a pseudonym solely for literary, cinema, television, radio or other entertainment purposes and in athletic events where the use of pseudonym is a normally accepted practice, no person shall use any name different from the one with which he was registered at birth in the office of the local civil registry, or with which he was baptized for the first time, or, in case of an alien, with which he was registered in the bureau of immigration upon entry; or such substitute name as may have been authorized by a competent court…. The name shall comprise the patronymic name and one or two surnames.
