      Legamia v. IAC (131 SCRA 479, 1984)

      Corazon Legamia lived for almost 20 years with Emilio Reyes, who was married to another; he introduced her as his wife and she used the name "Corazon L. Reyes". After his death she signed as "Corazon L. Reyes" in claiming benefits for their son Michael, and was convicted of using an alias under C.A. 142. Held: acquitted. "It is not uncommon in Philippine society for a woman to represent herself as the wife and use the name of the man she is living with despite the fact that the man is married to another woman. The practice, to be sure, is not encouraged but neither is it unduly frowned upon…. None of the women has been charged of violating the C.A. No. 142 because ours is not a bigoted but a tolerant and understanding society." She used the name "without any sinister purpose or personal material gain in mind", for the benefit of her son; "the lawmakers could not have meant to criminalize what Corazon had done especially because some of them probably had their own Corazons."

      Ursua v. CA (G.R. No. 112170, April 10, 1996; class reviewer)

      Cesario Ursua, asked by his lawyer to get a copy of a complaint against him from the Ombudsman, signed the visitors' logbook as "Oscar Perez" once, out of reluctance to be identified. He was convicted under C.A. 142. Held: acquitted. An alias is a name used publicly and habitually, usually in business transactions, in addition to one's real name; a single isolated use, with no sign of intent to be known by it, is not punishable. "A man's name is simply the sound or sounds by which he is commonly designated by his fellows."

      People v. Estrada (G.R. Nos. 164368–69, April 2, 2009; class reviewer)

      Former President Estrada was charged with illegal use of the alias "Jose Velarde" for signing bank documents to open a trust account on February 4, 2000. Held: the demurrer to evidence was properly granted. Under Ursua, the use of an alias must be public and habitual; the information limited the charge to a single occasion, and use in a bank transaction covered by the secrecy of bank deposits (R.A. 1405) is not public. Legal names "comprise the patronymic name and one or two surnames."

      Dapar v. Biascan (G.R. No. 141880, September 27, 2004; class reviewer)

      A man's lawful wife sued his common-law partner, who had used his surname, for usurpation. Held: to be actionable under Art. 377, usurpation requires: (1) actual use of another's name by the defendant; (2) the use is unauthorized; and (3) the use is to designate personality or identify a person.

      Tolentino (Arts. 377–380): the right to a name is a right of personality, protected even for a person without a good reputation. A pseudonym is "a conventional fictitious name freely chosen by a person to disguise his personality"; it is protected only when well known as the designation of a particular writer or artist in his field, and may be used only in that activity, never in relations with the State.
      Syllabus note: the syllabus lists "R.A. 8805" under Surnames; it is not in your materials. The surname laws you need are FC 176 as amended by R.A. 9255 (2004), C.A. 142 as amended by R.A. 6085, and R.A. 9048 as amended by R.A. 10172 (see Civil Register).
      Quiz traps (surnames): "A married woman must use her husband's surname" → false (Art. 370: "may"). "A legally separated wife may resume her maiden name" → false (Art. 372: shall continue). "An innocent wife in an annulled marriage must resume her maiden name" → false: the guilty wife must; the innocent wife may choose. "An illegitimate child recognized by the father shall use the father's surname" → false: may (R.A. 9255; Grande). "An adopted child takes the surname the adopter acquired by marriage" → false (Johnston). "Any change of name requires a court order" → false since R.A. 9048 (first names and clerical errors). "A single use of a false name is a violation of the anti-alias law" → false (Ursua; Estrada).

      Absence

      Civil Code, Title XIV, Arts. 381–396, with FC 41 (syllabus XX). The three stages of absence (provisional measures, declaration of absence, presumption of death), administration of the absentee's property, the 7/10/5/4-year rules, the absentee's reappearance, and contingent rights. Cases: Reyes v. Alejandro, Eastern Shipping v. Lucero, Tol-Noquera v. Villamor; from the class reviewer, Jones v. Hortiguela, Valmonte v. Villaroman. (The Persons section has a short summary of absence as a modification of capacity.)

      Provisional measures (Arts. 381–383)

      Art. 381, NCC. When a person disappears from his domicile, his whereabouts being unknown, and without leaving an agent to administer his property, the judge, at the instance of an interested party, a relative, or a friend, may appoint a person to represent him in all that may be necessary.
      This same rule shall be observed when under similar circumstances the power conferred by the absentee has expired. (181a)
      Art. 382, NCC. The appointment referred to in the preceding article having been made, the judge shall take the necessary measures to safeguard the rights and interests of the absentee and shall specify the powers, obligations and remuneration of his representative, regulating them, according to the circumstances, by the rules concerning guardians. (182)
      Art. 383, NCC. In the appointment of a representative, the spouse present shall be preferred when there is no legal separation.
      If the absentee left no spouse, or if the spouse present is a minor, any competent person may be appointed by the court. (183a)
      Tolentino (Art. 383): unless the wife has been appointed administratrix or trustee of her absent husband's property, she cannot sue to recover it. The petition to declare the husband an absentee and the petition to place the conjugal property under the wife's management may be combined. Garrido v. North Camarines Lumber Co. (C.A.): a guerrilla's employer paid his unpaid prewar salaries to his wife in Japanese military notes during the occupation; the payment did not bind him, because the wife had never been judicially appointed his representative.

      Declaration of absence (Arts. 384–386)

      Art. 384, NCC. Two years having elapsed without any news about the absentee or since the receipt of the last news, and five years in case the absentee has left a person in charge of the administration of his property, his absence may be declared. (184)
      Art. 385, NCC. The following may ask for the declaration of absence:
      (1) The spouse present;
      (2) The heirs instituted in a will, who may present an authentic copy of the same;
      (3) The relatives who may succeed by the law of intestacy;
      (4) Those who may have over the property of the absentee some right subordinated to the condition of his death. (185)
      Art. 386, NCC. The judicial declaration of absence shall not take effect until six months after its publication in a newspaper of general circulation. (186a)
      Tolentino (Art. 384): with no news at all, count from the disappearance; with news, count "not from the actual receipt of the news but from the time referred to by the news, or the time when the news was sent" (Jones v. Hortiguela). Why five years when he left an administrator: his affairs are attended to, so there is less urgency.
      Reyes v. Alejandro (141 SCRA 65, 1986; the syllabus prints 41 SCRA)

      A wife petitioned to have her husband, who had left the conjugal home years earlier, judicially declared an absentee; the petition alleged no property of his that needed administration. Held: dismissed. "The need to have a person judicially declared an absentee is when he has properties which have to be taken cared of or administered by a representative appointed by the Court (Article 384, Civil Code); the spouse of the absentee is asking for separation of property (Article 191, Civil Code) or his wife is asking the Court that the administration of all classes of property in the marriage be transferred to her (Article 196, Civil Code). The petition to declare the husband an absentee and the petition to place the management of the conjugal properties in the hands of the wife may be combined and adjudicated in the same proceedings" (Peyer v. Martinez). A declaration of absence is not needed merely to establish the fact of absence.

      Jones v. Hortiguela (64 Phil. 179, 1937; class reviewer)

      Marciana Escaño's first husband, Arthur Jones, left in 1918 and was not heard from; she obtained a judicial declaration of his absence (published, taking effect in 1921) and married Felix Hortiguela in 1927. The validity of the second marriage was later questioned. Held: valid. Under the then General Orders No. 68, a spouse could remarry after seven years of absence; "the requirement of the 7-year prescriptive period before a spouse may enter into a second marriage is counted from the date the last news concerning the absentee was received, not from the date of the publication of the judicial declaration of absence." From 1918 to 1927, more than seven years had passed.

      Administration of the absentee's property (Arts. 387–389)

      Art. 387, NCC. An administrator of the absentee's property shall be appointed in accordance with article 383. (187a)
      Art. 388, NCC. The wife who is appointed as an administratrix of the husband's property cannot alienate or encumber the husband's property, or that of the conjugal partnership, without judicial authority. (188a)
      Art. 389, NCC. The administration shall cease in any of the following cases:
      (1) When the absentee appears personally or by means of an agent;
      (2) When the death of the absentee is proved and his testate or intestate heirs appear;
      (3) When a third person appears, showing by a proper document that he has acquired the absentee's property by purchase or other title.
      In these cases the administrator shall cease in the performance of his office, and the property shall be at the disposal of those who may have a right thereto. (190)
      Tol-Noquera v. Villamor (211 SCRA 616, 1992)

      Remigio Tol disappeared. His daughter, Daya Maria Tol-Noquera, petitioned for the declaration of his absence and for appointment as administratrix of his estate. The trial court dismissed it because a lot he claimed was titled to someone else, and because she, as heir, might inherit the property. Held: reinstated. "It is not necessary that a declaration of absence be made in a proceeding separate from and prior to a petition for administration" (Reyes v. Alejandro; Peyer v. Martinez). "The purpose of the cited rules is the protection of the interests and property of the absentee, not of the administrator. Thus, the question of whether the administrator may inherit the property to be administered is not controlling. What is material is whether she is one of those allowed by law to seek the declaration of absence … and whether she is competent to be appointed as administratrix." Ownership of the disputed lot should be resolved in another proceeding; she may use reconveyance or damages if appointed.

      Tolentino (Art. 388): there was a conflict between this article and old NCC 197 (which gave the wife administering all the marriage's property the husband's full powers); it was settled by the omission of NCC 196–197 from the Family Code, so Art. 388 stands: no alienation or encumbrance without judicial authority. Compare FC 96 and 124: a spouse who assumes sole administration because the other is "otherwise unable to participate" also needs court authority or the other's written consent to dispose or encumber; otherwise the transaction is void (but a continuing offer). Sale or encumbrance of the absentee's property follows Rule 98, Sec. 9, like a guardian's.

      Presumption of death (Arts. 390–392; FC 41)

      Art. 390, NCC. After an absence of seven years, it being unknown whether or not the absentee still lives, he shall be presumed dead for all purposes, except for those of succession.
      The absentee shall not be presumed dead for the purpose of opening his succession till after an absence of ten years. If he disappeared after the age of seventy-five years, an absence of five years shall be sufficient in order that his succession may be opened. (n)
      Art. 391, NCC. The following shall be presumed dead for all purposes, including the division of the estate among the heirs:
      (1) A person on board a vessel lost during a sea voyage, or an aeroplane which is missing, who has not been heard of for four years since the loss of the vessel or aeroplane;
      (2) A person in the armed forces who has taken part in war, and has been missing for four years;
      (3) A person who has been in danger of death under other circumstances and his existence has not been known for four years. (n)
      Art. 392, NCC. If the absentee appears, or without appearing his existence is proved, he shall recover his property in the condition in which it may be found, and the price of any property that may have been alienated or the property acquired therewith; but he cannot claim either fruits or rents. (194)
      Art. 41, FC. A marriage contracted by any person during subsistence of a previous marriage shall be null and void, unless before the celebration of the subsequent marriage, the prior spouse had been absent for four consecutive years and the spouse present has a well-founded belief that the absent spouse was already dead. In case of disappearance where there is danger of death under the circumstances set forth in the provisions of Article 391 of the Civil Code, an absence of only two years shall be sufficient.
      For the purpose of contracting the subsequent marriage under the preceding paragraph the spouse present must institute a summary proceeding as provided in this Code for the declaration of presumptive death of the absentee, without prejudice to the effect of reappearance of the absent spouse. (83a)
      Samplex (Uribe quiz compilations): "X, who was not in danger of death, disappeared at the age of 76 … presumed dead for purposes of succession after an absence of: (a) 1 year (b) 5 years (c) 7 years (d) 10 years (e) 2 years" → (b) 5 years (disappeared after 75). "X, in danger of death, disappeared at the age of 76 … (f) 4 years from his disappearance" → (f): Art. 391 governs; age is irrelevant. "X, not in danger, disappeared at age 69" → (d) 10 years. T/F: "The absentee shall not be presumed dead for the purpose of opening his succession till after an absence of ten years" → keyed false: the statement omits the five-year rule for one who disappeared after 75 (and Art. 391 cases).
      Tolentino (Arts. 390–391): the presumption of death arises by law, without any judicial declaration, and may be invoked in any action; there is no independent proceeding to declare a person presumptively dead, except for remarriage under FC 41. A judicial declaration adds nothing to the presumption, which stays prima facie and yields to proof that the absentee is alive (Szatraw; Lukban v. Republic). FC 41 amended Art. 390 (4 years for remarriage) and Art. 391 (2 years). Art. 391 covers "missing persons", whose disappearance points to a catastrophe: "vessel" includes all watercraft and "aeroplane" all aircraft; the vessel must be lost on a sea voyage (including river mouths and canals, but not inland waters). "War" covers all military operations, and the persons covered include nurses, doctors, guides, guerrillas and reporters with the armed forces, but only if they disappeared during military operations. "Other danger" includes earthquakes, fires, explosions, floods, mine cave-ins, volcanic eruptions and landslides; count from the last day of the danger, or, for expeditions, from when they should have ended.
      Eastern Shipping Lines v. Lucero (124 SCRA 425, 1983)

      Captain Julio Lucero's contract was to end on the arrival of the M/V Eastern Minicon in Manila. On the voyage from Hong Kong, the ship sent three messages reporting a leak and that the crew were abandoning ship; it was never heard from again. His wife refused death benefits and claimed the monthly allotments instead, arguing that under Art. 391(1) he could not be presumed dead until four years had passed, so his contract continued. Held: she is entitled to death benefits, not allotments. "There is thus enough evidence to show the circumstances attending the loss and disappearance of the M/V Eastern Minicon and its crew. The foregoing facts, quite logically, are sufficient to lead Us to a moral certainty that the vessel had sunk and that the persons aboard had perished with it. Upon this premise, the rule on presumption of death under Article 391(1) of the Civil Code must yield to the rule of preponderance of evidence. As this Court said in Joaquin vs. Navarro, 'Where there are facts, known or knowable, from which a rational conclusion can be made, the presumption does not step in, and the rule of preponderance of evidence controls.'"

      Valmonte v. Villaroman (class reviewer)

      Heirs of a long-absent owner, invoking the presumption of his death after seven years, sued to recover land held by others in open, continuous and adverse possession. Held: the action fails. "When a person's right to recover property had already prescribed during their lifetime due to another's open, continuous, and adverse possession for the statutory period, that right is extinguished and cannot be transmitted to heirs. Likewise, the presumption of death after seven years of absence does not revive or preserve any extinguished property right."

      FC 41 vs. Arts. 390–391: for remarriage, the FC rules (4 or 2 years, a well-founded belief after diligent search, and a summary judicial declaration) displace the Civil Code periods; for all other purposes the presumption needs no declaration. The FC 41 judgment is immediately final and executory (FC 247); the State's remedy is certiorari (see Summary Proceedings). The subsequent marriage is terminated by the recording of an affidavit of reappearance (FC 42); see Void Marriages.
      Tolentino (Art. 392): the reappearing absentee recovers his property as it is found, plus the price of what was sold or the property bought with it, but not the fruits or rents: those who held it in good faith keep them (compare Art. 396). His action is imprescriptible as to his ownership, subject to acquisitive prescription by others.

      Effect of absence on the absentee's contingent rights (Arts. 393–396)

      Art. 393, NCC. Whoever claims a right pertaining to a person whose existence is not recognized must prove that he was living at the time his existence was necessary in order to acquire said right. (195)
      Art. 394, NCC. Without prejudice to the provision of the preceding article, upon the opening of a succession to which an absentee is called, his share shall accrue to his coheirs, unless he has heirs, assigns, or a representative. They shall all, as the case may be, make an inventory of the property. (196a)
      Art. 395, NCC. The provisions of the preceding article are understood to be without prejudice to the action of petition for inheritance or other rights which are vested in the absentee, his representatives or successors in interest. These rights shall not be extinguished save by lapse of time fixed for prescription. In the record that is made in the Registry of the real estate which accrues to the coheirs, the circumstance of its being subject to the provisions of this article shall be stated. (197)
      Art. 396, NCC. Those who may have entered upon the inheritance shall appropriate the fruits received in good faith so long as the absentee does not appear, or while his representatives or successors in interest do not bring the proper actions. (198)

      Tolentino's illustration (Art. 393): X disappeared in 1940. Y died in 1942, leaving a will instituting X as heir. In 1950, X's children, invoking the presumption that X is dead, want to take the inheritance Y left to X. May they?

      Only if they prove that X was alive when Y died in 1942. The presumption of death does not help them, and a dead person cannot succeed by will; whoever claims a right of an absentee must prove he was living when his existence was necessary to acquire it (Art. 393). Otherwise the share accrues to X's co-heirs under Art. 394 (or, X being only an instituted heir, follows the rules on accretion and intestacy), subject to an action for petition of inheritance if X turns out to have been alive (Art. 395).

      Quiz traps (absence): "A friend of the absentee may ask for the declaration of absence" → false (Art. 385; a friend may ask only for a provisional representative under Art. 381). "The declaration of absence takes effect upon its publication" → false: six months after publication (Art. 386). "If the absentee left an administrator, his absence may be declared after two years" → false: five years (Art. 384). "After seven years, the absentee is presumed dead for all purposes" → false: except succession (Art. 390). "A person lost at sea is presumed dead for all purposes except succession after four years" → false: including the division of the estate (Art. 391). "The reappearing absentee recovers his property with its fruits" → false (Art. 392). "A wife-administratrix may sell the absent husband's property" → false without judicial authority (Art. 388).

      Funerals

      Civil Code, Arts. 305–310 (syllabus XXI). Who has the right and duty to bury, the deceased's wishes, retention and exhumation of remains, autopsies, disrespect for the dead, and tombstones. Cases: Eugenio v. Velez; from the class reviewer, Valino v. Adriano.

      Art. 305, NCC. The duty and the right to make arrangements for the funeral of a relative shall be in accordance with the order established for support, under article 294 [now FC 199]. In case of descendants of the same degree, or of brothers and sisters, the oldest shall be preferred. In case of ascendants, the paternal shall have a better right.
      Art. 306, NCC. Every funeral shall be in keeping with the social position of the deceased.
      Art. 307, NCC. The funeral shall be in accordance with the expressed wishes of the deceased. In the absence of such expression, his religious beliefs or affiliation shall determine the funeral rites. In case of doubt, the form of the funeral shall be decided upon by the person obliged to make arrangements for the same, after consulting the other members of the family.
      Art. 308, NCC. No human remains shall be retained, interred, disposed of or exhumed without the consent of the persons mentioned in articles 294 and 305.
      Art. 309, NCC. Any person who shows disrespect to the dead, or wrongfully interferes with a funeral shall be liable to the family of the deceased for damages, material and moral.
      Art. 310, NCC. The construction of a tombstone or mausoleum shall be deemed a part of the funeral expenses, and shall be chargeable to the conjugal partnership property, if the deceased is one of the spouses.

      Who buries (Art. 305 with FC 199)

      Eugenio, Sr. v. Velez (185 SCRA 425, 1990)

      Vitaliana Vargas's full-blood brothers and sisters filed a petition for habeas corpus, alleging she was being unlawfully detained by Tomas Eugenio, Sr., with whom she lived. She had in fact already died, and Eugenio, claiming to be her common-law husband, refused to surrender the body for burial. The trial court treated the case as an action for custody of the corpse. Held: custody goes to the siblings. A writ of habeas corpus cannot issue for a dead body, but the court could proceed on the question of custody. "We hold that the provisions of the Civil Code, unless expressly providing to the contrary as in Article 144, when referring to a 'spouse' contemplate a lawfully wedded spouse. Petitioner vis-a-vis Vitaliana was not a lawfully-wedded spouse to her; in fact, he was not legally capacitated to marry her in her lifetime." With no spouse, descendants or ascendants, her full-blood siblings had the right to bury her.

      Valino v. Adriano (G.R. No. 182894, April 22, 2014; class reviewer)

      Atty. Adriano Adriano, long separated in fact from his wife Rosario, lived for many years with Fe Floro Valino, who cared for him in his illness and paid his medical and funeral expenses. When he died, his wife and children were in the U.S. and asked Valino to delay the burial; she buried him in her family's mausoleum anyway. The legal family sued for damages and the transfer of the remains. Held: for the legal family; the remains are to be exhumed and transferred. Under Art. 305 with FC 199, the right and duty to make funeral arrangements belong to the surviving spouse, then descendants, ascendants and siblings, "to the exclusion of common-law partners", however long or close the relationship. The deceased's wishes (Art. 307) govern only the rites and form of the funeral, and must be proved clearly and expressly, preferably in a will; in case of doubt, the law favors the legitimate family. Valino's claim that the deceased wanted to be buried with her was not proved.

      Tolentino (Art. 305): the person preferred may waive the right, expressly or impliedly, and it then passes to the next in order; a spouse must assert the right promptly. A wife living separately when the husband died, or who neglects or refuses the duty, impliedly waives it; but waiver is not presumed and needs clear proof of a free and voluntary intent. The person entitled to custody of the corpse cannot exclude the deceased's friends and other relatives from the wake and funeral without just cause; that would be an abuse of right (NCC 19) or contrary to good customs (NCC 21). Family members can never be excluded.

      The corpse: rights, wishes, limits

      Tolentino (Arts. 306–310): Art. 306 has no sanction of its own, but others supply it: if the surviving spouse spends lavishly out of proportion to the deceased's position and small estate, the other heirs may object to charging all of it to the estate; if the spouse gives a miserable funeral to a prominent person with a large estate, the relatives may sue for disrespect to the dead under Art. 309. Actionable disrespect includes withholding the body from those entitled to it, an unauthorized autopsy (a physician who did one to fill in a death certificate, without consent, was held liable), mutilation, unlawful disturbance of a grave or removal of remains, an undertaker's refusal to disclose where the body is, and unauthorized use of a photograph of a malformed deceased child. Revised Administrative Code limits: burial only in authorized places, a death certificate is needed, and an unembalmed body must be buried within 48 hours (12 hours if the death was due to a dangerous communicable disease), unless legal investigation or the health authorities require otherwise.
      Quiz traps (funerals): "A common-law spouse of many years has the first right to bury the deceased" → false (Eugenio; Valino). "Among ascendants of the same degree, the maternal side is preferred" → false: paternal (Art. 305). "Among descendants of the same degree, the youngest is preferred" → false: the oldest. "Habeas corpus lies to recover a dead body" → false (Eugenio; the court may still decide custody). "A tombstone is a personal expense of the surviving spouse" → false: funeral expense chargeable to the conjugal partnership (Art. 310). "The deceased's wishes on the funeral always prevail" → false: subject to law, and they cover only the form and rites.

      Civil Register

      Civil Code, Title XVI, Arts. 407–413 (syllabus XXII), Rule 108 of the Rules of Court, and R.A. 9048 as amended by R.A. 10172. What must be registered; the evidentiary value of entries; and the three routes to change an entry: the civil registrar (clerical errors, first names), Rule 103 (change of name), and Rule 108 (cancellation or correction, summary or adversarial). Cases: Republic v. Sayo, Republic v. Valencia, Republic v. Marcos, Labayo-Rowe; from the class reviewer, Cagandahan, Braza, Magpayo, Olaybar, Gallo, Bartolome, Felix, Ontuca, Barcelote, Cua Ko.

      What is registered (Arts. 407–411, 413)

      Art. 407, NCC. Acts, events and judicial decrees concerning the civil status of persons shall be recorded in the civil register. (325a)
      Art. 408, NCC. The following shall be entered in the civil register:
      (1) Births; (2) marriages; (3) deaths; (4) legal separations; (5) annulments of marriage; (6) judgments declaring marriages void from the beginning; (7) legitimations; (8) adoptions; (9) acknowledgments of natural children; (10) naturalization; (11) loss, or (12) recovery of citizenship; (13) civil interdiction; (14) judicial determination of filiation; (15) voluntary emancipation of a minor; and (16) changes of name. (326a)
      Art. 409, NCC. In cases of legal separation, adoption, naturalization and other judicial orders mentioned in the preceding article, it shall be the duty of the clerk of the court which issued the decree to ascertain whether the same has been registered, and if this has not been done, to send a copy of said decree to the civil registry of the city or municipality where the court is functioning. (n)
      Art. 410, NCC. The books making up the civil register and all documents relating thereto shall be considered public documents and shall be prima facie evidence of the facts therein contained. (n)
      Art. 411, NCC. Every civil registrar shall be civilly responsible for any unauthorized alteration made in any civil register, to any person suffering damage thereby. However, the civil registrar may exempt himself from such liability if he proves that he has taken every reasonable precaution to prevent the unlawful alteration. (n)
      Art. 413, NCC. All other matters pertaining to the registration of civil status shall be governed by special laws. (n)
      Evidentiary value (Art. 410): entries are public documents and prima facie evidence only. A birth certificate naming a father who did not sign is not competent proof of paternity (Reyes; Vda. de Alberto: see Proof of Filiation). And the status of a child is what the law says, not what the record says: "A child born during a valid marriage is a legitimate child by law. Not even the birth certificate of the child can change her status for the information contained therein are merely supplied by the parents" (Cua Ko v. Republic, class reviewer). Likewise, the mother's declaration against legitimacy does not affect it (Art. 167; Ordoña).
      Barcelote v. Republic (G.R. No. 222095, August 7, 2017; class reviewer; see also Paternity)

      Jonna Barcelote's two children by a married man were registered by him, without her knowledge or signature, under his surname. Held: the birth certificates are void and cancelled: they violated the FC rule that illegitimate children use the mother's surname and the Civil Registry Law requiring the mother's signature. "It is mandatory that the mother of an illegitimate child signs the birth certificate of her child in all cases, irrespective of whether the father recognizes the child as his or not."

      Changing an entry (Art. 412; Rule 108)

      Art. 412, NCC. No entry in a civil register shall be changed or corrected, without a judicial order. (n)
      Rule 108, Secs. 1–7, Rules of Court (summary). Any person interested in an act, event, order or decree concerning civil status recorded in the civil register may file a verified petition with the RTC of the province where the civil registry is located (Sec. 1), for the cancellation or correction of the entries listed in Sec. 2. The civil registrar and all persons who have or claim any interest which would be affected shall be made parties (Sec. 3). The court fixes the hearing, gives reasonable notice to the persons named, and publishes the order once a week for three consecutive weeks in a newspaper of general circulation in the province (Sec. 4). The civil registrar and any interested person may oppose within 15 days from notice or the last publication (Sec. 5). The court may expedite and issue a preliminary injunction (Sec. 6). After hearing, it dismisses or grants; a certified copy of the judgment is served on the civil registrar, who annotates it (Sec. 7).
      Republic v. Valencia (141 SCRA 462, 1986)

      Leonor Valencia, a Filipino, petitioned under Rule 108 to correct the birth records of her two children by Go Eng, a Chinese national: their citizenship from "Chinese" to "Filipino" and their parents' status from "married" to "not married", on the ground that she and Go Eng were never married. The Republic argued that such substantial changes cannot be made under Rule 108. Held: the petition may proceed. "It is undoubtedly true that if the subject matter of a petition is not for the correction of clerical errors of a harmless and innocuous nature, but one involving nationality or citizenship, which is indisputably substantial as well as controverted, affirmative relief cannot be granted in a proceeding summary in nature. However, it is also true that a right in law may be enforced and a wrong may be remedied as long as the appropriate remedy is used. This Court adheres to the principle that even substantial errors in a civil registry may be corrected and the true facts established provided the parties aggrieved by the error avail themselves of the appropriate adversary proceeding." Here the petition was published, the registrar and Go Eng were notified, and the Solicitor General opposed: the proceeding was adversarial. "A proceeding under Rule 108 is not necessarily a summary proceeding" (class reviewer).

      Labayo-Rowe v. Republic (168 SCRA 294, 1988)

      Emperatriz Labayo-Rowe petitioned to correct the birth records of her two children: her first name from "Beatriz" to "Emperatriz", and the entry on the parents' marriage (date and place) to "not married", which would make the children illegitimate. Only the local civil registrar was notified. Held: only the correction of the misspelled name, a clerical error, may be allowed. "A mere petition for correction of entries under Rule 108 of the ROC cannot change a child's status from legitimate to illegitimate. Rule 108 'shall not diminish, increase or modify substantive rights.' If Rule 108 were to be extended beyond innocuous or harmless changes or corrections of errors which are visible to the eye or obvious to the understanding, so as to comprehend substantial and controversial alterations concerning citizenship, legitimacy of paternity or filiation, or legitimacy of marriage, without observing the proper proceedings …, said rule would thereby become an unconstitutional exercise which would tend to increase or modify substantive rights."

      Republic v. Marcos (182 SCRA 223, 1990)

      A petition sought substantial alterations in a birth record (including the child's citizenship and filiation) in proceedings that did not implead or notify all who would be affected. Held: not allowed as filed. "When a petition for cancellation or correction of an entry in the civil register involves substantial and controversial alterations, including those on citizenship, legitimacy of paternity or filiation, or legitimacy of marriage, a strict compliance with the requirements of Rule 108 of the Rules of Court is mandated. If the entries in the civil register could be corrected or changed through mere summary proceedings and not through appropriate action wherein all parties who may be affected by the entries are notified or represented, the door to fraud or other mischief would be set open." (The class reviewer also cites it for the rule that a change of name should not give a false impression of family relationship.)

      Republic v. Sayo (188 SCRA 634, 1990)

      A petition for correction involving a person's citizenship was granted in what amounted to a summary proceeding. Held: "If the subject matter of a petition is not for the correction of clerical errors of a harmless and innocuous nature, but one involving nationality or citizenship, which is indisputably substantial as well as controverted, affirmative relief cannot be granted in a proceeding summary in nature." (Your sources give only this doctrine.)

      Tolentino (Art. 412): a clerical error is "visible to the eyes or obvious to the understanding; an error made by a clerk or transcriber; a mistake in copying or writing, or some harmless or innocuous change, such as correction of a name that is clearly misspelled or of a misstatement of the occupation of the parents." Substantial changes (citizenship, civil status, sex, paternity and filiation) need the adversary procedure: the civil registrar and all who claim an interest that would be affected must be parties, with notice and publication, so that "all relevant facts are fully and properly developed, opposing counsel are given the opportunity to demolish each other's case, and the evidence is thoroughly considered and weighed." A false entry naming the petitioner as a child's father, made by an interloper without authority, may be ordered struck out and replaced with "unknown" (Alisoso v. Lastimoso).

      Administrative correction (R.A. 9048 as amended by R.A. 10172)

      Sec. 1, R.A. 9048 (as amended by R.A. 10172). Authority to Correct Clerical or Typographical Error and Change of First Name or Nickname. – No entry in a civil register shall be changed or corrected without a judicial order, except for clerical or typographical errors and change of first name or nickname, the day and month in the date of birth or sex of a person where it is patently clear that there was a clerical or typographical error or mistake in the entry, which can be corrected or changed by the concerned city or municipal civil registrar or consul general in accordance with the provisions of this Act and its implementing rules and regulations.
      Sec. 2(3), R.A. 9048 (as amended). "Clerical or typographical error" refers to a mistake committed in the performance of clerical work in writing, copying, transcribing or typing an entry in the civil register that is harmless and innocuous, such as misspelled name or misspelled place of birth, mistake in the entry of day and month in the date of birth or the sex of the person or the like, which is visible to the eyes or obvious to the understanding, and can be corrected or changed only by reference to other existing record or records: Provided, however, That no correction must involve the change of nationality, age, or status of the petitioner.
      Sec. 4, R.A. 9048 (grounds for change of first name or nickname). (1) The petitioner finds the first name or nickname to be ridiculous, tainted with dishonor or extremely difficult to write or pronounce; (2) the new first name or nickname has been habitually and continuously used by the petitioner and he has been publicly known by that first name or nickname in the community; or (3) the change will avoid confusion.
      Republic v. Cagandahan (G.R. No. 166676, September 12, 2008; class reviewer)

      Jennifer Cagandahan, registered as female, had congenital adrenal hyperplasia (intersex anatomy), produced high levels of male hormones, and had matured with male features; she petitioned under Rule 108 to change her name to "Jeff" and her sex to "male". Held: granted. A change of sex is a substantial change under Rule 108, and procedure was substantially complied with. Where a person is biologically or naturally intersex, "the determining factor in gender classification for an individual who has reached the age of majority is what the individual, with good reason, thinks of his/her sex", respecting the person's choice about sexual development. (Contrast Silverio v. Republic, G.R. No. 174689, October 22, 2007, not in your sources: no law allows changing the sex entry on the basis of sex reassignment surgery; the first-name change was likewise denied.)

      Braza v. City Civil Registrar of Himamaylan (G.R. No. 181174, December 4, 2009; class reviewer)

      The widow and legitimate children of Pablo Braza petitioned under Rule 108 to correct the birth record of Patrick, recorded as Pablo's legitimated son by Lucille Titular, alleging that Pablo's marriage to Lucille was bigamous. Held: dismissed. The petition was really a collateral attack on the validity of a marriage and on legitimation and filiation, which must be raised in a direct action by the proper party (FC 170–171), not through correction of entries. "Substantial or contentious alterations may be allowed only in adversarial proceedings, in which all interested parties are impleaded and due process is properly observed."

      Republic v. Olaybar (G.R. No. 189538, February 10, 2014; class reviewer)

      Merlinda Olaybar learned from her CENOMAR that she was "married" to a Korean, though she had never married; her identity had apparently been used by a travel agent. She sought cancellation of the "wife" entries in the marriage certificate under Rule 108. The OSG argued she was seeking a declaration of nullity in disguise. Held: Rule 108 is proper. Cancelling the wife's entries does not declare a marriage void, since there was no marriage to speak of; and all parties had the chance to contest. "As long as the procedural requirements in Rule 108 are followed, it is the appropriate adversary proceeding to effect substantial corrections and changes in entries of the civil register."

      Republic v. Magpayo (G.R. No. 189476, February 2, 2011; class reviewer)

      Julian Coseteng Magpayo, claiming his parents were never married, filed a Rule 103 petition in Quezon City to change his name, which the RTC granted by ordering the Makati civil registrar to delete the parents' marriage date and his father's name. Held: void. Changing one's status from legitimate to illegitimate is not a mere change of name under Rule 103. It requires a Rule 108 petition filed where the registry is (Makati), with the civil registrar and all affected persons (including the parents) impleaded.

      Republic v. Ontuca (2020; class reviewer)

      A mother sought, under Rule 108, to correct her misspelled names in her daughter's birth record and to change her civil status there from "married" to "not married". Held: the name corrections stand (the RTC may resolve clerical errors to avoid multiplicity of suits), but the marital-status change is void: it affects the child's legitimacy, and the father and the child, indispensable parties, were not impleaded. Substantial errors are those that "establish or affect the substantive rights of a person (civil status, citizenship, nationality, legitimacy or marriage/filiation)."

      Republic v. Gallo (G.R. No. 207074, January 17, 2018; class reviewer)

      Michelle Soriano Gallo, recorded as "Michael", "male", with no middle name and no parents' marriage date, sought correction under Rule 108. Held: proper under Rule 108, not Rule 103: she was not changing her name but correcting an obvious misspelling (she had always been Michelle), and the other corrections were clerical. A clerical error is one "visible to the eyes or obvious to the understanding, and can be corrected or changed only by reference to other existing record or records."

      Bartolome v. Republic (G.R. No. 243288, August 28, 2019; class reviewer)

      Ruben Cruz Bartolome, recorded as "Feliciano Bartholome", went to court under Rule 103 to change his name. Held: denied without prejudice. R.A. 9048 governs changes of first name and clerical corrections (including inserting a middle name and correcting a misspelled surname); "typographical or clerical errors in a person's surname must likewise be corrected through the administrative proceeding under R.A. 9048." Judicial remedies are available only after the administrative petition is denied.

      Republic v. Felix (2021; class reviewer)

      A man with two birth records, one with errors, filed a Rule 108 petition to correct one and cancel the other; the Republic argued the RTC had no jurisdiction because R.A. 9048 covers clerical errors. Held: the RTC had jurisdiction. R.A. 9048 "did not divest RTCs of their jurisdiction to hear and decide petitions for correction of entries"; failure to exhaust the administrative remedy does not affect the court's jurisdiction.

      Quiz traps (civil register): "No entry in a civil register shall be changed or corrected without a judicial order" → incomplete today: true as Art. 412 reads, but R.A. 9048/10172 allow administrative correction of clerical errors, first names, the day and month of birth and sex. "The year of birth may be corrected administratively" → false (age). "A Rule 108 proceeding is always summary" → false (Valencia). "Legitimacy may be changed by a petition naming only the civil registrar" → false (Labayo-Rowe; Ontuca). "Entries in the civil register are conclusive" → false: prima facie (Art. 410). "The civil registrar is absolutely liable for unauthorized alterations" → false: he may exempt himself by proving every reasonable precaution (Art. 411). "Rule 108 publication: once a week for two weeks" → false: three consecutive weeks.

      Bar-style: Ana's birth certificate lists her as "Anna", born "June 5, 1998", "male", and as the legitimate daughter of spouses Jose and Maria, who in fact never married. What remedies apply to each error?

      "Anna" → "Ana" (misspelling) and "male" → "female" (patent clerical error, with a medical certification of no sex change): administrative petition with the local civil registrar under R.A. 9048 as amended by R.A. 10172. A wrong day and month of birth would also go there, but not the year. The parents' marital status (which changes her legitimacy): only through an adversarial Rule 108 proceeding in the RTC of the province where the registry is located, impleading the civil registrar and all affected persons (both parents, and anyone whose rights would be affected), with publication for three consecutive weeks (Labayo-Rowe; Ontuca; Magpayo). If the claim is really an attack on a marriage's validity or on legitimacy, it must be a direct action by the proper party (Braza).
